                                 _Fog_

    “_You have heard the beat of the off-shore wind_,
          _And the thresh of the deep-sea rain_;
    _You have heard the song--how long? how long_?
           _Pull out on the trail again!_”




                               CHAPTER I


CLEMENT MARLEY was waiting for his tea. The table was laid near the
open fire, the muffins were cooling under their cover, the teapot had
long since ceased to steam. And Marley was prey to the melancholy
emptiness of the methodical Englishman tea-less at five o’clock on a
foggy afternoon.

Still, it did not occur to him to raid the table before the muffins
got quite cold and the tea too strong. Alexandra always poured the
tea. It was a wife’s duty--one of them--to pour her husband’s tea. And
Alexandra was missing.

He went to the window again and peered out into the Bloomsbury twilight
and fog. Impossible to see as far as the corner. He was becoming a
little anxious. Only a little. Alexandra had been missing like this
before, and she had never yet been run over or lost. She would turn up.
She always did turn up, conscious of truancy, but bright-eyed, aglow,
and not sufficiently apologetic.

He turned back into the room and prowled about it gloomily. It was not
a helpful room on a depressing afternoon; fusty with honorable age;
aridly neat; impersonal even to the pictures on its walls; the sort
of room which must become either a sacred tradition or a prison. To
Clement Marley it was home. To Alexandra it spelled duty, which is at
best a sort of compromise with fate.

The furniture was mid-Victorian, a bit faded, and without the sybaritic
softness of modern upholstery. The piano stood out from it; warm,
polished wood, and when it was played, warm, rich tone. Alexandra’s
piano, a stranger ten years ago like its owner--a stranger still, in
the surrounding desert of horsehair and carved black walnut upholstered
in a relentless red. It stood a dumb yet somehow sentient thing, as
though awaiting release from a spell. She never closed it, being
careless of her things as a boy, Marley frequently pointed out. But she
never played it either, any more.

The window beyond the piano bench gave upon the square, and when in
the old days one had stood on the hearth-rug watching her while she
played, her clear young profile and slender throat were silhouetted
against the light. And sometimes when the late sun came in, haloing
her smooth hair, pale gold like the London sunshine, sometimes she
sang. And if she had only sung the right things, Clement Marley might
very well at such times have been badly in love with his wife. But the
songs were likely to be not quite what is expected of a saintly-looking
yellow-haired woman: sailor songs, often, chanteys with a troublesome
rhythm, with words which fell disconcertingly on the chaste ears of
the Bloomsbury born; or wild, wordless Eastern things with the beat of
drums under her fingers and the wail and whine of pipes in her taut
throat; or love songs of the harem lattice--well, really! No, Marley’s
Saint Cecilia had always been a subject for a husband’s kindly censure
rather than a lover’s uncritical worship.

They thought very well of Marley at the British Museum, where he was
known as an authority on Oriental art. He read glaze and color and
carving as few men could. He wrote expensive books about ceramics
and ancient jewelry. Unutterably dry books they were, for all their
lovely colored plates and gold edges. Other men brought the priceless
treasures across the sea to Bloomsbury--brought them at great cost of
money and effort and sometimes of life and limb--and Clement Marley
wrote the books.

You always knew where you were, with Marley. His manner was weighted
with the slight ponderosity of men whose work is done at close range
among the dead echoes of the ages. He was ruddy and near-sighted,
kindly by nature, a little patronizing, a little absent-minded, a
little inclined to be fretful about things he could not understand.
Alexandra had discovered in nearly ten years of marriage that there
were a great many things he could not understand. And just now he was
wishing not very patiently that Alexandra would not behave like this.

The mantel clock struck five. He looked at it reproachfully and then
at his watch. The clock was slow. He set it right to the minute by the
loud, bulbous watch in his hand. Really, Alexandra, this is becoming
unpardonable....

Rather aimlessly, then, he rang the bell for Susan.

Susan did not appear silently, as the perfect maid is trained to do.
Susan arrived. She stood now in the dining-room doorway, the knob
having rattled under her hand, a scraggy little Cockney girl, too small
for her aprons.

Marley cleared his throat.

“Susan, just when did Mrs. Marley go out?”

“Directly after luncheon, sir.”

“And she didn’t say where she was going?”

“For a walk, sir.” They had been all over it before.

“She was quite alone?”

“Oh, yes, sir. She always is, sir.”

“But she should be home now,” he pointed out.

“Yes, sir. But if you was to ask me, sir, I’d say it was just one o’
those days.”

Marley looked over his spectacles.

“One of what days?”

“Well, sir, there’s times when things ’ere gets on ’er nerves, like,
an’ maybe she cries an’ more often she goes for a walk.”

“Cries?” The word carried its usual quota of masculine horror.

“I’ve caught ’er at it twice, sir.”

“But--surely she’s perfectly well!”

“Yes, sir.”

“Well, then, what--” He checked himself. After all, Susan was only a
child. “That will do, Susan.”

“If you please, sir----”

“Well?”

“You wouldn’t be too ’ard on ’er, sir?”

“Be--!” Marley was dumfounded. “_What?_”

Susan stuck to her guns.

“She can’t ’elp it, sir. She’s one o’ Them.”

“One of--whom?”

“One o’ _Them_.” Susan waved a hand to include horizons.

“What on earth do you mean?” he demanded.

“My old man’s a sailor, and _I_ know. My mother says it’s like
drink, sir. You never ’ave no warnin’--just all of a sudden they’re off
again.”

“Drink?” A man must have patience with these people. “What has drink to
do with Mrs. Marley?”

“Not drink, Lor, no, sir. But when she gets these spells o’ wantin’
to be Out There--” (another wave of her hand) “--it’s all the same as
sailors, sir. It’s the Call. They ’ear it and they got to go.”

“I haven’t the faintest idea what you’re talking about,” said Marley.
Nor had he.

“No, sir,” agreed Susan hopelessly.

“You may go, Susan.”

“Yes, sir.” She turned on the threshold. “My mother says it’s the wind,
sir.”

“But there’s no wind today,” he objected. “It’s fog.”

“There’s always a wind--Out There.”

“Susan.” He stopped her as the door was closing. He would go to the
bottom of this.

“Sir?”

“Does--does Mrs. Marley speak to you about all this?”

“Oh, no, sir! But I’m from Poplar an’ I’ve ’eard ’em talk. There’s them
as nothing can ’old, sir, once they’ve got to go. My mother knows.”

“But Mrs. Marley is a woman--delicately reared--and in Buckinghamshire,
too!” He was arguing with his own serving maid for his peace of mind
and he deeply resented the fact. “Where’s your wind and sea there?”

“In ’er blood, sir. My mother says----”

“You’d better make fresh tea, Susan,” he closed it abruptly.

“Yes, sir.”

She went, taking the teapot.

Marley looked after her, frowning. It was disquieting, this talk of
wind and sea and the things in his wife’s blood. How much did Susan
know? How much did that shrewd little brain, cheated of childhood,
comprehend of the perplexing creature who was his wife? How much did
Susan’s slavish devotion to her erratic and unexacting mistress enable
the girl to guess concerning her; concerning him; and their way of life
together? _In her blood._ The girl was uncanny.

It brought up a picture of Alexandra’s father, a tawny-bearded giant
who had loomed Olympian in the stuffy drawing-rooms of the ’Nineties--a
man who spoke and sang and swore and laughed like Baldur the Beautiful,
his own everlasting god of youth and light--a man, however, who
unaccountably tripped over the skirts of a woman and measured his
great length at her flattered feet, and somehow married her and finally
left her, and so died miserably, as was only fitting, alone, with
his face to the African sky. In Alexandra’s blood--a heedless Nordic
paganism, a blindness to private obligations and public opinion, a
carelessness of life itself, a streak of madness, even, boasting the
wind’s will, and without the fear of God!

But on the other side was Clement’s own second cousin Emily, a
Marley too, a plump, capable robin of a girl with no imagination; an
excellent wife if properly appreciated; a conscientious mother for
all her fretful ill health in later life. How very singular, then,
that Alexandra should be so exclusively Norse, so entirely without
Marleyisms. It set all one’s notions of heredity askew. All very well
for her to look like her father’s side--Clement had always rather liked
her looks--but might she not still have possessed some inward evidence
of the restraining Marley inheritance?

He got out his pipe, poor man, and stood on the hearth-rug filling
it and frowning. Things he wanted to forget, things he had chosen to
regard as forgotten, skulked about the edges of his well-ordered scheme
of life. Alexandra was his wife. She ought not to behave like this.
Must he tell her so--again? Surely after nearly ten years the daily
necessity for disciplining even such a very young wife as Alexandra
should abate?

His mind went back reluctantly along the years, and came to the bride
Alexandra. And he saw as he had not taken time to see for years her
white face, remembered acutely that it had been white as her dress,
recalled her icy fingers and whispered responses. He had supposed at
the time, in his colossal ignorance of women, that all brides were
like that--sheer nervousness. And he had pressed her hand with extra
fervor as they left the church, by way of conveying to her how very
safe she would be with him, and how he never meant to let her go now
that he had got her. He remembered her eyes, wide and watchful like
a child’s in the dark, and how he had seen the pulse beating in her
throat--a phenomenon he had never before beheld. And it occurred to him
to wonder, standing on the hearth-rug nearly ten years later, if all
brides looked as starkly, pitiably frightened as his Alexandra, after
all--if, when one came down to it, she had quite wanted to marry him.

Such a doubt was of course absurd. Look at the life she had been
living. Running wild at seventeen, with her long, straw-colored plait
carelessly looped and tied on her neck, always out of breath about
something unless caught and reproved and made to sit down. Poor Emily,
with her martyred widow’s tears, her headaches, her smelling-salts,
her alarming shortness of breath, her fastidious appetite, had little
strength to spare for curbing a spirited daughter. But once Alexandra
was caught and provided with a book or a bit of becoming needlework and
seated submissively beside her mother--once she was momentarily tamed,
as it were, and placed where one could look at her without following
her about until one was out of breath oneself--how fascinating became
the shadow of her lashes on her cheek, the smooth undulations of her
hair, the strong, sweet lines of her profile!

The truth was that Marley had never looked with acquisitive eyes on a
woman before, and so could not know that this girl was half goddess
as well. He saw, however, that she was a swift, enlivening, adaptable
thing to have about, and from this it was but a step to the conclusion
that the deference she paid him was perhaps not wholly due to his very
distant relationship with her mother, whose affairs he had come to
straighten out. Which latter reflection rather went to his sober head.
Moreover, his masculine fingers itched for the reins.

With a sigh of relief and some maternal tears, his cousin Emily heard
his plans regarding Alexandra’s future. Looking back on her own
exhausting years of marriage, she regarded Clement Marley as a very
restful and desirable husband for anybody. Alexandra would never be
exposed to the strenuosities she herself had weathered. And in time,
she confidently assured her cousin Clement, Alexandra would become less
strenuous herself.

“It was her father,” she explained. “He fostered it. There was nothing
I could do. I hope you realize my position. Even after he--went
away--in fact, even up to the time of his tragic death, he wrote to
her. And he would send her things--such heathenish things! If she
had been a boy--!” Her open hands expressed utter hopelessness. “But
marriage,” Emily assured him, brightening, “marriage will bring out her
womanliness. She’ll have that from me,” Emily assured him complacently.

It did not occur to either of them that Alexandra might not want to
marry him. Marley was ten years late with that idea, and Emily never
achieved it this side of the grave. “_I_ was married at sixteen,”
she was accustomed to observe impressively, so that poor Alexandra was
made quite properly to feel that it was high time she found a good
husband. Anyway, she allowed Clement to kiss her cheek, and appeared
next morning with her hair suitably dressed, and a seemly air of
pensive dignity. Observing which, Marley began to fall in love, and
watched her with already a proprietary pleasure. He even paid her
a discreet compliment, and noting the flush it brought resolved to
indulge her often in expressions of his approval. But he found himself
not overly fertile in these, and abandoned the idea philosophically as
the idle pursuit of a younger man.

It can be seen that Marley was not imaginative, and it was never
given him to suspect the complicated emotions behind Alexandra’s new
passivity. She had been like a colt, racing hilariously at the heels
of life, before the news came of her father’s sudden death. Her mother
had told her, weeping, how he died. Alexandra had stood a moment, dumb,
quivering, cold--then turned and walked blindly out of the room. No
one saw her cry, no one ever heard her regret her loss. No one, least
of all herself, could have told you the devious ways she traveled to
the realization that though she would never see him again the sky he
had loved was still blue. After that she lived for him too, who had so
loved life; saw for him, sang for him, laughed for him, and in spending
his lavish legacy of life ceased to mourn for him.

Then Marley.

Staggering as the idea of marriage was, rebellion did not enter her
head. You grew up and got married. It was life. Her time had come.
A little soon perhaps, but-- Anyway, Clement was good and kind and
she would go to live in London. She had been in London once with her
father, and liked it. They had watched the boats and gone to the
play. She told herself that to live in London would be like having
the sea at the bottom of the garden. Perhaps they could live near the
Embankment--? Clement said, No, they would live in Bloomsbury. She
supposed one could walk from there to the River--? Clement said there
were omnibuses. What fun, insisted Alexandra to her often faint-hearted
self, what fun to live in London! One would see life, in London!
Clement spoke vaguely of concerts and parks.

And then, most alluring of all, she was allowed to choose where they
should spend the honeymoon, and after a great deal of mental stress
she settled on North Devon. It was there that she met her father’s
mistress, the wind from the sea.

Thus, between the two of them and her own pellucid views on life,
Alexandra was married and went to live in London. She took with her the
humiliating memory of how her teeth had chattered over her responses;
and of how when Clement pressed her hand at the end she would have fled
in panic but for the sick knowledge that there was nowhere to flee to
now, that it was too late, that she would only be brought back, shamed
and helpless, to this stranger who had put a ring on her finger; an
implacable memory of a naked, unreasoning fear; a memory which not all
the winds of the world could blow from her.

If she found London not quite the Baghdad that she remembered it, that
was doubtless because it was only Clement now and not her father.
Clement was very good, and she loved him--she was quite, quite sure she
loved him, for was she not his wife?--but, after all, a husband was
not one’s father, was he! She tried very hard to please him, though.
That was a difference between husbands and fathers, one couldn’t
please husbands just by breathing, and they were sometimes hurt and
reproachful if one wasn’t careful. But really, it might be rather jolly
after one got used to things.

By imperceptible degrees this valiant, hopeful bride had become the
wife who was missing at tea-time. Marley could remember how assiduous
she had once been about tea and clocks and his many preferences about
such things. Once she had cared to please him. Once she had thought of
nothing else. He had even invented small duties to amuse her. Once....

Something was forming at the back of his brain. There was a pinpoint
of time when he dreaded its actual conception. Relentlessly it shaped
itself in words. If and granted that Alexandra had really wanted to
marry him in the beginning, was it possible that now his wife no longer
loved him?

And even as he stood aghast before the enormity of such a thought, the
door opened and Alexandra came in.




                               CHAPTER II


ALEXANDRA--slim, with a boyish length of limb; hair and eyes that
revealed the Viking strain; a wistful mouth with humorous corners;
and the chin that had seen her through years of this room. Her suit
was dark and trim and in its second season. Her hat was small and
plain against the smooth sheen of her pale hair. Her long hands were
black-gloved. No fur, no touch of deft color, not even violets to set
her off. And when she entered a room, seemingly borne on the wind of
her own swift coming without a footfall to herald her, something of
youth and light, something brave and very beautiful, something that
caught at the heart, came with her.

Now her cheeks were flushed and she was breathless from hurrying, a bit
guilty above a secret lilt. And she had on a new leash a very dirty,
very hungry, very sad little dog, chiefly Irish terrier. Her smile was
ingratiating.

“Hello, Clem.”

Marley looked over his spectacles.

“Alex, I’ve been worried--” He halted as though an abyss had opened
between them. “My God, what’s that?”

“Oh, that?” She looked down at the dog, seemed to meet his questioning
gaze and silently reassure him. “Just a fellow vagabond.”

The dog sat down, leaning wearily against her skirt.

“But you can’t bring things like that into the house! It’s nasty, dirty
and bound to be full of germs!”

“Germs? I didn’t think.” She looked down at the dog speculatively
and he sank still lower, half his weight across her feet, as though
crowding closer to the sound of her voice. “Well, Susan can keep him
downstairs,” she concluded comfortably.

“But, my dear Alex----”

“Oh, he won’t stay long, Clem, don’t fret. I shan’t try to keep him. A
few good meals and he’ll take to the road again, won’t you, old man?”
She stooped and rubbed the scrubby ears, almost roughly as a boy would,
and covered even that moment of tenderness with a resounding slap on
the lean shoulder as she straightened. “You don’t mind if I stake him
to a dinner, do you?”

“Where on earth have you been?”

“Down to the Bridge.” She pulled off her gloves and tossed them into a
chair, moving on to ring the bell. The dog dragged himself to his feet
and followed, trailing his leash, his nose at the hem of her skirt.
“You know, Clem, he’s been a different dog since I bought that leash.
I didn’t know how to get him home without it, but it weighs on his
spirit!”

Marley allowed the things he did not say to shriek in the silence.
Again the dog sat down, or rather folded up, bonily, with a tired sigh.

Susan came in, bringing fresh tea. She set down the teapot with a cry
and stood gazing rapturously at the despondent stranger huddled at
Alexandra’s feet.

“Oh!” gasped Susan. “Oh, ma’am! He’s a dog!”

“He was meant to be.” She smiled. Sensing it, the dog looked up into
her face and snuffled engagingly, his stumpy tail entreating favors.
“Are you afraid of germs, Susan?”

“Germs, ma’am?” Susan had fastened yearning eyes on the dog.

“Mr. Marley thinks he may have some.”

“They do ’ave fleas, ma’am.” Susan was drawn irresistibly toward the
waif. “Aw, ’e needs a bath, ’e does!”

“My poor friend!” Alexandra stooped for the dragging leash and the dog
nuzzled her hands affectionately. “It’s an effete age we live in!”

“I could wash ’im, ma’am--if you was to let ’im stay!”

“He’s to stay as long as he likes, which will be as long as he’s hungry
and no longer.”

Susan had come to the dog as a needle to a magnet, reaching down
motherly hands with little croons and cluckings.

“Well, there, now, wuz ’e, wuz ’e, wuz ’e! Yus, ’e wuz a booful baby,
that’s wot ’e wuz! Did ’e wanna ’come wiv Susan an’ ’ave a bone an’
some nice biscuit an’----”

“Yes, do give him a good dinner. Look at his ribs!” Alexandra handed
over the leash.

But Susan’s arms were round his neck, his dirty paws smirching her
crisp apron, germs, etiquette, service, all swept aside before a child
and a dog as they are the world over.

“Yus, ’e would be jus’ a booful angel once ’e gets fattened up a bit!
Susan knows wot ’e likes to eat----”

“That will do, Susan, take it away at once,” Marley’s voice cut in
decisively.

“Yes, sir.” Susan stumbled to her feet, clutching the leash.

“And, Susan.” The eyes of servant and mistress met with a mutual
understanding, a half smile in Alexandra’s. One mustn’t mind men. “He’s
not to be tied up.”

“But, ma’am--!” Susan’s grip on the leash was convulsive.

“Take the leash off, Susan. When he has learned that he can get food
here he’s to come and go as he likes. I’ll have nothing tied in this
house.”

“Yes, ma’am.”

“And, Susan.” It was Marley again. “See that it does not come upstairs.”

“Y-no, sir.”

Susan went, leading the treasure.

There was a silence, loud with a husband’s disapproval. Alexandra
took off her hat and dropped it in another chair. Then Marley, having
weighed his words, spoke, he was sure, more in sorrow than in anger.

“My dear, I wish you wouldn’t do these things. How do you know where
such a dog may have been, or----”

“But that’s just it! He has such possibilities! He may have been
anywhere! He may have got lost from a ship!”

Her face was alight with the infinite desirability of owning a dog
which had been lost from a ship. He knew that look, did Marley.

“But--where on earth have you been all this time?” he demanded again,
fretfully. “It’s nearly six.”

“Poor dear, you want your tea, don’t you! I’m sorry.” She went to the
tea-table hurriedly. Men got so hungry. It made them cross.

“It is not entirely a question of tea,” he insisted. “Though you know
very well that I like things on time. But you are also aware that I’m
bound to worry when you disappear on these wild enterprises.”

Looking back on it, he was surprised, positively surprised, at how
anxious he had been. And then she had come walking in, as always, quite
safe, and not sufficiently apologetic. Anything might have happened.
How was he to know? And now that she was here, quite safe, and pouring
his tea as she should have been two hours ago, what was the good of
it, this tardiness? What had she gained by keeping him waiting for his
tea and giving him a bad fright besides? Where was the fun of tramping
about in a fog picking up strange dogs? What were dogs compared to a
husband’s comfort and peace of mind?

“It all seems so--so useless, Alex,” he pointed out.

“Yes--doesn’t it!” Her hands came to rest among the tea things. “I only
went down to the Bridge to listen to the ships. I love these early
twilights with a fog to blot out the sharp edges and hard corners of
London. I stood leaning on the wall in that muffled babel--how can
one lose one’s temper in a fog?--looking down the River, watching for
those queer rifts in the white that showed a light or gave up a voice
shouting things I couldn’t understand--till the stone wall under my
arms became a ship’s rail and I wasn’t in England any more--till I
could see and hear and almost smell South Africa--Suez--Shanghai--” She
drifted, unseeing, adream.

“Darling--aren’t you going to pour the tea?”

“Oh!” She rather leaped at it. Things clinked under her hands. He
wished she weren’t so jumpy. “I _am_ sorry!”

“Fortunately,” pursued Marley in the even tones of marital forbearance,
“fortunately Dorin is late too--or isn’t coming.”

“Dorin?” She was spearing a slice of lemon. It fell off the fork and
she jabbed at it again, viciously, almost, her teeth set on her lower
lip.

“Blaise Dorin,” amplified her husband and waited, his eyes on her
hands. Beautiful hands. But jerky.

“But--is this Tuesday?” She lifted startled, guilty eyes to him. “Oh,
Clem, I forgot today was Tuesday! How silly of me!”

Her smile as she handed his cup was fleeting, nervously propitiatory.
He reflected that when one was being most patient, Alexandra often
behaved like a punished child. He had said nothing, he was sure he had
said nothing--so far--in the way of a justly deserved rebuke. Somehow
that smile and the way her lashes fluttered down before his mildly
reproachful gaze infuriated him. He couldn’t understand why Alexandra
should act--well, almost as though she feared him. He spoke with what
he felt to be heroically concealed annoyance.

“How could you forget, Alex? Will you never stop being the same
irresponsible child that you were when I married you? Will you never
take your duties seriously as mistress of my house? How could you
forget when a guest is coming to tea?”

Alexandra sat with bent head, eyes on her tense, clasped hands. She
was not going to cry--oh, no!--but she terribly wanted to scream. She
wished herself out in the fog again. She wished she had not come home
just yet. Inside, the fog made for echoes. Outside.... Out there....

Marley was speaking still.

“And so it’s time we came to an understanding, Alex. Now, wherein have
I failed?”

“Failed?” she repeated faintly.

“To make you happy.”

Oh, he wasn’t going to begin _that_ again! They hadn’t gone into
that for months--years!

“I--I’m perfectly happy, Clem.”

“Then why do you cry?”

“I don’t!” How had he known?

“You’re fretting again,” he accused. “Things go along well enough for
a while and then something comes over you and you fret. Don’t think
I haven’t seen. Why, even Susan sees! And something she said this
afternoon set me thinking.”

“Why, what could Susan say that--that--?” She felt betrayed. Outraged.
She and Susan understood each other. Even Susan saw!

“Never mind, it set me wondering about things I had almost forgotten.
You’ve got Viking blood. Your father had it, and his father before him.
He used to talk a lot of nonsense about Leif the Red and King Olaf. I
might have known, I did know, he had left you his own roving foot. But
I thought because you were so young when I took you that this--” his
gesture took in the room and his own not inconsiderable self “--would
do as well in the end.”

He came to a full stop. There was no applause. Alexandra said nothing,
tensely. It was a way she had. He stood looking down at her, at the
slim grace of her body, the sweet line of her averted cheek, her meek,
shining hair in its great coil on the nape of her neck. To look at
her one would never guess, thought Marley. She looked like a quiet,
sensible woman--a treasure of a wife. And she behaved like a mad,
undisciplined boy. He was too near-sighted to see that in every line
of her was the hopeless droop of broken pinions.

“I remember,” he pursued after a silence in a tone which tactfully
ignored sulking, “I remember on our wedding journey you stood on a
cliff overlooking the sea and held out your arms to the wind like--like
a lost child! You had the same look just now when you spoke of the
fog. And I’ve seen it--other times. It--it--well, I don’t like it!” An
ultimatum.

She spoke at last, with submissive, lowered eyelids.

“I suppose it must be that old storm-king inside me, Clem. I suppose he
dies hard.”

“But, my dear--” (It is not cricket to clothe the exaggerated patience
of conjugal argument in my-dears.) “But, my dear--it does seem to
me--That is, after all, you are my wife!” As though that didn’t settle
everything! “And you can’t change things much this way, can you!”

“No.” She drew a sudden breath between her teeth. “Sometimes the
thought of all the days that are still to come--!” She broke off with a
gesture.

“But how long is this to go on, Alex?” Marley was still being patient.
“There may have been some excuse for it once, I saw that, but----”

“Oh, you saw that,” she murmured.

“I knew your father.” The statement spoke volumes in its simplicity. We
need not, it implied, go into this.

“Poor dear,” breathed Alexandra.

“He was a man without the fear of God,” said Marley.

“I’m sick of hearing about fearing God!” she broke out. “It’s wrong!
It’s wicked talk!” She flushed pitifully under his astonished gaze.

“This,” said Marley, “is what comes of never being taken to church when
you were a child.”

“My father’s God was not a thing of wrath and vengeance! My father’s
God was love. That’s in the Bible too,” she added defiantly, with
scarlet cheeks.

“A very comfortable doctrine,” said Marley. “Trust your father for
that.” He cleared his throat. “Nevertheless, I can never forgive him
for treating your mother as he did.”

“She couldn’t understand. And he meant to come back.”

“Oh, I’m not saying he intended to desert her.” Magnanimous Marley!
“Nor to die like a dog in South Africa, for that matter!”

“He died--happy,” muttered Alexandra.

Marley stared at her, surprised anew at her reprehensible
ideas of things. Died happy! Alone on the veldt, fever-ridden,
thirst-tortured--_alone_, beneath the sun! Not even he was mad
enough to choose to die like that!

“It broke your mother’s heart,” he said conclusively.

“A man like my father,” she lingered lovingly over the words, “a man
like my father ought never to have married.” She sat with parted lips,
thinking it out. “Unless perhaps,” she added slowly, “a woman like me.”

“A woman like you?” repeated Marley, vaguely shocked.

“I should have gone with him, if I had been his wife.”

“Your mother had a child,” he argued. “A woman’s first duty is to her
child.”

“The tiger’s cub,” smiled Alexandra, distant-eyed.

“You’re your father over again!” he said impatiently, and paused,
struck by the thing he had accused her of.

“Yes,” she agreed serenely.

There was a silence.

Marley felt bewildered, hurt, ill-used. The hypersensitive complacency
of the egoist was injured. She had said that her father ought never to
have married, and in the next breath had admitted her profound likeness
to him. Was her husband then to infer that she felt she herself had
made a mistake? But how could she have made a mistake? He was a
generous, virtuous man, and she was a woman without a large fortune in
her own right. Had he not been good to her? How could she regret having
married him? The idea was preposterous. It was not a woman’s place to
go traipsing about the world, no matter what her inheritance of madness.

She sat quiet, apparently dreaming. For perhaps the millionth time he
was baffled by a sense of her utter remoteness, her inaccessibility to
his honest affection. He had done his deserving best all these years
and there she sat--still somehow beyond his reach. She was his wife
and he had cherished her, given her all the money she wanted, justly
praised her, tenderly chastened her, in short, loved her. And there she
sat, no more one spirit and one flesh with him than was that elusive,
self-contained bride he had brought home nine years ago. She did not
love him. She had never loved him. He felt very sorry for himself.

“I thought--surely I had the right to think that you would forget
your father’s legacy of restlessness here,” he complained. “It--it’s
unnatural in a woman.”

“You were wrong to set your will against my ancestors’. And I was too
young then to know what I wanted. I was seventeen. To me then even
marriage looked a Great Adventure.”

“And what else is marriage but that, for a woman!” He now permitted
himself more than a trace of legitimate annoyance. That she could be so
thoughtless as to say such things, to wound him so deeply! “And you are
a woman now, Alexandra--a nine years’ wife!”

“Nine!” Plainly the sum of them startled her. “Why--it _is_ nine
years! Why--I shall be thirty soon!”

“When we were married I was as much past thirty as you are this side of
it today--just double your age then. You’re catching up!” he rallied
her kindly.

“Thirty.”

Her eyes went slowly round the room. So much of life gone already--to
this! So little of living--yet! And somewhere there was hot sun and
dazzling sand, somewhere still that mystic line where sky and water
meet, and the wind that sang to her like a seashell to a child’s
enchanted ear! Less than four years away--thirty. Why, thirty years ago
her father had been still in India!

So Marley’s little jest failed. And now he spoke more sharply, and said
not quite what he had intended to say.

“What I mean to say is, can’t you settle down?”

“And get in a rut, like you?” She shook her head. “I’ve tried.”

“I like ruts.” And so he did.

“Yes.” She spoke half to herself still, not looking at him. “And you
think it’s every one’s Christian duty to be in a rut!”

“This is how it always ends!” cried Marley helplessly. “I can’t match
words with you! I can’t make you see reason! I can’t make you see my
viewpoint for one minute!”

“But you can’t see mine, Clem.”

“Your viewpoint,” pedantically, “is not reason.”

“Other people’s viewpoints so often aren’t,” she sighed, without malice.

“There it is again!” Marley threw out his hands. “I can’t understand
you, Alex! I can’t reach you!” And with unconscious pathos, “All I can
do is--is mean well!”

She turned to him then on a warm, quick impulse to atone, to explain,
to convey to him something of her captive spirit. Clem was so good. It
wasn’t his fault. She must be fair to Clem. Clem was so very good, so
very dear, as far as he went. She had been behaving like a beast again.
She was forever hurting Clem. She wondered how he bore with her at all.
Poor Clem!

“Oh, Clem, I mean well, too; truly I do! Only--don’t you see,
dear--sometimes it seems as though I must get out of this house--away
from all this--quickly, before I suffocate!”

“But that’s exactly what I’m driving at!” He began an irritable
pacing. “What’s the good of getting away from it, I say! Your life is
here--your duty is here--” (his gesture was eloquent) “--here in this
room!”

She stood up suddenly, a hand to her face. The low words leaped, with
the movement.

“Oh, I hate this room!”

“Now, Alex, you know very well that we----”

“I know, I know, we’ve been all over it a thousand times! If we changed
it your mother would immediately turn up for a visit and there would
have to be explanations, apologies, and so forth! But I----”

“She likes it as it is,” he reminded her, becoming patient again with
this lesser folly of hers, this unreasoning desire for change. He
could understand, a little, that a woman might like to furnish her own
home. It was fitting that she should wish that privilege. And it was
regrettable to have to deny it again. But after all, a man’s mother--!
“She was happy here, in her way,” he said.

“Until I drove her out.”

“Oh, don’t say that, old girl.” Clumsily kind, now, he put out a hand
that fell short of her. “Very sensible of her to go. Brides, you
know----”

“Oh, I know!”

How well she remembered that first awful week in Bloomsbury! Her
mother-in-law’s half-packed boxes, the harried servant’s endless trips
up and down stairs, the persistent allusions to the uprooting of
life-long habits--as though she herself had not felt uprooted too!--and
the continuous cold, furtive scrutiny of a pair of prominent blue eyes.
“My only son,” was always on Mrs. Marley’s lips. “My only living son,”
like a dirge. Alexandra was made to feel hopelessly an interloper,
inept, unwanted, a misfit. When Mrs. Marley finally departed, tearless,
stony, chill, to the end, Alexandra felt as though she had callously
turned an old woman out into the streets, whereas Mrs. Marley was going
to live quite comfortably on her income with a spinster sister in
Tunbridge Wells. At the last minute Alexandra had begged her, trembling
and with tears, to remain in her old home, not to be turned out if
she didn’t want to go, not wholly to surrender her only son; and Mrs.
Marley turned upon her those bleak blue eyes, freezing the tears on
Alexandra’s cheeks, and said, “You will want my room for the nursery
soon. It faces south.” And she got into the carriage and drove away,
looking straight ahead of her, relentlessly a martyr.

“But,” resumed Clement more cheerfully, “she likes to come back and
find it just as it’s always been. Surely we are reasonable enough to
allow an old woman--a lonely old woman,” he emphasized, “what few
small pleasures are left to her? Surely we, with youth and love before
us--” (it was even thus he had spoken nine years ago) “--can afford
to be generous to an old woman’s whims? After all,” he summed up
overwhelmingly, “after all, my dear, she is my mother.”

Alexandra’s spirit cried out rebelliously within her, “But it’s
_not_ youth! It’s thirty! It’s _not_ love! It’s--!” Her
spirit was silent, aghast.

Not love? But she was married to him! They had lived together a long
time; sat across the table from one another at breakfast; he liked her
hair when it was down; she had seen him at odd times like shaving;
they had spoken together intimately, sometimes they had even laughed
together intimately.... _Not love?_

Her mind fled headlong from heresy. What had they been talking about?
Oh, yes.

“I--I only thought--” she began, and found that she was interrupting
him.

“I keep forgetting to tell you,” he was saying, his hand going from one
pocket to another in search of something, “I----”

“Clem.” She took a heedless step toward him, twisting her fingers
nervously. “If I take all the blame next time she comes--couldn’t I
have some bookshelves built in over there and--and perhaps get new
curtains? I just can’t _bear_ red--!” She hurried on, reading
refusal in his face. “After all, she may not come again for months--and
I could put these curtains back while she’s here! She needn’t know I’ve
changed things--except perhaps the bookshelves. Oh, Clem, please let
me----”

“I keep forgetting to tell you,” he continued, producing an envelope at
last, “that I had a letter from her yesterday----”

“She’s coming--!” There was horror in the gasp.

“She has decided that Tunbridge Wells doesn’t agree with her any more.
And she’s coming here, next month, for an indefinite stay.”

Alexandra dropped into a chair as though her knees had gone suddenly
weak. Things were bad enough, insisted that other, insurgent self she
was forever quieting lest Clem hear and be hurt, oh, things were bad
enough without _this_!

“It means only one thing, I’m afraid,” he went on, oblivious to
atmospheric conditions. “It means that, indomitable as she is,
she feels the end coming on. We must persuade her--tactfully, of
course--not to leave here again. This must be her home henceforth.”

“Of course,” she assented dully.

“Now, my dear,” said Marley, “a word to the wise. Her visits have been
short heretofore. You’ve accommodated yourself to them fairly well. But
now that she is coming to live with us, I’m very much afraid----”

“But, Clem----!”

“She won’t understand these queer excursions of yours into the fog. You
can’t expect her to. I--I confess I don’t quite understand them myself.
It seems as though the worse the weather is, the worse you want to be
out in it. It’s madness. It--it doesn’t look well. I’m sure I don’t
know what she’d think!”

“But if I manage the house satisfactorily and still have time for
myself--need she think at all?”

“But she will. You know Mother, my dear.”

“Yes, I--I do,” faintly.

“Well, then, don’t you see----”

The doorbell rang. Marley, interrupted in mid-air, frowned. Alexandra
was on her feet, relief in every inch of her.

“That must be Blaise Dorin at last!”

“He’s confoundedly late!” said Marley.

“I suppose poor Susan must make still another pot of tea!”

“Certainly. You have a tendency to spoil that girl, Alexandra.”

She did not hear. Her eyes were on the door, frankly expectant. It was
the face of a child before the curtain at a pantomime.

For when Blaise Dorin came her father came too, a little. They had
not known each other, those two who could have been such friends, and
she thought it a great pity. But something of her father lived in
Blaise Dorin’s deep eyes and spoke to her through the tales Blaise
Dorin sometimes told--at least as much of him as though he sent her a
message--even almost as much of him had come in his treasured letters.
Blaise Dorin would have loved her father.

Marley, who hated being interrupted, felt in an unpleasantly chaotic
state of mind. And though he placed some trust in the steadying
influence of his mother, soon to become a permanent member of the
household, he had nevertheless some uneasiness as to her real
opinion of Alexandra, whom she was known to have none too privately
described as flighty. She would not suspect, of course, that a perfect
understanding did not exist between himself and his wife. A man does
not speak of these things, even to his mother. But with him dwelt the
doubt: Was it possible that his wife, his Alexandra, would rather have
not married him?




                              CHAPTER III


BUT it was not Blaise Dorin, after all, and Alexandra, swallowing
disappointment, gave up hope that he would come that day. Lone wolves
like Dorin are likely to be a bit hazy about engagements, remembering
them too late and then being very contrite and funny about apologies.
And it never occurred to Dorin that it really mattered to anybody
whether he turned up or not. Her father had been like that.

The visitor was a Mr. Starke of New Orleans, an unholy mixture of
New England and Louisiana French, a millionaire and an acquisitive
connoisseur of old ivory and jade; in fact, of anything ancient and
priceless and hard to get. Oddly enough, he was not equally well-versed
in horses and women.

He was a rugged, seemingly ingenuous giant, heavy-shouldered,
heavy-chinned, with a heavy geniality. His clothes were good because
he could afford to place himself in the hands of the best tailor.
His manners were fair because he had the self-made man’s pathetic
appreciation of things he can never hope quite to attain.

Alexandra’s clear, cool fairness caught him at first sight. He looked
at her as he looked at Gainsboroughs--with a measuring, merciless
appreciation of what he unerringly recognized as beauty.

Marley and he had met a few weeks before at the Museum, where he had
come in quest of further records and rumors concerning his current
enterprise. He was obsessed with the desire for a new treasure which
had been described to him by a chance-met Frenchman in Saigon, a
jewelled fabric supposed to be hidden in the wildest hill regions of
Central Asia. The Frenchman’s expressive shoulders had risen to his
ears when he was driven into a corner and pressed for facts. He knew
nothing definitely, he had heard this, had heard that. Perhaps he did
not quite believe, he could not say. It was what the Americans call a
good yarn. Yes, others had heard it. There was a Babu at Delhi who said
there was once a Russian at Bokhara who made a bet with a Jew.... No,
the Russian had not won. In fact, he had disappeared.

The Museum itself had heard tales of the thing. A fabled sacrificial
robe, men said, of woven gold encrusted with unbelievable yellow
topazes. It was fantastic. Chimerical. Still, there was the myth.

Starke had gone beyond legend to names and places. Vague, contradictory
clues at first, but by process of patient elimination they had become
enticingly possible. Probable, even. Worth a long chance, said Starke.
All he wanted now was a trustworthy man, fearless, with a charmed
life. All he wanted was Blaise Dorin. Marley had put him in touch with
Dorin a week ago. And to Marley Starke came now in perplexity and some
annoyance.

“Say,” he began without preamble, having refused tea and ensconced
himself behind a cigarette. “Tell me more about this man Dorin.”

“Well, I don’t know--let me see--” Marley found it taxing. He had not
given much thought to Dorin, who was a man nobody seemed to know well
and yet whom everybody seemed to--well, to exaggerate. “He’s a queer
sort. For one thing he knows more about jade than any man on earth. He
seems to smell it out, like a setter. By the way, he’s coming here this
afternoon, unless he’s forgotten all about it!”

“Coming here? Fine!” Starke settled back to wait.

“He promised to bring a piece of nephrite carving he spoke about the
other day. My wife was interested in its story. He’s a dashed queer
sort, you know! He wouldn’t let the thing out of his sight, apparently,
except under lock and key.”

“He’s a little superstitious about it, I think,” ventured Alexandra.

“All those fellows are superstitious, the whole lot of ’em!” Starke
disposed of them with a sweep of his cigarette. “Regular Hindus for
superstition!”

“They’re all mad!” said Marley. “Take Dorin, for instance, risking his
neck the way he does again and again, just for the sake of some trinket
not a hundred men in the world can appreciate! I’m one of the hundred.
I know the value of the stuff. But make it my business to hunt it down?
Not for me! It’s not worth any man’s life!”

“Oh, it isn’t the trinket itself that counts.” Alexandra’s voice came
slowly on the emphatic period. “It’s fun of smelling it out--the risk
of making it your own--the Big Handicap, with the odds against you
forty-to-one and no takers! There has come to be such a premium on
adventure. Time was when something happened every time a man showed his
nose outside his own front gate! Nowadays the places where a man can
risk his neck in peace are numbered!”

Marley looked over his spectacles.

“But why should a man risk his neck nowadays, that’s my point,” he said.

Her eyes came back to his face with a jerk.

“Perhaps to keep museum curators busy.”

Starke laughed, and Marley, after a moment, conceded the joke.

“Below the belt, Alex! You’re married to one, you know.”

“Oh, I didn’t mean it like that, Clem!” She was instantly penitent.
“It’s because it’s in his blood, I suppose, really. The primeval
instinct to dare the gods and win! When men do stop gambling with life
and death-- Oh, well, I shan’t be here to see! And neither will Blaise
Dorin!”

“They call him Dodo, did you know that?” Starke asked.

“Silly name!” worried Marley. “It sounds like a--like a lap-dog!”

“It means they love him,” explained Alexandra. “By their nicknames ye
shall know them.”

Marley sighed, and turned to Starke.

“Well, how did you get on with him? All satisfactory, I hope?”

“Not so good,” grinned Starke.

“No? What’s the matter?”

“Well, here’s how it is. I’ve got a nice little scheme worked out for
this Asian job. All Dorin has to do is put it over. I understand he’s
a cracking good shot and uncommon handy with a knife. He’s been in
tighter places than this would ever be. It’s a cinch. If he follows
directions he can’t fail.”

“What’s wrong, then?”

“He balks. If it was a case of his not having the nerve I could
understand it. But it isn’t that. What he wants is to nick the old
bankroll for a fair purchase price.”

“I see,” said Marley, a great light breaking on his trusting soul.

“Well, what’s the use?” Starke spread well-kept artisan hands. “I know
a better way.”

Alexandra spoke unexpectedly.

“I believe Mr. Dorin does always pay a fair price.”

“Oh, rubbish!” He swept this aside. “How do you suppose half the stuff
is brought out? Stolen and smuggled and hacked out! No argument like
three inches of cold steel. Cold cash can’t compare with it! Dorin
knows that as well as I do! But he won’t see it!”

“No, I confess I don’t quite see it either!”

“Oh, well, you’re a woman,” he reminded her indulgently. “But Dorin’s
been around. He knows the ropes.”

“I’m afraid there’s no getting round the fact that Mr. Dorin does play
fair.”

“You got any influence with him?” he asked abruptly.

“I?” Alexandra looked bewildered. “Not the slightest!”

“Well, he’s got to see reason, that’s all, if I have to knock it into
him! No agent of mine is going to Asia on tiptoe for fear of hurting
their little yellow feelings! My men go to do business!”

“And do you call murder business?” she demanded indignantly.

“Eh?” said Starke, staring.

“Alex, my dear--!” said Marley.

“You can’t hire assassins in England, Mr. Starke!”

“It has been done, I believe.” Marley was oil on the waters. “However,
I’m sure Mr. Starke doesn’t mean anything so melodramatic.”

“Nothing melodramatic about it.” Starke disclaimed it in all honesty.
“Plain business proposition. I want what I want and I get it. There’s
always a way.”

Again the doorbell. This time it was Marley who spoke with relief.

“There’s Dorin at last!”

Alexandra rose and slipped out into the hall, her ready loyalty up in
arms. Blaise Dorin should be warned that this man was here.

“Mind if I have it out with him right now?” Starke inquired of Marley.
“If he’s going I want to see him on his way. Got to come to terms. Put
in a word, will you? You’re a reasonable man yourself.”

“Dorin makes his own terms, you know.” Marley was dimly aware that many
people had cause to know this.

“Not with me, he doesn’t! Of course that pretty wife of yours would be
on his side. By George, I like her spirit, going for me that way!”

“My wife is an enthusiast always,” admitted Marley, a bit stiffly
perhaps.

There were men’s voices in the hall and Alexandra returned, laughing as
she came, with Blaise Dorin and a stranger in her wake.

She was aglow with frank hero-worship like a boy. These were the men
who did things, kinsmen of her ancestors. Her gaze as it rested on them
was somehow possessive. They spoke her language, thought her thoughts,
heard what she had once heard in the wind and the sea. They were
splendid.

Dorin was lean and humorous, and spoke as Englishmen speak with the
tongues of men and of angels, though he used the slang of three
continents and could swear engagingly in half a dozen languages.
His gray eyes had seen things no man can speak of, and his hair had
whitened round his ears with fever, and other things.

Bob Taunton was younger, solidly built, sunbleached and tanned. He
brimmed with a boyish exuberance and made no attempt to conceal his
idolatry of Dorin. Starke and he were already known to each other by
reputation, and his private advice to old Dodo had been to go slow. A
friend of his, a maharajah and a gentleman, who knew all about horses
and women _and_ pearls had yet learned about swindles from Starke.
It was all quite legal and correct--and very clever. The maharajah,
being a gentleman, had been able to see the joke. But he would never
see those pearls again.

They were surprised, as much as their kind is ever surprised at
anything, to find Starke there. And they neglected to shake hands with
him, but no one, least of all himself, noticed this. The air cleared
before the largeness of them. The room was somehow windswept, no longer
stuffy, no longer bounded by red plush. Yes, they were splendid.

They explained that they had run into each other in the club. They
explained that they were forever running into each other, even in
the Kimberley, and that they were inevitably late to appointments
thereafter. They explained that they had left the club with a due
regard for the time, however, Bob coming along to be introduced since
he was to be in London for a while, and Dorin was leaving tomorrow for
Algiers. No, they had not got lost in the fog. But there was a most
singular bookshop on the way....

“Never mind, we can guess the rest!” said Alexandra.

“Find anything of value?” The connoisseur speaking.

“Nothing we could buy,” admitted Dorin, and grinned. He had an
astonishing grin for one so grave. It spread all over his face. It made
little crinkles round his eyes.

“No, the old cove who owned the place was the attraction.” Taunton
grinned, too, and it made him look like a friendly bull-pup. “He rowed
Dodo the whole time we were there.”

“Rather fancies himself as a Buddhist, and was fretful because I hadn’t
made a pilgrimage of some sort during four years in Asia,” added Dorin.

“But why Buddhist?” Alexandra hung breathless on the answer.

“That’s what I said. And he replied, ‘My son, for fifty years I watched
Christianity work out!’ Well, I mean--!” grinned Dorin. “That did it!
I’m not a missionary, even in London!”

“Now, look here, my boy.” Starke snapped the case of his large gold
watch upon irrelevancies. “I’ve got just five minutes to come to terms
with you.”

There was a silence. Dorin glanced over his shoulder as though he was
the last possible person to be so addressed.

“With me?” he inquired.

“I’ve been laying for you. Let’s talk business.”

“Here?”

“And now.”

“Changed your mind?”

“No. Have you?”

“No.”

Dorin had become suddenly rather like a coiled steel spring, for all
his loose grace in the big chair. Taunton winked at Alexandra, and
settled down on his spine prepared to enjoy the ensuing half-hour.

“Well, let’s get together on it,” proposed Starke. “Assuming that you
agree to go----”

“But I haven’t.”

“Assuming that you do--just what would be your plan of campaign?”

“Heretofore you haven’t been much interested in my plan,” Dorin
reminded him warily.

“Well, suppose I am now. Now, on the basis of, say, fifty bearers--good
shots all--I could arrange about the rifles, I think----”

“Assuming that I go,” interrupted Dorin softly, “I shall leave Bokhara
without ostentation.”

“Oho! Disguised as a native, eh!” Starke looked pleased.

“N--no,” said Dorin thoughtfully. “N--no, I don’t think that would help
much this time.”

“But a lone game in the hills--it’s dangerous!”

“So is--the other.”

“Well, go on. How would you work it?”

“I should go to the monastery and open negotiations.” It sounded simple
enough.

“They won’t sell it, man!”

“You seem to forget the complications about their possession of it.”

“You’ll never get it if they find out what you want!”

“_You’ll_ never get it if they aren’t sure exactly what I want!”

Starke leaned forward.

“You’ve got something up your sleeve.”

“My knowledge of priests. And those--complications.”

“You actually mean to buy it?”

“That does come into it.”

“What else?”

“A fair offer--a warning--and some tact.”

“But, my God, it’s worth a king’s ransom!”

“You are a rich man, Mr. Starke. And I’m a tactful one. And we know
what we know. I fancy they’ll be glad enough to be rid of it--at a
price.”

“I’m not made of money!” Starke pointed out petulantly.

“Well, be that as it may, my way will cost you less than your way in
the end, and it gives me a chance of getting back alive, which you must
admit is a point in its favor.”

“But my plan----”

Dorin cut in crisply.

“Your plan is bound to fail, Mr. Starke!”

“I don’t see why!”

“Have you never discovered that blood is always slippery?”

“You’re squeamish, that’s all!”

“If you like.” Dorin smiled, but it did not reach his eyes.

“Well, what’s a few Chinks?” demanded Starke querulously. He was not
accustomed to this sort of thing. “Plenty more!”

“The yellow man’s blood is as red as mine.”

“So you’re a sentimentalist!” It came near to insult.

“Am I?” said Dorin.

“Then you refuse, do you? You actually sit there and calmly refuse to
take on a job that ought to be meat and drink to one of your tribe? And
you give a womanish reason, a barefaced excuse, a mere prejudice about
the red blood of the noble heathen Chinee!”

“A prejudice,” Dorin corrected, “against making a needless mess.
Blood,” he explained, and this time the smile was in his eyes only,
“even English blood, is unpleasant stuff to work with. Did you ever,”
he inquired pleasantly of Starke, “feel the warm, slow crawl of it
outside you, where it didn’t belong? Did you ever carry it about with
you, stiffening on your hands, so that when you finally got a chance
to wash it off, in cold water, perhaps, hours later, miles along the
trail----”

“I know what’s the matter with you!” roared Starke. “You’ve lost your
nerve! I’ve heard that when you fellows do break up you go all at once
and have the general horrors ever after about getting a knife between
your ribs any night in Piccadilly! So it’s turned on you now, has it!
You’ve had enough! Well, there’s some younger man to take on the job, I
guess!”

Taunton drew in his breath with a little hiss, and Alexandra
instinctively laid a quick hand on his arm. Dorin was getting out a
cigarette.

“He would certainly have to be young to the point of childishness,”
he said at last, “to undertake to filch the thing as you suggest.” He
turned courteously to Alexandra, holding up the cigarette. “May I--?”
he asked, and she nodded, spellbound.

“Well, since you’re not interested--” Starke rose. His neck was red.

“But I am interested,” objected Dorin, searching his pockets for
matches. “As I told you the other day, I am very much interested
indeed. But--Bob, have you got a match?” He caught the box Taunton
tossed. “Thanks. But----”

“But you have flatly refused the job!” said Starke.

“Oh, no. I’ve refused the terms.” He tossed the match-box back to
Taunton, so that it missed Starke’s head by scant inches. “I was only
going to say----”

“Who says terms? I’ll pay anything within reason! Come, now, what will
you take to go up there and do the job my way?”

“If the time ever comes when your way is not the only one, let me know.
Meanwhile, I’m off for Algiers in the morning.”

“You’d let this chance slip for a ten-twenty-thirty holiday in the
Sahara?” Starke stood over him, bellowing.

“A letter addressed to the Travelers’ Club will always reach me,” Dorin
told him sweetly.

“All right, I guess that settles it! Good-afternoon, all.” He stalked
toward the door in a huff.

Alexandra had got uncertainly to her feet.

“But--Mr. Starke----”

“You’ll pardon me, Mrs. Marley, but I have a dinner engagement.”

“Dear, dear--most unfortunate--I’ll see you out--” Marley followed him
from the room in great distress.

Dorin looked at Taunton and they laughed silently, like terriers at a
rat-hole. Alexandra was all but wringing her hands.

“Oh, what a pity!” she moaned. “Oh, to think of your having to miss it!
He’ll never get it now, will he----”

“Oh, he’ll come round!” prophesied Taunton. “Dodo knows what he’s
about. Look at him! He knows he’s got Starke on toast! Give him time!”

“I’ll pop over to Africa,” grinned Dorin, sheepishly conscious of
having played his hand rather well. “He’ll still be here when I get
back.”




                               CHAPTER IV


“WEIRD cove,” remarked Dorin comfortably behind his cigarette, when
Marley had returned. “He’s got a house in New Orleans which must be a
museum in itself, nothing less. And according to all accounts, it’s
full of things which have no business in a private collection. How he
gets them seems to be another story!”

“But look here, Dorin.” Marley drew up a chair. “Do men actually go the
limit in these secret enterprises?”

“Oh, yes,” said Dorin cryptically.

“You mean that men, less principled than yourself, actually steal and
sometimes murder for the whim of a man like this fellow Starke?”

“And are murdered. For the same whim.”

“But it’s such a senseless business!” protested Marley. “I mean to
say--getting yourself murdered!”

“It’s because they’re fools, usually.” Dorin’s eyes were lowered to
his cigarette, so that his ridiculous lashes cast a child-like shadow
on his cheek. Dorin’s looks took a lot of living down. He was not even
blessed with a serviceable scar. Too thin, and somewhat weather-beaten,
but young and unmistakably Eton, Oxford, and the West End. Nothing
brawny, nothing grim, nothing at all ruthless about him. A quiet,
low-voiced man with little crinkles round his eyes when he laughed. And
then you caught the lean line of his jaw, or a glance like a scalpel on
the soul.... “It’s because they’re fools,” he said. “Fools not to like
the Asian and treat him well when he deserves it. Worse fools to risk
his vengeance.”

“But you yourself----”

“Oh, I’m a different kind of a fool. I admire the native in several
ways. Sometimes I--almost--trust him. It’s not quite as suicidal as it
sounds,” he grinned.

“Dodo’s got heaps of pals up Kashmir way,” boasted Taunton. “The Sikhs
are good children if you know how to handle ’em.”

“The Sikhs have nothing to do with the case,” murmured Dorin.

“Unfortunately!”

“But what is it all about? Do tell me everything!” Alexandra sat with
clasped hands, looking from one to the other.

“Poor Bob’s been through it already, hunting for hitches.”

“Oh, don’t mind me!” Taunton picked up the _Times_ from a table
and retired to a chair by the fire. “It’s a beautiful story. Tell it.
I’ll sit over here and improve my mind.”

“Well,” began Dorin, putting out his cigarette, “once upon a time there
was a goddess named Shir Shan. She had not been seen within the memory
of man, but she was known to have sun-colored hair and eyes like the
heavens at midnight. She was beautiful and she should have been good,
but she had an unfortunate weakness for human sacrifice. Even so, she
was neat about it. At certain intervals her priests would find a golden
robe, supposedly her own, lying across the long-deserted throne in her
temple. Bells were rung and drums were beaten and there was feasting
and ceremony, and at the end of three days the usual luckless virgin
was dressed in the golden robe and seated on the throne and left there,
quite alone. The trick was that she vanished without a trace and was
never seen again. Evaporated, the legend runs. Consumed by the magic
fabric of Shir Shan’s robe. Gone up in smoke! And the empty robe,
spotless and shining, always came back for more.”

“But the priests! They must have--” It was again the little girl at the
pantomime.

“Aha! The priests!” said Dorin.

“Never look for trouble in that direction, Mrs. Marley,” advised
Taunton from behind the _Times_. “You’re sure to find it.”

“And the magic robe still exists?”

“So Starke says. He’s run it to earth, he thinks, some distance from
the temple where it flourished, which was long since abandoned. It’s in
the keeping of a little-known religious order who might be induced to
part with it--for reasons of their own.”

“Stolen?” she whispered, tingling.

“A hundred times over!”

“And you’d go off on a wild-goose chase like that--?” began Marley
incredulously.

“Try me!” said Dorin.

“But you’ve no kind of proof that the robe ever even existed! Perhaps
it’s just a myth!”

“Perhaps!”

“Like the Golden Fleece!” nodded Alexandra. “_He_ found it!” she
nodded again, sparkling at them.

“He did, he did!” murmured Taunton to the _Times_.

Marley turned on him.

“But Dorin’s mad!” he cried. “Why doesn’t somebody talk him out of
this?”

“Well, after all,” reflected Alexandra, “Bruce came home from a
thousand perils in Abyssinia and fell downstairs and died!”

“Why, I--I feel a certain responsibility!” worried Marley. “It was I
who introduced you to this man! I had no idea-- Dear, dear, I supposed
you’d put him off somehow; I never dreamed you’d take it seriously--”
Again he turned to Taunton. “And are you going to sit there and let him
do this?”

“Who am I to stop him?” queried Taunton modestly.

“But--it’s dangerous! It’s suicidal! He won’t come through alive! Why,
Starke says there was a Russian from Bokhara who went up there on a bet
and was never seen again, but the story goes that they----”

“Russians,” said Taunton, “have no social tact. And I’ve heard they
torture well.” He turned a page. “Dodo will turn up. He always does.”

“Well, of all the cold-blooded, sinful--” began Marley, eying him with
incredulous horror.

“My dear fellow.” Taunton sat up. “My dear fellow. Would you tie a man
by the leg to the Nelson monument for fear some snipin’ Asiatic wit
might miraculously hit him? I quite see your point; I realize as well
as you do that some day good old Dodo will inevitably fail to turn up
at all--and God grant that it be not yet. But we are all destined one
way or another for the front page of the _Times_, and he takes his
standing up--as I do!” Having delivered himself of which he returned,
reddening, to the paper and was seen no more.

“What a way to go!” said Alexandra, half to herself. “No fuss--no
tears--no dying wish--no procession with plumes--no marble weight
pressing down, down above your head-- Just--!” She snapped her fingers,
so that Marley started, frowning, and took up the argument again.

“Why don’t you go along and look after him, then?” he demanded
indignantly of the _Times_.

“Haven’t been asked,” complained the voice behind it.

“Oh, get along,” advised Dorin, grinning fondly. “You know you’ve
already promised to go to South Africa!”

“What for?” Still the little girl, begging for more stories.

“Alex, my dear--!” said Marley.

“Some camera Johnny wants to shoot lions,” Dorin told her. “Bob’s got
to coax ’em to come out and sit for their portraits.”

“Just with cameras?” queried Alexandra, looking rather dashed.

“Alex, my dear--!” said Marley.

“Daresay that depends on how they behave themselves,” admitted the
invisible Taunton. “Been trying to get Dodo to wait and go as far as
Gibraltar with us, but he’s off tomorrow in spite of me. Unsociable
cove, Dodo.”

“Seems as though everybody’s going somewhere!” sighed Alexandra.

“Which reminds me--” Marley rose briskly. “I’m going out to dinner.
Making a speech--that sort of thing. You chaps excuse me while I dress?
I won’t be long.”

He went, and was not missed.

“Where is the robe, now, supposedly?”

Alexandra fixed expectant eyes on Dorin. He was to her at the moment
far less a hero than a talking-machine from which further details of
this fascinating quest might be unwound. The man, the adventurer, the
protagonist of a possible tragedy, all were lost in the immensity of
the thing he stood for: _Hazard_.

“Supposedly there is a monastery in the Hills south and east of--” he
was beginning.

“Wait! I’ll get a map! I love maps! Could you show me on a map?”

“Approximately.”

“There’s an atlas in Clem’s study--and a guidebook. Wait, I’ll fetch
them!” She hurried out, light-footed.

Dorin retrieved her handkerchief from the floor, looked at it with
a half smile, tossed it to the table, glanced about the chill,
commonplace room, back to the handkerchief--and lighted a cigarette.

Taunton was still out of sight behind the _Times_. Dorin drifted
to the piano, and as he sat down before it he perceived for the first
time its mute tragedy amidst the red plush. It was her piano. All that
was hers in her home.

Poor little devil, he thought, as his foot went home to the pedal.
There was something about her like--he fumbled about rather shyly in
his mind for something to describe her, for he was unused to describing
women even in the privacy of his own mind--like the beating of wings,
he decided, and smiled, grave-eyed, above the keys as the piano awoke
to the touch of a lover. That was it. A dauntless eaglet warring with
the bars of a cage....

“Mandalay” throbbed softly under his fingers. Bob began to sing, and
Bob had a tenor so sweet that it ached.

    “‘If you’ve ’eard the East a-callin’ you won’t never ’eed naught else;
        No! You won’t ’eed nothin’ else
        But them spicy garlic smells,
        An’ the sunshine an’ the palm trees an’ the tinkly temple bells;

    On the road to Mandalay,
    Where the old Flotilla lay;
    Can’t you ’ear their paddles chunkin’ from Rangoon to Mandalay?
    On the road to Mandalay....’”

Across the hall Alexandra was crouched by the bottom shelf, tugging at
the atlas. She paused and sat back on her heels to listen.

The song she and her father had sung that night, sitting by the window
with his arms round her, waiting for the moon to rise ... and finally
the moon had come, scarved with cloud.... Alexandra could almost feel
his beard brushing her cheek now, and the rumble of his great chest as
he sang, she leaning against him ... and the excruciating strength of
him when he caught her close at the end, and her ecstatic “Tighter!”
which made him laugh ... and he had said, “What’s the good of sons,
when they make girls like you!” ... and then he sighed, looking down
at her straw-colored plait in his big fingers--“Moon-gold,” he said
... and then-- “But girls get married, don’t they, and leave their old
dads!” ... and she, crowding closer to him-- “Not this one! Not my
dad!” ... but he shook his head, fingering her thick plait-- “You’ll
see--some younger fellow--not long now--” ... and then at last,
crushing her-- “By gad, it’s been worth it--having you!” The next
morning he was gone.

    “‘For the temple bells are callin’ an’ it’s there that I would be----
    By the old Moulmein Pagoda, lookin’ lazy at the sea!
      On the road to Mandalay,
      Where the flyin’ fishes play....”

She stumbled to her feet and gathered up the books. He had reached her
again. Another message had come through. And so life went on, must go
on, somehow.




                               CHAPTER V


“THAT was my father’s song,” she said, from the doorway, as they
finished.

“I’m sorry!” said Dorin quickly, dropping his hands from the keys.

She shook her head.

“He would have liked you.” She dumped the books on the table and sat
down beside them. “I brought everything I could find on Clem’s shelves
about Central Asia. You must tell me what to read.”

He came and bent above her and the open books, turning the pages. He
began to talk, briefly at first, unemotionally, even, of supplies,
transportation, frontiers, difficulties. And then, as she made no move,
said nothing to remind him that she was a woman and this was London,
he went on. While Alexandra, with yearning eyes on a few square inches
of red and yellow and pink and green, saw a tiny party picking its
perilous way across desert, timber, and rock--tired plodding beasts, a
syce sulking in the rear, a man in khaki on a horse, a very good horse
it would have to be--a blinding sky above them with the sun scorching
down while a biting wind ripped by.... Sun--and Wind! And round the
next ledge of rock the Unknown. Behind them, Russia’s restless power.
Ahead--far ahead--the British Raj. And between them and the goal....

Fifteen minutes later found them still at it, the floor littered
with discarded books and sprawling maps. It found Taunton frankly
fast asleep before the fire, his feet outstretched before him, the
_Times_ slipping from his fingers. His attitude was of such
childish abandon that it seemed only by the grace of God that he
did not snore. Alexandra sat with her chin in her hands, Bloomsbury
forgotten. Dorin was perched on the table swinging a foot. Her
almost hypnotic receptiveness had as usual momentarily dispelled the
Englishman’s holy horror of talking “shop” and he forgot to stop at all
the most interesting places and leave out all the best parts, as is
likely to be the way of his kind.

“Of course,” he finished, “it all happened so long ago that none of it
makes sense, I suppose. But it is fairly safe to assume, isn’t it, that
after the tumult and the shouting had died and the blood no longer ran
in rivulets nobody ever did go near the place again. It was natural
enough for them to harbor ideas about the goddess’ vengeance. In that
case, the temple itself is still there somewhere, gone to wrack and
ruin, and haunted by all the pagan souls which assisted at the carnage.
Nobody seems to know its exact location. It’s not much of a country
to go prospecting in just for the look of the thing. But the robe was
carried off and has had many adventures. If my luck holds it will have
one more.”

“And that’s your job,” she said slowly.

“That’s my job. When I get it!”

“Oh, what fun!” she whispered, with clasped hands. “What fun!”

“Oh, yes,” he agreed with a touch of irony. “And a suffocating wind
blows for days and the air is thick with sand, and there’s never enough
water. And then in the hills you freeze, and everywhere you go you’re
generally unwelcome. It’s great fun! But back I go, just the same!”

“One always does go back,” she nodded, distant-eyed.

“Like the pitcher to the well.”

Reminded of something, he took from his pocket a bit of greenish stone,
a carven knot with an inscription. Through it, apparently a part of it,
ran an odd streak of dull red. He dropped it in her lap and watched her
fingers close over it as she lifted and held it lovingly.

“Why--I never saw anything quite like this!”

“Nor I,” he said.

“You called it a gift-stone--the other day.”

“With blood on it.” Half smiling, he touched the red streak with one
finger. “Magic, you see. A magic lost centuries ago. Bought or stolen
or found--the thing’s no good. But given freely for love--oh, yes! Or
so I was told by the Chinese gentleman who put it in my hand when he
died.”

“Murdered, you said.”

“Yes.”

She waited, eyes on the stone in her hand, watching it as though it
were a crystal ball, waiting for its story to unfold. Again the spell
of her intent silence worked. He went on, dreamily, as one spins a tale
at twilight for a child.

“It was in a little village beyond Su-Chow. The old chap had a sort
of shop, and we had done business together for years. So once when I
turned up from the interior, somewhat the worse for wear, he took me
in and gave me a place to sleep, and no questions asked. I saw this
thing one day lying in a tray full of more or less worthless stuff and
asked him to set a price on it. He refused, and when I went to look
for it again it was gone. He read my thought, as those fellows do, and
said, ‘Often the best way of concealing a thing is not to hide it. But
plainly what your eyes saw at once could not be invisible to those
who search.’ I tried to get the story out of him, but he sheered off
at once and I could see it wasn’t any good. Though why any one should
want to steal a thing with such a reputation-- However, that’s the way.
Well, that same night I woke with a feeling I had been called. My head
felt queer and there was an odor in the room I couldn’t recognize--dope
of some sort. And there was a something in the stillness--well, I had
felt it before. I got up and went into the other room and fell over
something--he was dying, and the thief, whoever he was, had gone on
before. When I took his hand he pressed this into mine and said, ‘Too
late--yours now--will serve you better--’ and--cashed in.”

Eyes on the stone, she did not answer his wry smile.

“He might have told you before, of his danger.”

“He was an Oriental.”

“What does it say--there in the carving?”

“It seems to be a sort of ‘God keep you.’”

“He loved you--the Chinese gentleman.”

“We were friends,” he said simply.

With a small, satisfied sigh she held out the stone to him.

“Thank you for letting me see it.”

“Won’t you keep it?” This was an impulse he was to wonder at later.

“Why--I--” She drew it toward her again, wistfully.

“Freely given--for love.” Again she failed to answer his smile, that
enveloping smile which robbed the words of any ulterior meaning. His
voice softened then, deepened. “Please keep it. God knows it’s an odd
enough thing for a woman to love like that. But if you’ll have it-- The
truth is, I’ve got a sort of hunch this time.”

“A hunch?” She looked up at him quickly.

“One has them.” He shrugged. “It’s only that I think you’ll be surer
of having it if I leave it with you now--than if I were to promise to
bring it back to you from Asia.”

Her eyes were on his, gravely.

“From all I can gather you’d better have all the luck you possess in
your pocket, if you go.”

“Oh, I’ll go! But no gift-stone is proof against the ultimate hunch.”

“You really mean you think things may not go right this time?” she
asked quite calmly.

“Oh, bless you for putting it like that!” Briefly, his fingers pressed
hers round the stone. “You should have been a man yourself--one of Us.
You’d shoot straight, you’d go till you dropped, and you never would
say die! Teach you to shoot and you could take on anything and pull
through!”

“One of--Us.”

She sat staring down at the stone, while he told himself ruefully that
he shouldn’t have said it, and wondered what temporary insanity had
loosened his tongue at both ends. It was not his way to talk too much.
He wondered just how it had happened.

“If I were a boy,” she said slowly, “I’d take you up on that. I’d run
away and go with you. I’d ask nothing better than one day of burning
sand--one night of tormenting cold--one hour of a great uncertainty
between life and death! Oh, just one little glimpse of the things that
make just existing from one hour to the next a great adventure!”

He was silent, appalled at this sudden giving way of barriers,
this unforeseen overflow into words of hidden, sacred things, this
unpremeditated and embarrassing confidence for which he was himself
to blame. He had been right, then, he thought. And she knew she was
caged, too, and was acutely miserable, as he had suspected. It was not
just tucked away at the back of her consciousness, buried under her
wifehood and her housekeeping, mercifully dormant. It was a thing
which possessed and tormented her. He could see that now.

She had risen and paced away from him, her movement, her hands, her
very voice, a blind, unreasoning beating of wings.

“Oh, I grate on rusty hinges here! But it isn’t just that I’m
bored--dissatisfied--malcontent! It’s something driving--dragging!
Something as insistent as hunger! When I was small I once tried to know
what starvation felt like, and when they caught me at that and made
me eat, I went without water to know thirst. I rebelled, even then,
against the smug snugness of life in England! I missed my heritage of
hardship--craved it--groped for it! I was seventeen before I saw the
sea, and heard the wind that walks on the water. It was on my wedding
journey I found that wind, and knew that I was a girl, and so not free
to follow it!”

She threw wide her arms, there in the stolid room with the fog outside
and the red plush inside choking the bright, insurgent flame of her
love of living; that fatal spark, handed down from father to son
through the years--to a girl! To just this mad, shackled creature,
slim and shining and keen as a blade! The pity of it, thought Dorin
helplessly. The pity of it!

“All my grandfathers were free men! And one of them fell with Wolfe at
Quebec, and one of them died at Cawnpore! And I had an uncle once who
came home from Natal and told me stories--as you do. My father--” (her
eyes grew eerie) “--my father made just one little mistake. He thought
because I was a girl he must leave me behind! He went back There
without me. But we’re rovers, all of us, always! Men who rode the wind
and died young, happy to have had so much of life, but yearning still
over things undone! It is hard for me, the last, to see life pass me
by!”

“I know,” he said, inadequately enough, he felt, but what could a man
say?

“I’ve tried so hard to forget my grandfathers. I’ve tried to be a
Marley. I can’t.”

“I know,” he said again, impotently.

“I wonder if they know--those splendid, ruthless, gallant grandfathers.
I wonder if they know--” She blinked up at him, dazed, and suddenly
timid. “Oh, I forgot--I-- You had me half drunk with your talk, I
think. You--you do understand?”

“So very well,” he said.
