They smiled at each other briefly. Then she passed him and dropped into
the chair at the table, drawn again to the maps.

Bob Taunton still slept. He had spent the night in the smoking-room
of a Channel boat, exchanging views on the Congo with a colonel of
the Indian Army, on leave. They didn’t think alike, which made it
interesting, but they had parted good friends, and the Congo was no
better off than before.

“If it’s in the Hills,” said Alexandra above the maps, “why don’t you
go up through India?”

“I’d prefer to go in by way of Bokhara and come out into India through
the Pass here, if it’s all the same to you.”

“Just as you like!” she grinned. “Tell me about Bokhara.”

“Well,” he began obligingly, “it’s an Aladdin city, with toothed
walls and covered alleys--mosques where the storks are encouraged to
nest--pink doves feeding under foot--fine old doorways, and a dignified
people--luxurious bazaars--oh, you never saw such silks and such
color----!”

Marley came in, in evening dress, and glanced about the book-strewn
room.

“Good heavens, have you fought the whole campaign? Where’s Mr. Taunton?”

“Oh, Bob!” said Dorin loudly, and Bob sat up.

“Hullo?”

“It’s all right, I’ve finished talking about myself for a while.”

“Oh, but it’s been splendid!” cried Alexandra.

“Did he ever tell you about the time we----”

“Now, Bob.”

“--about the time we completely lost ourselves in the Pamirs, and there
wasn’t even anything worth shooting at until one day----”

“Bob, that’s not a pretty story! Please don’t encourage him!”

“Oh, be quiet!” Alexandra quelled him with a gesture. “Go on,” she
commanded.

And then Taunton told a tale whereat Marley winced fastidiously and
Alexandra crowed with a heathenish satisfaction. But Dorin knew and
praised God for what had been omitted in the telling.

“Now, look here,” complained Marley at the end, “do you expect me to
believe that you _enjoy_ these experiences--that you _like_
being without food or water----”

“The only thing we really resent being without is cartridges,” said
Taunton. “That’s tough. _That’s_ hardship.”

“But you can’t eat cartridges!”

“There’s not much choice between a cartridge and a biscuit in the
Hills,” said Dorin.

“But the Government--” argued the man who wrote books.

“Oh, God bless the Government!” cried Taunton gayly.

“Well, it’s beyond me, risking your neck pursuing a will-o’-the-wisp!
You’re always on the move!”

“Life’s none so long,” Dorin apologized.

“And you pick such fantastic schemes! I could understand the desire to
plant a flag at the poles----”

“But that’s been done, Mr. Marley!” objected Taunton.

“--or some sort of relief expedition----”

“But there are so few people to rescue!”

“But this robe!” fretted Marley. “It’s such a--such a pipe-dream!”

“Oh, it isn’t what lies at the end, or even whether it’s there or not,”
said Alexandra. “It’s the getting there one goes for.”

“Exactly! _She_ knows! It’s the call of the off-shore wind--it’s
the spell of the trail that’s always new--it’s the lure of the happy
roads that take you over the world! One man has said it all. Listen!”
Carried away, Taunton began tramping up and down the room, his hands in
his pockets.

    “‘It’s like a book, I think, this bloomin’ world,
    Which you can read and care for just so long,
    But presently you feel that you will die
    Unless you get the page you’re readin’ done
    And turn another--likely not so good;
    But what you’re after is to turn ’em all.’”

“Bobby, in heaven’s name, dry up!” said Dorin in affectionate horror.
“I’ll leave you at home next time!” He rose. “Come along. We promised
to feed that fellow Whatshisname at the club and it’s getting late.”

“Oh, Lord, yes, I forgot! He’s starving by now. Let’s go be a relief
expedition!” He pranced toward the door.

“The club?” said Marley. “I’m going that way. We’ll have a cab. I’ll be
late tonight, Alex.”

“Yes, Clem.” She gave her hand to Dorin. “I do hope I can see the robe,
when you get it!”

“I hope I get it!” he grinned.

“But suppose the robe isn’t there!” Marley turned in the doorway.
“Suppose there simply _isn’t_ any robe. Suppose----”

“Oh, suppose there was no such word as suppose!” Laughing, she waved
them out, and stood alone in the middle of the room looking after them.

She was tired. Tired to the soul of being left behind. She went
forlornly to the window and watched them getting into a cab, and
wondered what she was to do with herself the rest of the evening. She
didn’t mind being alone, but she hated emptiness, and the room seemed
somehow bereft. The walls closed in again. It would have been easier,
almost, if they had never opened and let her out.

She stood disconsolately in the middle of the room, looking at the
abandoned books, becoming conscious of the clock, hearing the distant
clink of silver and china as Susan laid the table for dinner. She might
go and look at the dog.... But she stood still, strangely indifferent
now to dogs. Besides, it had annoyed Clem. Almost she wished that Clem
hadn’t had that engagement tonight. She would have liked him at home,
solid and kind and comfortable, reading in his study with the door
open, and the smell of his pipe drifting out....

It might have been better, Clem, to have let that lecture go.




                               CHAPTER VI


BLAISE DORIN had happened to look back as he stepped into the cab. He
saw that slim figure at the window, silhouetted lonesomely against the
lighted room. And as they drove away his mind’s eye saw too clearly for
comfort the heap of books, the deserted chairs, the open piano with its
empty music rack, the red plush. He wondered what she would do with
herself the rest of the evening.

Poor little devil, he might have helped her pick up the books. Awful,
the way a room must feel when people went out of it, several people
laughing and talking together, and you were left, with things to
pick up. He wished there was time to call in again before he left
London. She might have liked to see that dagger he had picked up in
Rangoon--the one with the elephant’s head and trunk for a handle. She
was such a bloodthirsty little thing. Little? She would come to his
chin!

He dismissed her with a mental shrug, but she kept coming between him
and the talk. He decided that he might take her the dagger when he
returned from Algiers. Perhaps she might like to own it. She would
think it great fun to give him sixpence in return, to scotch the
hoodoo. A luck-piece for him. He would need it!

They deposited Marley on the pavement at his destination and proceeded
fitfully in the cab toward Pall Mall. Dorin was wondering if there was
anything he could bring her from Algiers.

“It seems too bad,” he said at last, into the silence.

“What seems too bad, old son?” queried Bob.

There wasn’t much in Algiers that one could conceivably bring away in
one’s pocket.

“I’m sorry for her, hanged if I’m not.”

“Sorry for who?” said Bob, cheerfully ungrammatical. “Oh, you mean
_her_? You know, Dodo, if she’d been born a boy she’d have run
away to sea, as I did!”

“Why on earth wasn’t she born a boy, I wonder!”

“Might just as well have been! There’s about as much of the eternal
feminine in her as in the first Eton jacket you meet!”

“Yes. You forget she’s a woman, somehow.”

“Yes, but _is_ she!” There was a silence. “Wonder how she came to marry
him,” said Bob.

“Loved him--I suppose.”

“Loved _that_?” Bob got out his cigarettes. “Garn!” he jeered.

More silence, with the scratching of matches.

“Good Lord, Bobby, think of all that joy-of-life buried in that house!”

“Awful hole!” agreed Bob round the light. “Not even a _Punch_!”

“It’s a beastly shame,” Dorin ruminated aloud. “It’s wicked. How would
_you_ like it?”

“Oh, me!” said Bob airily. “I’d clear out.” He thought it over. “That
woman,” he pronounced then with emphatic forefinger, “that woman is
what they call a throw-back! She--she’s-- What’s the word I want?
What’s that beauty of a word I want?”

“Atavistic?”

Bob gazed at him admiringly.

“Now you see,” he pointed out, “the value of an education!”

“But she isn’t, you know,” grinned Dorin. “That is--she comes by it
honestly enough through her own father.”

“Where’s he?”

“Valhalla.”

“I see,” said Bob, more soberly.

“He was Ingarsen.”

“_Ingarsen’s daughter?_ Oh, well--!” Bob threw out his hands.
“All the Ingarsens are like that!” he said. Again he thought hard.
“No--brothers or anything of that sort?”

“No. She’s the last of the line, I think.”

“Golly.” Bob scowled intently out of the cab window. “Why didn’t he
stick round and look after her?” he demanded. “Where does _this_
bloke come into it?”

“Ingarsen died.”

“No way to do,” decreed Bob. “Leavin’ a girl like that. God only knows
what girls will marry. Should have stuck round.”

“Africa,” said Dorin, and sighed.

“Mmmm,” said Bob. “She’ll get me too, you know. Africa will.”

Dorin was silent, thinking of the Hills. He was not for Africa.

“No way to do,” repeated Bob. “Chap marries--kids have some rights.
For hundreds of years there have been Ingarsens. That’s what India
needs--more Ingarsens. And now this girl--the quintessence of Ingarsen,
mind you--think of the sons----”

“_Bobby_, my God!” said Dorin, badly shocked, and again there
was silence. “Well, I thought perhaps you might like to go and talk
to her sometimes when you’re in town,” he suggested. “That is, if you
can behave yourself. There’s precious little we can do, but she’s like
a kid for stories. Of course,” he added, thinking of that time in the
Pamirs, “you’ll have to censor a bit sometimes, as you go.”

“But I haven’t any parlor tricks,” worried Taunton. “I don’t belong in
a place like that.”

“Neither does she belong there.”

“Yes, but after all, she is a woman, and----”

“Yes, but _is_ she?” No reply. “Lord, how she’d live the life we
love!” he muttered.

“I say, you know--please don’t shoot--but after all, it’s no good
sentimentalizin’ over--over----”

“Can one be sentimental over an Eton jacket, you ass? I only said----”

“Besides, the world is full of people married to the wrong ones.”

Dorin threw away his cigarette.

“That’s not what I meant.”

“Perhaps not, but----”

“Oh, don’t talk rot.”

“But all the same, if----”

“Stow it, Bobby!”

“Right-O!”

Thus the subject was amiably closed between them.

Months later, reading his mail by the light of a camp-fire in South
Africa, Bob remembered this conversation incredulously, and rose up and
called the world a liar in the face of it. Later still, when life for
Bob had resolved itself into just the single idea of finding Dodo alive
somewhere, somehow, when nothing else mattered and everybody could go
straight to blazes, it began to haunt him most horribly--it, and the
eager eyes of Ingarsen’s daughter, who should have been born a boy.




                                _Storm_


     _“The days are sick and cold, and the skies are gray and old_,
              _And the twice-breathed airs blow damp...._”




                               CHAPTER I


TAUNTON did go back to the house in Bloomsbury Square, however, and
they talked lions and Kimberley diamonds and the Boer War--among other
things. She knew all about the Boer War, he found to his amusement.

“Of course we were all wrong in a way,” she said with her quaint
earnestness about such matters. “But, after all, we _can_
colonize--we _do_ colonize--better than anybody!”

He wanted to pat her on the head.

“Imperialist,” he said fondly.

But always they would return, by this way or that, to the subject
which if they left it at all lay just under the surface of the talk
and of which they were constantly being reminded by something--the
life and works of Blaise Dorin. The saga of his not uneventful career
was faithfully unfolded in jerky, graphic chapters told in Taunton’s
colorful language, for now that Dorin’s restraining influence was
removed to Africa, Bob rather let himself go and became simply a modest
Roland singing of his Oliver. It was a diet of sheer hero-worship,
shining and unashamed, that Alexandra’s greedy imagination fed on now.

So she heard, among other things, how once in the Congo Bob had
lain with a broken leg, weakened by fever and pain, and watched the
bull-like rush of a mad black giant toward where Dorin stood with a
revolver in his hand. “You see, I didn’t dare try to shoot, I wobbled
so I’d have hit Dodo instead--black fellow came on swingin’ four feet
of iron chain and bellowin’--_musth_, you know, _musth_
as any elephant, and no prettier to see--all over mud and blood he
was--hijjus-lookin’ nightmare--” And Dorin had stood there waiting, his
finger ready on the trigger, but waiting, until it seemed no bullet
made on earth could stop the fatal impact of that black body. “I had
time to think of all my ill-spent life, while I waited for Dodo to
shoot--like drowning, it was--and I heard the rattle of the chain,
and the giggle of the river beyond--I smelt the brute, too--I did,
I _smelt_ him!--and I felt the breath of the jungle on my face
like the breath of a hot ghost, with never a leaf stirring--I saw the
flash of a bright bird out of a tree over Dodo’s head--and I heard
Dodo breathing--he’d had quite a run up the bank after I yelled--by
God, I even had time to _pray_!--and Dodo stood there, solid as
though he was watchin’ a bloomin’ parade go by, holding his blessed
fire!” Bob had been afraid to shout to him to hurry, though his every
shattered nerve shrieked for the sound of the gun--afraid to move,
for fear of disturbing for a flickering second the steady, measuring
gaze of the man with the gun. He had huddled there, spent and sick and
scared--“whistling with funk each time I breathed”--till finally the
gun barked twice and the black doubled forward, coughing--“as though a
taut wire had caught him across the stomach”--and pitched on his face
at Dorin’s very feet. Dorin looked down at him a moment, reflectively,
it seemed, then shook out the used shells and stepping over a huge
black arm and the sprawling length of chain tossed an empty revolver to
Bob with a request for the loan of a cartridge or two. “Those two were
his last, do you see? First _I_ knew we’d run as short as that! My
gun still had its full quota--I’d been laid up for days. Oh, yes, we
got through to the coast without much more trouble--had three to spare,
I think.”

Another time----

“Unless you know his little ways you always think he isn’t going to
fight,” said Bob. “They always think it doesn’t look like Dodo’s day
to shoot. That’s their fatal mistake. He goes about his business, you
know, sort of absent-minded and sweet-tempered. Harmless-looking sort
of cove, Dodo is. But when he begins to squint, look out! Of course,
I’ve only seen it happen a couple of times myself--but other chaps say
the same. His eyes get queer, just before he lets fly. How? Oh, I don’t
know--slits, you know--light gray--chilly sort of look--” He hunched
his broad shoulders in a boyish shiver. “_Glittery!_” he explained.

“You can’t hurry him either. He always takes the whites of their eyes.
Cheaper in the long run. Neater, too. Dodo hates a mess. There was once
he wasn’t quite tidy, though.” He pulled up suddenly. “_Just_ once
in all history.”

She waited tensely, her hands pressed together. She _had_ to have
that story. Mutely, she willed him to go on, uttering no sound to bring
his thoughts to focus in Bloomsbury. If she kept very still he might
go on ... he must go on....

“Something gave, somewhere,” he went on slowly, almost unwillingly,
speaking more to himself than to her. “Nothing to apologize for, I
suppose. One isn’t quite oneself sometimes--civilization caves in-- Oh,
I wasn’t there, I heard about it. Wish to God I had been there----”

Again that tight silence. He looked up at last, as if drawn by her
intent eyes, caught her look, surrendered to it....

“Well, if you must--! Seems there were a lot of fuzzies lying
round dead--trickiest native of all, fuzzy-wuzzy--but _you_
know that--there’d been a bit of a row, you see, and one of Dodo’s
particular pals had been downed in the middle of it. _He_ was
bendin’ over this chap lookin’ out the damage--and all of a sudden the
nearest dead fuzzy rolled over and took a swipe at him with a knife.
Damned near thing, just missed--important mechanisms. Nasty gash,
anyway. Dodo’d been through a good deal that day--he was nervy, no
denyin’--there was a scrabble, of course, knife and gun, and his first
bullet did for the fuzzy, who was about done anyway--but Dodo laid
back his ears and emptied his gun into It. All six. Came to when the
trigger changed its tune--thought it had jammed--found he’d used ’em
all--and was rather sick very soon after, of course. But I mean to say,
it _was_ irritatin’, wasn’t it! That is--a dead fuzzy suddenly
hackin’ at you like that--what?”

Alexandra had put a question, large eyed.

“How many--?” said Bob in surprise. “Oh, I don’t know--perhaps--” He
checked off sundry fingers, waggled another vaguely, gave it up. “Dodo
doesn’t notch his gun. The War and all--no good dwellin’ on it, is
there? You do it when you’ve got to, and let it go. But there’s one
thing--if ever he’d been inclined to be the least bit hasty twice as
many more would have gone shoutin’ home to glory various ways. And half
of _those_ are still looking for him. He’s a bit careless-like
with his feuds. Forgetful. Or maybe it only looks as though he is.” Bob
pondered this. “No. I don’t think you could call Dodo exactly careless,
after all. _Lenient_ is the word, I think. He’s dretful lenient,
sometimes. The fact is,” added Bob slowly to his boot-toes, “the fact
is, he’s not quite hasty _enough_, to my way of lookin’ at it.
Lots of loose ends hangin’ out, in Dodo’s life--one of ’em will trip
him up some windy night. The Congo, now--big place--hard to get about
in to find a man in a hurry--low visibility, as it were--but I’ll keep
him clear of the whole damn’ works from now on if I have to sit on his
head!”

“Why?”

He looked at her queerly, seeing something else.

“We’ll let that go,” he said.

There was the other side, too, the less spectacular, wholly lovable
side--the man who doctored native babies, endured hunger or thirst
or risked infection for the sake of a favorite servant or a faithful
headman or merely an obligation of long standing, who spoke all tongues
and was made welcome in many places, and carried in his head the
etiquette and idiosyncrasies of a dozen wilderness kings. There was the
Dodo who could soothe a sick man in his arms when delirium razed the
barriers of consciousness, loosing things that were better not babbled
aloud; once all one night, white-faced and patient, he had answered to
a woman’s name and thus forgiven an ancient wrong, lost at this long
last in fevered incoherency. Once there was a Bhil, one of those little
apparently unloving, unlovable savages, who had thrown his own body and
soul to a tiger that the _sahib_ might live with but the mark of
claws on his shoulder--the Bhils are small men, but quick. Once a whole
village had pelted him with flowers, to his chagrin, and once a child
had crept into his lap to die.

All this Alexandra heard, and much more, often laughing with wet eyes,
while Taunton talked as he had never talked to woman before, pouring
out the shy, sacred love of man for man, unembarrassed. She echoed
to it all, like a harp to remembered music, caught at it with hungry
hands, took it to bed with her and dreamed it again in the dark,
vividly, lying taut between waking and sleeping, seeing the far-flung
camel-lines marching across her eyelids, hearing the beat of torture
tomtoms in the pulses in her own ears.

“‘Frabjous’ times,” Bob called them gayly. Frabjous’ times, when he and
Dodo worked together. He shared them with her, the best he could. He
even shared a cheerful scrawl, two weeks old, relayed from Marseilles,
which spoke lightly of inevitable trouble pending in Morocco,
feelingly of a _pukka_ sandstorm, and vaguely of a probable
errand in Paris. “Paris,” puzzled Bob. “What’s he up to now, I wonder!
Paris--it doesn’t seem to fit in.” This was to remain a mystery to them.

Then a packet arrived for Alexandra, containing a bangle with a charm,
heavy, thrilling, seeming still warm from an arm brown with the African
sun, but of small intrinsic value--so Clem said she might keep it.
She had hidden the note which accompanied it, in a groundless fit of
childish naughtiness.

  “I was able to make myself useful to a damsel in distress,” it
  read. “There was a lover or something in a bit of a fix--I helped
  him out--nice chap, too--bless-you-my-children--_that_ sort of
  thing. She gave me this for my sweetheart, and thought it no end
  funny I hadn’t got one. No offense, but--thought you might care to
  have it!”

She hid the paper under her handkerchiefs in the top drawer, beside the
knot of carven nephrite with its heathen blessing. One could always
keep notes. That was no affair of Clem’s.

Then Bob Taunton went away to his lions and there were no more stories.
But she went over and over the ones she knew, building them, filling in
the gaps in Bob’s vocabulary, visioning, hoarding, dreaming....

Yes, she dreamed of Blaise Dorin now. Not tenderly and gladly as women
dream, but exaggeratedly and in secret as children and men, both of
which dwell in the fear of ridicule, think on their gods.




                               CHAPTER II


MR. STARKE returned one day to make his peace, he said, and was
graciously absolved. Then he came to inquire Bob Taunton’s London
address--which he probably already knew--in order, he confessed,
grinning, to learn from him the approximate date of Dorin’s return from
Algiers--which he also probably knew. And again, with a carved jade
necklace which Marley named, dated, pigeonholed, and forgot, and which
Alexandra touched with reverent fingers for its beauty’s sake.

Finally--it seemed somehow quite a natural thing--Starke kept on
coming, not too often, of course, and welcome for his genial presence
and his way of producing casually from his pocket some priceless
trinket with a history.

His eyes would go wistfully from Alexandra’s blonde perfection to the
thing of his in her hand. He could never decide in his own mind the
fine point of what object of sufficient value to be worth the offering,
she would not decline as too lavish a gift. Yet he always experienced
an almost uncontrollable desire to bestow upon her everything she
admired.

One satisfaction the conventions did allow him, and he showered her
with books of travel and adventure, most of it in Asia. She seemed
never to tire of hearing his varied reasons for believing in the
golden robe of Shir Shan, which became to her the shining symbol of all
the romance left in a dreary world.

Starke had no parlor tricks either, but he never for one moment forgot
she was a woman.

Meanwhile, existence was getting a strangle hold on her spirits.

The elder Mrs. Marley, an indomitable dowager in black taffeta, had
reëstablished herself in the south room, hung her canary in its gilded
cage above the mute piano, and commanded the restoration of the
antimacassars to all the chairs.

Alexandra shut herself up in the linen closet to look for them, and
having found them much too soon mislaid them again by placing a sheet
on top, and sat down in a disconsolate heap and told herself that once
things became adjusted, once Susan learned to make that tea-cake, once
she herself learned never to express ideas even about the weather,
life might become more simple. But after the first frenzied weeks of
striving to please one who was by nature and inclination incapable of
being pleased, Alexandra felt the waters of despair close over her
aching head; felt herself sinking down, down, into utter blackness and
inert misery.

Her long, solitary walks were forfeit. The pace of her circumspect
daily airing was either reduced to suit the majestic gait of a stout
old woman with a stick, or driven with the responsibility of a dozen
small errands to be accomplished before tea-time. To be alone became an
obsession. Freedom became a madness. Life slipped past her while she
danced attendance on a born tyrant.

The faithful Susan retrieved and confiscated sundry small, hard, damp
balls which had once been handkerchiefs. Susan closed doors with great
presence of mind when one dissolved without warning in the pantry or
the linen closet, overtaken by a general blurriness and limpness. Susan
patted one’s shoulder understandingly and said, “There, now!” till
one’s sorry pride got on its feet again.

And then at last one morning in the pantry where she had come upon
Alexandra huddled on a stool with her head on her knees, very still,
Susan spoke to the point.

Alexandra had long since discovered that the closed door of her bedroom
only brought about questions when she was at length forced by hunger
or conscience to emerge. Or if she withstood both these too long the
door was tapped upon and the questions fired through it. There was no
sanctuary. But the pantry was safest.

“This won’t do, ma’am, it won’t,” said Susan. “You’ll be ill, and think
how you’d like _that_, ma’am!”

Alexandra forced herself, blinking, to contemplate being ill. No, most
decidedly that would not do. She had been ill once....

She sat quiet, contemplating memory, holding her reluctant mind by the
scruff of its neck, as it were, making it look. Of course that had been
different, that time. But, after all, if one was ill one was ill; it
all amounted to much the same thing so far as she could see. A shiver
ran through her. It was not the pain she minded so much. Pain holds you
there, gives you something to get your teeth into. It is after pain
recedes, taking everything with it, leaving you floating, blind, deaf,
half-dead--half-dead!... She remembered that she had roused from that
to a voice suddenly quite distinct in ears which had so long heard only
blurs. A man’s voice, saying quietly to whatever was on the other side
of her bed, “That doesn’t fetch her. Nothing will. She won’t last the
night out.” Was it a ship he meant, she wondered vaguely. What ship?
Was something sinking? She puzzled over it, lying there half-dead,
until a little frown showed between her closed eyes. She couldn’t
remember a ship.... Some one bent over her, there was an exclamation of
triumph, there were fingers on her wrist.... Then she knew. Death was
waiting for her. For _her_! And they were going to turn her over
to him already--they, whose business it surely was to fight him off
for her, to get her well again in spite of him--and they had abandoned
her now that he had almost got her. She wondered where Clement was.
Had he deserted her, too? Very well, she would fight alone, but it
was hardly fair of them to go back on her now--she was so tired--it
wasn’t fair.... Complaining bitterly, grumbling resentfully, feeling
much abused but quite undaunted, more hurt than frightened, her fagged
spirit girded itself for battle. Leave her in the lurch, would they!
Go back on all their fine promises! Perhaps they thought she didn’t
mind dying! She _would_ not die--she _could_ not die--she
had only begun to live--it was her right to live.... She began to
count her breathing conscientiously. Breath--death. Odd they should
rhyme.... There seemed to be a lot of activity all of a sudden--what
were they saying?--it didn’t matter now, she hadn’t time to listen--not
if she had to bring this off alone.... She wished they would let go of
her wrist--she was sure she could breathe better if they would let go
of her wrist--it smothered her, that small pressure on her wrist....
She tried to free herself, but nothing moved. No matter. There wasn’t
time now.... Hours passed. Eternities. She gave up counting because
it seemed to make her sleepy. She got her eyelids up a little way and
could see the foot of the bed with the lamplight across it, and the
shadow of some one who moved. If they would move oftener it might help
her to keep awake. Was it sleep or Death that plagued her so? He had
as many shapes as the Old Man of the Sea. She must be careful--must
keep awake--it seemed a very long night she had to last through....
Hours. Eternities. While she kept Death off with one hand and held
to Life with the other.... What was that, there on the wall? A bit
of something gray--smoke?--daylight?--dawn between the curtains? She
wished they would open the curtains, but there was no time to tell
them.... She lay watching the gray place on the wall, her eyes a little
wider as it widened. She was sure it was daylight; why didn’t they
open the curtains and put out the lamp? How could she be sure she had
lasted the night out so long as they kept the lamp burning? Another
hour, perhaps. Then it would be day. Another hour--another day. And
what then? Would she be safe, once it was day? Then would they take
hold of things again, and let her rest? She had done her share. It was
their turn at Death. Apparently they hadn’t quite deserted her--there
seemed to be something going on over there--she wished they would let
her alone.... The minutes crawled by, while the gray streak grew and
grew. At last before her very eyes it reddened faintly, deepened,
brightened, and was sunlight! Sunlight on the wall! Her eyes opened
wider, and there came a face. Not Clement’s face. But she had seen it
somewhere before. It smiled. “Hullo,” it said. Its eyes were kind--they
_knew_. Her gaze went back to the patch of sunlight. She wanted to
say something, too. She wanted to show them she was still alive. She
looked up at the face again, earnestly, into its eyes. It bent nearer,
inquiringly. A flicker, a mere wan wish to smile, passed over her lips.
“Sun,” she said, and went to sleep.

That was what it meant to be ill. Just an exhausting determination to
live, one’s whole being fastened with sick longing on the glory of a
miserable little patch of sunlight reflected on the wall.

She lifted helpless, questioning eyes to Susan.

“What shall I do?” she asked meekly.

“It’s those walks you don’t get nowadays, ma’am. It’s pullin’ you
under, bein’ shut up like this. For one thing, it’s too sudden. You
can’t just turn off a ’abit like turnin’ off water in the sink, ma’am.
You’ll be ill.”

“But I mustn’t be ill!” she argued apprehensively.

“No, ma’am. That’s what I say.”

“But I never am ill!” she protested hopefully. “Except that once,” she
added, averting her eyes from it.

“No, ma’am. But _she_ ain’t never been ’ere this long before.”

This was logic. Alexandra went down before it.

“Do you think--? I mean--you don’t think--?” she began, and stopped.
Through the house shrilled the soprano ecstasy of the canary, driven
out of his witless head by a rare sunbeam athwart his cage.

“Yes, ma’am,” said Susan. “You got to be out more, that’s what.” She
jerked her head toward the front of the house. “_You_ ain’t a
canary-bird, ma’am.”

“I’ve tried,” said Alexandra vaguely.

“It’s killin’ you, ma’am,” Susan comforted her. “_I_ can tell. You
can’t go on like this, not noways you can’t. You’ll be ill.”

Alexandra sprang to her feet, her hands over her ears.

“I won’t be ill!” she cried wildly. “I won’t! I won’t!” And she ran out
of the pantry and through the house and up the stairs for her hat.

She did not come home to luncheon that day. Susan, under
cross-examination, admitted that she had gone out without saying where
nor when she would return.

“How very extraordinary,” said Mrs. Marley.

Clement sighed.




                              CHAPTER III


DESPERATELY, then, Alexandra set about the business of not being ill.
She walked alone by the River till the old sweet weariness came upon
her. She dreamed on the Bridge and went home through the dusk to a
belated dinner amid the coolness and formal converse of a politely
disapproving household; gratefully ate the hot food Susan had kept for
her; wondered a little through a pleasant tiredness and plenitude how
things had ever seemed so important in the linen closet days a century
or so ago; went to bed very early, and to sleep.

At first the mere regaining of her lost privileges put new life into
her, privileges grown doubly dear through long abstinence. It was as
though she had discovered life all over again. It was like getting well.

She was so very happy about it, so very glowing, that Starke on one of
his pilgrimages to the shrine was smitten anew, and if opportunity had
offered would certainly have pressed upon her a bracelet of old wrought
silver from the arm of a dead queen. There was coming to be quite a
collection in his rooms at the Cecil of historic trinkets designed
to delight the most capricious of her sex. They accumulated, locked
rather carelessly into a lacquer box, for once she had seen them,
once they had been produced for her entertainment, like rabbits from
a conjuror’s hat, they had served their purpose and appeared to have
no further destiny in his eyes. I have already said that many of the
diversions of his kind were a closed book to him.

But she found it only temporary, this regained paradise of
quasi-freedom. As time went on, the atmosphere surrounding her belated
meals and erratic absences became more and more chilled with reproof,
less and less painfully polite. Life again closed in on her. It became
imperative when she was out to stay out and when she was in to flee.

_To get away._ To feel the wind on her face and to smell the sea
and to hear the hundred intimate and precious sounds that water makes
on wood, rock, or sand--to tread turf instead of pavement, even to
empty sand from one’s ridiculous low shoes--to lie face down and watch
what happened in the mysterious insect world underfoot--to lie face up
and watch the white kaleidoscope of clouds--to play recklessly at being
a child again--_to get away_! So she went farther and farther
afield, and sometimes was gone so long that even Susan, who had every
confidence in her immunity from disaster, watched anxiously for her
return. And then she would be seized with spasms of remorse and stay
close at home for days, a disarming, yellow-haired saint doing penance.

Clement washed his hands of her.

It was now that she became really acquainted with the vast loneliness
of her own soul, stranded in a world of other souls lost in their
respective lonelinesses. She turned, as her forefathers had done
throughout the ages, to the sky for comfort. The sky, where the wind
came from and where mystically God dwelt--the God of her childhood,
builded upon the somewhat haphazard foundation of her father’s
casual-seeming faith, the religion of a man who had lived and died
ignorant of fear. It was a kindly, even humorous God she had known as a
child, of Whom one asked and if in His infinite wisdom He thought best,
it was given. He sat somewhere beyond the sun, meting out His gentle
justice, never angry if people meant well, always willing to listen to
reason, like her father--and, like her father, never too busy to stop
and hear.

Somehow she stumbled back along the road now to that child’s God in the
sky, of Whom it was possible to ask things, even to point out angles
of the situation which might have escaped his attention. And while no
tumbling incoherencies shaped themselves on this grown-up Alexandra’s
lips, she would sit watching the clouds or the stars, and in her eyes,
in her stillness, in her very hands clasped loosely on her knees, was
prayer.

So there were days when she stood listlessly at the window, nursing
vague plans. And there were nights when she lay awake with feverish
eyes on the moonlight marching along the carpet--it was surprising how
fast that moonlight moved--mentally equipping in minutest detail an
expedition into the Hills for Shir Shan’s robe. She was crammed with
facts and theories about this, accumulated greedily from a hundred
sources in the forlorn hope of seeing Blaise Dorin just once before
he started, and perhaps having a share--just a glimpse--of his own
mysterious arrangements.

Dodo Dorin. There was magic in the name. Men loved him, his friends
were legion, of all colors and creeds; men had voluntarily died for him
as he had in turn offered his charmed life for other lives he loved.
God still made men like her father, then, and the art of living was
still practiced by a fortunate few. And the knowledge that she belonged
among them, that she was missing her divine heritage, became veritable
torment. Then, quite unexpectedly, she discovered a way to ease the
misery of it. She learned to shut her eyes and go!

No longer just a wistful looker-on at a distant drama on a mental
motion-picture screen now, for she had found she could _remember_
things. It was the only word she could find for it. Remembering. It
was as though when she had come to a blank wall and could no longer go
forward the doors in front of her had swung softly ajar. Breathlessly,
she peeped and listened at their tantalizing cracks--and this one
showed a deep blue sky curved above a strange red desert city whose
streets were given over to pigeons and the winds--and that one would
reveal, if only she could have touched the door to swing it wide open,
long lines of yellow-robed men, passing, passing, endlessly, with
whispering bare feet--beyond another was the source of nameless music
trickling from unseen, unguessable instruments played by houris or
beggars, there was no telling which--behind another lurked an unknown,
inevitable evil, to which some one would presently pass in--still
another shut her out from some unimaginable paradise of warmth and
kindness and low laughter and fellowship--and none of the doors
would give way an inch more, though her spirit pressed against them
pitifully, its ear against the panel, pleading.

“It’s very odd,” her mind would murmur to her consciousness as it
pattered busily from door to door, eavesdropping, “it’s most unusual;
perhaps we’re going mad--or perhaps it keeps us sane--or perhaps it’s
only natural to Us.”

By piecing together a sort of legacy wrenched by her dire need from
ancestors rich in all such things, a legacy of beauty and discomfort,
of heat and smells and sounds and motion, and adding these to what she
knew and what she could guess of Dorin’s impending venture--she found
she was able to almost go along! This was a new and thrilling game.
More than ever before she pored over books and pictures--raw material
for the Dream, grist for the mill of her omnivorous imagination. So
that bit by bit, rock by rock, mile by mile, and sun by sun, she set
herself to build a world and saw it spread, mirage-like, beyond the
desert at her feet. And here at last was sanctuary.

She was able at times to be very sorry for her mother-in-law. Dreadful
to be like that, dreadful for life to mean so little. Not that her
mother-in-law took life easily. But all the wrong things mattered,
and all the real things, the tremendous things, might just as well not
be there. Rain meant merely that the pavement would be wet. Sun only
relieved one from one’s umbrella. Fog delayed the butcher’s boy. Her
mother-in-law, she decided, had no sense of proportion.

Dreadful, too, to have outlived love. She supposed that that nebulous
being, Clem’s father, had loved his wife, at least in the beginning,
at least when he had asked her, in effect, to become Clem’s mother.
And she supposed Clem’s grandmother had loved her daughter, at least
when she was a child. And the spinster sister, with whom Mrs. Marley
had implacably quarreled--they must have been fond of each other years
ago when they were girls together and had secrets and borrowed each
other’s things. Everything seemed to have had its beginning in love.
And then you came on along the way and love lagged behind, and finally
you turned round to look for it and--it wasn’t there! That was the way
it was with Clem’s mother. She had come so far and left so much of love
behind. There was only Clem’s love left, and Alexandra suspected that
it was mainly scriptural. Dreadful to have outlived love. That left
only pity.

She saw less and less of Clem these days. He was absorbed in the
writing of his new book on the pottery of the Sung period, and there
were beautiful things in the library, loaned for his study and minute,
dispassionate description. She loved to pass her fingertips across the
cool glaze.... But of course the library was kept locked most of the
time. Locked when Clem was in because he must not be disturbed, except,
of course, for meals. Locked when he was out because other people’s
valuable belongings must not be disturbed.

Once when she knew Clem had gone out for the day she stealthily tried
the library door, hoping he might have gone just this once without
remembering to turn the key, hoping to steal in and touch the lovely
whites and greens and buffs without Clem’s nervous admonitions. It did
no harm just to touch....

But Clem always remembered things like keys. The door was locked and
the keyhole was empty. And Alexandra, like her impatient spirit at the
haunted doors to the past, shed swift, unreasonable tears against the
panels because for the moment it was as though the key to Life itself
was in Clem’s pocket.




                               CHAPTER IV


ONE day she paused beside a flower-girl in the Strand and lifted her
nose to the scent of violets. She had promised herself Tilbury and
a sight of the big ships today. She had declared another truce to
conscience. And then--violets. Quite suddenly she wanted some.

“Violets for consolation and tea at home like a good girl,” she told
herself firmly, “or no violets and Tilbury. Which shall it be?”

She hung on one foot deciding for Tilbury, when the flower-girl
smiled at her. It was a smile of artless flattery, tribute to the
golden-haired princess of the fairy tales. Alexandra smiled back, and
sighed as she put the violets in her belt and turned homeward.

She entered hastily with a nervous laugh.

“Well, I did it this time!”

“Did what?” inquired Mrs. Marley coldly. She had come downstairs after
her nap only to find an empty house. And Dicky was not well and would
not sing. It must have been that bit of lettuce. She would have liked
to discuss his symptoms and reject all suggested remedies. And she had
found an empty house. “Did what?” she inquired coldly.

“Got home in time for tea,”

“Tea is late, as usual. Where have you been, pray?”

“Oh, just round the square. It’s a beautiful day.”

“Where did you get those violets?”

“Aren’t they lovely?” Alexandra took them from her belt and buried her
nose in them. “See, there are two bunches, I’ll share with you.” She
held out the violets. “Smell! Aren’t they sweet?” And she pushed them
impulsively into her mother-in-law’s unsmiling face.

“I asked you where you got them,” observed Mrs. Marley when she had her
breath again.

“I bought them on my way home.” She dropped them as an offering in the
sloping black taffeta lap.

“Oh, did you!” sniffed Mrs. Marley. “Take them away, Alexandra, before
they spot my dress with their stems. Put them in a vase where they
belong. That pink one on the mantel will do. Be careful of it. It was
my mother’s.”

Meekly Alexandra took up her violets, and without even a glance at the
pink vase replaced them in her belt.

“Nothing will induce that girl to bring tea on time,” said Mrs. Marley.

“She does her best. Perhaps the kitchen clock is slow.”

“The minute your husband’s mother ventures to suggest that the service
in this house is abominably slack you begin to find excuses for the
kitchen maid!”

“But I--” Alexandra looked troubled. “She’s very young.”

“You couldn’t be more tender of her feelings if she were your own
daughter. Mine don’t matter.”

“I--I’m very fond of Susan,” faltered Alexandra unluckily.

“I see. Your implication is plain.”

“Oh, _no_, Mother!” flushing pitifully. “But you see----”

“You spoil her, Alexandra. You haven’t children, so you indulge this
little Cockney.” She paused. Alexandra had turned away, tugging at
her gloves with futile fingers. “I’m always sorry for a woman without
daughters and a man without sons,” pursued Mrs. Marley, along a
favorite theme. “Clement’s boy would have been a great comfort to me
now and to him in his old age.” She glanced sharply at Alexandra’s bent
head. “Now what’s the matter? You always act as squeamish as a girl.
If your own mother-in-law can’t say these things to you, who can?”
Silence. “Children,” resumed Mrs. Marley, “give a woman something to do
besides coddle her complexes, as they call them nowadays. In my time
we had nerves as an excuse for not doing our duty. But it’s my opinion
you’re not sorry you don’t have children. And from what I see of you,
it may be just as well----”

Susan came in with tea, and the attack shifted.

“Oh, there you are at last. Tea is late.”

“Yes, ma am.

“Why?” ruthlessly.

“It was the cake, ma’am. _Your_ cake.”

“What’s the matter with it?” Mrs. Marley leveled a lorgnon on the
tea-table.

“Nothin’, ma’am,” hastily. “I--I ain’t used to makin’ it yet, that’s
all.”

“I suppose you forgot to start it in time.”

“N--no, ma’am.” Susan sent an appealing glance toward Alexandra, who
could only basely pretend not to see.

“What then?”

“It--well, it didn’t come right the first time.”

“So you threw it out and made another.”

“Y-yes, ma’am.” It was no good lying. Nothing could be concealed, not
even with lies, from this terrible woman.

Mrs. Marley bent a severe gaze on Alexandra.

“That’s waste,” she said, and “Do something,” was in her tone.

“You may go, Susan,” said Alexandra.

“You may take two weeks’ notice.”

“Mother!”

“I’ve had enough of this incompetence. I shall engage a girl myself.”

Susan became tearful. Exile from her adored and lenient mistress would
leave little to live for.

Now, Alexandra had an almost masculine horror of scenes. Already the
situation had got out of hand. Life was resolving itself into dozens of
these small daily crises, which left her faint and sick with something
between white rage and the utter slackness of despair. Gently she
turned the weeping Susan about and gave her a push toward the door.

“That’s all, child. It will be all right.”

Susan went, her apron to her eyes.

“Come back,” spoke Mrs. Marley, “and close that door behind you.”

But Alexandra was there first, leaning against the panels, her hand on
the knob, her voice a little shaken, very low.

“All that fuss about ten minutes, Mother!”

“It’s not the first time. I’ve borne all I can from that girl. She’s
got to go.”

“I engaged Susan. She’s a good girl--faithful, and tries hard.”

“She’s incompetent.”

“She’ll learn.”

“Not here.”

Alexandra drew a long breath.

“She’s not going.”

“Alexandra--” began Mrs. Marley in an awful voice, and Alexandra’s
fingers flew to the growing ache between her eyes.

“Oh, _please_ don’t call me by that horrible name!” Always she had
hated the unwieldiness of it, which seemed to carry the weight of a
rebuke. She was Alex when she was good. Even Clem knew that.

“You’ve answered to it for near to thirty years, now. I fancy it will
serve for the next thirty.” She waited. “You understand me, Alexandra.
The girl goes. I shall speak to Clement.”

Susan too! She was to have nothing left. And Susan would cry and beg
to stay, and nothing would get her a reprieve. Nothing. It was no
good resisting. You got mowed down and the juggernaut passed over you
and left you flat and maimed, but never quite dead. Something in you
always rebelled, cropped up, dragged you painfully to your feet, and
you made one last stand and went down again, endlessly....

Alexandra found herself on the way to the door, heard herself saying
submissively:

“Very well, Mother.”

“Aren’t you going to pour the tea?”

“I--” She had learned that automatic acquiescence was cheaper in the
long run. Listlessly, she returned to the tea-table and prepared a cup
with cream and two lumps.

“And whom is that for, pray?” inquired Mrs. Marley when she had quite
finished.

“Who--why--” What had she done? She glanced up, puzzled.

“You’ve put in two lumps and cream. I take cream and one lump, and for
some absurd reason you don’t take cream at all.”

Alexandra set her teeth. It was Clem who had two lumps. And she had a
silly aversion to murking the clear amber of good Ceylon with cream.

Her fingers shook over the second cup. She dropped a spoon in the
saucer with a clatter, snatched at it, and tipped an empty cup
sickeningly.

“Did you break anything?” Mrs. Marley’s cold blue eyes were on those
shaking hands. “You’re getting as clumsy as Susan.”

“Why not dismiss me too?” Alexandra handed the cup, childishly at arm’s
length, and laughed with an odd defiance. “I’ll take two weeks’ notice!”

“That’s hardly in good taste, Alexandra. You are my son’s wife. I’m
sure I do my best to further an understanding between us. I can’t reach
the cake.”

Alexandra handed the cake.

“Aren’t you going to have tea?” demanded Mrs. Marley.

“Not today.” She turned away, picking up a book from the table, a
handsomely bound offering from Starke.

“Now, don’t sulk. You’ve had your nose in that book for days. What is
it about?”

“Central Asia. The Hill country.”

“Uncomfortable region. Extremes of heat and cold, I understand. Why do
you read about it?”

“It’s more interesting than London.”

“Nonsense. There are no English there.”

Alexandra managed to smile faintly. Mrs. Marley sipped her tea, which
was too hot, and munched her cake, still warm as she liked it, while
Alexandra experienced that unreasoning hatred of people who eat or
sleep when we ourselves for any reason under the sun cannot. Then Mrs.
Marley spoke again.

“Is any one coming to tea?”

“I don’t think so. Clem should be here soon, of course.”

“Did you see that man Starke on your walk this afternoon?”

“Starke?” She lifted surprised eyes. “Why--no, of course not!”

“I may as well tell you, Alexandra, I do not like that man.”

Now, if the truth be told, there was that about him from which
Alexandra herself instinctively withdrew. But he was a link, almost the
only link now, with that never-never-land her aching spirit craved.
That, and criticism from this source, drove her headlong to his defense.

“He’s an interesting talker--a man of wide experience--he’s traveled a
lot--I like the things he has to tell----”

“You’re often alone with him.”

“Only if Clem is late or has another engagement.”

“He doesn’t look at Clem when you’re in the room!”

The fact that Alexandra was dimly aware of this only tried her patience
the more.

“But really, Mother----!”

“You’re not a plain woman, Alexandra, and you dress as if you knew it.
This fellow Starke has the rich man’s eye for pretty women----”

This went beyond all reason. Her convulsive movement shut the book with
a snap.

“Mother, don’t you think a man like Clem knows----”

“A man like Clement is always as blind as a bat!”

“Then you think--” She was dangerously quiet now, level-eyed with
outraged dignity. “You think I am the sort of woman who----”

“I think you are the sort of woman my son ought never to have married!”

Anger flared again, and was mastered. Her voice was very low.

“I’ve tried not to be that.”

And then Mrs. Marley said an amazing thing, a thing which left
Alexandra wide-eyed and groping among its infinite possibilities.

“It’s no good trying, in these things. A woman either is or she isn’t.”

“You say--it’s no good trying----?”

“A woman is either a born home-maker or she isn’t. I was never so happy
as at some little task about the house, though my husband thought as
Clement does that a lady should fold her hands and be waited upon. My
husband was a remarkable man, but he knew too much about the wrong kind
of women. He never liked to see me in an apron. But I liked to cook and
I cooked. I was a born home-maker.”

“Yes, Mother,” said Alexandra mechanically at the pause. She had
heard all this before. Her mind was busy with something new and
disturbing--something that opened vistas. _It’s no good trying...._

“But then, _I_ had sons,” continued Mrs. Marley, complacently. “A
childless woman----”

The words beat in on Alexandra’s abstraction. Words that she had told
herself would some day drag her screaming from her chair with murderous
intent. They brought back the lurking memory of the only illness she
had ever known--the awful endlessness of it, stretching into leaden,
wasted weeks, crawling with lowered voices and firm, gentle hands,
quick professional hands of hateful efficiency.... And then the horror
of that long weakness when she tried to move, she who had been so light
and strong. The indignity, the impotence, the utter misery of having to
be waited upon. The impatience of slowly returning strength that failed
her ignominiously again and again....

She rose with a little cry.

“Mother, I----”

The doorbell rang.

“There,” said Mrs. Marley with a kind of triumph. “It _is_ that
man Starke! You knew he was coming to tea today! That’s why you came
hurrying home!”

“I _didn’t_ know!” cried Alexandra, passionately innocent. “Why
should it be Mr. Starke? Why do you always----”

“You intentionally deceived me, Alexandra, when I asked you. I shall
speak to Clement about this. It’s gone on long enough.”

Something snapped somewhere. Alexandra heard her own voice, outside
herself, as though another woman spoke, a woman she tried in vain to
hush.

“If you don’t stop ‘speaking to Clement’ something dreadful is going
to happen! Clem and I were muddling through well enough, but since you
came it’s been horrible! _Horrible!_”

“Be quiet!” commanded Mrs. Marley, just in time.

“It’s Mr. Starke, ma’am,” said Susan from the doorway.




                               CHAPTER V


HE surveyed Alexandra with pleasure from the threshold as she turned,
dark-eyed, a little flushed.

“Well, well!” he began with that weighty, well-meant geniality of his
that seemed somehow to make one’s answering smile compulsory. “Thought
I’d get in yesterday, but was detained.”

“How do you do?”

With a swift reversal of mood, she gave him her slim, boyish paw almost
gratefully. Her lips twitched. Her eyes fell to hide the sudden,
unholy glee which surprised even herself. He was too opportune, too
theatrically pat upon Mrs. Marley’s unfounded suspicions. She was all
at once perversely delighted to have appearances so against her. It
made Mrs. Marley so completely a fool. It served her so jolly well
right to have been wrong! It was delicious. Life was a joke, if you
stopped to think!

“We were just speaking of you,” said Alexandra, with hidden eyes.

“Speak of the angels, eh!” boomed Starke.

She recovered her hand hastily. It was positively almost as though he
had tweaked her chin. Things were still funny, but she was the only one
who knew they were funny. That was the worst of life’s best jokes. One
laughed and was misunderstood. It made a sense of humor a liability.

Meanwhile Mrs. Marley was frigid. Mr. Starke remained oblivious to
temperature.

He lighted a cigarette, and having done so asked permission to smoke.
Alexandra gave it, with one eye on Mrs. Marley, in whose presence not
even Clement’s briar pipe went unchallenged.

“Sure you won’t light up with me?” he queried, and as always she
shook her head, thinking of Clem. That was funny too. “You’re a real
old-fashioned woman, aren’t you!” he said admiringly. “You know,
some day some clever woman is going to make it fashionable to be
old-fashioned.” He turned genially to Mrs. Marley, who sat wrapped in
an icy silence. “She could set the style, eh?”

“But I’m not clever!” protested Alexandra. No one had ever told her
otherwise.

“Unless you know you are, you aren’t!” he grinned at her fondly.

Mrs. Marley rose with a rustle of black taffeta.

“If you will excuse me--” she announced. “There’s a little sun coming
in my window. I think it might be good for Dicky. He’s not been well.”

“Birdie a bit off his feed?” queried Starke sympathetically. “Now,
that’s too bad. Try him with a bit of red pepper on the yolk of a
hard-boiled egg. That’ll set him up. It’s your crazy climate. I know
how he feels!”

“He’s only sick of his cage,” said Alexandra. “It will pass.”

“What’s that?” Mrs. Marley paused accusingly, the cage in her hand,
Dicky swinging dizzily with protesting, piercing chirps.

“He’s dreaming of tree-tops and the sky today.”

“Nonsense. He’s used to a cage. He was born and reared in one.”

“It doesn’t matter where you’re born.” A sullen restlessness possessed
Alexandra’s white and gold. “Whatever is born in you will raise the
devil just the same.”

“Really, Alexandra----!”

Mrs. Marley majestically withdrew. Not every one can move majestically
with a bird-cage in one hand. Life had left her behind, stranded in
the backwater of a mind more Victorian than Victoria’s own, and wholly
without the intense sympathies of the great queen. Looking at the thing
impartially, it can be seen that a canary-bird was the inevitable
affinity for Mrs. Marley.

“But how on earth did you know about the red pepper?” asked Alexandra
curiously.

“My mother used to have ’em,” he replied succinctly, and stretched his
legs as he sat down. “Well--! Got you all to myself now!”

“I can’t think what’s keeping Clem.” It was at such times that she was
really rather glad of Clem, and of his leisurely habit of taking tea at
home. One always knew where one was, with Clem.

“He’ll turn up, I guess.” That settled Clem. “Things are looking up,
anyway. Dorin’s back,” he announced with satisfaction.

“Blaise Dorin--back!” She caught at the name as she snatched at
Shanghai or Kublai Khan--a name spangled with romance, foreign to
Bloomsbury. Would she see him?--could she see him?--they were such old
friends, now that she had ridden with him into the Hills.... She would
like to tell him how she had learned to remember. He would understand
that--he wouldn’t laugh--he would so splendidly understand what it
meant to her to be able to remember. Would he come to see her, she
wondered, or would there be time for her now, on his way back to the
jealous Hills?

“Got back from Africa last night. Been up to some mischief or other in
the desert. I’ve got him with me at the Cecil now. Don’t intend to let
him out of my sight for long till I see him actually on the boat. He’s
a card, that fellow! I like him, darned if I don’t, for all his crazy
notions!”

“But are they crazy? That’s the question!” said Alexandra.

“Yes, well, women always agree with men who look like Dodo Dorin,” he
remarked dryly.

“That’s hardly fair!”

“Maybe not. Anyway, we’ve both come round. I know I can’t get anybody
to do the job the way he can, and he knows he’ll have the time of his
life bringing it off. Well, there we are! I’ve got him now!”

“On his terms?” That was tactless, but she had to know.

“Largely. He’s worth it. I believe he’s the only man in the world who
can deal this game and win. And I want that robe. I’ve wanted it for
years. And I’ve as good as got it once he’s on the way.” Starke blew a
smoke-ring and destroyed it with a breath. “Provided he gets back,” he
added.

“You think there may really be trouble, then?”

“Well, there’s a lot of superstition to contend with in those parts--we
all know that. And those beggars will play horse with a bargain any
day. And the region is full of roving gangs accountable to nobody. But
I guess he’ll pull through all right,” he concluded comfortably. “There
ought to be two of him, to make sure. But Taunton’s blowing bubbles in
South Africa--can’t get hold of him for another two-three months. And
Dorin won’t hear of taking anybody else.”

“When does he start?”

“Tonight.”

“Tonight!” Disappointment engulfed her unbearably. She wouldn’t see
him, then. She couldn’t tell him about that other world she had
made--_her_ world, where she rode in the heat and the silence as
her ancestors had done, _their_ world, hers and his, where they
were old, old comrades in arms and talked together exactly as they
pleased of things other people didn’t comprehend and couldn’t approve.
Except Bob Taunton. She had wanted to tell him how kind Bob Taunton had
been. And now there wouldn’t be time. Life wasn’t kind, she cried out
sickly within herself. It stripped one so. It might have let her see
him just once--hear his plans--tell him her little news and hear him
say it was good. Life might have helped her that much, when she loved
it so! Oh, life _wasn’t_ kind! “Tonight!” she cried.

“He’s a fast worker, Dorin is! Barring something very unforeseen, the
robe is as good as in my hands right now. Which only goes to prove my
pet theory.”

“What’s that?” She was sitting very still, her great eyes gauntly
on his face. Tonight! The Dream was in shards at her feet. Could
she ever build it again from the beginning, if he went without even
knowing it had once miraculously existed? Could she ever face again
that endless labor of love, if she were actually left behind? Had she
been--hoping? For what? She could never get away. “What theory?” she
asked mechanically, because he seemed to be waiting for her to ask.

“Why, simply that if you want a thing bad enough, there’s a way to
get it.” He perceived that he had made a gratifying impression, and
elaborated. “No matter what you want in this world, if you want it long
enough and hard enough, there’s always some way to get it. You may not
like what you have to do, but there it is if you’ve got the guts. You
can go through with it or not as you please. I didn’t like crawling on
my knees to Dorin, but I did it! And I’ll be glad, about a year from
now when I’ve got Shir Shan’s robe--” He clenched a mighty fist slowly.
“--in my hand.”

There fell a tiny pause, while Alexandra followed her own thoughts down
this new and somewhat terrifying vista. It was only another version
of faith in an answer to prayer, wasn’t it. Anything you wanted--if
you had the courage! But what if you wanted the sea ... hot sand....
Himalayan cold.... What if you wanted to die with your boots on?

With an effort she recalled his last words.

“A year,” she said. “Will it take that long?”

“He’s got a stop-over somewhere in the desert on the way. More business
with that sheik pal of his, there. Take a month or two, maybe. Then on
to Port Said.”

“Port Said!” she echoed softly, still with a separate consciousness
at work within her. That sultry city of iniquities, sprawling on the
fringe of shifting mirage, not by any stretch of the most fatuous
imagination inviting, not even picturesque. And yet--a man who knows
has written that it is there that the great Smell of the East begins.
Port Said!

“Dirty hole,” said Starke. “Ever been there?”

“No.”

“Ever been anywhere?”

“No.”

“Well, personally, I like to travel.” His narrowing eyes missed nothing
of the wide abstraction of her gaze. “But I must say I like to do it in
style. Got a nice little yacht--all the comforts of home.” His glance
round the room was eloquent. “No roughing it in mine. I leave that end
of it to these crazy fools like Dorin. He goes for the sake of going. I
want to be comfortable on the way.”

“The idea,” said Alexandra, almost unaware that she spoke, “is to get
there.”

Starke leaned toward her.

“Say--I’ve been wanting to talk to you. Only been waiting for a chance.”

There was a portentous silence, which she broke at last, preoccupied.

“Well?”

“You know, I like to play a sort of game with myself. I like to look at
people and decide what they want worst--what they need worst to round
out their lives--what they’d ask for first if their fairy godmother
came along. I wonder--if you know yourself what it is that you want.”

Still he had not her usual keen attention. Her eyes came slowly to his
face. She answered automatically.

“Why should you think I want anything?”

“I don’t think. I know. Besides, everybody wants something they haven’t
got, if they’re any good at all.”

“You think there is no such thing as contentment?”

“Show me the man who has stopped seeking--craving--hankering for
something, no matter what he may have attained already, and I’ll show
you a man who’s as good as buried. With a woman it’s usually different.
But not with you.”

She was a little confused now, conscious of the steadiness and
hunger of his gaze, and she rejected several half formed replies
instinctively. How had this got started? She had no desire to talk
about herself or to be talked about. Not by this man whose eyes took
liberties, however humbly.

“And you, Mr. Starke--will you never have everything you want?”

“I hope not!” His smile was oddly whimsical for so big a man. “When I
stop wanting things I hope to God they come cover me up with leaves
quick! Oh, yes, I keep thinking ‘Now if my luck only holds good for
just this one thing more, I’ll never want anything so bad again.’ But I
always go back on it, sooner or later. I’ve just done it again.”

“You mean the robe,” she puzzled.

“Oh, yes, the robe!” He waved it aside. “I’ve wanted that for years.
And now that I’ve practically got it, I’ve come on to the next thing.
This time I want--the moon.”

She laughed briefly, not quite keeping up with him, not quite at ease,
not quite knowing why.

“I’m afraid that _is_ hopeless!”

“They said that about the robe. But I’ll have it. You’ll see. And
you’ve told yourself that what you want is hopeless--haven’t you. But
I’ve got what you want. Money.”

She shook her head with a dim feeling of relief.

“Wrong.”

“Not the glitter of the gold itself. That doesn’t satisfy me either.
But the things that Money will buy. That’s what you want. You love
beauty. You _are_ beauty, in your queer, cool way. Lord, I’d like
to see you with a few million behind you!”

“Mr. Starke----!”

“Why, you were made for palaces!” he swept on. “You could carry
a fortune in jewels better than any one I ever saw! And look at
you! Violets wilting in your belt and not a diamond to your name!
Look at this room! There’s a room in my house done in peacock and
ivory that would set you off! And a conservatory, with five kinds
of orchids! You’re wasted here--you’ll be an old woman in five
years--stifled--mummified!”

He leaned closer, clasping his big hands loosely lest they betray him,
clumsily in earnest. He meant it so. This fact stood out through her
bewilderment. He meant it so!

“There’s nothing like an unlimited clothes allowance for keeping a
woman young,” he was saying. “And for all your brains and coolness
you’re a woman. Cloth of gold is your style. I’m not joking. Woven
gold, like that robe I’m sending Dorin after. _Would you dare to wear
it?_”

He seemed to be waiting for her to say something. Her mind fumbled
desperately. What did one do when things like this happened? Presumably
one was indignant, insulted, outraged. That is, if he meant-- Well,
what did he mean? He hadn’t touched her. He hadn’t made love to her. He
wasn’t the sort of man who made love to people. What did he mean? She
wasn’t quite sure.

“I don’t think I--understand all this,” she said.

“I guess you do.”

He watched her anxiously. His eyes went to her hands. Queer how they
had always fascinated him. Quiet, slim, helpless hands, cool, he
thought, to a man’s lips. They reminded him of pearls. Pink pearls,
a little warmed by the sun. Some men, he knew, could have contrived
to kiss her hands before now. He didn’t know how to kiss a woman’s
hands like that.... Still he waited, his eyes on her hands. What ailed
the girl? It was not like her to pose. Had she been brought up in a
convent? Why did she only sit and look at him? Couldn’t she understand?

“Well, then, I’ll make it plainer,” he said at last. “You haven’t by
any means got what you want out of life, little girl, and you know it.
But you remember what I said just now, and I’ve proved it again and
again. If you want what you want bad enough, there’s always some way to
get it. Now you see, don’t you? I’ve got what you want. Money to dress
and travel and gratify a thousand whims. And I want you.”

For a moment she stared at him and through him. So that was what he
meant! Odd she didn’t feel outraged. Not even angry with him. Only
rather numb. And she was suddenly, illuminatingly aware that he meant
to be kind. He was sorry for her. He wanted to help. He was offering
the best bargain he knew.

Dizzily, she rose and turned away.

“Now, take it easy,” his voice went on, reassuringly. “Take your time
about it. And get this. I’m in dead earnest. It’s on the level, do
you hear? Marley would divorce you. And Shir Shan’s robe would be my
wedding present to the most exquisite woman I’ve ever known.”

She was standing motionless, her face hidden in her hands. He rose
uncertainly and remained where he was, half the room between them. Why
didn’t she say something? Had he bungled it? He had done the best he
could, but he was a blunt man. At least she hadn’t shown him the door.

“I expect I’ve been pretty clumsy about it,” he admitted humbly, as
she still said nothing. “There wasn’t too much time, and I can’t make
pretty speeches anyhow. But I--” His forehead was damp. The words
came jerkily, torn from his inarticulate emotion by his terrible
earnestness. “Well, you won’t--be sorry--if you come. I swear it. I’ll
give you everything on earth you want, little girl. I--I’ll treat you
square--you know that--don’t you--and I’ll bow down before you and
worship.”

At last she spoke, her voice muffled with her hands.

“Please go now.”

He hesitated, frowning like a worried mastiff.

“Does that mean Yes--or No?”

“Oh-h-h-h!” It was half moan, half sigh. “Need you ask that?”

He had refused to contemplate failure, before now. He had formed no
arguments beyond the stating of his case. She was miserable here--a
man with half an eye could see that--and he had so much to offer. And
he wanted her so. That would make up for a lot, in the end, wouldn’t
it? It was a fair bargain. She would be his wife--eventually. That made
it all right. They would cruise about the Orient for a while. Then,
when it was all settled, he would take her home to America. Already he
saw her at the other end of his table. The finest woman wearing the
finest jewels in the room. And his. _His._

He was a man who dies hard.

“Now, just a minute,” he said. “Take a look at your life here. Look
ahead. What do you see? Drab old age. Canary-birds. Black silk. We all
have the right to a splash of color.” A telling shot. He felt it hit
and came toward her, a hand out. “I’ll be good to you--can’t you see
that? What’s a man’s money for, if not to amuse a pretty woman?” His
fingers touched her sleeve, ran down it to close on her wrist. “What
are you afraid of, little girl?”

She faced him quietly. Her knees felt queer. She wondered if he could
hear her silly heart thumping. After all, what was she afraid of? He
was kind. He was good. He meant well. She didn’t have to go with him.
All she had to say was “No,” and he would go away. Nothing to be afraid
of.

“No--please,” she said.

But he stood there, clutching her hand helplessly.

“But--I’ll take you out of this!” he expostulated.

_Out of this!_ She caught her breath, and her eyes swept the
room, wincing anew at its red plush ugliness. She hated it so! It
was all she had, all she ever would have, and she hated it so! To be
taken out of it--never to have to come back to it--to be free of it,
forever--_to get away_....

His fingers were hot on her hand. He bent his head and his breath was
hot on her cheek.

“They’ve no right to keep you here,” he said, and seeing her hesitate
while her eyes went round the room he became suddenly eloquent,
driven by the fear of losing even what little he had of her, and by
the leaping hope.... “No more right than the oyster to its pearl!”
he cried. “Pearls--that’s you. Not diamonds--not rubies--nothing
hard, to hurt you. No sharp corners for my little girl. I’ll buy you
pearls--ropes of them! And white satin--velvets--ermine! I’ll make you
a queen! There’s nothing soft and warm and beautiful you shan’t have,
little girl! Paris--Nice--Monte--New York--Miami--we’ll show ’em, eh?”

She was trying dizzily to think. Paris--ermine--pearls--orchids....
But she didn’t want conservatories--that would be as bad as the red
plush! She didn’t want Paris--she wanted the Hills! She didn’t even
want the robe--all she cared about was going after it! Still--to leave
Bloomsbury forever--even for Paris--even for conservatories.... It
would see an end to this. It would be a sort of freedom. It would
be ships, and the sea, and moving about in the world. It would
be adventure, in its way. It would be to dare madly, to gamble
greatly.... Gamble? But with what chance of winning? Ropes of pearls.
Bonds. Always bonds, because she had been born a girl. And it was the
sharp corners that she wanted. It was not just getting out of this,
after all, but getting into the desert that she wanted. He didn’t
understand. He didn’t understand a bit better than Clem did. And they
both wanted her, both loved her, both were doing their best. It seemed
too bad, all that kindness, all that loving, going to waste. But there
was nothing she could do. Nothing but stay where she was. Clem had
loved her first. Poor Clem.

“Please go,” she said, very low. And then, quickly, “I--I’m sorry.”

What a cool, white thing she was! How she took her time about things
and thought her way through! No heroics. No tears. No cant. How she
kept her head up! Honest, too. She played fair. Lord, what a woman! He
snatched at her awkwardly.

“For God’s sake, don’t be a fool, little girl!”

With a gasp she flickered out of reach and rang the bell. He stood and
watched her go.

“All right,” he said quietly. “Think it over. I’m at the Cecil, you
know. A telephone call any time----”

The latch rattled under Susan’s hand. Alexandra heard it with a dull
thud of her heart. The decision had got itself made somehow. She had
elected to stay. The chance was gone forever. Thrown away. She had
been a fool--but she was glad.

“Did you ring, ma’am?”

“Yes, Susan. Mr. Starke is going. Please show him out.”

The sentence dwindled away in her throat. Clement had appeared in the
doorway behind Starke, who put the lid on it by passing him without a
word, not seeming to see him. She stared after Starke helplessly. He
looked round-shouldered, and old. Had it mattered so, to him? Did she
matter that much--to anybody?

She turned toward Clem, troubled, pathetic, feeling small and to blame,
desperately wanting to be told that she had done the only thing. She
met his eyes across the room, and something within her stumbled and
went down. She was cold and tired and had a headache. And she was not
at all sure she had done the only thing.




                               CHAPTER VI


MARLEY waited until the front door had closed and Susan’s footsteps
died away. The atmosphere became almost unbearably charged. Then he
spoke.

“What’s the matter?”

“Nothing, I--I’ll have fresh tea in a minute, Clem. You’re very late.”
She was wondering how she was to touch the cups with hands that shook
like this.

“Never mind tea. What happened between you and Starke just now?”

“I asked him to go. He won’t come here again.” She started blindly for
the door. “Please don’t let’s talk about it any more. I----”

Mrs. Marley stood on the threshold, blocking the way. Alexandra
swerved, hopelessly trapped.

“Didn’t I hear Clement come in?”

“Yes, Mother.” His eyes were on his wife.

“You’re late, my son.”

“I’m sorry, Mother.” What had happened to upset Alexandra like this?

“Where’s that man?”

“Starke? He’s just gone.” She was white. He was sure her hands were
shaking.

“Odd,” said Mrs. Marley, “that he should take himself off just as you
come in.” In the silence she struck her stick on the floor. “Well, out
with it! What’s happened?”

“Clem, I’m very tired,” pleaded Alexandra. “I--I was just going to my
room----”

“You were not so tired an hour ago,” said Mrs. Marley. “Sit down and
pour your husband some tea.”

“He--he said he didn’t want it----”

“Sit down!” Mrs. Marley pointed with her stick. “I’ve got something to
say to Clement.”

Alexandra gripped cold fingers in foolish panic. She had had about all
she could bear.

“Clem, I--I’ve got a headache----”

“Clement, will you ask Alexandra not to leave the room until I have
finished?”

“Oh, good heavens, can’t you see my position?” he cried. “Can’t you see
that this atmosphere of constant strife and dissension is bad for my
work? I’m getting nervous--I don’t sleep well--I--I--my food doesn’t
tempt me! I’m all upset!”

“It’s time you paid a little less attention to your work and your food
and a little more to what is going on under your very nose,” said his
mother. “What _I_ want to know is--how much longer is it to go on?”

“Very well, we’ll come to an understanding here and now, and then I
shall expect to be undisturbed. Alex--” He indicated a chair, and she
took it listlessly. “Now, Mother?”

Mrs. Marley seated herself expansively on the sofa and the tribunal was
on. Weeks of suspicions, fancied slights, misunderstandings, years of
prejudice and brooding, lurked behind her cold eyes. She had promised
herself a reckoning. She had nursed the idea of a reckoning, pictured
it, planned it, a sort of Judgment Day _à trois_, which would
leave this yellow-haired young woman in a properly penitential frame of
mind. There could be no extenuating circumstances this time. This time
she had overstepped. The Taunton business had been a little different.
There was a matter-of-factness about it all. One couldn’t lay hold of
the man. And she had heard them talk. Madness. But impersonal madness.
But this fellow named Starke--he brought her things--he looked at her.
Their voices were low. Too low to be heard from the stairs. Clement
should be undeceived at once, should know once and for all that the
woman he had married and whom he had dared to defend against his own
mother was not fit to be a Marley. One could have seen all along by the
color of her hair that she was not. Reckoning. It was high time.

“Did you know that man Starke was coming here this afternoon?” she
inquired of Clement, in the complacent tones of one who is perfectly
sure the answer will increase the unpleasantness of the situation.

“No. What’s that got to do with it?”

“_She_ knew.”

“I didn’t!” Alexandra bit her lip over the foolish denial.

“She knew he was coming and she didn’t tell you and she didn’t tell
me. It looks very odd, to my way of thinking.”

“But I didn’t know he was coming!” protested Alexandra with the guilty
vehemence of innocence. “You certainly don’t think I’d be planning
anything clandestine at my own tea-table!” This shocked them both.
Unexpectedly her inconsequent sense of the ridiculous tittered again
within her. “In the first place, there’s no screen for Mr. Starke to
hide behind when Clem came in, the way they do in the French farces!”
She laughed incomprehensibly, in their stony faces. Things were
getting out of proportion. It made her dizzy. And her head ached.
“Oh, it’s simply too absurd! Why shouldn’t I have told you? I didn’t
know--I--didn’t know--” She faltered, sobered, over what she hadn’t
known. She saw again in her mind’s eye that unfamiliar stoop to
Starke’s thick shoulders. It wasn’t funny. But it made her dizzy.

“No women ever come to tea.” Mrs. Marley brought forward her next
point. “Where are all your women friends?”

“I haven’t many.” Then, defiantly, “We don’t seem to speak the same
language.”

“What’s that?” said Marley. This was going to be one of her difficult
flights which so confused and annoyed him.

“We’ve nothing to talk about--nothing to be friends _with_. Women
whose ideas are bounded by puddings and prams make the best wives
according to your mother’s standards. I’m outside the pale!” she told
them, jeering, quite mad.

“Whose fault is that?” said Mrs. Marley from the sofa, and Alexandra’s
eyes darted angrily in that direction only to slide off ignominiously
from the ice in the gaze which was fixed upon her.

“Can’t you take this situation a little more seriously, Alex?” Clem was
