inquiring patiently. He did wish she could talk sense in an argument.
“Can’t you try to be a little more considerate----”

“Seriously!” She was looking at him now with an odd intentness.

“Yes, seriously!” he repeated crossly. “It is getting serious. I----”

“Oh, you see that at last, do you!” said his mother.

He turned to her courteously, a man almost ludicrously between the
devil and the deep blue sea.

“I beg your pardon, Mother?”

“So you are beginning to realize at last that your house is not in
order. How do you know where she goes or whom she sees or what she does
all day long? Yes, and nights too! She disappears for hours--she’s
late to meals--she comes in looking as though she had been up to
something--! It seems very odd to me!”

So that was it! The old, old question. Well, he had warned her. He
turned on his wife severely.

“Now, Alex, I’ve mentioned this to you before. This is the last time.
These mad excursions of yours at all hours must stop. Do you hear?
They must stop!”

“Stop--my walks?”

“It won’t do. I’ve told you that before. Hereafter, you will be more
careful of appearances. Less free!”

“Appearances!” snorted Mrs. Marley. “Are appearances all you think of,
then?”

“What--what--?” His eyes went to the door through which Starke had
passed without a word. She had asked him not to come again. _Why?_

“You went out last night about nine o’clock, Alexandra,” Mrs. Marley
observed, settling to it.

“Yes.”

“Where did you go?”

“Why--nowhere.”

“You were gone more than three hours. What did you do all that time?”

“I-- Does it matter?”

“I begin to think it does.”

Marley clutched at reason.

“Mother, I--I think we’ve had quite enough of this. If--if you’ll just
leave this to me----”

“That will do, Clement!” she rounded on him. “I’m handling this! Well,
Alexandra?”

“I sat for a long time in the square.”

“Alone?”

“Yes, I-- That is, there was a policeman.”

“A policeman?” Clement was thoroughly horrified.

“He asked me if I was all right. I said--said yes, that I lived just
over the way and couldn’t sleep,” she stumbled on, knowing the futility
of trying to make them understand what even the policeman, looking into
her white face, had understood--her desperate need to be let alone.
“He--he just walked up and down on the other side--till I came in. I--I
was looking at the stars. They were so near--if you look at the stars
long enough they come down to you. You can get in among them, even here
in London----”

“Never mind the stars. You didn’t come in until after midnight. Not
until after Clement came home from the club. You weren’t with him--were
you?”

“No, but--I--I saw him come in----”

“Oh, you saw him come in! Where were you then?”

“There in the square--I--” She was becoming confused, hunted, with a
horror that was like guilt.

“How long had you been in the square?” the relentless voice pursued her.

“Why--all the time--I don’t know--it must have been quite a while-- Why
do you question me like this! I’m not a child!”

“No, and neither are we children, Alexandra! Yet you want us to believe
that you saw no one and expected to see no one between nine and
midnight?”

“Yes--no--I--why, of course--!” She was bewildered, at the
breaking-point. “I don’t understand what you mean--I----”

Once more Marley interfered, torn between a good man’s loyalty to his
mother, right or wrong, his own knowledge of his wife, and a hideous,
creeping doubt of her.

“Mother, this is--! Oh, this is unheard-of--preposterous----!”

“I tell you, Clement, it’s time you put an end to her unaccountable
absences from this house! Take this man Starke who was here today. If
you used one-tenth the intuition God gave you you wouldn’t trust him
alone with her for one minute----”

“_Clem!_”

“A word to the wise, Alexandra!” Mrs. Marley turned on her at the cry.
“I’ll say no more--this time.”

For a second their eyes held. Then Alexandra began to laugh, her own
brave sanity and guiltlessness in pitiful revolt against her own cold
horror. This thing could not be! It was nightmare--these things being
said to her in her own home while Clem stood by in a silence that could
mean only doubt! Nightmare, but while it lasted she was afraid. And so
she laughed, stiff-lipped, at terror.

“Oh, how perfectly ridiculous!” she laughed. “Oh, how perfectly
incredible it all is! And this is what you want me to take more
seriously, Clem! Don’t you see the joke?” She dropped her head in her
hands, rocking, laughing. “You want me to take the creeping paralysis
of this house more seriously! You want me to grieve over the ghastly
process of being buried alive in this house! You object to my levity at
my own funeral--levity being unseemly in a corpse! I must preserve the
dignity of the inquisition--I must wear my martyr’s crown with a long
face--my ghost must not walk at night--” The laughter rattled on.

“Alex!” Clement shook her with a hand on her shoulder. “Alexandra!
I’ve never seen you like this! For God’s sake, Alex, be quiet!
_Alex_--!”

“Oh, go away!” she cried wildly. “Go away, both of you, or I shall
_scream_!” And then the laughter crossed the borderline into tears.

Clement fell back aghast, at sea. This madness meant one of two
things. But it is so hard to distinguish between flagrant guilt and an
innocence that is well-nigh divine!

Mrs. Marley’s sharp voice clove the air.

“Now, stop that, Alexandra! A foolish woman’s last resource is always
hysteria. Stop it!”

They waited, while Alexandra became chokingly quieter. With all his
honest soul, Clement Marley wanted to believe in her. He told himself
futilely that he did believe in her. And yet he did not go and take
her in his arms. He left her huddled there beneath his mother’s eyes,
alone. And then it was too late.

Mrs. Marley, having done her duty and relieved her mind, rose at last
and smoothed her taffeta skirt. She was agreeably aware of a crisis.
She had, to put it crudely, started something. The rest was up to
Clement. Now he knew. She had done enough for the time being. One might
have known that Alexandra would cry. Women with that color hair always
cried. They thought it was becoming. Clement’s taste in women was like
his father’s. Why had her life had to be so littered with blondes!

“A word to the wise, Alexandra,” she repeated crisply. “If you mend
your ways at once, I fancy nothing more need be said of this. Don’t
think I don’t perceive how things are between you and my son--” This
was for Clement too. “But Marley is too old a name to court a needless
scandal in the divorce courts.” She moved toward the door. “But for
Clement’s sake--mend your ways.”

The sound of her stick died away on the stairs at last.

Alexandra turned shaking to Marley in the bleak silence that was left.

“You--heard that? _You heard what she said to me?_ She is able to
suggest--to _believe_ that of me--and yet--_if_ I mend my
ways--!” With a gasp of shame she buried her face in her hands.

Things had been going a little fast for him. He did feel, of course,
that he knew Alexandra too well for this. But after ten years what
had they? Nothing. Less than nothing. A closed door. He felt dimly,
too, that she had been deeply hurt--wronged, even. But, after all,
what could he have said or done more than he had done? An old woman’s
notions--one must make allowances--the past generation--after all, a
man’s mother--! Besides--three hours--the square at midnight.... Poor
Clem.

“Oh, my God, why don’t you say something!” Her head was back, her eyes
blazing up at him darkly.

“Even then, Clem, you might have-- But no.”

“Now, Alex, I hardly know what to think of all this, it’s--it’s most
unfortunate. I suppose we must try to forget it. But you had fair
warning, didn’t you? Didn’t I tell you before she came that she would
never understand your odd comings and goings? And besides, that--that
business in the square last night was a bit thick, you know. I mean
to say--a policeman--! Suppose some one had seen you! I think I’m a
fairly reasonable man, but there is a limit. As Mother said--for my
sake, you really must-- Understand, I do not--er--doubt you myself.
But hereafter, oblige me by taking such walks as are necessary to your
health at a respectable hour, and don’t turn up missing at half a dozen
meals in the week. You--you can see my position, can’t you?”

He patted her shoulder perfunctorily, as she sat looking up at him with
a face gone blank, expressionless, while life swirled about her. What
was happening to her? Where was she being driven? What had they done,
between them?

“You know I hate scenes,” said Marley, with the air of a man heroically
coping with a grievance. “I shall dine at the club; I’ve had about all
I care for in one evening. A man does like a little harmony in his
home, if nothing else.” He crossed the room and turned, a hand on the
door-knob. “Remember, now--no star-gazing tonight!”

The door closed smartly behind him. A good man, blind as a bat, bound
for his club.

For a long time she sat staring at the door. Then hideously into the
silence the clock began to strike five. With a gesture that was like a
scream, her hands came to her ears.

She paced up and down the room, her hands pressed over her ears, long
after the clock had finished. At last she paused, staring at it,
unseeing, her brain beginning to work again, numbly.

_A woman either is, or she isn’t_, groped her brain. _It’s no
good trying._ But she had tried. For ten years she had tried, and it
was no good, just as Clem’s mother had said. Clem, after ten years of
her trying, did not know quite what to think. Were they wasted, then,
those ten years? Ten whole years out of a lifetime--gone for nothing?

_Canary birds. Black silk. We all have the right to a splash of
color._ The blue depths of the desert sky. The white radiance of a
desert moon. Or the yellow fire of topazes. Or even the red ugliness
of blood.... Color, as her ancestors had understood it. Life up to the
hilt, as her grandfather had lived it for a few crowded years in the
Sudan. Death as her father had died, with room to die in....

_If you want a thing long enough and hard enough--there’s always a
way to get it._ You might not like what you had to do, but the way
was there, if you wanted to go through with it. The way was there. But
was it? The way to what she wanted--the way to the Hills--the way....

_You should have been--one of Us._ And Blaise Dorin was at the
Cecil with Starke, who did not intend to let him out of his sight....

Her heart was beating thunderously in her ears. If she could go
along--if only he would take her with him--he _must_ take her
with him--that was the way--they didn’t really want her here--she
couldn’t fit in, no matter how hard she tried--she only made them angry
and miserable--she shouldn’t have married Clem at all--she had never
been much of a success as Clem’s wife--she hadn’t quite understood
things, when she married Clem--it would be better now, for everybody,
if she went--no good bothering Clem any more, making mistakes, having
scenes--she would go--the Dream--she would have it--it was her right to
have it--she had wanted it so long-- Blaise Dorin would understand....

Fumblingly, with cold, moist fingers, she got the telephone directory
and looked out the Hotel Cecil number. Stammering, clearing her throat,
not able to hear anything but her own heart, she spoke it into the
instrument. And at last, after interminable waiting, came Blaise
Dorin’s voice, indistinctly, beyond the thunder of her heart....




                              CHAPTER VII


HE was coming.

He would be there any minute now. Rushed as he was, he could drop
everything long enough to answer an inarticulate summons from a woman
he had seen hardly a dozen times altogether. He understood only that
something was wrong, and that she had turned to him. A soldier of
fortune, son of a soldier of England, he wasted no time in questions
once the course of action was clear. He said he would be there.

She went to the window. He was not yet in sight. Suppose he shouldn’t
come, after all. Suppose Starke reached the hotel and prevented him.
Suppose he went away tonight to the desert--to her grandfather’s
desert--without her! No, he had said he would come. Not even Starke
could stop him now.

Alexandra pressed against the window-pane, staring feverishly down the
street and into the future.

She had a little money of her own. How far would it take her--if he
shouldn’t come? Could she manage alone--if he shouldn’t come? Would she
know the way, she who had hardly journeyed across the county alone?
Would the same torturing instinct that had hounded her all her life
turn, now that she had yielded, to guide, philosopher, and friend?

She confronted the tremendous fact of her surrender, breathless but
unafraid. She was going to stop trying. She was going to give in. Her
nomad heritage was to have its way at last. Tomorrow would find her
homeless--and free. It was over. All over.

Odd, how suddenly one turned the corner. This morning life had
stretched drearily from her feet to the horizon, complete in each drab
detail: a flat, gray expanse of leaden duty and small, stolen, secret
joys. Then violets; the dismissal of a servant-girl; an old woman’s
grievance; an unexpected guest at tea-time; cataclysm.

And now she could not see the length of her own shadow on the path
ahead, but life was precious as it had never been before. She had
crossed over. There remained only to fire her bridges. They would give
a lovely light!

“I am leaving Clem,” she thought, amazed at her own calmness, mentally
pinching herself. “Perhaps I’ll die without ever seeing Clem again. And
he loves me--at least--I thought he loved me.... I am going away--right
away from England. Tomorrow morning everything will be different. I am
leaving my husband. I am running away.”

Still no remorse, even less elation. Just the serenity of an immense
decision.

“The sea,” she thought, trying to make herself realize what had really
happened. “The dance of it in the sun--the heave and dip and roll of
it--the clean sea-smell that comes far out from land--horizon--on
all sides, sky and water meeting--_the sea_--I shall know soon!
Gibraltar,” she went on wonderingly, “and the Mediterranean--the tip of
Spain behind me--Africa----”

Her heart skipped at that.

_Africa._

She whispered it against the pane. She shut her eyes and saw--a map.
Africa was mostly pink and purple, patched with scraps of yellow and
green for the Congo and German East. She shut her eyes tighter. Across
the dots that mean desert a golden glare came glowing. She felt the
light--actually _felt_ the brutal desert sun on her eyelids! She
heard--what was it? Voices--singing--a kind of chant--and the dry,
husky whisper of camels’ feet in sand--and everywhere the cruel light,
beating down till one felt faint and bruised beneath it....

It faded. She let go her breath with a sob. _She had remembered
Africa!_

“Please, ma’am----”

Susan stood uncertainly in the doorway, her apron crumpled, her face
blotchy and swollen from crying. Alexandra looked at her as from a
great distance.

“Yes, Susan----?”

Tears rose again in Susan’s reddened eyes, and her mouth squared
ludicrously as she stood twisting her thin little fingers in her apron.

“I--I could do with less wages, ma’am--so long as I can’t please
_’er_--if only I didn’t ’ave to--go! I’d work fer you fer nothin’,
ma’am, only--my mother needs what I send ’ome. I don’t want nothin’
fer myself, ma’am--if only I can stay with you----”

Vaguely it reached Alexandra’s consciousness that this piteous child
was crying over the thought of leaving her--that other lives must go on
as before, after tomorrow. It seemed too bad....

“I--I don’t see what I can do--now--” she said doubtfully, half to
herself.

Susan came to her, sniffling, her ravaged face lifted hopefully.

“I was thinkin’--you might let _’er_ get somebody else--an’ let me
stay an’ work for _you_. I could stay for ’alf, an’ wouldn’t make
no trouble, an’----”

“I’ll--think about it,” Alexandra promised gently. “I’ll see--what can
be done. Now serve dinner as usual tonight. Mr. Marley is dining out.
And I’m going for a little walk and may--may be late.”

“Don’t you--don’t you feel good, ma’am?” Susan’s eyes were searching
Alexandra’s face. She came nearer, her eyes on that white, rigid face,
and her voice shrilled sharp with a nameless apprehension. “Don’t
you--feel good?”

No answer. Alexandra was looking at the window, but it was not the
window that she saw. Susan clenched her bird-like claws in her crumpled
apron. She had seen that look before, in the eyes of men who followed
the sea--a look as of listening for something beyond the rim of the
world.

“Take me with you, ma’am!” she cried sharply.

“_What--?_” Alexandra whirled.

“D’ya think _I_ don’t know they’re killin’ you between the two
of ’em?” Susan was crying openly now, shamelessly. “Every time you go
out--lookin’ white like this--I get afraid, thinkin’ o’ the things
you might do, rather than come back! _’Er_ givin’ me the sack
today--she ’adn’t no right! Think _I_ don’t know you won’t be
takin’ things like that lyin’ down forever? Goin’ fer a walk, you say!
An’ can’t I tell by the looks of you that _this_ time you ain’t
comin’ back--” Alexandra’s hand covered the rest of it.

“You mustn’t say such things!” she commanded, in a guilty whisper.

“T-take me with you, ma’am----?”

“No, I-- No--” Alexandra swung away toward the window, and felt panic
grip her. Blaise Dorin was getting out of a cab in front of the house.
How should she begin?

He would understand, of course. But suppose he refused to help her. It
was Bob Taunton he wanted. Nobody else. Suppose he should regard her
only as a possible burden. Her task was to convince him that lacking
Bob Taunton he would find her better than nothing. No other aspect
occurred to her now. To get him to see that she would not be in the
way--a tremendous undertaking, but she would not, could not, be beaten
now. And Blaise Dorin would understand.

The doorbell rang.

“Never mind that,” she said quickly to Susan. “I’ll go.” Stooping
suddenly, she set her lips on Susan’s wet cheek--Susan felt them cold
through her tears--and pushed her toward the other door, and waited
till it had closed behind her.

Then she went herself to answer Dorin’s ring.

He followed her into the room, his hat still in his hand, silent before
her whiteness, aware of her pushed-back hair and trembling hands;
aware, too, of the crushed, fragrant violets in her belt; but still not
dreaming that the scent of violets was to go with them both all the
rest of the way.

He had not been able to make much of what she was saying over the
telephone. It had sounded as though she was crying, or had a sore
throat--both irreconcilable with his ideas of her. Two facts at last
emerged from the chaos--she had to see him before he went--and she
couldn’t come to the hotel on account of Starke. Naturally if she
wanted to see him he would find time to go to her. Odd, her calling
him just then. He had been thinking of her--regretting that he
couldn’t see her again, and ask her to wish him luck. And then she had
sent for him. Very odd. Where did Starke come into it? Why had she
sounded--frightened? Why, in any case, had she turned to _him_?
Where did _he_ come into it? Had Starke been up to something....
He made nothing of it in the cab. And now--_had_ she been crying?
It didn’t seem to fit in. He wasn’t quite sure how she ought to look,
but surely she looked different--? He was prepared for almost anything
but what was about to happen to him.

She faced him without embarrassment, purposeful, but shaking with
tension. As always, his flesh and blood presence was lost in the
immensity of the thing he symbolized. He had never seemed less a man,
more a means to an end.

“You’re leaving tonight,” she said.

“Yes.” There was a puzzled question in the word.

She plunged.

“I’m going with you.”

He was staring dumbly, incredulously, obviously doubting his ears. She
repeated it, distinctly----

“I’m going with you.”

“But--Mrs. Marley--!” He half gasped, half laughed. It was his own
stupidity, of course, but for the life of him he couldn’t see--! “I--I
don’t quite----”

“Yes,” she conceded gravely. “I suppose it does seem a bit sudden to
you.”

“But--you can’t be serious!” This was far worse than he had feared.
That is--_going with him_!

“Oh, yes,” she assured him with a small smile. “I’m serious--now.”

“Won’t you--” He passed an agitated hand across his hair. “Well, could
you explain a bit? I--” He paused appealingly.

“It’s quite simple,” she said patiently. “I’m not going to be a Marley
any more. I’m not going to try to be. It’s no good trying,” she added,
to clinch it.

“But,” said Dorin helplessly, “I--you--that is--we----”

“You said we could take anything on and win. You said I should have
been a man. You said----”

“But unfortunately the good God in His wisdom made you a woman. He may
know why. I don’t. But----”

“There’s not much time to talk,” she interrupted. “I can pack a bag and
be at the station in an hour. Will that do?”

Dorin called inwardly upon his gods. He was as near to being floored as
he had ever been in an adventurous life.

“But, Mrs. Marley, I can’t let you do this thing on an impulse. Think
what it means! Think what you’re doing! That is--I mean--think--” He
floundered.

“I am leaving my husband.” She put it into words for him,
unemotionally. “I know. It will hurt Clem. It would have hurt him more
a year ago. Since _she_ came--things are different.”

“I--I don’t think I--” he groped.

“His mother,” explained Alexandra.

“Oh.” His eyes widened. “Oh,” he said, thinking it over.

“This afternoon,” she went on, perceiving that she must make things a
trifle clearer for him, “something happened. I can’t go on here after
that. I won’t! And, anyway, it isn’t any good. Clem is a good man, and
good men always take their mother’s part. I don’t blame him,” she added
conscientiously, and indeed her soul was swept clean of rancor by the
ghost of a wind from the sea. “One can’t blame him. But I’m going with
you. I’ve got to love life,” she pleaded, “before I die!”

Well, yes, Blaise Dorin understood. He was an observant man, for one
thing, and, too, he had learned to think quickly for very life’s sake.
He had by now assimilated her reasons, her intentions, above all, her
heartbreaking need. But all this he set aside as his mind leaped ahead
to the inevitable results of the course she had chosen.

“But have you thought carefully about what it would mean for you?” he
probed uncomfortably. “Disgrace, you know--divorce--scandal--all that
sort of thing. You see, the world is pretty hard on a woman who----”

“Oh, don’t talk like that!” she cried. “Besides, if you take me on to
Asia--I might never have to face that.”

“Now, look here, if you’re thinking only of the chance of getting
yourself killed, it’s a slim one! You _would_ have to face it. And
the injustice of it _would_ very nearly kill you! If--if you--” He
stammered a little here. She was so clear and fine. Such things would
not have occurred to her, of course. “If we were in love with each
other--that sort of thing--it might be different, but----”

“But we’re not!” she cried, honestly horrified.

“No, that’s what I say! And so----”

“And so there’s nothing wrong about it!” she cut in triumphantly. “Why
shouldn’t I go with you?”

He grasped his patience firmly as he grasped her slim, straight
shoulders, and the violets sighed against his coat. Was she a child,
an utter, impossible urchin of six? One oughtn’t to have to explain
these things to a married woman. He wanted to shake her for being such
an exasperating and inconvenient anomaly. Couldn’t she see _his_
side of it? A fellow can’t do these things.... His irrepressible levity
quirked through his mind here, as it was bound to do in a crisis. He
had too much perspective not to see the funny side of every crisis.
Well, then, was he to be run away with, scandalously, by a tow-headed
schoolboy in a wedding-ring? It was like dreams. It wasn’t real. It
couldn’t be happening.

“But, my dear, sweet, unsophisticated soul, no one would ever in this
world believe anything but what is customary, and----”

“Customary?” She blinked at him a moment, then a shade of real
embarrassment crossed her upturned face. Not a blush. Nothing so
encouraging as that. “Oh, but they couldn’t be so silly! It’s not an
elopement! God knows there’s nothing romantic--that way--about--what
we’d be going into! It’s not a--it’s no kind of honeymoon trip! If
you l-loved me--that way--you wouldn’t let me go,” she argued wisely.
“Women men love _that_ way stay safe at home. I’m just--just like
_you_! Surely people would see exactly how it is!”

“But I’m telling you they won’t! I----”

“But they’d have to! Look at us! Beastly uncomfortable climate--both
of us wearing khaki--hard going--short rations--our lives in danger,
perhaps---- Wasn’t it Loti who said that hunger and thirst come first,
and----”

“No, it wasn’t.” He had to smile at that, though a bit grimly. “And
you’d be surprised how silly the world can be. Anyway, you’re not
coming with me. I wish you could. It would be jolly. But you simply
must not think of it.”

“But----”

“No,” he said. “My blessed innocent, you’ve no idea of the hardship and
the danger, especially to a woman!”

“But I _want_----”

“Look here. I said your chance of getting killed was a slim one. It
probably is, for all I know now. But think a minute. Suppose I was mad
enough to take you on this Asian job. We must cross miles of wilderness
with the smallest possible equipment--we can take no armed escort--we
must camp when and where and how we can--we must be alone, the pair of
us, without seeing another English face for weeks--Government washes
its hands of us because it has formally forbidden me to go--and we may
meet up with very undesirable native company. If anything should happen
to me-- Can’t you see how impossible it is?”

“But if anything should happen to you, that’s just where I’d come in!
I’m as strong as any boy! I’ll do anything you say to get fit! I can
learn to shoot and all the rest of it--I’ll _remember_ all that
too, as soon as I have the chance! I won’t be a hindrance--I’m not a
whimpering girl!” She caught at his sleeve. “Oh, let me come! Please
let me come!”

“I can’t,” he said gently.

“Make this little bargain with me, then! Take me as far as
Algiers--into the desert. Try me--see how I get on there--don’t spare
me--put me through it--anything, everything you can think of! And then
if you honestly feel I’d be a handicap on the big job, I won’t snivel
or argue--I’ll go away!”

“But don’t you see, the result would be the same, even if you only went
as far as Calais! That is--you couldn’t come back here----”

“You’re afraid of having me on your hands when this is over, is that
it? You’re not to worry about that!” She hurried on, twisting her
fingers in an agony of effort, trying piteously to read his face.
“If--when we come through--that will be all I’ll ask of you, ever.
When we get down to India I won’t trouble you any more. I can take
care of myself. I’ll have had my fun. I can stay there in Lahore or
Delhi--somewhere where there is light and color and work. I can teach,
or learn nursing. I’ve got a little money of my own. You can forget all
about me! But let me come with you, just this once! Starke said two
men would be better than one. I’d be better than nothing. Take me! You
can’t wait for Bob Taunton. Take me--in his place!”

He steeled himself against her white entreaty, and the insurgent
knowledge that it would be somehow wrong to refuse her. Not only
cruel, but wrong. And yet--it would be wrong to take her. Oh, not the
traditional wrong of the broken marriage vow. That sort of thing didn’t
trouble him now. But the wrong the world would do her. That was what
he balked at. The things it would convict her of, unheard. The things
it always looked for and that never occurred to her. That would be
wicked--to let her in for that.

“No,” he said again. “I’m sorry--but it just wouldn’t do.”

She drew back, looking at him oddly.

“Is that final?”

“It’s got to be.”

“Very well.” She turned away.

“Hold on a minute. I don’t like the way you say that. You’ve got
something up your sleeve.”

He waited, watching her. Her mouth was mutinous. She was capable of
anything. He was afraid for her. Afraid to leave her like this.

“Good-by,” she said, her back to him.

“Oh, poor little kid, I-- Look here, promise you won’t do anything
foolish while this fit is on. I know how you feel, indeed I do.
But--it’s no go.”

She would not answer. Manifestly, he could not leave her like this. He
went to her and turned her about by the shoulders. She drooped in his
hands like a sulky lad. He was reminded vividly of the Eton jacket.

“Promise you’ll be a good boy while I’m gone,” he begged whimsically.

She shook her head, looking down.

“Word of honor that you’ll stick it out--say, till I come back,” he
said, and held out his hand.

She put both hers behind her and faced him, then.

“What would you do,” she asked evenly, “if some pagan ritual required
that Bob Taunton be shut up in a box and driven slowly mad by beaten
drums? Would you stop to consider the ethics of the case? Or would you
simply get him out of it the quickest way you could?”

“As bad as that?”

“Oh, I was doing the best I could!” Her fists came to her temples as if
the torture drums were beating there in Bloomsbury. “But sometimes I’ve
run away for hours, down to the docks--Wapping, Limehouse, even Poplar!
At first I skulked, knowing I had no right there. But now--well, either
they think I’m just a harmless mad thing or else they understand--a
little. Anyway, they let me alone down there. I’m free to pry and sniff
and poke about as I please. But that wasn’t enough. The time came when
I had to go farther--down to Greenwich and Tilbury where the big ships
come in--I don’t know quite why, I--I had to go till I felt free of
this! Each time I have to go farther, and it’s harder to come back.
And the water--the smell and the depth and the sound of it beside the
piers--it has a fascination----”

“Good God!” he murmured.

“It has, it has! At first they treated me like a naughty child when
I came home. I was always in disgrace. I didn’t mind that--much. But
this afternoon they said--things. She said them and--Clem-- Well, Clem
wasn’t quite sure. You can see, can’t you, that now Clem will never
know quite what to think-- And so--whether it’s with you or not--one
way or another, I’ve got to go away and not come back. I can go alone,
I suppose--one way or another--” Her voice died away.

“Easy, now.” This was different. He took her hands down from her face
and held them against his coat, the violets bruised beneath their
fingers. Hers were icy cold, and damp. She had had all she was good
for, he thought. “Easy, now. If you’ve thought this out--if you really
mean it--I’ll stand by, you know that.”

Her fingers clutched his gratefully.

“You’ll let me come?”

“Yes. At least as far as the desert. If you must.”

“The desert!” She looked up at him, laughing with suddenly quivering
lips, with happy, flooded eyes. “My grandfather,” she boasted
tremulously, “loved the desert better than anything!” Like a child she
caught up their clasped hands so that her wet cheek rested for a moment
against his fingers. “Oh, I knew you’d see how it is! You’ve been so
good, I--I can’t ever say thank you enough!” This passed swiftly, in a
glance at the clock. “I can pack a bag and be at Charing Cross station
in an hour,” she said, laying plans. “I’ll wait for you there.”

“Right,” he agreed briefly, and dropped her hands and strode out of the
house.

Not until he was outside on the pavement did the thing strike him
with full force in all its awfulness. _He had contracted to run off
with another man’s wife!_ In a moment of complete aberration he had
saddled himself, for the most ticklish job of his life, with a woman.
You forgot she was a woman, somehow. But no, she should not go on to
Asia. Africa was hers. He had let himself in for that. But it would end
with Africa. She should not hypnotize him again. He was all kinds of
a fool and he would look it, when this thing got round. Oh, this was
horrible!... Poor little beggar.

The violets fell from her belt on the stairs as she ran to pack the
bag. Clement stepped on them the next morning, as he went up to see
why she did not come to breakfast. Susan cried over them, hours later,
crouched against the banisters in a stricken house. And the time was
to come when Blaise Dorin would remember them and hold to them when
everything else was slipping away.




                                 _Wind_


    “_For I know of a sun an’ a wind_,
    _An’ some plains an’ a mountain be’ind...._”




                               CHAPTER I


THE Mediterranean’s fairy blue and gold and pearl flung open the doors
of Alexandra’s spirit to the four winds of heaven.

“It’s the sun!” she would try to explain, with a catch in her breath.
And then, throwing out her hands to it, “It’s the water!” And then,
laughing, with tear-pointed lashes, “Oh, I know you think I’m an idiot,
but--it’s the wind!”

Viewed from the harbor, terraced Algiers delighted her, but after
landing it left her restless and still unsatisfied. This was not quite
what she had come for. There was more.

Neither the exotic French section with its boulevards and cafés, nor
the rabbit warrens of the Arab town crawling with beggars and tiny,
laden donkeys was enough. She loitered in the heat and seethe and
changing color of the market-place. She expressed a docile appreciation
of the fortress, which Dorin went to the trouble of showing her. But he
noted with an inward grin that she was continually sniffing upwind, as
it were, and they pushed on next day, southward toward the sands.

She tried not to chafe at the inevitable delay in the tattered town
huddling at the edge of the desert, a place which had won no star from
Baedecker. Dorin had no time now to listen to inarticulate rhapsodies,
nor to take her sightseeing. Her presence amounted chiefly to further
difficulties, and while he coped with them he left her to amuse or bore
herself as might be, in the best room the inn afforded. He gave her
audience at meals, however, and she gratefully gathered the crumbs of
his esoteric doings and begged, terrier-eyed, for more.

She made only tentative excursions by herself, fearing to miss a
summons from him, staying like a good child where he had stowed and
forgotten her. She felt humbly enough that she was a bother at best,
and that the least she could do was to be at hand if by some miracle he
should happen to want her. She ached to help, but her Arabic was still
very weak, and he seemed only to desire her out of sight.

Meanwhile time dragged, and the desert lured.

Never had she seen such sunlight. She spread her hands to it, lifted
her face till it blindingly kissed her closed eyelids, soaked in the
tremendous vitality of it, perversely preferred it to the glorious full
moon of their arrival. She was up at dawn, watching for the wonder of a
new day. She lingered wistfully at the window while the quick African
night closed in on the heels of sunset. She hinted pathetically to be
taken for just one look at the desert between sun and moon. But Dorin,
his mind on horses and camels and an extra boy who would not steal more
than was expected of him, remained impervious to hints.

On the afternoon of the fourth day she slipped guiltily away from
the inn and was gone until after sunset. Harassed by details of
transportation, Dorin was slow to miss her. At first confident of her
ability to look out for herself, he became uneasy, then annoyed, and
finally as the swift desert dark drew in, frightened.

He strode out of the inn with his stick at a militant angle in search
of her and of the vanished servant he had dispatched to find her. And
just as he reached the street she turned the corner and came toward
him, flushed, dusty, radiant. He understood suddenly the primitive
parental impulse to smack a runaway child miraculously restored intact.
He had yet to learn, like Clement, that nothing ever happened to her.

“Where have you been?” he barked.

“Out there.” She waved a vague hand back toward the desert. “The sun
went down,” she explained further, with a beatific smile.

“Yes, I know it did.” His swift glance took in her dusty white frock
and returned to her hot, ecstatic face. “I suppose you can’t eat dinner
like that,” he observed.

The radiance faded. Men got so hungry. It made them cross.

“I’m sorry I--kept you waiting.”

“Well, pop along and wash your face. You must be starving, if you only
knew it!”

She looked up quickly to find him grinning down. Relief flooded her.
He wasn’t cross! She felt somehow reprieved.

“I won’t be ten minutes!” she promised fervently, and disappeared up
the steps of the inn.

As a matter of fact, it was less than twenty minutes later that she sat
across the table from him, clean and cool and meek, eating her dinner
with an undisguised appetite. But meek. It was exasperating.

“Look here,” he said abruptly. “It wasn’t that you kept me waiting and
it wasn’t that your face was dirty. It was only that I had let you
start off alone and I felt a fool.”

“Oh, but I didn’t at all mind going alone!” she assured him hastily.

“It won’t do.”

“But----”

“Tell me all about it. Where did you go and what did you see?”

And glowing again, she told him, eloquently and with gestures, until
long after the coffee was brought; while he watched her from behind
his cigarette, marveling anew at the extraordinary situation in which
he found himself. He knew by heart all that she spoke of. And yet
it was curious, pitiful, almost, the way it went to her head. As
far back as he could remember there was sand and heat, the chill of
altitudes, and the glory of sunset and dawn. His had been a vivid
childhood passed under the tutelage of an Indian cavalry regiment,
which one day returned from the Border without his father. Death and
a jest, Oriental loyalty and Oriental treason, fatigue and the courage
of strength, the value of ten drops of water and the nothingness of
life--these things had been clear to him almost before she was born.
Poor little soul, what a thin time of it she had had, all these years!

After that, she was attended by an adoring Arab boy who kept ever at
her heels, while she haunted the edge of the desert, yearning eyes on
the sea of sand. She detested the boy for his proprietary airs, and
tried repeatedly to dismiss or lose him, but young Ahmed had his orders
from the tall Englishman, and stuck like a limpet, silenced, hangdog,
devotedly watchful.

“Please call Ahmed off,” she begged one morning at breakfast. “I won’t
get lost. Truly, I won’t.”

“Does he talk too much?” Dorin frowned.

“No, he’s lovely. But I’d rather be by myself, really.”

“My dear child, this isn’t London, you know!”

“But surely there’s no danger! Surely an Englishwoman----”

“Quite so. But I’ve enough on my mind without you, too,” conclusively.

“I thought--this morning--since I was only going as far as----”

“You’re not allowed to think.” He smiled his transfiguring, squint-eyed
smile, to take the bite out of his tone. “Not yet.”

“Of course I don’t want to be a bother--” She bent her head beneath
the rebuke. “Of course you do know best----”

“Don’t be an ass.” Her downcast eyes missed the humorous understanding
in his. “Ahmed knows his way about, and he’s to be trusted. I’m afraid
you’ll have to put up with him.”

“Very well.”

“Besides, he’ll do to practice your Arabic on, won’t he?”

“Yes.”

She drank her coffee contentedly. What did Ahmed matter? What did
anything matter beside the stupendous fact that she was _here_,
with all the Sahara before her? And Blaise Dorin wasn’t cross when one
was late to meals.




                               CHAPTER II


DAWNS of pearl and saffron; brief, opalescent twilights; days when she
seemed to move waist-deep in a dizzy, shimmering flood of heat, and
distance lost all meaning in the glare that beat like thunder on her
consciousness; blue velvet nights, star-strewn, when she grudged the
sleep her weariness demanded.

She thrilled to the dry suck of sand under foot, and the wail of the
Arab pipes and the musical Arab prayer, and to a silence that was
somehow a tangible thing. She watched her long, sharp-cut shadow on
the sand as she rode, rested, dazzled, loving eyes on the wind-carven
dunes, and cried out rapturously at the mirage. She snatched at each
hour and devoured it with its wealth of unexplored sensation. It was
all holiday.

And her grandfathers, that ghostly host of gallant gentlemen, must
have smiled to see her stretch out greedy hands to the wilderness,
even while she paid its price of discomfort. She lived in boots and
breeches, Dorin’s lean length in miniature. There was sand in her long
hair and in her clothes and in her food. She forgot the taste of a
civilized cup of tea. She suffered heat tortures, the worse for her
delicate fairness. But her eyes grew steadily bigger and brighter, and
she learned to laugh aloud. No doubt her grandfathers swelled with
celestial pride.

Often dog-tired, aching, and very thirsty, she went about the arduous
business of “remembering.” Dorin’s rigorous system of training included
a grilling target practice, and she sniffed the sharp, sweet smell of
powder, along with other less exhilarating odors of hot leather and hot
horse, and told herself that at last she had life in both hands. She
acquired a painful knowledge of camels and mules and struggled with
dialects and the native mind.

Dorin said it was as good as a play, and stood by impassive with secret
mirth much of the time. Sometimes his tactful gravity gave way under
the strain and they laughed together helplessly and began again. Always
impersonal, never impatient, he seemed to regard her as somewhat more
dependable and a little less useful and infinitely more amusing than an
ambitious boy of her size.

She had not been given a rocking-horse to ride. The black brute which
carried her was a very different animal from the country mare of her
girlhood.

In the beginning, she was fly-weight on his back and her hands were
light on the rein. This puzzled him. He danced experimentally. The fly
sat still. He plunged, with a sea-going motion, and the fly laughed
like a boy. He shook himself till he clattered, and the fly chaffed
him. This was impertinence and not to be borne. He rose and walked on
his hind legs, and something slid off over his tail without a sound.
He paused then, disdaining to kick out. It was no man.

Next, some eleven stone arrived expertly in the saddle and his mouth
felt a hand that meant business.

“Now, then, damn you, march!”

This was more like it. He could carry a man as prettily as anybody. He
marched, stepping delicately.

Three times they made the circuit of the camp, in all his paces, as
though at a sale. Then Dorin swung down.

“Seems to have worked off his mad,” he said. “Feel like trying him
again?”

“Of course!” snapped Alexandra, who, having lit in sand, nursed only an
injured dignity.

The fly was up again! The black brute stood still, quivering with
indignation.

“Well, get along!” advised the speck atop him. “Do your stuff!”

His fine Arab soul rebelled. This was colt’s play. He would be laughed
at. He did his stuff, and he had a neat bag of tricks. Again she went
off, over his head this time. Some one swore at him vividly, and he
stood still, more than pleased with himself.

“He won’t have me!” gasped Alexandra, spitting sand. “He’s got a crush
on you! But I’ll ride him if it takes all summer!”

“He’s no gentleman,” said Dorin, lifting her to her feet. “Sure you’re
not hurt?”

“It’s nice soft sand,” said Alexandra.

“That’s enough for today. I’m going to reason with him.”

But with Dorin up again the black brute became as a horse with wings.
They had a most amiable time of it.

Alexandra refused to try Dorin’s mount the next day. The black one was
hers and she would ride him. And ride him she did, in the end, though
not without slight mishaps.

The first three minutes were the hardest. If she managed to stick
that long the rest of the day was fairly peaceful. Dorin would stand
watching, so interested that he often had to dodge rather suddenly,
while with set teeth and pink cheeks Alexandra silently stuck her three
minutes out.

“Ride ’em, Sandy!” he would shout, squinting into the whirlwind, and
the name stuck.

They called the black brute Brugglesmith, for no reason at all except
that they considered it--and no doubt so did he--opprobrious.

Men said that Dodo Dorin was “handy with a knife,” which meant only
that if deprived of his white man’s weapon, the neat and honest gun,
if brought to close fighting, or if silence meant very life itself,
his work would be swift and conclusive. He had compromised with the
Englishman’s natural fastidiousness in such matters by a certain
deftness and minimum of fuss, and this fact was clearly set forth in
the subtle, wind-written lore of the far places, so that they gave
him room in a row. There was only a man in Somaliland and another in
Mexico who could really tell, first hand, of witnessing the famous
short thrust and draw which Dorin now set himself patiently to teach
a fair-haired girl. “Might need it some day,” he explained almost
diffidently. “It’s all in getting home with the point. Any one can
jab and gouge and make no end of a mess. You hold it--so.” She gave
breathless attention. And when at the end of the lesson he gayly pinned
a corner of a tarpaulin on the ground with a ten-foot forward flip, she
shrieked with delight and ran to fetch the knife, and begged to learn
that too.

Gradually, Dorin’s sense of the queerness of it wore off. She was a
jolly little thing. He was not sorry he had brought her.

Like a boy she rode beside him, learning his easy, tireless seat,
enduring the longest day’s travel without complaint. Boylike, she lay
on her stomach by the fire after the evening meal, a cigarette in her
fingers, the firelight dancing in her eyes, and coaxed stories from
him. And like a boy, she was up at his first shout in the morning,
eager for the new day even though it was of a desert sameness with the
one which had gone before. No, he could not be sorry he had brought her.

Shy of personalities as any Etonian, she had never asked questions
about the mysterious errand which took them thus into the heart of an
unfriendly desert region. And perhaps because it did not occur to him
to do so, Dorin never told. Twice they were followed suspiciously by
a chain of horsemen flung along the skyline, and once they rode at
night well-nigh beyond all endurance, because of certain fires to the
north and east. Alexandra, noting that Dorin nursed a gun across his
knees and that his eyes became quicksilver slits at the murmurings of
his men, held her peace and reeled in the saddle as the sun came up.
Long, blind, parching hours later, they came to a staggering halt in
a tiny oasis where they seemed to be expected and were ceremoniously
welcomed. Some one lifted her down, and there was fresh water, and she
slept where she was, amid voices and movement with which she felt no
concern. When she awoke it was dark, and Dorin sat nearby, smoking.
She sat up swiftly, clutching at consciousness, guilty, apologetic.
“It’s all right,” he grinned. “We made it. And that’s that.” He sighed
with contentment and lay back, communing with the stars. A priceless
packet of ancient jewels whimsically reset by a great Parisian firm
for the covetous fingers and round brown throat of some favorite
dancing-girl--a verbal message from a man in Marseilles. Both delivered
safely, intact. And that was that.

It was not until they had turned north again that Alexandra really
looked beyond the twelve hours immediately in hand. But on the return
journey, as she lay one night in her tent, hearing the parched rustle
of some sad desert herbage and the last nameless sounds of a drowsy
camp, she was snatched back from sleep by the horrid thought that this
part of it was almost over. At what point would he turn eastward
toward Port Said? Would he return to Algiers first? Not, she decided,
unless he meant to go on alone.

With dreadful accuracy she counted the days that would be left. They
were appallingly few. In sudden panic she crawled to the flap of her
tent and peered out. The fire was low, the Arab pipes were still. The
camp slept, and the desert moon rode high, a luminous silver plaque on
the wall of heaven. Dorin’s tent, a short distance away, was black and
quiet.

Was he pleased with her, she wondered. She had been game, she knew she
had. She had loved every minute of it. She had not once said she was
tired. She had even reached some sort of compromise with Brugglesmith,
lately. She had not been a failure here! And yet Shir Shan’s robe had
not been mentioned for days. Not for weeks.

Suppose he sent her back, after all, like an importunate puppy. Suppose
he left her behind, and she never saw the Hills, with him. With him.
She regarded the addition curiously. She wanted above all to go with
him. She could get to India alone, somehow, with her little money. But
without Dodo--she was among the elect now and privileged to call him
that--without Dodo things would seem very queer. He knew how she felt
about it all. And they laughed at the same instant, always. He--she
sat back on one foot and contemplated this--he had taught her to laugh
like that. He had given her life as surely as though he had picked
her dripping from the Thames, and she owned him now with a doggish
devotion which had nothing to do with the skirts she had shed, and
partook of the mute worship of his native boys.

She wanted to explore Port Said at his heels. That is where the East
begins. She wanted to go to Bokhara and see the storks. She wanted to
penetrate to that monastery in the Hills and watch the bargaining.
She pictured it, hugging one knee in the moonlight. Dodo so grave and
respectful and keen of eye. And all the while thinking what rot it was,
and laughing down inside. Always those imps inside. But if the robe was
at the monastery Dodo would be sure to have it before he had finished.
He would come away with it in his pocket. The robe was as good as in
Starke’s hands--provided Dodo got back.

Then there would be the thrilling journey down to the Pass and so to
India--Dodo, again, beloved of his kind. They would fall on his neck at
the Fort and there would be high jinks. She knew, from the tales he had
told.

Dodo, always, in the center of things, but taking it all quite calmly.
Arabs, Asiatics, or Englishmen, priests or subalterns--Dodo, playing
the game, leading it, loving it, winning it. And perhaps herself, proud
as any possessive canine, wagging and smiling at his heels....

The joy of it! The freedom of it! The heat and the cold and the
breathlessness, the heavenly tiredness! The intolerable strain
triumphantly endured, the possible danger encountered, the thrill of
wit against wit like the ring of steel on steel! The risk and the dare
of it--Out There!

“O God,” prayed Alexandra suddenly toward the desert moon, “let me go
on like this always!”

All the next day she watched his face, while hope and fear and a tact
that was more than woman’s kept her dumb. She must not make it harder
for him. If he meant to leave her behind he must be allowed to break
it in his own way. He was fond of her, she knew that. She must not
press him. He would hate to disappoint her, but he would undoubtedly do
exactly as he thought best. He was a soldier, first of all. Her chin
quivered, as an overstrung terrier whimpers for action. She would be a
soldier, too!

There were things, you see, which did not occur to her. Things which
Dorin, facing a decision, was compelled to consider.

What, for instance, about their necessary stop at Port Said if he
took her on with him? An obscure hotel, a hole-and-corner business,
or--glances, perhaps even snubs? Not at all the sort of thing either
of them was used to. An ordeal at best for both of them. And what
about taking her into India later, where each colonel’s lady sharpens
her claws for infinitely less than poor Sandy could imagine? She had
no idea of the chill blast of public opinion. Of course it might not
precede them. But even so, how could he explain her to fellows he
couldn’t avoid? Of course they might never get to India....

And it wasn’t as though he hadn’t got devilish fond of her. She was
the gamest little beggar, and too heartbreakingly happy over this mild
lark in the Sahara. Had he the courage, he wondered, to turn her back
even for her own good, when this job was finished? Could he watch her
take it as she would take it, on her two feet, but with her great eyes
gone suddenly desolate? How in heaven’s name could he bear to put out
the light he had seen there? The light not only of complete beatitude
toward life, but of such ridiculous--he rejected several words
hastily--well, the way she looked at him. As though he had himself made
this desert in all its hideous beauty and tossed it into her lap. He
would miss that look. Yes, hang it, he would miss her!

And yet, somehow, he couldn’t quite see himself riding serenely into
British India with her at his side. And yet neither could he just
dump her down somewhere to get along on her few hundred pounds a
year--he was sure it couldn’t be much--and perhaps become the prey of
God knew what. To suggest that Ingarsen’s daughter couldn’t take care
of herself was absurd. Never was such a valiant soul. But there were
so many things that never occurred to her. And it was borne in upon
him sickeningly that this Sahara business of theirs would give her a
certain reputation.... He always swore a little here. He had seen women
in his time who had for several years away from Home worn that sort of
reputation.

He had been mad, to bring her. But what would have become of her if he
hadn’t? She would have walked out of that house that night, regardless.
Nevertheless, what was to become of her now that he had brought her?
And he himself--it would make a difference to him too. A fellow can’t
do these things....

Was it her imagination, she wondered, or was he silent and preoccupied
that day? At the evening meal he hardly spoke at all. And she, her
whole being concentrated on his unreadable thoughts, choked on her
bitter tea and was thumped perfunctorily on the back, without comment,
and forgotten again, while he retired within himself, filling his pipe
by the fire.

Silently, then, he felt in all his pockets. Silently she tossed him her
own match-box. In silence the match was struck and applied.

He kept the box in his hand long after the pipe was alight, and she
waited meekly with an unlighted cigarette, dreading to intrude herself
upon his notice. At last he laid it down between them and stretched
himself full length, eyes on the fire. She reached out cautiously and
struck her own match. He did not notice.

Minutes, perhaps an hour passed. She had begun to nod above her
hunched-up knees. Then he spoke.

“You’ll want another pair of boots,” he said. “We can pick them up at
Port Said. Have to stop there for some stuff I sent on ahead.”

Thus lightly he tossed the Dream into her lap.




                              CHAPTER III


GOLD fabric, of an ancient mystery. Gold in a woman’s hair. Gold that
clinks. Trouble, three times over.

As hidden water draws the diviner’s rod, so hidden gold exerts its
unholy magnetism. They were not a week out of Bokhara when there began
to be furtive whisperings, watchful eyes, among the three servants.
Dorin had allowed himself only three, so that his little party might
the better melt into the vast, uncaring landscape. These three soon
had their heads together over certain luggage which was heavy and
which slept in the _sahib’s_ tent at night, under his hand, like
a dearly loved woman. Or like treasure. Stealthy fingers pinched and
poked at it during the loading--it was assuredly very heavy--ears were
attuned to catch a sound which imagination readily supplied. Gold. The
_sahib_ carried gold into the wilderness. And they were three. The
woman-- They did not like the woman, with her pale hair and level eyes.
_Was_ she--woman? Then a silence would fall, while eyes avoided
eyes, and a great uneasiness went unvoiced.

Dorin, not at all unaware that he rode into triple trouble, chose to be
oblivious to signs, but his trained nerves registered cross-currents,
his sleep was light, and he would wake in the night without apparent
cause.

He was not satisfied that the heavy khaki-swathed bundle which lay
beside him every night accounted for all that which subtly charged
the air. Nor could he feel that the absence of a known destination
alone would cause this growing unrest among his men. No. He sniffed
superstition, an unreasoning apprehension, mutiny, even. And it did
not tax his practiced perceptions to trace it to Alexandra’s glowing,
joyous presence, her almost unearthly grace and zest. She was amazingly
handy, and possessed of an endurance almost equal to his own. She
was fast becoming unbelievable even to him, tanned now to a clear
creaminess which made her eyes seem bluer, her hair fairer than before.
And she lived in an exultation that was like white flame. Small wonder
that they murmured of her, apart.

Slowly his beloved Hills rose before him, shouldering the clouds. He
watched them reaching out their ridges to him, perceptibly nearer each
day, and as he looked his gray eyes darkened with something sad and
wise and yearning, something old as the Hills. Alexandra would dance
and throw wide her arms in pagan joy, and talk happy foolishness to
her stoical pony. To her the Hills meant heaven unalloyed. Perhaps
there were, after all, a few things she had forgotten.... But her nose
came up to the first whiff of the snows with a jerk identical with
Dorin’s own, and a shadow crossed her face, like the shadow of a great
bird flying low, or of the spirit of him who had died at Cawnpore;
but it was gone again in a cry of sheer rapture. Dorin smiled
sympathetically, and from then on, while the Hills gathered him ever
more closely to their rugged, ruthless hearts, he rode preoccupied,
like a man who keeps a rendezvous.

And now there began to be talk among the three of magic, and of men
lured to a horrible undoing, of the need of certain forgotten deities
for sacrifice, and of divers methods whereby victims were secured. This
strange, laughing creature with yellow hair--whither was she leading
them? This tireless blue-eyed one, this goddess-woman who was obviously
no woman at all, but-- Silence and nods. And the treasure? A pity that
so much good treasure should be abandoned forever to the avarice of
some long-lost evil spirit. It was still possible to return the way
they had come--not, of course, forgetting the treasure--_if_
the _sahib_ were not in a position to interfere. There were
certain villages to the north.... One called Mohammed objected here
that the _sahib_ was not a man to be lightly disposed of, and
that the other, the blue-eyed one-- He was scornfully overruled.
The _sahib_ was but one man, and they were three. And the
goddess-woman would doubtless be powerless until her own country,
somewhere beyond the realms of possibility, was reached. She would
doubtless die of hunger and thirst in due time if left to herself here,
where her needs were as yet quite human like other people’s. Had they
not all seen her eat and drink, like other people?...

One morning a swift, unerring instinct turned Dorin about suddenly
just as he was going to mount, and a long knife drove past him into the
saddle. His fist shot out and the man rolled between the horse’s feet.
Dorin covered the scene with a revolver and got his breath. Alexandra
sat silent, rigid with astonishment, with a brown hand still gripping
her wrists on the pommel. The third man, he who was called Mohammed,
dropped a rifle as though it had burned his fingers, and busied himself
with a pack.

Then Dorin spoke briefly and to the point behind that unwavering
revolver. The prostrate would be murderer was unceremoniously doubled
groaning across a pony and the day’s march began without further
incident.

Toward evening Mohammed, who had plainly been a prey to conflicting
emotions all day, fell back beside Dorin’s horse at the end of the line
and lifted the somber, inscrutable eyes of the East.

“If the _sahib_ permits his servant to speak--” he suggested in a
confidential whine.

“Yes--well?”

“It is--_that_.” Mohammed’s skinny brown finger indicated
Alexandra where she rode just in front. “The gold--it is nothing to
_me_.” His oblique gaze slid away, half sullen, half ashamed, to
the horizon and beyond. “The _sahib_ is my master and I obey. But
I do _not_ like--that.”

“What’s the matter with it?” demanded Dorin, grimly amused.

“They say--” There was a sidelong glint of the opaque brown glance.
“They say _she_ leads us--nowhere.”

“Nonsense. _I_ lead. And I have a destination, but that is my
own affair. You all knew it would be so when you agreed in Bokhara to
follow.”

“We did not see _that_ in Bokhara,” complained Mohammed.

“That is a woman of my people, only. All Englishwomen are like that.”
Again grim humor touched his tone. It was perhaps overstating the case
a bit.

“I do not understand,” sighed Mohammed. “But the _sahib_ is my
master and I obey.”

“It is well.” Dorin closed the subject, and rode on, looking thoughtful.

There was undeniable humor in it. Forthright, vivid Sandy, being
suspected of witchcraft, savoring of the supernatural, in the face
of her passionate mortal love of the earth she trod and the air she
breathed! And now, as she rode before him in the slanting sunlight
of late afternoon, she began to sing in a muted tone, eerily sweet,
swaying slightly to the motion of her horse in a small private ecstasy
of her own at the dear immensity of things.

    “I got wings! You got wings!
    All God’s chillun got wings!”

crooned Sandy happily, as he had taught her.

Dear old thing, thought Dorin, fond eyes on the supple back ahead of
him. It was worth it, having her, no matter what happened. Too bad,
though, that she had to be a girl-- Something clicked in his mind and
turned over. _Was_ it altogether a pity that she was a girl?
That slim delicacy of line overgrown into masculine proportions--that
hair cut short--that voice--Here, he told himself abruptly. Hold on a
minute. Was hers a merely decorative value, like other women’s? Oh,
most decidedly not. And yet--that spirit in another shell, speaking in
other tones-- Sandy, by any other name----?

    “Lots o’ folks talkin’ ’bout hebben ain’ goin’ dere!
    Hebben! Hebben!
    Goin’ to fly all ober God’s hebben!”

Then, as the weird little melody began again, wordless this time, in
her quaintly sexless choir-boy pipe, he straightened and his eyes came
sharply to focus where Mohammed had rejoined the others. The three
were casting glances over hunched, secretive shoulders as they rode.
And suddenly Sandy’s harmless crooning among the lengthening shadows
assumed a new aspect in his eyes.

He pushed forward and aimed a kick at her stirrup.

“Stow it!” he hissed as he passed. “Shut up!”

He had a glimpse of her amazed face, its naïve surprise complicated by
the added injury of her kicked ankle, and this abode with him while he
shouted orders full of a studied fractiousness about the pitching of
camp--a good hour before he had meant to halt.

But even though harried by their _sahib’s_ incomprehensible
querulousness, his many fretful and useless exactions, the three found
time to ponder this new development of their destiny--the singing of
spells and incantations at twilight by the blue-eyed one.

The evening meal was eaten almost in silence, polite and puzzled on
Alexandra’s part, remorseful but inarticulate on Dorin’s. He deemed it
unwise for them to appear to confer and so gave her no very detailed
explanations. She wasn’t to sing, he said. It made these beggars
fidgety.

She accepted the dictum philosophically, and his heart smote him anew
with how he had taught her that song and then kicked her when she sang
it so that he listened too long. It wasn’t that he didn’t want her to
be happy. Her happiness was to him suddenly beyond price. It wasn’t
that he didn’t like her to sing.

“Sorry,” he mumbled inadequately. “Ticklish job--no chances--queer
chaps, you know--weird notions----”

“Yes,” she agreed serenely, her mind already drifting away to the
sunset and the picturesqueness of Mohammed outlined against it where he
stood peering intently across at the opposite hillside and the shadows
of the valley between. “Do you think he sees something?” she queried,
minutes later, into the silence.

“Who?” Dorin sat up. “Where?”

Economical of movement, she nodded her head in Mohammed’s direction,
and Dorin, too, scanned the hillside, and the shadows, until Mohammed,
seeing himself under observation, became ostentatiously busy.

Dorin roused several times during the night to a phantom movement and
whispering, but the open flap of his tent gave an unobstructed view
of Alexandra’s quarters a few feet away, and nothing seemed to be
stirring. Each time he reproached himself for nerves and napped again.
He was quite sure before morning, however, that he wished she wasn’t a
girl.

Alexandra slept with utter confidence in the goodness of life and in
Dodo’s guardianship. The episode of the morning had not badly shaken
her. She supposed such things happened occasionally. Natives were queer
and resented fancied slights. Dodo knew how to manage them, though.
Dodo was altogether wonderful. Everything was wonderful. Being a girl
hadn’t mattered, after all.

When Dorin stepped out of his tent soon after dawn into a strangely
quiet camp a spatter of earth rose at his feet and something else
struck _whack_! on the tent-pole behind him.

“Hullo!” said Dorin mildly, thinking fast.

“They have gone, _sahib_.” Mohammed’s confidential whine came from
where he squatted placidly on his hunkers in the lee of the tent. “All
gone, but me. Gold--it is nothing to me. The _sahib_ is my master
and----”

“Gone! Oh, my hat!” Dorin gazed ruefully across the valley. “Stalky
brutes they were, too! But I might have known-- _Zut_!” he added
cheerfully, unstartled, as another bullet plopped on to rock three feet
to the right of him. “We can’t have this!” He dived into the tent for
his rifle. “What did they take with them?” he demanded, emerging gun in
hand and making for the stores piled on the far side of the burnt-out
fire.

“A good share, _sahib_. Two horses, two guns----”

“They’ve got my little Enfield, confound ’em!” Dorin was making swift
inventory of what remained. “I liked that gun. She was a lady.” He
cocked the rifle in his hand briskly, his gaze raking the hillside
opposite.

“The _sahib_ sees where the rock dips down to the timber.”
Mohammed’s skinny brown finger pointed across the valley. “One of them
is there--behind the large round stone which overhangs. The other----”

“Above and to the left. Dashed good at taking cover--” The rifle
snuggled lovingly into Dorin’s shoulder. “I don’t think he’d be
missed,” he murmured, and the rifle spoke.

The answer came promptly and scattered the ashes of the fire.

“The ledge,” remarked Mohammed regretfully, “projects too far.”

“Dodo, what _is_ it?” Alexandra stood breathless and blinking in
the morning light.

Dorin whirled. He had clean forgotten her.

“Go into the tent and lie down, you,” he commanded. “_Ek dum!_”

“But what----”

_Ping!_ one of Mohammed’s cherished cooking utensils was disabled.
_Plop!_ to Alexandra’s immediate left.

“Oh, here, I say, this won’t do!” cried Dorin. “Get out of sight, I
tell you, and keep still!” He glanced at Mohammed’s expressionless
countenance as she vanished obediently within the tent. “Got your
revolver handy?” he called after her.

“Yes, but----”

“Hang on to it.” He started dodging along the slope to the left, rifle
in hand. “Shan’t be long. Keep still, I say.”

“But where are you going?” A reckless head appeared at the tent flap.

“Round the end. Can’t have them firing into camp like this. Lie down,
you idiot!” He was already out of sight.

The firing was occasional but persistent while Dorin made his zig-zag
way along the side of his hill, into a rock chimney, out again, and on,
unhurried, methodical, sure-footed. It came inevitably to his mind that
he had had a hunch. He hoped things weren’t going to be awkward for
Sandy....

Once he glanced over his shoulder at a blob of lead on the rock,
then at the hillside opposite, and grinned. “Not bad, that one,” he
commented approvingly. “Good gun you’ve got, my boy.” Again, working
along an exposed ledge, flat to the cliff wall, he paused as though a
hand had held him back, while lead flattened on the rock six inches
ahead. He shook his head at the hunch, then, a trifle thoughtfully.
“No,” he decided. “This isn’t it.”

He came to the end of the ravine and began working up toward higher
ground. The range had lessened and he had to be more careful about
keeping to cover. He had forced them to change their position, and the
balanced rock no longer blanketed the man in its shadow. He found a
ledge with a deep crevice and fitted himself to it, breathing hard,
dusty, somewhat cut and bruised, but happy enough. He could see the
stolen horses and the second man from where he lay. Now, then.

Almost immediately a bullet spat dust into his face. “Oh, shut up,”
he said, not impatiently. “Wait a minute, can’t you?” His eyes had
gone cold and bright and narrow. Again the rifle snuggled against his
shoulder and spoke once. The hillside answered twice. “Must be getting
old,” he complained, shifting a little. “Better make my will.”

He fired again, with the same result. “_I_ know,” he sighed. “I’m
nervous!” His third shot brought a yell, and the man beside the rock
moved incautiously and then lay spraddled out and visible, one arm
flung wide into a patch of early sunlight. Dorin waited, tight lines
around his mouth. The humor was now quite gone from the situation.

The man behind the ledge which Mohammed had deplored apparently lost
his head and fired several times rapidly. The bullets went wild. Dorin
kept very quiet. At last the man raised himself and curiously surveyed
his comrade, who was ominously still. Dorin watched him grimly, while
he crawled from behind the ledge toward the widening patch of sunlight,
in the edge of which huddled the bundle of rags and villainy which
seemed so indifferent now to fate.

Something in its stillness struck the late conspirator with sudden
panic. He rose and made for the horses at a dodging, drunken run,
finally abandoning all thought of cover as he flung himself at the
saddle and dug his heels into the horse’s sides. Dorin sent several
bullets after him not too wide of the mark, to lend color to his
escape, and watched him gallop out of sight round a shoulder of rock,
the second horse clattering aimlessly behind. “Break his silly neck,”
he muttered. “Save trouble all round.”

He got to his feet a little stiffly, and with a sigh of resignation
started for the balanced rock. And as he went the hunch went with him,
puzzlingly, until-- “Look here,” he said to it. “Look here, let me see
her through, can’t you? I’ll come back,” he promised it. “I swear I’ll
come back. But I’ve got a bit of a job on, this time. Hold off a bit,
can’t you...?”

The bundle lay there on its face, deserted, inert, the sun creeping
along its shapeless length, warming it. He turned it over, to make
sure. Yes, one might as well leave it there, now. He rolled it back on
its face and stood looking down at it a minute. Beastly business. But
what was a man to do?

As he turned away he caught sight of something out of the tail of
his eye, and stooping he picked up the gun who was a lady. “No good
here--either of us,” he told her apologetically. “Let’s go home.”

Mohammed was getting breakfast with Oriental impassivity when Alexandra
looked out at last into the silence.

“It’s--very quiet,” she said.

“Breakfast now,” he opined brightly. “I think no more shooting today.”

“What’s happened? Could you see?”

“One died. One ran away. The _sahib_ will be hungry. Allah! It is
a man!”

Alexandra peered down the ravine against the rising sun. Dorin was
headed for camp. One died....

“Snipers,” said Mohammed virtuously. “Gold--it is nothing to
_me_.” He spat eloquently into the fire. “A wise man could see
that the _sahib_ is not an easy man to kill.”

“They meant to--to murder him and--and----”

“For the gold, yes. A wise man could see it could not be done. The
_sahib_ is not a child.” Mohammed pondered this a moment. “He
_need_ not have let that one run away,” he said.

Alexandra stood still in the sunlight, working it out, contemplating
the stupendous idea of a Dodo who had just-- She knew, of course, that
he had killed before, knew well from Bob Taunton that one does kill at
need. But on her holiday--! B-before breakfast--! stammered her mind
incredulously.

And now he was coming back, carrying two guns. He waved to her with
his free hand, and she waved back, absent-mindedly, and he came on,
stepping lightly, almost gayly, she thought, watching him, from rock to
rock, and there was the smell of cooking in the air....

She wondered how it felt to kill a man, how it felt to know that a
crooking of your finger had robbed some one of long, warm, thrilling
years, of dawns and moons and winds and laughter, and the feel of a
good horse between his knees. A life gone out, finished, because you
crooked your finger....

_A wise man could see that the sahib is not an easy man to kill._
They had meant it to be Dodo who forfeited this day, this precious
early sunlight--and all days and all sunlight to come. Suppose they
had brought it off. Suppose it had been Dodo’s life which had gone
out, instead of that one there by the rock. Dodo’s splendid love of
living--or that man’s mere existence. Well, but did that make a real
difference? The dead man would have killed Dodo if he could, and she
was immeasurably glad that he was dead. But was a life, then, to be
valued according to how it was lived and loved?

It was hard to look at the thing impartially. But the idea of
Dodo--dead.... With a little gasp she ran down the slope to meet him.

The _sahib_ was indeed hungry. Alexandra watched him at
breakfast, awed and almost silent before his new distinction. The
day’s work. That was all he made of it. Of course that would be all.
But--_breakfast_! There was reverence in her gaze. He was a very
great man indeed, and he had let her come along.

Dorin, too, was watching, and he smiled in his sleeve. He had wondered
how she would take this necessitous slaying of an acquaintance. He had
been, on one side of his mind, cold-bloodedly interested in its effect
on her. On the other side, being ignorant in the main of the educative
influence of Bob Taunton for one thing, he had half dreaded to meet her
eyes. He had been less pleased with things than he looked from above,
striding back to camp with the recovered Enfield. And then she had
come running to meet him, carried one of the guns, inquired the range,
praised his marksmanship, and superintended the cleaning of his rifle.
She was beyond belief. His pride of her was enormous.




                               CHAPTER IV


THE odd part of it all was that Shir Shan’s robe did exist in that
monastery in the Hills--a breath-taking thing, truly, when its ageless
splendor was gingerly unfolded before them; supple gold, like Danae’s
shower. An incredible thing, even though shorn now of all its largest
topazes, its clasp dangling an empty setting, its hem bare of the great
stones which once had weighted it. Still, the skirt and sleeves gave
back the light in a thousand pin-points of yellow flame, and the rich
fabric sighed against itself under its burden.

Later, when there was time to laugh, Dorin said it was Sandy’s _beaux
yeux_ which turned the trick. It is possible that without the
blue-eyed goddess he would never have touched the robe. It is certain
that because of her it came very near to being one of the last things
he ever did.

To go back a little----

Arrived within sight of the monastery, Dorin cached her in a nullah
with the pack animals, while he and Mohammed went on. She was somewhat
aggrieved about that, but she submitted gracefully. Dodo knew best. She
watched them out of sight round the shoulder of the hill with envious
eyes, and then sat down on her saddle with a cigarette.

He had said he would be back by dark, or as a last resort would send
Mohammed with a message. They did not entirely trust Mohammed. But no
one came that night. Nor the next night. Alexandra was not frightened,
but she trusted Mohammed less and less. And she wondered if there was
not something she could do.

On the third morning she got the packs together alone and followed
Dorin’s track round the shoulder of the hill, taking the pack animals
with her; a slim, valiant figure with alert, anxious eyes, and a
revolver at its hip.

Meanwhile Dorin, that very tactful man, was having his troubles at the
monastery. Things were not quite as he had been led to expect, and his
original plan was thrown badly out of gear. And just to make things
more interesting, Mohammed disappeared, whether voluntarily or perforce
he could only suspect. It was inconvenient, but by no means fatal.
Sandy would have to possess her soul in patience. Hastily reorganizing
his always elastic schemes of action, he broached the delicate subject
of his quest. At first they declined to understand what he was talking
about. Then they began to evince an almost embarrassing interest in
him. And finally they refused to part with him at all, which was
awkward.

On the morning of the third day he insisted upon another audience with
the authorities and got it. They talked. He talked. Time passed.

At last they came to the point.

“Who,” they desired to know, “is the one in the nullah beyond the hill?”

“My brother,” said Dorin, without blinking.

“Slender, with small hands and feet like a Rajput.”

“A lad only,” said Dorin.

“And long yellow hair.”

He glanced about for Mohammed and saw him in a corner looking detached
and innocent.

“Some one deceives you,” he said.

“It is a woman.”

“A woman? Here?” He smiled. “How could a woman of my people be here?”

“It is a woman.”

“Are these magic hills,” he queried, “that one can leave a boy and
return to find a woman?”

“It is,” they assured him, “a woman.”

“I know of no woman.”

“You lie.”

“I will ride down to my camp and fetch the boy,” he proposed blandly.

“No,” they said.

“I would leave my servant here as security,” he offered craftily.

“No,” they said. “She will be sent for.”

And at that moment Alexandra, driving the pack animals before her, rode
into the courtyard.

Dorin followed the crowd. At sight of him she waved her hand and called
out in her clear voice.

“Hullo!” she called. “I thought perhaps they’d eaten you!” She swung
down, unassisted, and walked, as though it was not there, through the
mob which parted before her to where he stood on the steps. “Have you
seen the robe? Is it here?”

“Do you know what you’ve done?” he demanded. “You’ve walked straight
into the trap!”

“Trap?” She glanced out over the heads of the watchful crowd, packed
below them. “What’s all this? Going to make a speech?”

“They were told--Mohammed, of course--that I had a yellow-haired woman
up my sleeve. And they were all for making me produce her.”

“Well, then, it’s a good thing I came on in, isn’t it!” she beamed.

“Is it?”

He was looking down at the crowd, from which a spokesman advanced and
