delivered himself of a message. She listened with a puckered brow. It
didn’t sound at all like the sort of thing Dodo had been teaching her.

“What’s he talking?” she asked, deeply interested. “It’s beyond me.
What’s on his mind, do _you_ know?”

“He wants to see your hair.”

“Oh.” Obediently she took off her helmet.

A murmur ran through the crowd as her blondeness was revealed. Dorin’s
eyes were on those upturned faces. He was thinking hard. It was at work
again, that weird illusion she unconsciously created of being--not
quite mortal. They had to deal with a mob which was literally ready for
anything. And it was a pet conviction of his that almost any crisis
could be turned to account if only you were good for it.

For a breath he hesitated, weighing Sandy’s untried nerve with the
possible consequences of failure. Both unknown quantities. Might as
well give it a run.

“Listen, now.” He began to speak rapidly, close to her ear. “There is a
long chance--if you want to take it. They remember that Shir Shan had
yellow hair, too, and they’re wondering. It might be possible to run
a colossal bluff. I don’t know what will happen if they call it. One
never knows. Anyway, we’re in a fix as it is. But I could tell them
that Shir Shan has come for what is hers.”

“Try it!” she urged instantly. “Oh, what a lark! Try it!”

“Sure you want to?”

“We can swing it! It’s worth a try!” Her eyes were blazing. “Tell them
I’m Shir Shan and see what happens!”

She went up a step and stood above him, looking out fearlessly over the
crowd, which waited, expectant, incredulous, murmuring, uncertain.

After a moment he stretched his arms for silence and spoke. He told
them that she was the rightful owner of the robe and that owing to
their obduracy and stupid ways with her emissary she had come herself
for what was rightfully hers, and that it had pleased her to come in
this guise. He told them that acting on her orders and for their own
good he, who was her high priest and as the dust beneath her feet,
had thought to conceal from them her presence in these hills, but that
now she had come and they had best walk lightly. He told them that
owing to her all-embracing clemency they should be unharmed if they
returned to her the sacred robe which was in their keeping, and that it
was her gracious wish that they should even be rewarded for holding it
safe until she came for it. He said that they had thus so far acquired
merit, and advised that the robe be brought forth at once.

It was a beautiful speech.

The spokesman conferred with others. There was a priest with turquoises
in his ears who objected to everything and whom they sought to placate.
He was the one who had sat highest in the council hall all morning,
and he had taken no active part in proceedings hitherto. So aloof had
he seemed on his uncomfortable pedestal that Dorin had wondered if
he weren’t a deaf mute. He spoke now, with gestures. They seemed a
little afraid of him, but they argued. Then suddenly he withdrew his
objections. It was as though something had occurred to him.

Alexandra waited, bare-headed, pink-cheeked, her weight thrown on one
foot, her thumb hooked into her revolver belt, while her blazing eyes
missed nothing. Dorin, who was himself ready for almost anything now,
saw that she looked quite plausibly of another world, with a thousand
years of life and death and mystery in those eyes. She caught his
glance and laughed silently. This was living!

The spokesman came forward again. They were humbly invited to enter
the building. Alexandra shook her yellow head.

“Bring it here,” she said, with an imperious gesture.

They understood the gesture.

And so, amazingly, they brought it, and unrolled it on the steps before
her, half in sunlight, half in shadow, shorn of its largest stones and
with a rifled clasp, but unbelievably magnificent still.

And she, playing her part, frowned over the clasp, held up the barren
hem. Volubly, they explained that it had come to them so. Still she
frowned, turning it over and over.

A mutter started among those gathered in the courtyard round the man
who had objected, and spread to those about them on the steps. It
passed from lip to lip that none but Shir Shan could wear the robe and
live. When this reached Dorin’s ears he heard, as it were, the fall of
the next card, and his lips tightened. He drew closer to her and bent
his head.

“Put it on,” he said. “You’ve got to put it on. Quick!”

“Here.” She thrust her helmet into his hands. “Hold this, then.”

It was ridiculous, but he felt something, a sort of twinge, as he
watched her getting so matter-of-factly into the magic robe. Of course
nothing happened. But he had held his breath, there in broad daylight,
conscious of the cobra-like glitter in the gaze of the man with the
turquoises in his ears. She was so game, so pitifully unquestioning.
And now they were in for it.

She faced the crowd again, muffled to the chin in supple gold, her blue
eyes blazing, the sun on her pale hair.

“Well?” she demanded of them impudently.

They gaped. Then there was a movement, a bending of backs.

“Done it!” murmured Dorin, his face inscrutable. “Now to get out of
this.”

“We mustn’t seem to hurry,” she warned him wisely. “Wait----”

She moved down the steps toward them, looking them between the eyes,
and they gave back before her. She went to her horse, which stood
against the wall, and returned with a heavy bag which clinked as she
set it on the steps.

“Now. Get your horse. I’ll wear this thing till we’re out of sight.
Hang on to my hat.” She turned again, as coolly as though she had given
him orders many times before, and mounted, the robe dragging behind her.

A shout of protest went up at that. Hands caught at her stirrups and
bridle. The mob closed in about her. Yelling, chanting, jostling each
other, they swept her forward so that she rode a bewildered, stumbling
horse up the steps and into the great hall. Heavy doors swung to behind
her, shutting out the sunlight, shutting in the exultant noise.

She had caught one dazed glimpse of Dorin, struggling to get to her
through the crowd. Looking about now in the dim light of the interior,
she could not see him. She rose in her stirrups and loudly demanded
him, but they did not hear nor would they have understood. Alexandra
felt disconcerted. She had been so very clever, everything was going so
beautifully, and now.... She was still not badly frightened. But it was
getting a bit thick, wasn’t it!

Red fires were kindled, and swinging lamps cast weird shadows on great
gray walls. The clamor was deafening. And she realized at last, with
a queer feeling in the pit of her stomach, that Dodo was on the other
side of those metal doors.




                               CHAPTER V


ALL the rest of that day and all night, Dorin waited on the steps
outside the metal doors. So far as he knew, it was the only entrance to
that part of the building. He could not tear down stone walls with his
bare hands. He could only wait. She might find a chance to slip out.

His head ached furiously from the sun and the noise, and his tongue was
rough with thirst. After the doors had slammed in his face, turning the
mob back upon itself, he retrieved her helmet from the corner where it
had been kicked while he was trying to get to her. It was dusty and a
little bashed in. He sat brushing it off, worrying at the dents, and
waiting.

The place was now wholly _en fête_. The man with the turquoises
had apparently got inside. Those who had been shut out, and there
seemed to be hundreds of them sprung from somewhere, were celebrating
in their own way the acquisition of a private deity. Weird-sounding
musical instruments wailed above the steady, maddening throb of drums
and the babel of voices. As night drew in, fires sprang up and torches
danced.

He could hear nothing through the doors. She would probably be safe, he
told himself, if she kept to the horse and didn’t get trampled. They
would not willingly harm one hair of that sacred golden head. At least
not yet. And she had her revolver. He wondered if he could hear a shot,
out there.

He had for comfort the knowledge that whatever happened to her as a
result of her impromptu deification would be his fault. He had told her
to put it on. And she had unhesitatingly obeyed him in that as in all
other things, trusting to him to tell her what to do next. And here he
was. It looked like rather a bad business.

Fingering the battered helmet, he waited helplessly beneath the
Himalayan stars. He wondered if they’d give her anything to eat. He
wondered, wincing, what manner of revels and homage she would be forced
to witness. His clear-eyed, joyous Sandy--those beasts. Once he rose
and beat upon the closed doors with his hands like a madman, and then
dropped down beside her helmet again, remembering to save his strength
for whatever came next. At 3 A. M. he remembered to wind his
watch.

He got the packs off two of the ponies, which huddled in a corner where
she had left them, and shifted the kits so that they each carried water
and a little food; fed them and ate and drank, himself. She might
have to run for it now. Dawn was coming. Things were quieting down.
The place was littered with lax, exhausted figures. Perhaps she would
manage to slip away. Hang on to her hat, she said....

At last the doors swung open. He whirled, a hand going to his hip.
Some of them came out, tenderly leading a dissipated-looking horse with
an empty saddle.

They told him she was sleeping, and they tried to stop him. He sent two
of them flying, and rushed into the hall, shouting her name. The place
smelt abominably, a horrible mingling of a hundred unnamable odors, but
among them.... He sniffed. A dead sheep with its throat cut accounted
for that.

He went on through endless corridors, calling her. At last in an inner
chamber hung with fine silks and rugs, the air heavy with a sweetish
smoke despite the beautiful carven lattice open to the dawn, he found
her, lying on the stone floor with an arm beneath her head, her cheek
pillowed on the other hand. The robe had been dropped in a shimmering
heap beside her.

On his knees he raised her in his arms, felt her hands, her temples,
groaned with relief when she opened heavy eyes. She sat up, pushing him
from her futilely with one hand.

“I’m all right,” she said, holding her head. “It seemed best--to drink
the stuff. It made me sick.” A shudder ran through her. “I’m all
right,” she said again. “Help me up.”

He lifted her to her feet. How light she was, for her strength! Her
hair brushed his cheek. How tall she was!

Then there were footsteps outside and they rushed him from behind,
pinioning his arms, chattering angrily, and she reeled back against
the wall. There was the flash of naked steel.

Without time to scream she flew at them, struck up an arm blindly,
began to splutter at them in English, calling on her small stock of
epithets--somehow gave them pause. They stared at her, holding him
between them, his arm oddly twisted, his face very white.

“Loose him!” she commanded in English, pulling at him. “Let him go, I
say!” Her palm cracked smartly on the cheek of the man who was twisting
Dorin’s arm. “_Let go!_”

Astonished, the man let go, in order to rub his face. It appeared that
some one had made a mistake.

“He is mine!” she cried, striking her breast. “_Mine_, do you
hear? And I am Shir Shan! Now clear out of here! _Go!_”

Dorin had dropped to his knees and crouched there, sick with the
pain in his shoulder. Stooping swiftly, she caught up the robe and
threw it over her shoulders so that he, huddled there at her feet,
was half within its protective folds. So she faced them above him,
adding figurative cubits to her stature, seeming to tower in offended
divinity. They retreated unwillingly, muttering among themselves, eying
him with increased respect and puzzlement, abasing themselves before
her.

As the curtain fell into place behind them she drew a long breath,
pushing back her hair boyishly.

“_Well!_” she said. “Well, I’m blowed! Whatever touched them off
like that!”

“Suppose it’s what I get for laying hands on your sacred person.”

“Oh, what rot! Is your arm all right?”

“Think so.” He rose stiffly, rubbing it.

“And here we are!” She walked to the window, the robe whispering in her
wake, and stood leaning against the casement, panting a little. “Nice
view,” she said.

_He is mine._ Dorin followed her to the window and together they
watched the sun come up, while they made and rejected plans for escape.
_He is mine._ And it had stopped them like a shot. She had kept
her head. Any one else would have cut loose with a gun and there would
have been the devil to pay. But they were still alive, together again,
plus the robe, and stood one chance in ever so many of getting away.
_He is mine._ It had occurred to her to say that, unmistakably,
in every line of her, instead of pulling her gun. They owed their two
lives, perhaps, to her having said that in the nick of time. Rummy
feeling. And here they were.

They made their zealous hosts understand that she wanted him with her
throughout the day, and the two of them snatched sleep in turns until
dusk. Exploring after dark, they found they were guarded, surrounded,
bottled up. Then they made a plan.

She was to speak always in English, lots of it, with him as
interpreter. That would help to make him indispensable and free of the
place. They would stay there as they were and give no trouble, until
the time came. He would make unostentatious investigations among the
servants in the kitchens and the stables. She, speaking through him,
would sound the priests, one by one. And finally they would know just
how they stood.

The next day he delivered an address from her to the authorities, which
said that she was pleased with their zeal and their many kindnesses,
and since they so desired it would make this place her home. But it
was her wish not to be disturbed with ceremonies in her honor. She
was to be left to herself for rest and meditation, after her journey.
Furthermore, it was her will that he, her high priest and the dust
beneath her feet, should have the preparation of her food and should
come and go as he pleased, for without him she was as the moon without
its star, and lonely.

They listened attentively and seemed impressed. It should be as she
wished, they said.

And so the long siege began.

Dull days and weary weeks of waiting followed; of laying plans that
came to nothing, of setting word-traps that were never sprung, of talk,
talk, talk. Just what their hosts meant to do with Shir Shan, now
that they had got her, was not clear. Perhaps they could not agree
among themselves. Meanwhile she was kept virtually a prisoner. Queer
things happened, queer foods were offered her, she was surrounded by
intrigues, whisperings, plots. And Dorin knew well that her life hung
on the mad whims of a mob of undisciplined, all-powerful fanatics.

Small attention was paid now to his movements, but there was nothing
he could do. The pack animals and their kits remained undisturbed and
in readiness. But every exit from the suite of inner chambers was
efficiently barred to the goddess. It was as though he was to be given
every opportunity to escape and leave her there. But even if it had
occurred to him to do so the chances are that he would not have gone
far without being overtaken by an accident.

The thing looked hopeless. Even Alexandra, with her capacity for
deriving satisfaction from the very air she breathed, began to chafe
as the weeks went by. There they were. And there, by the mercy of
Providence, they might live to a ripe old age and die.

He of the turquoises, it was plain, had been until now the local
representative of heaven on earth. And him Dorin chalked up for special
attention. As fellow priests they had long discussions, often ending in
rather heated arguments which Dorin, who had dabbled in many cults and
held views of one kind or another on all subjects, would have regarded
as priceless under happier circumstances. And as fellow men they took
one another’s measure, and each recognized an adversary worthy of his
steel.

The priest was inclined to be insatiable as regarded the
goddess-woman’s past. Dorin drew him always subtly toward her future,
and in this way was able to get home with a few good ones. He had
mingled with the multitude and he had heard things which served his
purpose. And he began at last to move cautiously toward his goal.
Gradually, cloaked with hints and deferential silences but looming
larger always, it dawned on the turquoised man that his position, his
very priesthood, was becoming untenable. He had been master there, it
was true. He had ruled unchallenged, and the post was a good one. Then
had come this goddess-woman out of the blue, and his pedestal, to say
nothing of his life, was threatened. It was a new idea to him and he
did not like it at all. He had been doing very well as he was. And now
it seemed that through no desire of hers there was a movement on foot
to dispense with him entirely and enthrone the heaven-born wearer of
the robe.

It was naturally not a notion which appealed to him. He said so by
the hour. And Dorin would spread his hands and lift his shoulders in
exaggerated fatalism. One knew how one’s people were. Superstitions
ran away with them. Like children, one’s people. But, he confided, it
need not go on. Shir Shan was weary for her own land beyond hills and
water. They had been very kind here, but it was not a life that she
was accustomed to. She pined. She drooped. Her beneficent powers were
waning. A sick goddess was no good to any one, and might even become an
incubus. But he, who was her high priest and who understood her ways,
would undertake even now to convey her safely hence to her own land if
it could be arranged--provided it were arranged soon....

The turquoised man was eying him betwixt suspicion and relief.
_Something_ was bound to be arranged soon, prophesied Dorin
philosophically, and left it there.

Repeated crises of nerves had finally taught the prisoners to sleep
when they had a chance, and they were necessarily fatalists of a
sort, anyway. And so one night Dorin, who slept on a pallet across
Alexandra’s threshold, woke from dreamless slumber to a hand on his
shoulder and another over his mouth.

Some one wanted a private word with him. And as he lay looking up
into the face so near his own, he saw by the star-glow through the
open lattice that there were turquoises in its ears. He signified a
willingness to listen, and they withdrew amiably enough to the window
and there conversed at some length in the sinister sibilances of the
whispered vernacular.

There was truth, said the turquoised man, in what Dorin had told him
of his own diminishing favor. He had threatened and stormed and made
magic to no avail. The idea of change gained ground. He admitted
ingenuously that it had occurred to him to try if the goddess would not
bleed to death like a human being. But her dead body would have been
an inconvenience to him. Besides--here the cobra eyes wandered over
Dorin’s lean and lazy length--he desired no dealings with her. But if
she were just to disappear without a trace it could hardly be called
any of his affair. _He_ was not interested in her. And goddesses
were undependable people. If she were simply to vanish into the blue
as she had come from out it, that day when they spoke her name in the
council hall, and leave him in peace....

Dorin thought it over gravely, leaning against the casement. He
conceded the entire reasonableness of the turquoised gentleman’s
aversion to Shir Shan’s continued presence there, and commended
his foresight with regard to violent measures. He agreed that the
suggestion that she should disappear was feasible. There would have
to be horses, of course, and many days’ supplies. He himself was but
human, with human needs....

He was graciously urged to take his own kits with him, as much as one
extra pony would carry. The departure of more than three animals would
involve too much of a stir and be unwise. His servant, regrettably,
must be left behind. Himself, the goddess-woman, and three ponies. That
was all.

Dorin thought it would do, but-- There could hardly be any objection,
he supposed, to Shir Shan’s taking with her that which she had come
for and which was rightfully hers? Of course, he added as a flicker of
doubt passed over the sharp features of the man before him, she would
ask no embarrassing questions concerning the reward she had brought
and which had mysteriously disappeared the night of the festival.
Moreover-- His fingers were busy at his waist a moment, and then a
small khaki-covered roll, stuffed stiff and heavy, was deftly inserted
into the girdle of the turquoised man’s robe. Shir Shan never failed
to reward her faithful ones with more than her good will, smiled Dorin
sweetly. And when might the vanishing be arranged? _Tonight!_ He
straightened against the casement. Very well, he would wake Shir Shan
at once.

He found her already awake, fully dressed, kneeling by the doorway
peering through the parted curtains to make sure everything was all
right with him. He noted that her revolver was ready to her hand. Dear,
valiant Sandy!

With the robe rolled into a bundle under her arm, they followed the
swift, noiseless shadow which was the turquoised man through a darkness
which felt as darkness feels when a clock has stopped ticking. Dorin
knew that feel in the air--lifted his chin to it with dilated nostrils,
like a wild thing--and saw with his trained cat’s eyes that the trail
was blazed with huddled shapes where he had been wont to encounter
watchmen. His hand closed on Sandy’s elbow, and he grinned grimly at
the wholesale slaughter which would be laid at his door when morning
came.

Thus they reached the steps in the star-glow, and so passed out to
the stables. And that was the last they ever saw of the man with the
turquoises in his ears. But no one stopped them as they rode forth,
silent, a little awed at the dreadful ease of it, shaping their course
for India.




                               CHAPTER VI


SINCE the annihilation of time and space by the telegraph, nothing
from a famous actress’ first child to the disappearance into space of
an Englishman’s wife can be accomplished in private. And so the lurid
word went forth that Alexandra Marley and Blaise Dorin were believed to
be lost in the wilds of Central Asia, whither they had gone together
in search of adventure and romance. Weird speculations were made as
to their probable fate. Old stories were raked up, dating back to the
Mutiny, and new ones were invented--blood-curdling tales of mutilation
and slow death. In a temporary lull in domestic murders and divorce,
wars and rumors of wars, the whole of Alexandra’s spectacular story
came to light. _Ingarsen’s daughter!_ Oh, well, all the Ingarsens
were like that!

Even allowing for accidents, the pair were long overdue on the Indian
Border, and no word had come through. Bokhara shrugged its shoulders.
Calcutta sighed a patient, official sigh, and wished there was
something that could be done. London looked very worried and said that
something ought to be done. And women from Edinburgh to Simla called
Alexandra sporting or mad, according to their lights, and some of them
were kinder to their nice, stoutish husbands, because home was not such
a bad place to be, after all.

On the Indian frontier, where the news was naturally worst and traveled
fastest, men either shook their heads or took it without blinking, as
the case might be. And those who did not know Blaise Dorin talked too
much, twisting the knife in those who loved him.

Starke was frantic--it was he who gave the interviews--and said that if
Blaise Dorin had but taken his advice in the beginning and done exactly
as he wished they would both be safe in Calcutta or Bombay at that
moment, and the life of a beautiful woman would never have been forfeit.

Clement suffered as acutely as only a kindly, mistaken, bewildered man
can suffer, and blamed everybody and every thing except perhaps the
utter helplessness of a seventeen-year-old girl pitched into marriage.
And he thanked heaven that his mother had taken to her bed, after
commanding him to institute divorce proceedings, and need not know
the rest. “A Marley!” she would say. “Her mother was a Marley!” She
seemed to feel that excommunication from the clan, a sort of public
drumming out of the ranks, would in some way wipe the stain from the
family escutcheon. I think in the end it killed her, it and nothing
else, so that she died of being no longer proud to hold up her head.
Meanwhile, carried bodily on the wave of her relentless will, the
divorce proceedings went forward--a dreadful mockery to every one else
concerned.

And Susan, who had known an angel and been cast out of heaven, instead
of crying herself to sleep for that all kindness and beauty seemed
to have been taken from her, now lay awake staring into the dark,
imagining horrors, remembering how once she had dared to touch that
bowed, golden head, hating with a murderous frenzy that drove her nails
into her hands, a harsh, hideous old woman who was somehow to blame and
who was at that moment dying comfortably in her bed.

But Taunton, after the first strenuous hour when he didn’t believe
anything and his vocabulary wouldn’t stretch, threw up everything,
stopped for nothing, and arrived gaunt-eyed and grim in India. It was
during the hot weather, and two of every three men he wanted to see
were on leave in Kashmir, Simla, Darjeeling--as far apart as possible.

Doggedly, he set to work. And finally one night toward midnight he
paced the flower-filled living-room of a bungalow in Simla, alternately
pleading with and swearing at a man who had earned the reputation of
being able to move mountains.

“But _why_ can’t you send troops up there? Dorin’s alive! I know
he is! _You_ know he is! They can’t kill Dodo just for fun! But
he’s in some beastly hole. He’s fighting some fearful odds, holding
out, hoping against hope that we’ll come for him in time! Oh, my God,
_how_ can you sit there smokin’ that damn’ cigar and quibble about
things with official names! Thirst--death--torture--are _those_ in
your sacred treaties and army orders? I tell you you’ve _got_ to
help me find him!”

The man who could move mountains watched him with tired, kind eyes.
The love of man for man is a beautiful thing, a pitiful thing. And he
had seen it on the rack before now.

“There’s really nothing I can do, old boy,” he said gently, when
he could. “It’s no case for the Army. He--he’s just one man, you
know--going his own way at his own risk. He--he’s just Dodo Dorin, a
madman who has always pulled through somehow--so far. He knew when
he went up there that Government would not, could not back his play.
And besides--we know only that they left Bokhara with just three
servants, for some insane reason, working east, purposely avoiding
the usual trade routes--we know that they deliberately struck out
into back-of-beyond and vanished into thin air. There’s no way of
tracing them, nor of knowing how far they have come. It was a suicidal
performance, but there it is. Dodo has as many lives as a cat, we both
know that, but--this time he’s been hampered with--_her_. And
there’s no reason to believe that a whole regiment scattered through
the Hills now could find them and bring them in safe. How--” He knocked
the ash carefully from his cigar. “How did he happen to take her--do
_you_ know?”

“No,” said Taunton, and drew a little whistling breath of pain through
his teeth. “I suppose she just--_went_.”

The man who could move mountains brooded over his cigar.

“Yes,” he said. “Yes, I suppose she would. All the same--no job for a
woman.”

“I’m not sure--” began Taunton, and stopped.

“Not sure--?” prodded the man who could move mountains, gently.

Taunton swung round on one heel with a sigh, and passed a hand over his
hair.

“Oh, _I_ don’t know--sort of queer feeling, when you’re with
her--sort of--well, _not_ the sort of thing you feel with--women.”

There was a silence.

“I knew her father.” The cigar glowed under a long pull. “I knew
him--well.”

“He was before my time.” Taunton spoke softly, suddenly shy before
something he had not guessed. “I fancy she’s like him, though. You
ought to see her. Tall and fair--and keen. God, she was _keen_!”

“I suppose,” said the slow, tired voice behind the cigar, “I suppose
it’s the way Ingarsen’s daughter would want it.”

As he spoke the words, she was riding headlong through the dark, with
Dorin’s horse pounding just behind, bullets singing over her lowered
head. And she was thinking with an irresponsible chuckle catching at
her breath how lucky they were that it wasn’t Dodo who had taught these
blighters to shoot!




                              CHAPTER VII


IT was one of those courts the lion and the lizard keep; a temple stuck
on to the side of a hill, with a broken parapet jutting out over sheer
space. Rank undergrowth encroached on its decaying symmetries, for it
was situated unwholesomely near the outlying corruption of a spring,
once pure and fresh, now bubbling a death-rattle through lush foliage.
It had never been a healthful spot, the temple of Shir Shan, and it
had become less so since her beneficent influence had been withdrawn.
Things crawled and scampered across its widening fissures in the
great jungle game of killing before you yourself are killed, and the
grandsire of all the cobras had his abode in an underground chamber,
where he no doubt reflected upon the legend of his fathers that a
decent, well-meaning cobra was fed at regular intervals.

No sound disturbed the long torpor of Shir Shan’s temple except the
lisp of its foliage invasion, the glide, patter, or pounce of its
silent, eternally warring interlopers, and the terrible, gasping gurgle
of the dying spring, which rose and fell like a labored breathing in
the stillness.

And then in the slow, clammy hour before dawn, the ghost of an old
clamor echoed down the valley--shouts and the pounding of many hooves,
and the more modern, business-like rattle of rifles. Twice the racket
converged on the deserted shrine of Shir Shan, and twice held off and
passed to one side. There were riders on the crest of the hill way
above it--riders in the river-bed far below. The dark spat flame.
And Shir Shan’s temple waited, cadaverous, breathing a death-rattle,
peering into the dawn.

Two came panting to the foot of the wall beneath the crumbling parapet,
feeling their way through the protecting blackness, and one of them was
half crawling, half dragged. They spoke in whispers, and the grandsire
of all the cobras, beyond a break in the wall, heard, but being old and
very incurious, paid no attention.

“I can climb it,” said Alexandra.

“Not alone.”

“There’s an easier way in for you, but I can find it better from
inside. It will be safe to use the torch inside.”

“But it’s ten miles straight up here,” he objected. “And those rocks
will give under you.”

“The railing of that parapet is not more than ten feet above my head!”
she told him stoutly. “And we can’t wait; it’s getting light enough to
see handholds. Soon it will be light enough to be seen going up. You
stay here. Take it easy. Lie low. I won’t be long.”

Swift and sure as a boy, she came up the jagged face of the wall. Small
landslides marked her passage--things tottered under her momentarily
and righted themselves again as she left them--until with a little
grunt of achievement she swung over the railing of the parapet and
dropped to the temple floor.

Her riding-breeches and boots, once so smart, were torn and smudged
with earth and foliage. Her shirt was open at the throat, her face
and neck were smeared with dirt and perspiration, and on the sleeve
of her jacket was a dark stain from Dorin’s wound. She wore her topi
militantly, with the chin-strap. So came the last of the Ingarsens,
breathing rather hard as she took her place at the end of the
line, hunted and tired and cool-headed, with the odds against her
forty-to-one and no takers.

She pulled the electric torch from her belt, where it had somewhat
unwielidy made the ascent, and turned the light on the interior of
the temple. Everywhere there was the débris of crumbling columns and
rotting masonry. At her left rose a decayed throne with an altar-like
platform in front of it, reached from three sides by a dozen shallow
steps. An enormous image, blind, for its eyes had been sapphires, was
smashed and pitted with missiles and black with ancient fires. Beyond,
the rear of the temple lay in indistinguishable shadow, with the
glimmer of yet more broken columns, and from there came the ghastly
respirations of the spring. To her right ran a great wall with an
opening and a fallen lintel at a crazy angle across it.

“Shocking bad repair the place is in,” ran her irrepressible thoughts,
as she ducked through the doorway, the torchlight preceding her.
“Kenilworth Castle was never like this!”

She came out into a kind of inner court, crossed it, squeezed through
a hole in the wall, and emerged a hundred feet up the hill and to the
right of where she had left Dorin. She stood a moment, taking things
in. The pursuit seemed to have drawn off on a false scent. The East was
still blank and cold, but would not stay so long. A chill wind, like a
sigh from the dead, touched her face. She drew a long breath of it, and
that odd blaze leaped up suddenly in her weary eyes. _Life!_ It
was still hers!

She took her revolver from its holster and examined the chamber. Empty.
With a shrug she snapped it shut and tossed it into a corner of the
wall; frowned at a twinge in her wrist as she did so and paused to
wrap her grimy handkerchief around the sprain, jerking the knot tight
between her teeth, before she started down the slope.

Painfully and with long rests, with much tugging and some happy
nonsense from Sandy, Dorin reached the parapet room and sank with a
groaning sigh at the foot of the steps. She surveyed him anxiously.

He was wounded in the hip, the stain had spread to his shirt, and he
looked generally done for. Clutched safe in his left hand he held the
khaki-covered bundle which was Shir Shan’s robe. She put it behind his
head for a pillow, without comment. It and the torch were all they
had left. The useless rifles were miles back along the road where
the cartridges gave out. The kits were on the winded horses they
had abandoned at the bottom of the hill. She had had her hands full,
without even a canteen. Hands that had been cold but steady, as Dorin
swayed from the saddle into her arms.

“Let’s have a look at this place.” He took the torch and the finger
of light explored the throne, the broken columns, and the blackness
beyond, where the spring went on choking to death. “Mmmmm--picturesque,
at least!” he said.

“We-ell--” Alexandra, her thumbs hooked into her pockets, looked about
her at all she could see of it. “Don’t you think they’ve overdone it
just a bit?” She stood before the image, a small, impudent figure,
staring up. “It’s all sort of gone-at-the-knees!” she complained.

“And nobody cares!” remarked Dorin, feebly sententious. “Nobody loves
her any more!”

“‘The Goddess of your sacrifice has flown away,’” quoted Alexandra,
and swung round on a derisive heel at her own cleverness. “Me, I’m the
‘Deity on wandering wing,’” she added, tapping her chest.

For hours now they had played a brave game against what was very near
to hopelessness. Dorin’s laughter ended on a half sob of pain, and she
sobered.

“Look here, we’ve got to do something about that hole in your side.”

“Let me see your gun,” he said, bracing.

“It’s--out there,” with a jerk of her head toward the court.

“Fetch it.”

“Not now. I think I’d better----”

“It’s empty, then.”

“Possibly.”

“I told you to keep one.”

“I needed it back there on the road.”

“Take my knife.”

“What for?”

“Take my knife, I tell you,” he repeated peremptorily, and added as she
fumbled with the buckle of the belt, “You know how to use it.”

“They’ve gone on East. They think we’re up ahead.” She was fastening
the belt round her own waist. “We’ll lie doggo here through the day if
necessary. The horses are too done in to go far on their own. We’ll
find them still there in the ravine, I fancy, when things quiet down.”

“Have we any water?”

“None. Do you want it badly?”

“No. I only wondered.”

“Listen.” The gurgle of the spring filled in the silence. “There’s
water back there. If I could get some cold water on that wound----”

“Never mind that now. Want to rest a minute. Sandy, I want you to
promise me--that if I should go off unexpectedly----”

“Stow it, Dodo!”

“Promise you won’t go fooling about trying for water while it’s light,
though. They’re not out of the neighborhood yet.”

“Then I’d better go-look-see now, before dawn. Perhaps----”

A distant yell broke in. They listened tensely, holding each other’s
eyes. Nothing more.

“You stay here,” he commanded at last.

“Who do you suppose these ruffians are?” she demanded in a half
whisper, much as one speaks with lowered voice in the presence of a
ringing telephone. “Could they have overtaken us from the monastery?”

“Easily. Or it may be some roving robber band who either got wind of
the robe or are merely looking for a bit of fun. In any case, I don’t
mind owning, I wish we were well out of here.”

“If it were only bandits, I suppose they’d hold us for ransom, or
something.”

“Or something,” he agreed, ironically, and grinned. “‘Only bandits’
puts it well!”

“I was thinking--if they’re a delegation from the monastery, we might
look for something else again,” she reflected.

“You’ve got the knife. Don’t be afraid of it.”

“Well, they haven’t got us yet!” She straightened cheerfully. “How far
do you think we are from the Pass?”

“Hard to tell. Especially at this rate.” He laid a hand over his wound
and drew breath between his teeth.

“We’d planned to sleep on British territory tomorrow night.”

“We’ll do well if we sight this end of the Pass on the day after, now.
And that’s provided we haven’t hopelessly mislaid the horses.”

“Is there a surgeon at the Fort?”

“Doubt it. It’s a native garrison, you know, with an English officer or
two.”

“Then they can jolly well send down for a surgeon! We’ll get you as far
as the Fort and there we stick till you’re patched up!”

“Oh, Sandy--if there were words to tell how splendid you are!”

“Don’t talk rot! I’m having the time of my life!” She moved away,
embarrassed but proud.

“Yes--you would say that.” His eyes followed her, hoarding the sight
of her. “There’s only one thing you’re really afraid of, isn’t there?
That’s sentiment. Don’t worry. I’m not going to blub over you now. But
I wish to God I hadn’t let you in for this!”

“We’ll pull through somehow! And besides--I wasn’t meant to die in my
bed. I’m sure of that, since I’ve been with you.”

“Had a good time?” he asked wistfully.

“Corking!” There could be no doubt about that!

“I know,” he said. “You were born to this, as I was. You’d rather it
was short, if need be, but swift. So would I. Oh, bless you, Sandy,
I--” He broke off, and lay watching her a moment with a somewhat rueful
grin. “Do you remember something you said one day in London about the
great adventure of an hour’s uncertainty between life and death?”

She laughed aloud, lifting her face to the thrill of it as to a kiss,
her arms embracing life.

“Yes,” he admitted. “You’ve got it now!”

“Yes, I’ve got it!” she cried exultantly. “I love life tonight! Will
you ever forget that ride in a million years? Oh, it was beastly luck,
their hitting you! But we’ll get through somehow, and----”

“And if we shouldn’t?”

“Why, then--you will still have given me exactly what I wanted.”

He was looking at her thoughtfully, his mind’s eye seeing a red plush
room and a naked, neglected piano--a tea-table practically untouched--a
white, tense face--a gray gown....

“There were violets in your belt,” he said.

“Violets? Oh, you mean that day--” Her eyes widened. She came and
sat down on the step beside him, her feet tucked under her. “Those
violets,” she began slowly, “those violets started everything! If I
had not bought those violets--if I had gone to Tilbury instead, that
day--if I had not gone home to tea--why, if I had not been there when
Mr. Starke came--_none_ of it would have happened! At least, not
that day. And then you would have been gone.”

“Starke?” He had raised himself a little to look up at her.
“_Starke?_” he insisted.

“I didn’t tell you--it didn’t matter--there hasn’t been time to tell
you,” she apologized. “Starke came that afternoon, you know. That was
how I knew you were leaving that night. And--well, he asked me to go
away with him--so that there could be a divorce, so that he could marry
me, so that I could sit in the lap of luxury all my days and wear
pearls and ermine. He--he thought that was what I wanted, poor dear!”

“Starke!” he repeated, trying to grasp it.

“Yes, and so you see--when she began to say those things to Clem about
his--Starke’s coming there--well, you see, _that_ having only
just happened--Clem came in while I was having him--Starke--shown out,
the way they do on the stage--_that_ being the case, though I
certainly never dreamed, and it wasn’t exactly my fault, was it----?”

“That being the case--?” he prompted, spellbound.

“Why, then, don’t you see, when she began to say those things to Clem
about--about-- Well, the whole business rather had me treed,” she
explained. “And so I sort of had hysterics, or something, and Clem went
off to the club for dinner and--and I came with you!”

He was staring at her, raised on one elbow, his eyes already big and
bright with fever, his mouth, still sweet and fine of line despite a
three days’ beard, ajar with astonishment.

“But you never told me,” he said stupidly. “You--you never told me
this!”

“There wasn’t time.” It was the way she looked at it. That part of it
was over. She had been too busy, since, to think of it. There had been
so many other things to talk to him about, since. Things that mattered.
Starke didn’t matter. Not even Clem mattered, now. There wasn’t time
for them any more. Still, she frowned back across the months. “And
that’s not all,” she said darkly. “She sacked Susan.”

“She--? Susan--?” he groped.

“My maid.” She set her lips. “I liked Susan. She tried so hard. She
liked me too, I think. And just because tea was late-- That was
hard--having Susan dismissed before my very eyes! She cried.” She
brooded a moment. “I _liked_ Susan,” she insisted softly.

He had always dimly surmised that there must have been some sort
of row. But now, from her half sentences, her pauses, her quaint
reticences, her almost Etonian laconics, it began to assume in his eyes
the proportions of one of the decisive battles of the world. What on
earth had she been up against? Her own servant dismissed--Starke gone
mad--her husband playing the fool--and the old lady.... He had never
met the old lady.

“_She_ never liked me,” said Sandy, at this point, “because I
hadn’t a baby.”

She meant the old lady. It was uncanny the way she followed a man’s
thoughts. He settled back against the step, veiling his eyes with his
lashes, keeping careful silence so that if she were minded she might
talk it all out now that she seemed inclined to begin--might get it
all out of her system, now, while there was still time.

There was a long silence, which he forbore to break.

“I _meant_ to have one,” said Sandy, looking back along the
path she had come. “I thought it would be--well, something to talk
to--provided it wasn’t too much like Clem.”

That opened another vista to him. Sandy wanting a baby. Or rather,
Sandy wanting something to talk to that wasn’t too much like Clem. He
waited, among these astounding revelations, for more.

She sighed.

“It didn’t come off, though. _She_ said that from what she saw of
me perhaps it was just as well--” Another silence. Then-- “Were you
ever ill?” she queried suddenly. “I mean--so ill you heard them say you
couldn’t last the night out?”

“No,” he murmured, watching, fascinated, while another huge block of
the puzzle fell into place.

She was staring out over his head at the sky beyond the parapet. Dawn.
Dawn between the curtains, reddening to a patch of sunlight reflected
on the wall. And one had lived to see another day. One had lived--for
this day, breaking now. For value received!




                              CHAPTER VIII


THEY sat so for what seemed a long time, but it was really less than
five minutes, her eyes lovingly on the pearling sky beyond the parapet,
his on her hand where it lay on the step between them, grimed and with
a barked and bleeding knuckle, the handkerchief bandage peeping from
beneath her cuff. At last he reached out and covered the hand with his,
almost diffidently, and she looked down at him with a quick, anxious
smile.

“Oh, Dodo, what a beast I am! You must be hurting--just like
anything--and I sit here----”

“Look here,” he said. “If we seem to have thrown those beggars off the
track in the morning I want you to try for the horses and run for it.”

“Run for it?” she repeated, amazed.

“Alone.”

“Dodo, that’s an insult--no less!”

“Half a mo.” He was looking down at the hand in his, at its slim,
straight fingers, its delicacy, its strength. He loved her hands.... He
roused himself to argument. “What did we come for, anyway? Just a lark?
Or are we on business? The robe is here, a man has invested a huge sum
in it--and one of us is whole. If there is any chance of getting his
property through to the Pass we must take that chance. I wasn’t just
staging a picnic for you when I brought you along. I knew it was a
two-man job. Alone, I should have failed. You’ve got to carry on.”

“And what’s to become of you?”

“I’ll follow--more slowly. You can send back for me.”

“No, thanks. I’ll take you with me.”

“You take the robe,” he said. “That’s enough.”

“Oh, what’s the robe!” she cried impatiently.

“Our job.”

She was unimpressed. Her eyes rested on the khaki-covered bundle behind
his head, and they held no love for it. A yellow rag with a few bits
of glass attached--a fine thing to carry tenderly down to the Pass and
chaperon back to London while Dodo died! The symbol of an ancient evil
when weighed in the balance with the splendid, laughing flame that
was Dodo’s life was found hopelessly wanting. Disdain for its utter
worthlessness grew in her gaze, so that Dorin, watching, in sheer
desperation gave himself away.

“Oh, for God’s sake, Sandy, take the robe and go! It’s your only
chance!”

“My--only--chance! So that’s your game! It’s not the robe you’re
worrying about at all. It’s me!” She grinned at him, amused at the
childishness of such a scheme, chagrined that she had not seen through
him at once. “And to think I nearly let you bluff me!”

“Now, Sandy, we’ve got to face this thing,” he said. “You won’t like
it. For that matter, neither do I. But here’s how it stands. This hole
in my side is bad medicine. In a few days--a few hours--I’ll be out
of my head--helpless--a dead weight. You can’t lift and carry me.” He
waited a moment, looking down at their clasped fingers because he dared
not look into her face just then. “You came in Bob’s place,” he went on
slowly. “Better than nothing, you said! But I know and so will you if
you stop to think--that Bob himself couldn’t get me down to the Pass in
time.”

“Perhaps Bob Taunton couldn’t, but I can!” she cried, secretly
appalled, but fighting it grimly. “I will! I’ve _got_ to!”

“No. You’ll only be throwing away every chance you have in the world.”

“Now, get this, Dodo. I don’t leave you.” With a quick, hard pressure
on his hands she rose and walked away. “There _are_ things no
fellow can do,” she muttered, kicking at the floor.

“But it’s no good bucking destiny, old thing. As you said a minute
ago--I’ve had my fun. But you’re not done for yet! You may go on, God
knows how long, riding the wind, as you call it--taking your chances as
they come----”

“Save your strength, Dodo. I stick.”

“Oh, Sandy--you gorgeous fool!”

He lay looking after her with shadowed, smiling eyes, her very danger
forgotten in the almost creative pride he had of her. She turned,
throwing wide her arms in a gesture of impotent energy.

“Oh, Lord, I wish we had a couple of rifles! I’d like to see them take
us here, and let the Government worry it out afterwards!”

He smiled.

“Nothing that happens here concerns the Government. We’re playing a
lone hand, at our own risk. It’s no affair of the British Army’s what
happens to us. I had fair warning that our present enterprise has no
international significance!”

“Well, in a way, that’s comforting!” she said brightly. “I had one of
those devils on my conscience! Teach me to shoot, you said! You did!”
she grinned, with satisfaction. “I can!”

“Fire-eater! The good God meant you to be a Lawrence or a Rhodes. And
to think you might never have come into your heritage!”

There was a spurt of distant yells and a shot or two. They listened,
staring at the blank, cold sky outside the parapet. Whatever trail the
pursuit had crossed led on in another direction.

“I don’t know just what is your heritage,” he added in a minute. “But
I’ve an idea that it’s on all sides of us now.”

“Well, whatever it is--we’ll go halves on it!”

“That--makes all the difference.”

His eyes closed wearily, and she caught her breath at his white misery.
It was no good making a fuss, but--she had to do something at once.

“I’m going to see if I can’t find some water and get you more
comfortable. Does it feel pretty terrible?”

“It’s all right,” he assured her, bracing again. “Come and sit down.”

“I wonder--” She was peering over the parapet into the half light
below. “I wonder if I couldn’t get to the horses and bring back a
canteen.” She leaned way out. “I see them! I’m sure I do!”

“Sandy, you heathen, come back here!” he commanded sharply. “Leave the
horses alone, wherever they are. We won’t take any chances like that
till later.”

“Wherever any of this is! I say, where do you think we really are?” She
came back reluctantly from the railing. Orders were orders as long as
he was able to give them.

“In some God and Government forsaken pocket of the Hills near the Roof
of the World.”

“We’ve been going in circles trying to dodge those blighters.
Impossible to tell how far we’ve come in a straight line.”

“Do you know what I think?” He turned the torch full on the eyeless
image, and it seemed there was the glint of gold flake about its
head-dress.

“Yes. We’ve struck it. The lost temple with the record. Those fellows
circled it when we first came toward it, and then they doubled back for
us and skirted it again. And they’re still giving it a wide berth. It’s
haunted.” She swept it with an interested glance. “Full of ghosts!” she
said with relish. “Wonder where they keep themselves!”

“Then that’s Shir Shan.” Dorin was still studying the image.

“Yes, that’s herself.” She went and posed beside it, looking up. “What
a resemblance!” she said, taking off her helmet. “Don’t you notice it?
Round the eyes----”

“Ass!” he chuckled, loving it.

“Fancy we’re safe enough here. No native will risk the spooks.”

“Superstition is a great blessing to the enlightened. Still--with Shir
Shan’s robe as the stake--if they know we’ve got it----”

“I’ll bet you a piece of real Chinese money with a hole in it that we
don’t see anything more of them!”

“Done! And I shan’t at all mind losing!” He looked at her a moment as
she stood before him, straight and slim and smiling, with smooth, fair
hair. “Are you really as game as this?” he queried. “Or haven’t you got
sense enough to be scared? Which is it?”

Laughing, she slapped her hip pocket and brought out her cigarette
case, man-size, his gift to her at Port Said.

“One--two--three--four,” she counted cheerfully. “And yours is empty
and my horse has the rest. Much good may it do him!” She lighted his
and then her own, with a steady hand. “Listen. I’m sure there’s water
back there. Hear it? A spring. I’m going to get some and look after
that wound.” She took the torch and started off briskly.

“No, no, I’d rather you didn’t. _Sandy!_”

She paused at the foot of the image, ridiculously small and fragile
looking in the lee of its clumsy bulk.

“You’ve got the jumps, old man. I’ll be within hailing distance.” And
she went on, disobedient after all, into the shadows. Her voice came
back to him gayly. “Golly! There goes the father of all serpents!”

He knew she didn’t like snakes. It was not fear, it was the recoil of
a warm and vital creature from something swift and cold which struck
unfairly--an instinctive revulsion as old as the Hills. But she went on
steadily, the point of light preceding her, until all sight and sound
of her were lost among the pillars. He lay back with his eyes closed,
surrendering to the waves of pain and sickness that broke over him once
the anesthetic of her presence was gone.

He knew, as such men often do fatalistically know, that his allotted
time was up. It was the hunch. He was done. How to get her out of it,
that was the question. How to make her leave him and go on alone, till
her last chance had been exhausted. He was perhaps still not too far
gone to plan for her safety. She must go on. Alone. And he must stay
here and die. Alone. Else they would both assuredly perish, but he
would go first. How to spare her that, he wondered. He must get her
away before fever and delirium claimed him--before her last memory of
him should become a horror unspeakable. A man cannot die like a man if
it be not given to him to know what he is doing. A man is best alone
when the cards are stacked against him.

He found himself wishing helplessly for Bob Taunton. Bob would find a
way. Bob would get her down to India, would make her understand that
she must not stay on his account. Bob would never let her know the
hideousness of watching some one die, and of being left alone with
something that had once been warm and quick and--fond of her. He could
not have her going through that. If he told her that he loved her--if
he made her understand what he himself had only just come to understand
fully--that she mattered to him more than anything.... No, that would
never do, then she would stick for his sake. And he mustn’t let her
stick. He mustn’t _let_ Sandy die.

The infinite preciousness of her. He kept coming back to that. The joy
of her gay comradeship, the wonder of her mad enthusiasms, the warmth
of her loyalty and love--for she did love him in her way, he knew,
her weird way, betwixt child and man, selfless and self-conscious. He
had known well in his time and become accustomed to the desolation of
that inevitable loneliness which must now and then engulf the hardiest
solitary soul. And then Sandy had come, laughing and strong and
beautiful, stretching her valiant stride to his, and it was unthinkable
now how lonely he had been, always, without knowing quite where it
hurt. Sandy fitted into one’s heart so. Her roots went so deep. She was
such a plucky little beggar....

He lay there, hardly breathing, his head pillowed against Shir Shan’s
robe, his mind already feeling clouded, frowning because for once he
could not seem to think clearly. Instead he kept seeing Sandy.

Sandy climbing the wall in the dim dawn while he crouched below,
following with bated breath the progress of a slim shadow he could
scarcely see, hearing things come rattling down, fancying she
slipped.... Sandy on the monastery steps, swathed in supple gold, her
blue eyes eerie with a pagan flame.... Sandy sitting Brugglesmith like
a little warrior, rather flushed and quite breathless, boundlessly
happy because he told her she had done well.... Sandy running
heedlessly with outstretched arms to meet her first camel, and how the
brute had tried to bite her.... Sandy in that house in Bloomsbury, with
violets in her belt....

Violets. If she had not bought them, she said.... He had smelt them as
he entered the room. He had felt them cool against his fingers that
time he took her hands. He loved her hands. She need not know, but--he
must touch--her hands--once more....




                               CHAPTER IX


AND as he lay there at the foot of the steps leading to the altar, very
still, scarcely breathing, a head rose cautiously over the railing,
while its scared Asiatic eyes probed the shadows of the interior. Then
a sole adventuresome bandit, badly frightened at his own rashness,
bestrode the railing and surveyed the scene.

A detachment of his comrades was not far off, but trespassing on
haunted ground among devils is a lonesome business, and he wished he
had not come. He hung there, astride the railing, clinging to the
unsympathetic company of his horse below, fortifying himself with
thoughts of yellow topazes and tribal glory, until a deeper shadow
at the foot of the steps caught his wandering eye. No devil, that
shadow. He hitched soundlessly along the railing to look more closely,
to verify his first impression that the shadow was shaped like a
man. Undoubtedly it was a man; dead, or something like it; helpless,
certainly. A man in khaki with a white face--one of the two they
sought--one of the two who possessed fabulous wealth. The Asiatic
astride the railing became convinced that this was his lucky day.

Whereupon Dorin’s ears were rent with a yell that seemed to have its
origin somewhere beyond the mouth of hell, and raising himself with
a jerk he beheld a ghoul dancing on the railing against the faintly
luminous sky, and the noise it made proclaimed it human in its way. It
was an excellent if lively target, but there were no cartridges. Sandy
had needed them back there on the trail. Well, it was all a part of
the dreadful nightmare of her danger. Perhaps even now if she wasn’t
seen----

“Sandy!” he shouted, without turning his head in her direction. “Oh,
Sandy! Lie low, wherever you are, do you hear? Stay where you are! Keep
still!”

The dancing demon turned at the first sound of Dorin’s voice and
dropped to the floor, a ready hand searching out a knife. As he
advanced, his darting gaze caught the bundle behind Dorin’s head, and a
glitter came into it and stayed there. First of all, he would have that
bundle.

Dorin waited, lying quiet, his gray eyes looking coolly into the eyes
of murder. Sandy had dropped her empty gun somewhere. His knife was
belted round her waist. He had no weapon, and little strength to use
one. He could only wait, quietly, so that she would not try to help him
and be caught herself. If they killed him and took the robe and went
without seeing her, she might still stand a chance. Oh, Sandy, there
were violets in your belt that day.... Life and death both different
because of violets in your belt....

The native had become suspicious of Dorin’s very stillness. He felt
that a man who lay and looked at death like that must have something
up his sleeve. He circled uncertainly, muttering to himself, and so
came between his victim and something that might well have driven Dorin
quite mad--Sandy’s stealthy shadow among the shadows at the rear of the
temple.

She had found the spring and discovered how to set her cupped hand
between the rock and the stagnant pool each time the thing breathed
out. Thus the spurt of fresh water could be caught, and she found it
odorless and without a corrupted taste. Good water, always, at its
source. She had washed her face, and selected a place near-by for Dorin
to rest while she dressed his wound. If only she could get to the kits
on the horses for some bandages.... What was that yelling? It sounded
very close. It must come from-- She was on her feet, listening tautly
with parted lips. Then Dodo’s voice. _Lie low?_ Why? The yelling
had stopped abruptly. _Dodo--!_ She started, instinctively on
tiptoe, toward the throne room. Something was moving in there. She
flitted from pillar to pillar, hugging the shadows, losing no time
but being very careful, her light step on the grit of the stone floor
blurred by the ceaseless bubble and suck of the spring. Reaching
for the knife, she found the torch still in her hand, and stuck it
into her belt again. Not wise to use it now. If only the place were
lighter! Something moved between her and the steps where Dodo should
be. Something that went on two feet, as he could not. She caught its
silhouette against the sky--a native! It swept her like fire. They had
found him! They would kill him, lying there....

She never knew quite how it happened. But then she had run into a man’s
broad back from behind, with Dodo’s knife held as she had been taught
to hold it at necessity, pointing slightly up, her weight behind it as
she came.... With a queer gasping grunt the man threw up his arms and
sagged to the floor. Again that wave of fire swept through her. She had
killed!

“One of the neatest things I ever saw,” remarked a voice.

Dodo was all right, then. She had been in time. But she could not get
her eyes off the thing which sprawled, twitching, half across Dorin’s
feet, half on the steps. There had not been much room to spare.

“Is it as easy as that?” she asked.

“If you know how.” His voice was purposefully philosophic. He wanted to
laugh, and he wanted to cry over her. He wished Bob Taunton had seen
it. Nothing could hold her. Nothing. Again his own reaction was lost in
sheer pride of her. The pluck of her! The gorgeous, crazy pluck of her!
He hoped she wouldn’t wobble now that it was over. “Now, don’t let it
get you, old thing,” he warned. “It was this thing here--or me. Thanks
to you, I’m here to tell the tale.” He peered up at her with a white
smile. “From the extraordinary cleanness of our hero’s face, I judge
she has found water.”

“Yes, I did.”

Something was creeping over her fingers, warm and wet.... She regarded
the knife with interest, shifted it to the other hand, and frankly
wiped her right on her breeches. Vaguely it flitted across her mind
that a revolver was preferable for such matters. Tidier. No sense in
running out of cartridges like that. One lost one’s head and wasted
ammunition, and this is what it brought one to. Beastly business. But
what was one to do? Dodo must have had a bad minute or two before she
got there....

She glanced up from her spread fingers to find him watching her
anxiously, and saw with a pang how white he was--how drawn and parched
and feverish. She must get him more comfortable somehow. Nothing else
mattered. She stooped and matter-of-factly dragged the dead weight off
Dorin’s feet.

“There’s a nice spring back there,” she said. “Clean water. You must
get there--I’ll help you to get there--and then I can----”

“Listen,” he interrupted. “What’s going on outside?”

A distant tumult was growing--murmurs of dissension, it seemed, and
shouts of impatience. Horses’ hooves were pounding up and down below
the parapet.

Out of the mists of Dorin’s pain and giddiness uprose the hunch, and
pointed a relentless finger. He stared at it aghast, and knew it to be
as real, at least, as the Irishman’s banshee. There were such things.
One always knew. But Sandy! What about Sandy! Oh, why had he let her
come!

“That devil spread the glad tidings and they’ve come back for us,” he
said.

She nodded judicially.

“You win,” she conceded. “Lord, what a row!”

The noise seemed much nearer now. Their eyes met, and lingered.

“Well,” he said, and smiled at her wearily, “the game’s up at last.
We’re through, Sandy. Come here.”

“Not the slightest chance of a last minute rescue, either,” she said
thoughtfully.

“Not this time, I’m afraid.”

He reached unobtrusively for the knife on the floor beside him, and
held out an inviting arm to her. He had still not quite finished. He
must have her within reach and decide what he must do quickly when the
time came. Then let them yell.

“The British Army’s missed its cue,” she murmured, still thinking hard.
“Have to take a bow all by ourselves.”

“Come here and sit down. You’ve done all you can, bless you.”

“Just a minute, Dodo, this is too ridiculous----”

“Sandy, come here to me!” he cried sharply, with a glance over his
shoulder.

“Wait, now--let me think.”

She turned the torch on the crumbling altar above him, the rotting
throne, the great bulk of the desecrated image. That was Shir Shan.
She, too, was Shir Shan....

“Give me the robe, quick. Unwrap it!”

Not so much as a by-your-leave. Her grandfathers spoke in her tone.
Together they ripped away the khaki coverings and the great golden
thing spilled out, murmuring to itself of sacrilege against the stone,
while the clamor outside deafened.

Daylight is the essence of logic and reason, the ultimate argument.
Not even the healthiest legendary devils are wholly proof against a
genuine, inevitable dawn such as the one now breaking over the temple
of Shir Shan. Moreover, these were obsolete demons, much stricken in
years, vague wraiths of wraiths, half forgotten shades of a forgotten
race. Some talk there was of waiting for the sun to dispel the
shadow-shrouded riddle of the interior, some question arose as to the
fate of him who shouted triumph no longer, but all this was swept
aside before the primeval desire for more tangible gold than the first
sunbeam. Yelling, the host foregathered at the foot of the wall, and
howling they dismounted and climbed the crumbling stone and reached the
railing.

And at the top of the steps before the altar they beheld, motionless
in a miraculous light, a figure of unearthly beauty in a pose of
divine vengeance, a knife glittering in its upraised hand. Its long,
sun-colored hair lay golden on the magic gold of the robe of Shir Shan,
and its fathomless, far-fixed eyes were unlike any eyes ever seen
before. It did not seem to see or hear or be in any wise aware--and yet
the gleam of its dazzling vestments was stirred by its unmistakable
breathing. It lived. At least it was not mere image. And in the shadows
at its feet huddled the body of a man, and at the bottom of the steps
was another....

The inhuman bay of the man-hunt stopped with a wrench. The mob piled
up, blocking the way to those below. Questions, ejaculations, squeaks
and whispers flickered across the sudden hush. No movement, no sound
came from the golden mystery before the altar. The white light which
showed her was steady, unwinking. They had never seen such a light.

For moments which seemed eons the thing hung in the balance. The gloom
of the interior was chilling with a gray dawn. The spring could be
heard, gasping for breath in the stillness. Dorin’s position hurt his
wound cruelly but he hung on, with set teeth, so that the light might
not waver. Then Alexandra, her eyes fixed on a point in the shadows
straight ahead, sensed rather than saw recognition of the dead bandit
and a movement toward him. They would see that he had died by a human
enough hand. Then they would come to investigate Dodo....

Again something outside her own will acted. The knife left her hand
unerringly and struck, quivering, in the corpse. “_Mine!_” it
seemed to say. She had spent patient hours learning to throw a knife
like that.

There was a yelp, then pandemonium. Resolutely she kept her eyes again
on that spot in the air above their heads, unseeing, unaware, while
with a rush and a scramble, chattering in superstitious terror, they
fled headlong over the parapet, to horse, and away.

Then at last she drew breath, and at the same instant the torch dropped
from Dorin’s hand with a thud. He tried to ease his position, sighed,
and lay still. The robe rustled about her as she sank to her knees
beside him, her fingers seeking the pulse in his throat, and her hair
slipped down heavily across his hands.

“Dodo, old man, we’ve done it again--they’ve gone--Dodo, you’re all
right----?”

With a great effort he opened his eyes and smiled at her. It was good
to have seen her like this--bending over him, her face quite close, and
her hair.... His fingers closed on it wistfully. He was very tired.

“We must get you down to the spring,” she was saying. “I’ll fix you
up, you’ll see!” Still kneeling beside him, she threw off the robe and
rolled it up again, and swiftly gathered her hair into a plait as thick
as her wrist. “Come,” she said, sliding an arm under him. “We’ll get
some water now.”

“Yes--water--must have water now--” he agreed hazily, wondering at her
strength, trying to help her with his own weight. “Sandy, that was
a soft-nosed bullet, I think--I knew a chap once--got a soft-nosed
bullet--where it did some good--these fellows--pretty clumsy--we must
be farther North than I thought--up North they--never could shoot for
nuts----”

They were making slow progress down the steps. Dawn was graying even
the farthest corners now. He sank back against the steps with a short,
impatient sigh.

“I--I think I’d like a cigarette,” he announced.

“Rest a minute, then. I’ll give you one.”

As she drew out her case, her fingers touched something smooth and
cool--she felt it with an inward grin, that carven knot with the
inscription. “So far so good,” she told it approvingly. “Just you keep
it up and I’ll do the rest!”

“Why, Sandy--what’s that rag on your wrist?”

“I gave it a wrench and a scrape getting in here. It’s nothing. Feels a
little stiff.”

“If anything should happen to you now--!” he muttered. “If--if any harm
should come to you--!” He began to laugh unsteadily. “It’s rather a
joke, isn’t it--my saying that--now!”

“Dodo, stop that!” She spoke sharply. “Pull yourself together!”

“Sorry.” He drew on the cigarette she gave him. “It must be the fever
coming on. I--I won’t be much good by nightfall. There _is_ a
bandage on your wrist, though?”

“Just my handkerchief.” She showed him. “See--it’s nothing.”

“I can do it better than that,” he said. “It wants to be tighter than
that--let me----”

“But it doesn’t matter, I only----”

“Please let me.”

Her hands. He had so wanted to touch her hands once more.... His own
were steady and sure for the moment by a tremendous effort of his will.
He untied the knot and wrapped the handkerchief again, neatly.

His fingers lingered over the job and she glanced sidewise at his
absorbed face, a glance of mingled surprise, puzzlement, and amusement.
He was getting to be a bit of an old maid about her! First he tried to
send her on without him, and now making all this fuss about a sprained
wrist! She supposed one must humor him. Fever made people queer. Good
old Dodo--she would get him through safe, somehow!




                               CHAPTER X


THEY found that one of the two horses was badly lamed, and Alexandra
loaded him with the canteens, the robe, and a sketchy kit. Most of
their belongings were lost with the third horse which they had left
behind early in the chase. She got Dorin into the other saddle, and
they set out before noon, working south and east, watching their
shadows creep up and pass them as the day wore on.

Again and again Alexandra, plodding at the head of Dorin’s horse, was
overtaken by drowsiness till she stumbled, and thus jerked awake spoke
to the limping pony, took note of her surroundings, and went on again,
putting one foot in front of the other methodically, listening for any
sound from Dorin, trying blindly to keep awake. At first he was able
to help a little, with directions from the saddle, but soon he drooped
silent, only half conscious, across the horse’s neck. And by nightfall
he had begun to talk rather wildly, disjointed, pitiful talk.

She had never heard delirium before and its starkness appalled her.
Most of what he said was meant for Bob Taunton and had to do with
things that meant nothing to her, she thought, trying not to hear,
trying to forget what she heard, with a guilty sense of eavesdropping.
Then her name came into it--those violets again--something about her
hands--what worried him so about her hands, she wondered--and how she
would fall if she tried to climb up there alone--and how she must tell
Bob something when she got back. But from having tried not to hear she
did not know just what it was that she was to tell Bob. And then there
would be long gaps when he said nothing, and in the dark she would
feel her way along the horse to him and make sure he was still there.
Then on again, making as little noise as possible, being very cautious
about using the torch, hating the jackals--on, on, into the dawn, a
stumbling, earth-bound Valkyr with streaming hair.

Another day and another night of this, with short rests and walking
dozes, not daring to stop long for fear she would never go on again,
doing what she could for Dorin in his precious lucid moments, while he
alternated between babbling delirium and a silent stupor that was even
worse. But somehow she kept on, hungry, thirsty, drugged with fatigue,
playing the absorbing game of putting one foot in front of the other,
and heading south and east.

It was during the second night that she lost the limping horse with
the pack. There wasn’t a moon and the stars seemed very faint and far
away. They rounded a shoulder of the hill and came out on flat, bare
rock. Instinctively she hugged the up-hill side of it, holding Dorin’s
horse by the bit so that he walked almost in her footsteps. There was
a clatter, a hideous sort of scream, and silence. Looking back, she
knew that the other horse was gone and looking downhill she knew that
they stood on a narrow ledge above a drop so bottomless that no further
sound of the horse’s fall reached her. That made her more careful.
Tightening her grip on the bit, she went forward inch by inch, the
torch recklessly pointing the way now, her voice steadying the tired,
overwrought pony which was Dorin’s only chance.

It was an endless business. More than once she waited sickly beside the
hard-breathing horse, speaking to him in a low voice, praying that Dodo
would stay quiet just a little longer, assuring herself that in a few
minutes, a few steps now, she would be able to sit down.

At last the steep rise on her left fell away and she felt gravel
beneath her feet again. The torch revealed a safe slope covered with
dry turf. She sat down where she was, the bridle over her arm, her head
resting on her knees.

Dorin’s voice roused her, demanding of Bob what in the name of
something picturesque he had done with Sandy.

“I’m here, Dodo--I’m still here----”

“Sandy,” he insisted, pushing her away. “Fetch Sandy at once--don’t let
her wear that thing--it’s not--it’s not at all a wise thing to do--she
shouldn’t have come--we mustn’t let her know--you won’t give me away,
will you--it always happens like this, I suppose--but she doesn’t
know--it’s because she’s Ingarsen’s daughter, and they’re all like
that, you said--tell her--tell her Eton jackets are best--” He became
suddenly savage. “_Bobby!_ In God’s name, go quickly and fetch
Sandy! I tell you she’s all alone up there! If you let her die I’ll
come back and haunt you, I swear I will!” His voice sank with a groan.
“She’s all that matters, don’t you see--don’t let her die--damn the
robe--Sandy, where’s the robe?” Then he was gone again, quite limp and
still.

She had been leaning against the horse, her arm across Dorin’s body,
and she straightened with a gasp. The robe was on the horse that had
gone over the cliff! She had not given it a thought since she strapped
it securely to the saddle of the lame horse, intent on giving Dorin’s
mount the benefit of every ounce that could be spared from his burden.
The robe was gone. They would never see it again. It would lie there,
at the bottom of the pit, till the end of time. But only Dodo mattered
now.

She ran her hands lightly over his face and found it burning hot,
though he had been shaking with chill. His lips were rough and dry. It
was then that she cried out sharply and turned as though to run back
to where the horse had gone over the edge. The canteens were gone too!
They had only one left, the one slung across her shoulder, the one she
had been using as she walked. It was not as heavy as it had been.

She fought down panic resolutely. She would find water when it was
light. They had seen none all day but--there would be water when it
got light. There _had_ to be water. Dodo would want it. She drew
closer to him in the dark, put up her hand again to his face, dreading
to go and take her place at the horse’s head. At last with a little
moan she left him, feeling for the bridle.

“Come along,” she said aloud to the staggering animal. “We’ve got
another ten miles in us.” She stepped out, almost briskly. “Come along,
you poor beast. We’ve lost the robe, perhaps our jinx has gone with it.
Who knows what we’ll see when morning comes!”

And so for another hour only. Then the horse’s legs folded under him
and he went down in a heap. Dorin fell clear and rolled twice over down
the slope, which jarred him back to semi-consciousness.

She stood a moment, silently regarding the horse, which lay heaving in
the torchlight, and then turned away to look for a niche that would
shelter them from the night wind. A few feet farther on she came upon a
gully, a mere pin-scratch on the face of the hill, but deep enough at
one end to protect a small fire and she had still a few matches in her
pocket.

Putting forth such strength as she had never dreamed of in better days,
she got Dorin, protesting deliriously every inch of the way, even
swearing at her, into the shelter of the gully and covered him with her
coat while she built the fire. Between his feverish convictions and the
feeble blaze she knew no peace for an hour. The stars departed and the
dawn held off. At last Dorin became quiet again and she crawled back to
where she had left the horse. It seemed very far. She got to her feet
and swept the torchlight round hastily. There was no horse.

She was crying through clenched teeth as she crept back to the gully.
Dodo had to have a doctor. How was she to get him to a doctor without a
horse? She had been a fool to let go of the horse even for an instant.
Of course he would stumble up and on as soon as he got his breath, with
dawn coming and his load gone.

She waited on the lip of the gully, straining her eyes through the dim
gloom, her breath coming in short, jagged sobs of sheer weariness.
Relentlessly the graying night showed her what she might expect of the
coming day. They were on an arid hillside which seemed never to have
known rain. There was no water in sight. There would be no water for
miles.

At last she crawled down out of the wind and tended the fire,
mechanically, and then dragged herself close to Dorin, who lay
unconscious still, and dropped beside him, her head on her arm, her
face almost on a level with his. For minutes she stayed so, memorizing
him, as it were, seeing him in the slowly growing light as she had
never had time to see him before, tracing the delicate nostrils and
jutting brow, mentally smiling at the child-like curve of his dark
lashes. His eyes looked painted, she thought, with an inward grin.
Chorus girl’s eyes. She wondered if he knew. How still he was. She
touched him fearfully. He was hot. So hot. If only there was water.
Suppose he slipped away from her like this. Suppose he never looked at
her again, nor spoke. Suppose--she--lost--him!

It was the first time in her life that she had known the blank terror
that wipes out thought and action. Then that receded and left the
situation naked before her. They were without food and water to last a
day, the horse was gone, and Dodo was dying. She could not get him down
to India. She could not get him another foot of the way. He could not
live. In a few hours he would be dead. She couldn’t quite take it in.

Dodo--dead. Why, in that case she might as well be dead, too. She faced
it, blinking. If Dodo had to die she didn’t care what happened. Fancy
