not caring what happened! Fancy life become so empty that one might
as well be dead! Oh, no, not even for Dodo--! But with the little
impatient shake of her head which accompanied the denial she knew
there was no denying. Life was dear and thrilling and beautiful. Life
was Dodo. Without him it would become mere existence again, abortive,
like sunlight lying cold on a pavement, rain beating warm against a
window-pane. He would take all the color and quickness of it with him.
No good going on without Dodo....

He stirred, and moaned. She was bending over him.

“Water,” he mumbled, stiff-lipped. “Water----”

“Yes, old man--half a mo.”

She went to the canteen, which lay beyond the fire, and tipped it
recklessly. A tablespoonful of water, perhaps, trickled into the cup
before the canteen went dry. She stared at it, more in despair than in
surprise, shook it almost with impatience, and her eyes went helplessly
round the arid gully. But Dodo had to have water!

“Hullo, we’ve slept!”

His voice startled her, natural for the first time in dreary hours. She
turned, with glad, shining eyes. He had raised himself on one elbow,
temporarily quite himself again.

“Why--Dodo, you’re--all right?”

“Think so. Was I queer?”

“You did wander a bit,” she admitted, and proffered the cup.

“Have you--?” He hesitated. “Is there--?” She nodded, and he drank.
“Now, while my head is working--where are we?” She shook her head,
watching him, thinking how good it was to have his eyes seeing and his
tongue obeying his will, once more. “God knows, eh?” He glanced round
at the fire, cunningly built, and up at the sheltering bank of the
gully. “You do go at it like a veteran, Sandy! I don’t remember coming
here. Where are the horses?”

“I lost--the lame one,” she confessed.

“Lost him!”

“I’m sorry,” she said humbly.

“Sorry!” He tried to laugh, laying a quick hand on hers. “Good Lord,
did you think I was blaming you?”

“Well, you see--he took the kit and the robe with him.”

“The robe!” His fingers tightened. “The robe--_gone_?”

“We’ll come back for it--some day.” Her chin lifted, valiantly. Perhaps
he needn’t know quite how things were. Not yet. “It will wait for us,”
she said.

“Will it?” He rubbed away a puzzled frown. “I--can’t seem to remember
just what happened.”

“I was at your horse’s head,” she told him unemotionally. “We were
simply feeling our way through the dark--the other horse was following
the best he could--stumbling, grunting, slipping--following my
voice--and then he just went over the edge.”

“That’s--hard luck, isn’t it,” he said after a pause.

“My fault.”

“Don’t be silly. You’ve done the very best you could.”

“It wasn’t good enough.”

“Better than any one else on earth could have done.”

“You--you really mean that?” She looked at him hopefully, eager even
now to hear that she had pleased him.

“Yes, yes, a thousand times I mean it! You couldn’t have eyes for two
horses. Nobody could. Where’s the one I was riding?”

Again a feeling of guilty apology came over her--a feeling that she had
somehow failed him. Miserably, she tried to give an account of herself.

“He stumbled and went down under you last night--just over there. I
couldn’t get him up again, so I left him and brought you here--and then
I didn’t dare leave you--and when at last I went back to look after
him--he was gone.”

Dorin’s eyelids flickered, but he said nothing. Now that the thing was
out, she went on brokenly, in a passion of self-abasement.

“Oh, I should have made him fast somehow! I shouldn’t have left him
like that! It was all just my stupidity----!”

“Sandy--” He tried to check her.

“It was, it was stupidity! I knew he wasn’t dead! But I forgot the
first rule you ever taught me: _Stick to your horse--half the time he
knows more than you do!_ Forgot it, as though by holding fast to you
and only you I could get you through to India, safe!”

“Oh, my dear--! To have you beaten now!” He took her hands, and his
were hot but firm. “The gods aren’t being generous!”

“They’re jealous gods. Perhaps we were too clever at the temple.
Still--this is better than that, isn’t it!”

“But you mustn’t stay here any longer.”

“Why not?” She smiled at him gravely.

“My dear, you must snatch at every chance there is left! You might be
picked up by a caravan, or-- You’ve been splendid, since I crocked up.
But you’ve done all even you can do. You must go on--alone.”

_Must._ It had been her pride always to obey orders to the letter.
And mutiny against a wounded captain made one feel a cad.

“I--I’d rather stay with you,” she objected delicately.

“But this won’t last, you know. I mean--as soon as the sun comes
I--well, I won’t be much good. I probably won’t even know if you’re
here, after that. It’s got to be--good-by--now--in any case.”

And while he smiled, his gaze clung to her face, her hair.... And then
her arms were round him convulsively, his face pressed against her
throat.

“I won’t leave you.” He felt it against his lips. “I won’t leave
you--ever!”

Mutiny. And he too tired to cope with the comfort of it. Close enough,
now, to see the pulse in her throat, and not daring to kiss it. And
there was a great grimy smear on her cheek. The kind of smear that
tears make on the cheeks of dirty urchins. With a tired little sigh, he
shut his eyes against the day.




                               CHAPTER XI


AT last she raised her head and with a glance at the pearling sky
shifted his weight a little, making him comfortable against her
shoulder, and spoke as one child to another, making a game.

“We’ve hours yet. Let’s talk,” she said.

So, while the cold dawn gained on them slowly, they talked as they
had never before talked, no longer shy of things, no longer tacitly
avoiding things, their quaint, school-boyish reticence laid aside for
this last great moment that remained to them. But habit was strong in
both of them, and there were many things that neither of them could
find words for, but these were all encompassed in their boundless
understanding, each for the other, which filled in the gaps and replied
to them.

The man in Simla had said that it would be as she wanted it, and but
for Dorin she might now have had no personal quarrel with fate. Her
grandfathers had known how to die when the time came. But Dodo. That
made it different. That wasn’t fair of something somewhere. Her old
passionate clinging to life for life’s sake was in abeyance before the
new and stupendous fact that Dodo wanted her for his own. And she felt
that in the face of everything Dodo should be allowed to have whatever
he wanted. And because Dodo was being deprived of something he wanted,
Death had no right to him yet, nor to her so long as he wanted her.
Things had only begun, for them.

“We’d have had such times together,” she said thoughtfully. “Such
times.”

“You’d have gone on--and on--with me?” He wanted her to say it in every
possible way. He wanted to hear it as often as he could.

“If you’d asked me,” she stipulated.

“I’m not sure I’d have had the nerve to do that! Besides----” He
hesitated.

“I know. You’re thinking of all that back there. It seems like another
woman--another incarnation.” She broke that with a smile. “How
frightfully obvious people become, don’t they, when they try to put
big things into words! Of course it was another woman! _I_ never
was Clem’s wife! Not this me! And I’ve an idea Clem hasn’t got a wife
by now.” She nodded to herself, distant-eyed. “_She_ would see to
that. And Clem is such a logical man. He would divorce me first and
eventually it might occur to him exactly how I came to do it. I can see
that now. He’ll marry again, too,” she added after a moment.

“Think so?” Dorin was lying quiet, looking down at her hand in his,
caring for nothing but the sound of her voice. He felt her nodding
again.

“Not straight off. But that will occur to him, too, eventually,” she
prophesied cheerfully. “He’ll find he needs some one to see that his
meals are right. Unfortunately for Clem, even the best cooks if left
to themselves regard mutton as one of life’s obligations. Clem doesn’t
like mutton--among other things. You know,” she went on absurdly, with
a sudden squeeze of his fingers to make him pay attention to this new
idea of hers, “you know, I’ve got a theory that boy children should be
trained in the nursery to eat everything and anything, for their wives’
sake! Why, when I was first married to Clem I used to write down the
things he wouldn’t eat, so that they could be avoided thereafter.” She
sat with wide, humorous eyes, regarding that faraway, conscientious
bride. “There got to be quite a list,” she marveled mildly.

He shook with chuckling.

“Oh, Sandy, you priceless idiot!”

“Thanks to you.”

“Me!”

“You’re why I’m a priceless idiot and not Clem’s wife.”

“Pygmalion stuff!” he jeered, much pleased.

“Yes,” she agreed. And then, wistfully, “I could have made you so proud
of me, Dodo!”

“Proud!” he murmured. “Good Lord----!”

“Oh, don’t think I’m regretting--this. I’ve learned to look the lords
of life and death between the eyes and laugh--as you do. I’m almost a
philosopher now--like you!” She smiled down at him. Oh, it was hard,
his not having time for everything he wanted! She put that away from
her, sturdily. “You know, the curious part of it is,” she continued,
“if I’d been born knowing what I know now I might never have done
what I did!” They laughed at each other, without effort, in perfect
comprehension. “_You_ know what I mean, Dodo--_little_
things!”

“Tell me--” He had made a game of bending her long, passive fingers
back as far as they would go and then collapsing them suddenly, both
joints at once. “Of course my interest is purely--academic. But suppose
I simply _wasn’t_, and you _were_. Knowing all this you
mention about little things, and so forth--couldn’t you go back and
make a go of it now--if you had the chance?”

“No,” she said slowly, with a shake of her head. “Because you see
I wasn’t born a philosopher. I learned it all--here. And so it all
belongs to you. All my laughter. All my love.”

There was a silence. His hand was quiet on hers. It was one of the
times when words wouldn’t come to him.

“I’m glad you said that,” he got out, at last.

“I wanted you to know,” she said simply.

“I-- You-- Oh, bless you, Sandy.”

“I know,” she replied again comfortably to his inarticulateness. “We’ve
both been homeless vagabonds of the spirit, born out of our time.
Leftovers, both of us. Flotsam of the ages. I had lived all my life on
the doorstep of other people’s lives. It was always the same, after my
father died. My own mother--or Clem--I seemed to them just a bit mad.
Then you came, and for the first time I’ve been _inside_. I can
talk to you. You always know what I mean and how I feel. You’ve felt it
all, too. We were bound to come home to this, I suppose--together.”

“How simple you make it sound!” he teased her, with worshipful eyes.

“I’ve always been a terrific joke to you, haven’t I!” she remarked,
almost boastfully.

“Oh, my dear--!” He buried his face against her. Then, muffled against
her shoulder, “Go on talking, Sandy. I love your--nonsense.”

“Well,” she went on, playing the game, “I was just thinking. It would
have been nicer for Clem if I’d got back to face the music, wouldn’t
it. This way he’ll never know quite where he is. Dodo, can one divorce
a woman who isn’t alive?”

“It isn’t usually considered necessary, is it?”

“And yet,” she frowned, “if Clem didn’t divorce me because it
didn’t seem to be necessary--he’ll probably never _know_, you
know--wouldn’t he always be afraid if he married again that I might
turn up after all and convict him of bigamy, the way they do in books?”

“Does he read that kind of books?” He grinned against her shoulder, at
the thought of Clem straying among popular fiction.

“No,” she admitted, soberly enough. “And Clem was never an imaginative
man. But somebody ought to warn him. Clem would hate being let in for
bigamy!”

“But it’s what they call a strictly hypothetical case, isn’t it?” He
was playing with her fingers again. He loved her hands....

“All the same--” A smile flickered across her face. “If I were Clem I’d
feel safer if I’d divorced me first. Do you follow?”

“Oh, quite!” he assured her.

“Of course it does save trouble for us--this way. You would have been
expected to marry me.”

“Frightful bore.”

“Yes, that’s what I say!”

Laughing, her cheek suddenly against his hair, they clung closer for a
moment, hugging their joke. Then he looked up at her, quite serious.

“Will you, Sandy? I mean--would you? I mean, not just because it
would be expected, but because it won’t ever be the same now if we
aren’t doing things together-- I mean, it wouldn’t be if we-- Oh,
hang, I’m all mixed in my tenses! But if we’d had better luck this
time--Sandy----?”

She looked down at him, quite serious, too, her hand along his cheek.

“I told you I wouldn’t leave you--ever.”

“Well, then--” He caught his breath, turning his face into her coat
again. “--that’s that, isn’t it.”

She sat quiet, her arms aching with his weight but knowing that
she would hold him like this as long as he was there to hold, and
after--looking out with heavy eyes on the relentless day that would
take him from her. And then everything would be over. Funny, to love
some one, even Dodo, more than she loved life, and to count his loss
the greater. Funny, how things turned out.

“It’s an odd feeling, isn’t it,” she said. “Knowing that it’s all come
to an end--and not minding.”

“But you do mind, Sandy. It’s horrid hard on you. You’re not afraid.
But you don’t like it.”

“It’s only----”

“Only the things you haven’t had a chance to do. I know.”

“With you,” she reminded him jealously.

“With me--bless you. And the hundreds of long, windy days you forfeit.
I know.”

“Oh, that,” she said. “Sun--and wind.” Then she glanced down at him
sidewise, making the game. “I should have liked a tiger!” she confessed.

“Yes. Do you remember the time we talked tigers--in the Hills south of
the monastery while it stormed?”

“Allah, that was a storm! And then it cleared, like a shot, and the
sun----”

“It was on the tip of my tongue that day to promise you a tiger hunt
when we reached India.”

“I hinted, all I could.”

“But I was afraid you might think--afraid it might sound as though I
thought----”

“As though I was bound to you by what we had done.” She nodded. “I can
see how it was.”

“You know--it _is_ funny,” he said after a pause. “I mean--if
things had gone right this time we might never have come to talk like
this. We talk such utter rot about nothing at all, usually, and shy
like anything when it goes more than skin deep. It’s the way it is
with Bob. I never think of telling him how frightfully fond of him I
am. And you--I’ve got you, thank God--that is--I might have had you,
for keeps. But if we’d had any kind of decent luck this time I might
even have been fool enough to try to let you go without--without----”

“Of course I might have demanded the tiger,” she murmured.

“Oh, Sandy, you’re so alive--so awfully keen! And you may be throwing
yourself away, sitting here like this! It’s been worth--everything,
to me. But now you must take the canteen and keep on as long as you
can--for the sake of the tiger!”

“Well, you see,” she said, driven to it, “the canteen is empty.”

“But--you said----!”

“I lied. I thought it would do the most good that way. It gave
us--this.”

With a little sound of pity and despair, he crushed her hand to his
lips, and her eyes went again to the oncoming glare of day. Quite
suddenly, then, she saw red with all her rebellious soul. He was hers,
and here she sat, doing nothing. The only thing she had ever really
owned, the only thing that had ever really mattered, the only thing
that had ever needed her and wanted her and depended on her--all
wrapped up in Dodo’s life, that was slipping through her fingers. Her
tired body stiffened under his weight, she clutched him close, and her
voice rang out piteously in the wilderness.

“The Hills shan’t have you! I’ve kept you alive, I’ve dragged you inch
by inch to all the comfort I could make for you, I’ve killed for you,
and thanked God I knew how to get home with a knife! I won’t give in, I
am _not_ beaten! I dare all the demons of India! _I’m damned if
they can have you now!_”

“Sandy--my poor dear----!”

“From the top of the hill we could see--” She got to her feet, putting
him aside, planning coolly, thinking aloud. “Yes, we must get to
the top of this hill. I daren’t leave you here--there are a hundred
pin-scratches like this. I’d lose you. Dodo, you’ve got to crawl up the
bank so we can signal each other.” She bent over him again, coaxing.
“Just that little way--come--I’ll help--why, I almost carried you last
night; you don’t know how strong I am--come!”

Obediently, white-lipped, he raised himself on one knee, only to
collapse without a sound into unconsciousness. She laid him down very
carefully, and got to her feet again, talking aloud in order to keep
her head, refusing to admit yet to herself that he was gone now for the
last time.

“The horse,” she was saying quite firmly. “Perhaps I can still find the
horse--he can’t have gone far--I must go on--a little way--I can get
Dodo down somehow--I’ll show them--I----”

She snatched her helmet from the ground and then wavered, looking back
at Dorin, up at the merciless sky, down at the empty canteen.... It
wasn’t any good. She had done all she could. She couldn’t go on--far
enough--without water. It would be better to be together.

Strength seemed to drain out of her without warning. She fell. Dizzily
she crept to him--found his hand--there was still a pulse in his
wrist--water--if she had had water she might have got him through ...
if they had had any kind of decent luck....




                              CHAPTER XII


LIEUTENANT ERIC AINSWORTH, hastily clad, stood on the watch-tower of
the Fort, his eyes glued to the binoculars with which he was following
a moving speck on the hillside opposite. Beside him was Lal Singh,
bearer of the news which had jerked his officer out of bed at dawn.
He had seen the speck in half as much light and without binoculars,
and his brilliant gaze was now fixed expectantly on as much of the
_sahib’s_ face as remained visible.

There was a clatter up the stairs and Burton, the senior subaltern,
appeared on the lope, clothed sketchily and much excited.

“What is it? D’ya see anything? What is it?”

“Lal Singh’s right. It’s a horse. Got a saddle and no rider. Tripping
over his bridle at every step. Nobody in sight.”

They looked at each other. Lal Singh’s fine eyes went from Burton to
Ainsworth and back again. The fate of the Empire was nothing to this.
All along the Border men were watching, hoping, praying for just such
a sign as the speck on the hillside opposite. A horse. A saddled horse
which had come a long way. Never was such a sight! Lal Singh licked his
lips, looking from one _sahib_ to the other.

Burton nodded slowly.

“Yes,” he said. He looked a long minute at the hillside, through the
binoculars. “Stripped,” he said. “No kit. No nothing.” He looked
harder. “Saddle hanging any which way. Had a fall, perhaps.” He lowered
the glasses. “Yes,” he repeated thoughtfully.

“Better take a dozen chaps with you?” offered Ainsworth. There was
heroism in the pronoun. Only one of them could go.

Burton wrenched his gaze from the hillside, to look at him and at Lal
Singh, eager-eyed behind him.

“You’re his friend,” he said. “You go. Take Lal Singh. I’ll keep shop
here.”

“Thanks.” With a glance at Lal Singh, Ainsworth turned and plunged down
the stairs, the delighted Sikh at his heels.

“Mind you,” said Burton some minutes later, as Ainsworth came out to a
little group of pleased men and impatient horses waiting in the dawn,
Lal Singh grinning beside his own mount and Ainsworth’s, “mind you,
the beast may have come miles and miles like that. Or he may belong to
somebody else entirely. Unless you’re fairly sure--unless there’s a
clue of some sort on the saddle--” He hesitated anxiously.

“Be back before dark, anyway,” Ainsworth promised, and swung up.

They found the horse and looked him over. He had been much too long
without water, his knees were raw, and the saddle hung rakishly with a
bullet scar on the leather. He had been stripped of every extra ounce
and there was nothing to identify his owner.

“He’s come a long way,” said Ainsworth, and sighed. “But still--” His
eyes went hopefully over the gaunt landscape.

“From up there he came,” said Lal Singh, pointing.

Ainsworth nodded. They remounted and rode on, a dozen pairs of
horizon-trained eyes raking every rock and hollow.

Lal Singh seemed keenest on the scent and Ainsworth watched him
enviously. Trust your Sikh to find a friend, he thought, and between
Lal Singh and Blaise Dorin lay some bond of service done, either to the
other, years before. He had watched the big Sikh fretting since the
news of Dorin’s disappearance reached them, and had half expected an
outbreak of some sort. And so there might have been if the riderless
horse had been pronounced none of their business.

They topped the hill and halted, looking down its scarred flank which
lay in its own shadow under the low morning sun.

“See, _sahib_! Something--” Lal Singh’s long arm swept out. “There
at the edge of the sunlight beyond where the rock ends.”

“Where? Sorry, got no eyes this morning. Let’s go down.”

They went down, preceded by a rattle of small stones.

Alexandra had roused incredulously to the sound of horses’ hoofs. There
was a ringing in her head. It must be that only, and not horses. She
was too tired to move. She must listen--it _was_ horses--she must
shout--anything, even Afridis, would be welcome now--she must get up,
and make them hear her....

Then Dorin was taken from her, lifted bodily into the arms of some one
who set up great howls in a strange tongue, rocking back and forth.

“Good God!”

It was the purest English, that! Hands came into her narrowed range of
vision. English hands. She turned heavily, and found herself resting
against a khaki coat. She touched a bit of colored ribbon on the breast
of it. It was real. What were they babbling about? She was very tired,
but there was something she had to do.... It ripped through her mind
and she jerked against the khaki coat.

“Dodo--water--for Dodo----”

“That’s all right,” they told her. “Don’t you fret. We’ll look after
him.”

The British Army had come, then. She rested against it, closing her
eyes. How nice. And they would look after Dodo. He needn’t die, now.
That was all right. The British Army said so. It ought to know....

As they carried her toward the horses the sunlight stuck full across
her eyelids, and the shadow of a frown appeared between her brows. She
looked up into the face above her, intently.

“Sun,” she said. “Keep him--out--of the sun.”

And she fainted dead away.




                                 _Sea_


    “_I remember the black wharves and the slips_,
      _And the sea-tides tossing free_;
    _And the Spanish sailors with bearded lips_,
    _And the beauty and mystery of the ships_,
      _And the magic of the sea._”




                               CHAPTER I


SO Ingarsen’s daughter came to British India, and there was rejoicing
in the land. For this one had known her father, and that one loved
Blaise Dorin, and the other one’s wife would be pleased to send up
anything that was desired from the Peshawur shops. Alexandra would lift
shining eyes from these messages. “Aren’t they kind!” she would marvel.
“Aren’t they _good_!” While certain subalterns who had taken care
that the exact manner of her coming should be known grinned fondly and
went their ways.

The tale of the two Shir Shans, shyly told as a good joke by the
second, had gone out in all its glory on the four winds. Men chuckled
pridefully, and spoke of Ingarsen _père_, and abruptly blew their
noses, chuckling still. Even the women of Simla were impressed, and
wondered what she would be like to know.

Further details leaked out, discreetly. How for two days and nights
she had walked at the head of a staggering horse which carried a man
half-dead. How she had kept on, without food, without water, almost
without hope, till horseflesh failed her. How then she had found
shelter and built a fire, and waited coolly without losing her head and
wandering off alone. How she had _stuck_, to the end. And how
when they came at last she had bade them keep him out of the sun.

Thus was the chill blast of public opinion tempered to Ingarsen’s lamb,
and Alexandra, all unaware, found every one bewilderingly kind.

It has been magnificently said that a hero is a man who does what he
can. It might be added that he is also a man who remains sublimely
unconscious of heroism. In this was Alexandra a hero. She had done
superhumanly all that she could accomplish of what there was to do,
but when they tried to praise her she would point out in all honesty
that the gods had been mercifully moved to finish the job for her.
“I was done,” she told them. “If you hadn’t seen the horse we should
have died there, within a stone’s throw of the Fort.” And she smiled
at them thoughtfully. “It was a damned near thing!” she said, with
Wellingtonian emphasis.

Taunton arrived from Simla in a cloud of dust, and he and Lal Singh
and the doctor among them completely monopolized Dorin. She would come
to the doorway and stand there jealously, forgotten, superfluously a
woman again in a Peshawur frock, looking on helplessly while they sat,
all three, silent and sleepless and terribly determined, watching him,
tending him, dragging him back each time he slipped away, gaining an
inch here, losing it again there, in their long battle with eternity.
She had done her part. Now she had only to keep out of the way.

But sometimes in the long, still hours before dawn, when Lal Singh’s
turban rested against the cot close to Dorin’s hand and Bob Taunton sat
watching the precious breath coming ever so little and going ever so
far and long as Dorin slept, he would remember her and how for a time
he had been very near to hating her. And then he would acknowledge his
debt like a gentleman, envious, meanwhile, that it should have fallen
to the lot of that slim, spooky-eyed creature to take his rightful
place between Blaise Dorin and an aggressive destiny. Moreover, Dorin
had talked--never one rational word since he was carried into the Fort,
but talked--addressing himself oftenest to the agonizing Taunton whom
he heartbreakingly desired and could not recognize. And the talk was
full of Sandy, so that Bob, forced at last to believe his unwilling
ears, perceived that in Ingarsen’s daughter he had a rival and a peer.

Lal Singh regarded her with respect, and with something of a father’s
pride, with the awe that is due an instrument of the gods, and with a
tinge of jealousy, too. But he had no time for her. And the doctor said
she must rest, and shooed her from under men’s feet.

They did not consciously shut her out, but they were men fighting for
a life and they knew their business. So she wandered forlornly round
the Fort, making herself small, and hung about outside Dorin’s room,
listening, searching the faces of those who passed in and out, trying
not to be a bother and make a fuss, vaguely awaiting a summons that
never came. Each day she told herself that tomorrow she would go in,
quite firmly, and feel Dodo’s hands and make him speak to her, so that
they all might know that he wanted her, that she was necessary to him
now, and that she had some small right to him herself. But when each
tomorrow came and they passed her with set, weary faces, she fell back
out of the way and stood looking after them wistfully, feeling by
virtue of the weak, foolish tears in her eyes incompetently feminine.

It was hard to have no part in this last great fight. One night when
Dorin’s voice rose plaintively, unceasingly, in the fever, she had
wrapped herself in a blanket and crouched on a cushion in the corridor
outside his door, just in case, she told herself apologetically,
anybody should be sent to call her. The doctor found her there early in
the morning and told her it was no way to get back her strength, and
went on, hurriedly, to telegraph. “But I’ve _got_ my strength,”
said Alexandra, running after him in the blanket. “Can’t I help?
Can’t I take my turn at watching? Can’t I--?” As he disappeared round
the corner she became aware of the trailing blanket and returned
crestfallen to her room. “They treat me,” she said resentfully, “why,
they treat me the way Clem did!” She had almost forgotten how it felt.

Then came a day when Blaise Dorin opened his eyes upon a face he had
long wanted to see. He contemplated it, momentarily expecting it to
vanish into those dreadful mental mists which rolled up from a sea of
pain, engulfing consciousness.

“Bobby,” he experimented faintly.

“Yes, old man. Been here all the time.”

Dorin lay quiet, coping with it. This was no fever-born wraith which
sat beside his cot only to fade at a touch. This was Bobby, come to him
at last. If one reached out one could grasp warm, solid flesh, one’s
hand would be caught and held in the excruciating grip of their love
for each other. Nice to be able to hang on to Bobby, if only one’s
muscles could be made to work.... These were the walls of the Fort,
then. And that was some one he knew--one of his Sikhs--they had pulled
each other out of some sort of a hole a long time ago, but he couldn’t
remember at the moment just which hole--a fine chap, though--what the
devil was his name?--you must always remember your chaps’ names.... And
all the while he was conscious of something missing. The pain? Yes, but
that wasn’t it. What had he lost? There was something that was his and
he very much wanted it. Something he was loth to lose sight of and they
had taken it away....

“Sandy!” His gaze flew to Taunton’s face. It was all of him that moved,
but the look was as though he had risen. “You’ve got Sandy--safe----?”

“Quite safe, old man. Keep still. She’s coming.”

Lal Singh left the room silently. It was a little hard on Lal Singh,
but his voice was gentle as he came up behind Alexandra, watching the
sunset from the tower-- “_Memsahib_ come quick,” he suggested
softly.

She came very quick, her heart in her throat, choking her. Taunton made
way for her without a word and she went on her knees beside the cot,
giving Dorin her hand. He lay smiling at her mutely, from the pillow.
He was never a talkative man.

Taunton turned, and motioning Lal Singh before him started to tiptoe
from the room.

“Bobby.”

He paused, looking guilty, and Dorin’s brows quirked faintly upward
while he gathered strength for what was in his mind to say. It was as
if his old, delicious chuckle shook him. They waited, fascinated, while
he came ever more surely to life before their eyes.

“Sentimental ass--come back,” he said. “Sit down.”

They wouldn’t let him talk any more and so he went to sleep, Sandy’s
hand held fast in his. Taunton looked down at her where she sat
patiently on her heels beside the cot, watching with parted lips as
he himself had watched the precious breathing. He had resented her.
He had been jealous of her. She was, after all, a woman. And yet--
He looked at her in the silence, noting again her smooth hair, her
quiet hands, that hint of the palpitant wild thing in her utter lack
of self-consciousness. And then, for the first time he saw her mouth,
wistful, with humorous corners, a mouth meant to be kissed. Resent
her? Poor little beggar, she’d earned anything she wanted in this
world. And if life chose to pay its debt to her with Dodo, she had
earned even that. For without her there would have been no Dodo now. He
felt that he wanted her to know that he knew that. He felt there was
something he ought to say to her.

“I say,” he said.

Her eyes, still clouded with her own thoughts, came slowly to his face.
He noted, too, that she did not try, woman like, to shush him.

“You--you won’t mind my always claiming my bit of him?” Thus humbly he
surrendered the keys of office.

She regarded him gravely, her usual direct gaze misted with an
indefinable appeal. It was not an Eton jacket look.

“You’ll help me?” she said astonishingly. “He’s--so tired. I must get
him back to England. I must get him Home. You’ll--help me?”

Taunton reached out so that three hands lay one on the other, and hers
the middle one.

“We’ll get him Home, don’t you fret. Allah is good.”

And then, because it was all over and there was nothing whatever to cry
about, Alexandra laid her bright head on the edge of the cot and wept,
and then laughed at herself with wet cheeks until she cried again, and
Bob blew his nose, grinning.

But the cause of it all was asleep, and missed the fun.




                               CHAPTER II


LONG, slow weeks later they disembarked, the three of them, at
Plymouth, and proceeded thence to a London hospital with Dorin, for the
wound was not right yet. The voyage had been a trying one, though every
one was kind. And Alexandra, looking about her, came to the conclusion
that England was, after all, England.

“Have to see Starke, I suppose,” sighed Dorin. “Hell to pay, what?” He
grinned at Bob, who grinned back contentedly.

“Tell him,” said Alexandra lightly, “we’ll go back for it if he likes!”
But something stirred within her as she spoke, so lightly. _Go
back?_ it whispered. _Risk Dodo again--back there?_ Risk? She
cold-shouldered the word. It was their job--hers and Dodo’s. Dodo would
soon be right again. The robe, lying there at the bottom of the pit,
would wait for them.

According to plan, she did not linger in town but went immediately to
a village on the Cornish coast, on the flowery fringes of which stood
a cottage which Bob Taunton had once discovered. “Shockingly like a
honeymoon cottage it is, too,” thought Alexandra, as she was being
shown about it by the bright-eyed old lady who kept the keys. “I’m
afraid Dodo will think it awfully _bridal_!”

“And would you be wanting it more than a month, ma’am?” inquired the
old lady, cocking a robin-like gaze.

“We--don’t quite know,” said Alexandra, finding it difficult.

The old lady nodded wisely.

“He--he’s been ill,” Alexandra went on.

“‘In sickness and in health,’” nodded the old lady sympathetically.

“Yes, it--it all depends on his recovery how long we stay,” explained
Alexandra.

“He’ll get well fast enough here. He’ll get well, for such a pretty
wife as you.”

“But--” said Alexandra.

“‘To have and to hold,’” nodded the old lady.

“You--you’re married, too?” It came out oddly.

“Twice, my dear, and good men they were, too, and both buried now,”
admitted the old lady with something of modest pride. And she added a
bit irrelevantly, “I was never so pretty as you.”

“Oh,” said Alexandra. “And--what about the linen?”

“There’s linen here.” The old lady led the way to the cupboard. “But
you’ll have better of your own, I fancy, a young wife like you.”

“But--” said Alexandra, and stopped. She could buy linen.

“And when would you be wanting the place, ma’am?”

“Now,” said Alexandra firmly, knowing it to be just the thing for Dodo
once he got over the shock of its bridal exterior. “That is--I should
like to settle in at once, myself, and then as soon as we can be--as
soon as he can be moved----”

“Ah, the poor man,” murmured the old lady. “And what was he ill of, if
I might ask, ma’am?”

“A--a bad fall--from a horse,” gasped Alexandra. “He--his hip--he
limps--it doesn’t mend----”

“Ah, the poor man!” The old lady clucked her tongue wisely. “And how
they fret, the men, when they can’t get about!” She sighed, an ancient
zephyr of a sigh. “Like children,” she sighed, “the men are! Like to
die of a broken leg, my first husband was! Ah, well--you’ve patience
and you’ve youth, and he likes to look at you, eh? You’ll do well
enough here, you and him!”

Alexandra thought they would. The chintzes were bright but not too
new, and the long living-room opened graciously upon a rocky, fragrant
garden above the sea. The sea, at the bottom of her garden.... She
gazed at it happily. If Dodo were in for a long period of inactivity
they would have the sea.

“Not much will grow in that garden,” the old lady apologized. “Half
wild it is--half rock--not much grows there.”

“That makes what does grow all the nicer,” said Alexandra absently, her
eyes on the sea.

The old lady chuckled, much pleased with her.

“He’ll get well,” she chuckled. “He’ll get well, for you!”

There was a piano, and a quaint library, and a lovely old desk where
Dodo could write. They had planned a book. Perhaps two books. And the
afternoon sun came in from the sea through long windows. He would get
well, she told herself happily.

So Alexandra settled in, while Bob stayed in London looking after
Dorin. And she spent long, quiet days pottering about the rocky garden
above the sea, arranging things for Dodo, making mental notes of things
he must be sure to have pointed out to him at once, devising ways of
making the time pass pleasantly for him till he was quite well again
and could get about without even a stick. She thought they could be
very happy here for a number of weeks, even months, writing the book,
while Dodo got well. “Of course we shall have to be married before he
comes down,” she thought, scratching about in the garden one morning.
“Married to Dodo. How funny,” she grinned. “How--how _quaint_!
People are so silly. Why couldn’t we just--” The thought drifted away
before her interest in a large and sociable beetle which emerged from
the geranium border.

She hoped he could come soon. One missed Dodo so. He became so much a
part of one’s scheme of things. Still, she wondered mildly at the word
“love.” It had all seemed quite clear, that morning in the Hills. But
now, with weeks of travel and Bob Taunton and England between-- Love?
She had read about it. It was fierce and tender and blinding and
sweet. It carried one away. One didn’t think, one only felt. But--Dodo?
She wanted to be with him always, no matter where he went. She wanted
to be with him now, when he seemed so quiet and tired. They belonged
together, they couldn’t be happy apart. But--_love_? She gave it
up.

It was a problem she returned to later, in the train after one of
her numerous visits to the hospital in London. She puzzled over it,
frowning out at the lovely Cornwall landscape. Ever since they had
returned to England Dodo had seemed not to want to talk about their
future. It was queer, when that, too, had been so clear in India. He
seemed to like to hear about the cottage and her many small activities
there, but he never spoke of living there himself and he was likely to
fall silent and preoccupied if she said something (as she often had)
beginning, “When you come down--” So that gradually a shyness had crept
upon her until she left off saying, “When you come down--” and talked
only of things already accomplished. And all the while he said not a
word about their marriage, when he had once been so funny about the
unquestionable necessity of marriage, for them. “It is unoriginal but
expedient,” he said, laughing at her. He hadn’t laughed at her like
that for weeks, now. And yet he was getting well. They swore their
several oaths that all danger and uncertainty were past. She frowned at
dear North Cornwall, thinking hard.

It might be, she thought, that even as certain things were less
dazzlingly clear to her than they had been that morning in the Hills,
to Dodo, too, they might seem more complicated. It might be, she
insisted sturdily to something inside her which desired to think
otherwise, that he would prefer to leave things as they were. It might
be that Dodo well, Dodo in England, Dodo already thinking of the
Amazon, looked upon their marriage as less inevitable.

She contemplated this, blinking.

Just where had this marriage business got started? He had done all she
had asked of him, that day in Bloomsbury. He had given her back the
desert and the Hills. She had promised to ask nothing more of him,
ever. And if he would rather go on alone, now.... They had both been
light-headed, that morning in the Hills. Life looks different, from the
brink of death. She must think this out. Things might be different, now
that Dodo was getting well.

Thus came the inescapable reaction in the world of men and trains.
One cannot, either figuratively or literally, live forever on a
mountain-top with the dawn of some Great Beginning turning the evilest
shadows into mere rocks, and touching no matter what future with the
unearthly glory of new-born light. One must in the nature of things
descend. The trick is to descend in time, to get one’s bearings, and
to proceed, if possible, in the same general direction that one faced
while on the heights.

To get one’s bearings. To adjust one’s compass. Life is a series of
anticlimaxes.

She got out at her station and stumbled into the cottage in the dusk.
The red-cheeked maid brought candles, and was glad to see her. But when
the door had closed softly behind her Alexandra stood in the middle of
the long room with the kindly, living light of candles on its walls and
its windows open to the murmur and beat of the sea--stood with her eyes
on the spent greenish glow of the sunset sky, wondering what would be
best for Dodo, feeling suddenly desolate and bewildered and alone.

“But this is ridiculous,” said Alexandra severely to herself. “One
would think--really, one would think--” A word popped out of her
perplexity, like a cuckoo out of a clock. _Love?_ said the cuckoo.
“Is it?” she demanded.

How was one to know?




                              CHAPTER III


THE nine days’ wonder of their return had subsided and with the divorce
decree out of the way the newspapers were no longer embarrassing.
Everything was settled. Everything, that is, which linked her to
Bloomsbury.

Dorin was improving slowly, and could get about with a stick now. But
she missed the old gay assurance of his laughter, the old untroubled
confidence of his outlook on life. It was as though he felt his star
had wavered, and was at a loss. His eyes clung to her, shadowed,
somehow puzzled, with an odd, mute look. And when she laid her hand on
his, his lay passive under it and she thought the little lines of pain
showed plainer round his mouth. And she thought, too, that she caught
Bob Taunton watching her with measuring eyes that held a question. It
was as though something was in the air and she stood at a disadvantage
with the wind blowing toward it.

Why wouldn’t they tell her? What had she done, to be left in the dark
this way? Dodo always told her things. She thought of cornering Bob
and dragging it out of him, whatever it was that they hadn’t told her.
But that wasn’t quite fair to Dodo. Her pride rebelled, too. If Dodo
wouldn’t tell her she couldn’t ask Bob. Perhaps it wasn’t anything.
Perhaps she was imagining things. Dodo was still very tired--still not
quite himself. He liked to have her with him, though. Even she could
see that.

This went on. Dorin limped badly, but there began to be talk of his
leaving the hospital. No one could get really well in a hospital,
decreed Alexandra, asserting herself. He needed air and the sea and
pretty rooms and things to do. He needed Cornwall and herself. She
tried it again one day, sliding her slim paw into his hand as she sat
in her favorite way on her heels on a cushion beside his chair, a book
open on his knees.

“And when you come down to the cottage, Dodo, _could_ we have a
dog? There’s a new litter of puppies--Airedales, such darlings, all
heads and feet--in the village, and the man said we could choose the
one we wanted. He said----”

Dorin’s fingers had tightened with a jerk, on her hand. Looking up, she
saw that his head rested wearily against the back of the chair, his
eyes closed.

“Dodo!” She caught at him. “You _are_ getting better? You
_are_ going to be all right? There isn’t any danger now--_is_
there? You’d tell me--if----?”

“Live forever.”

“Of course you will!”

He looked at her, without smiling, his gray eyes strangely dark under
their long lashes. She remembered irrelevantly how she had lain beside
him on the mountain and called them chorus girl’s eyes.... They had no
color at all today. Black diamonds, neither cold nor hard, but living,
fathomless, infinite with pain. She felt herself drawn into them,
not caring.... The queerest feeling.... She hid her face against his
sleeve, burrowing gratefully into its roughness, and felt him stoop to
her hair.

Dorin, for once in his life, was funking it. He knew that he ought to
tell her of this thing that hung over them, knew that she was puzzled
by his silence, knew that it wasn’t quite fair of him--but even so, he
never guessed the only explanation she had arrived at, that typically
Sandyish conclusion that she was perhaps of less importance than
they had thought, after all. He could hardly have borne that. But he
simply didn’t know how to tell her what he was facing. In his active,
inarticulate life he had learned no words for such emotions as he was
experiencing now. Love, sacrifice, renunciation--how on earth did
people speak of these things? Sandy and he had not needed many words,
until now. Things had looked so easy, until they reached London. So
miraculously easy, after that morning in the Hills. How in pity’s
name to tell her now straight out that he loved her too much to let
her marry him, after all? Besides--the doctor wasn’t quite sure....
Besides--doctors were sometimes wrong.... He kissed her hair, wistfully.

She went home quite happy that night. Dodo was going to be all right.
Everything was going to be all right. She had thought foolish things.
He had suffered so. That was all. He had died, really, and come back
again. She knew how it felt. One wasn’t sure of anything. One rattled
about in life. One had to begin all over again. But he would be all
right. She would make things come right for him, always. He was hers.

“There was a gentleman to see you, ma’am,” said Jenny, meeting her at
the door. “I told him you’d be down on the six o’clock train and he
said he’d call again this evening. Came in a motor, he did, a big blue
one, and went to the inn, ma’am.”

Alexandra was staring at her.

“A g-gentleman?” she said.

“Yes, ma’am. Left his card on the piano. Wrote something on it, he did,
ma’am.”

Bob Taunton had not been at the hospital that day, she remembered then.
Her first thought was that he had come down to see her, that it must be
something about Dodo, that there was something wrong just as she had
thought and that now at last she would know....

She caught up the card. It bore the name of J. Lucien Starke, and
across it, in pencil, “On business.” Dodo wasn’t it, then. _That_
was all right.

“Lucien,” chortled a far corner of her consciousness. “I never knew his
name was-- How funny!”

_On business._ What did that mean? She frowned at the card
speculatively. Business. That must be the robe. But the robe was at
the bottom of the pit. Once she had said they would go back for it.
Business. Hmmm. Lucien. She grinned.

He came in genially, enfolded her hand hugely in his, told her she
looked flourishing, lighted a cigarette, asked if he might smoke. How
it took one back, she thought. Odd, how people didn’t change. Odd, how
lives went on, untouched by upheavals in other lives.

“Pretty room,” he said, glancing about it. “Nice place. But too
peaceful to hold you long, I guess.”

“I’ve been--been very busy,” she replied, with hidden eyes.

“Getting tired of it?”

“No,” she said. Dodo hadn’t seen it yet.

“Given all that other up? Ready to settle down? That it?”

She hesitated. He asked such hard ones.

“No,” she said.

“Seen Dorin lately?”

“Today.”

“Then you know why I’m here.”

“No,” in surprise.

“Didn’t he tell you I’d been to see him?”

“No,” in still greater surprise.

“Well, great Scott!” said Starke. “What _did_ you talk about?” he
demanded almost indignantly.

“We--were reading a book.” She flushed. Rather hopeless trying to get
Starke to see that an unpretentious tale of gods and men may fill
several hours, except such chinks as are stuffed with “personal and
private things.”

“Then you _don’t_ know why I’m here?”

“On business,” she suggested humorously.

“He said you’d have to decide for yourself,” reflected Starke. “He said
he wouldn’t interfere one way or another. Still--I didn’t know he was
as close-mouthed as all this.”

“What is it?” she asked. “Interfere in what?”

“Want a job?” he queried abruptly.

“A--job?” Her eyes were fastened on his face.

“On the level. In your line. And enough risk to make it interesting.”

“A job.” Her chin was up, her eyes were bright. She hugged her knee. “A
job,” she chuckled. “Go on.”

“Well, here’s the proposition. Could you lead an expedition through the
Pass to where that horse went over the cliff with the robe, and then on
to the lost temple--with the Society to back you up and me to finance
the extras?”

“Back there?” She caught her breath. After all, it was not an entirely
new idea. “You’ve got permission to go through the Pass----?”

“The Society has taken this thing up. They want to know about the
temple. I don’t pretend to understand their jargon, but it’s something
about carvings. Anyway, negotiations are under way. An appropriation is
being made. Hell is popping on Olympus, but we leave all that to Lewis.
You know how they feel about _him_. He’s the curly-headed darling
of all the little tin gods and has wheedled Lieutenant-Governors out of
their eye-teeth before now. Wish _I_ could read Sanscrit. Well,
anyway, he’s made up his mind to go to the temple, and I’m betting
he’ll go. He wants to know about the carvings--I want to know about the
robe. The Society loans its prestige--I donate the robe. They pull the
strings--I write the checks. That’s fair enough, eh? But it’s no good
without you, and Lewis wants to see you at once. Dorin says he was out
of his head with fever the last few days above the Fort and-- Well, the
question is, have you any idea how to get back to the temple?”

“Y-yes,” she said slowly. “A sort of idea.” Her eyes grew distant.
Something was dancing within her that had been quiet a long time.
Something else tugged at its sleeve. Out on the road again! Out there!
She shook off the plucking at the sleeve of her spirit, not knowing,
not caring what it was. To go back and finish the job! What luck!

“Remember any landmarks?”

“Yes. A cairn of stones unlike any I had ever seen before--the sides of
a ravine, curving like the neck of a bottle with an unmistakable jag in
one side--a straggling letter S in a rock formation on a hill--a sort
of track that dwindled off into devil-stones. There are things printed
on my brain, I know--burned there, with thirst and fever. If I saw them
again I should know them. They would lead on to other things. The first
few miles beyond the Fort would be difficult. I was pretty far gone.
But once I picked up the trail--once my sense of direction got going--
Oh, it _would_ come back to me, I know it would!”

“Good! That’s what we wanted to know. Say, how did you happen to find
the temple in the beginning?”

“Luck. We simply fell over it in the dark.”

He was watching her, almost with awe.

“Must have been a pretty ghastly business for you, after Dorin got
plugged.”

“Oh, I got sort of numb,” she said. “Existence narrowed down to just
two things--putting one foot in front of the other, and keeping solid
ground under Dodo’s horse.”

“They say you walked all night,” he probed, incredulously.

“Two nights.” She paused, looking back. “The jackals were the worst.
And Dodo babbling in the saddle till it seemed my own brain had
snapped. And then long silences when I was sure I carried a corpse down
to India----”

“How’d you manage to keep going?”

“I had to keep going.” Her schoolboy laconics overtook her. “It meant
Dodo’s life,” she said.

“Well--!” He drew a long breath. “You’ll be more comfortable this time.
Though even Lewis admits that nobody knows what may happen.”

Magic words! They caught her again, flared in her eyes, tugged at her
lips. Her spirit turned handsprings within her. Nobody knew what might
happen. That was the game. Not to know till almost too late. To solve
it just in time. To cross swords with Circumstance, laughing to hear
the ring of steel on steel....

“I’ll talk to Dodo,” she said. “I’ll go back to town tomorrow and----”

“Well, here’s how it is.” He appeared to fumble for words. She watched
him, sitting very still again. “Dorin seemed to think that you--might
not want to wait till he was in shape to make the trip----”

“But of course I want to wait! I couldn’t go without him!”

“He seemed to think,” Starke insisted, somehow cautiously, “that since
he was unconscious most of the way down to the Fort he wouldn’t be much
use on this trip and----”

“But that’s absurd! Of course he must come! What’s the rush? A few
weeks or months here will put him right.”

“I think he would oppose your delaying the expedition on his account.”
Starke’s eyes were on his cigarette tip. She had again that fleeting
sensation of being upwind. “He says you’re able to handle it alone.”

“But I don’t want to handle it alone! That is--unless he’d really
rather not--” She broke off. “I’ll go up and see him tomorrow.”

“Like to ask you something,” announced Starke bluntly. And then, “You
planning to marry him?”

“Yes,” she said steadily, meeting his eyes.

“Well, you know what you want and you go after it, I give you that,” he
admitted. “But--is it him you want now or the things he does?”

“I--” She frowned over this one. “I like doing them with him. We--we
pull well together.”

“Then the life itself isn’t enough. You want him, too. Adventure in
the abstract--that isn’t it any more.” He seemed to be trying to
straighten something out in his mind.

“But I don’t see it in the abstract any more. Adventure means Dodo.
Dodo means adventure. They go together,” she tried to explain.

“I see.” He sighed. “Then you wouldn’t undertake this without him?”

She leaned forward suddenly, looking into his face.

“Have you any reason to believe that he wouldn’t go if he could?”

“Will a duck swim?” Starke asked grimly.

“Well, then--why not wait for him?”

“Just as you say.” He rose. “We only thought, since your own memory and
sense of direction were all we had to go on----”

“But he knows the whole country and has a way with the people! He’s
indispensable on any trip of this kind, I think.”

“Just as you say,” he repeated, but doubtfully. And he said good-night
and then drove to the nearest telegraph station, in the next town.




                               CHAPTER IV


THE telegram went up on Dorin’s breakfast-tray. He read it and groaned.
Bob Taunton came, and read it, and said, “I thought so,” with a
satisfied air, and was affectionately sworn at.

Then they went into conference, during which Bob waxed heated and
Dorin monosyllabic. The doctor was had in, a mammoth gray man, bearing
gallantly on his great shoulders more than his share of the world’s
suffering. And him they harried and bullied and badgered until he
brought down his fist so that things jumped on the table, and uttered a
few bald, unpleasant truths, and departed, still rumbling, Jovian.

Taunton went and closed the door and leaned his back against it,
sagging a little, and they looked at each other across the small, bare
hospital room, in Dorin’s eyes a great desolation, in Taunton’s a
stark, incredulous horror. It was the first time they had ever really
faced the thing.

“Dodo--!” he choked at last, and stumbled forward. “Dodo--old man----!”

They talked a while in low tones, and in the end Bob went out and sent
two telegrams just alike, reading: _Sit tight. Coming down._ And
though there were those who tried to stop them, they caught the noon
train for North Cornwall.

“Fine!” said Starke, on receipt of his orange envelope at the inn. “Now
we’ll know!”

Alexandra’s cheeks got quite pink over hers, and she said, “Good
heavens!” and then, “How sudden!” and then, “I’m _so_ glad!”

Things buzzed all afternoon at the cottage. Jenny went round and
round in excited circles, upsetting every other thing she touched,
and Alexandra flitted about the edges with inconsequent scraps of
song. The very chintzes looked expectant. And at the bottom of the pit
lay Shir Shan’s robe, forgotten in concern over the cream for Dodo’s
strawberries.

She came running to the gate to meet them, bare-headed in the golden
sunset light, and wearing a soft, slim, yellow frock. Dorin, who had
never seen her quite like this before, caught his breath.

She walked between them up the narrow path, holding to an arm of each,
seeming almost to skip, calling their attention to the sun-gilded sea
with the same air of comic achievement that she pointed out her fat
pansies. And Dorin, leaning rather heavily on his stick, looking where
he was bidden, praising where it was due, and laughing in all the right
places, was achingly aware that her hair swept more loosely in its
smooth waves to the great knot, that her throat was white and small
like a child’s, and that her hands were oddly clean and very beautiful.
He missed his sunburned boy acutely, but he wanted never to take his
eyes off this exquisite usurper.

So they came in the dusk to the room overlooking the sea. And, “Oh, I
say!” said Taunton from the threshold. “What a jolly place it is!”

She flashed him a grateful glance.

“We’ll have the candles,” she said. “You’re tired, Dodo, I know you
are. Sit here. The cushion fits--like that!” She inserted it deftly and
was off to the mantel for matches. “I suppose you know Starke is still
at the inn. Must we invite him to dinner?”

“Must we?” said Bob, busy with their cigarettes.

She was lighting a huge candelabrum on the table, and she looked up
laughing in the warm, magic glow of match and taper. Once more Dorin
caught his breath, and somehow looked away.

“Well--not unless Dodo insists--!” she laughed, and bent her head to
the candles again because Dodo was not looking at her. He must be very
tired. Perhaps it had not been wise for him to come. Perhaps-- A little
chill ran through her. Perhaps he would rather not have come.

“I think we can do without him.” His answer came slowly.

“At least till we know--exactly what we mean to do.” She was apparently
absorbed now in reaching to the high candlesticks on the mantel, her
lifted face saint-like in the gentle light. She was thinking that in a
very few minutes she would know what was in Dodo’s mind, that in a very
few minutes the wind must shift and bring the scent to her.

“Sandy--we may as well settle this thing at once. Are you listening?”

“Yes, Dodo.” The low candles on the writing-desk next. It was coming.

“You must go--I want you to go--without me.”

Her hand hovered, then went on to the last candle.

“I--I’d rather wait,” she suggested delicately.

“No. That won’t do.”

It was a little hard, she felt, with Bob Taunton there. It seemed not
quite fair of Dodo. But Dodo always did play fair.... She blew out the
match.

“I don’t quite see.” She faced them, chin up, and Bob’s lips tightened.
Good old Dodo was bungling it rather badly. “You mean you--have other
plans?”

“Yes,” he admitted with a small smile. “I suppose one might put it like
that.”

“Tell her what they are,” said Bob.

“That doesn’t matter just now.”

“But it does matter!” she cried, bewildered at how something was
hurting. “I’ll go on with this job if you say so. I can do it--I can
try--if you like. But--I would like to know--what you’ll be doing
instead.”

“Tell her,” said Bob.

“Later. This other thing comes first, since she’s willing to go. You’d
better let Starke know at once,” he advised her. “On second thought,
you’d better have him come to dinner, after all, and talk things over.
You must come up to town at once and see Lewis, too. He’s a whirlwind.
It won’t be long before you’re on the way.”

“Dodo.” She came and stood before him, straight and slender, her hands
behind her back. “Dodo--where are you going?”

“Not now, I said.” The old note of command, unheard since the days of
her probation, was in his voice. “There are any number of other things
to be----”

“Is it the Amazon? Why shouldn’t you tell me if it’s the Amazon?” She
waited. Her days of probation were over. “Is it?”

And after a dreadful moment, inaudibly, through his teeth--“Yes.” It
would have to do. He hadn’t the words....

“That’s a lie,” said Bob, and Dorin’s glance was like a knife-thrust.

She looked from one to the other piteously, biting her lip. You
couldn’t tell by candlelight. You couldn’t see people’s faces. You
didn’t know where you were. And Dodo wouldn’t look at her. A lie. Dodo
didn’t lie. It must be something quite unthinkable if Dodo lied--! She
dropped to her knees by his chair, trying vainly to see his eyes in the
candlelight.

“What is it? There’s something wrong. I’ve felt it for weeks. Why won’t
you tell me? I’ll not make a fuss.” She laid her hand along his thin
cheek, turning his face toward her. “Dodo--silly--are you worrying
about this marrying business? _Are_ you? Because that’s all rot,
you know! _I_ don’t care. Why, we could go just the same as
before. You--you don’t have to go to the Amazon in order not to marry
me!”

“Oh, child--Sandy--I’d give my blundering soul to marry you, but--”
He must be careful now. Mustn’t let her be sorry for him. She was so
loyal. Nothing could stop her from doing what she conceived to be the
right thing. She was fond of him, too. It would be hard on her at
best, when she knew. If only they could have got her off with Lewis
without her having to know. He mustn’t whimper now. He mustn’t let her
guess how he hated to see her go. Mustn’t be a ball-and-chain on her
sympathies. He was out of it. But she mustn’t be allowed to feel sorry
for him. Why on earth had he come here! Bob had bullied him. Bob was a
sentimental, optimistic ass. Then let Bob handle it. _He_ didn’t
know how! He stretched out a groping hand. “Bob,” he pleaded.

“But you _are_ getting well!” Her voice came clear with terror,
and she caught his face between her hands. “Bob--you swore to me he
would be all right--now----!”

Bob came and sat down on the arm of the chair.

“Tell her what the doctor said, old man.”

“The--doctor--!” She pressed white knuckles against her lips. She hated
doctors.

“Sandy--don’t look like that.” Dorin took her hands and held them. They
were slim and cool and so absurdly clean. He loved them so. How could
he ever let her go! But how could he ever let her stay! “It’s just--
Well, I thought perhaps you needn’t know--at least till you got back.
But if you must have it--I can’t ever ride again. That’s all.”

“N-not--not ride----?”

“Nor walk, much.” She didn’t seem to understand. He set his teeth and
dragged words through them, somehow, trying to make her understand. Her
fingers were clinging to his. There was so much he wanted to say. How
did people say what they wanted to say when their throats ached? Were
there words, somewhere, for what he wanted to say to Sandy? “I’m well
enough,” he was saying, jerkily. “I’ll last forever. But I’m tied to
that stick. Never be able to get about without it again. Now you see.
No good waiting for me. I can’t go.”

She knelt there, looking up at him, taking it in. He said it so
quietly, as though it was the weather. It couldn’t mean what it sounded
as though it meant.

“But--I brought you back--you didn’t die--you were getting well--you
_must_ get well--oh, but you shan’t stay behind!” Her eyes
widened, tears hanging on their lashes. “Then _I_ shan’t go!” she
cried, and Dorin groaned.

“I was afraid of that! But get it out of your head at once. Of course
you’re going.” She had to go. She would still want to go, once she got
a little used to this. Hard on her. But she had to go.

“Back there--alone?”

“Not alone. At the head of a nice little chartered expedition with its
worthless little papers all in order.”

“But--I couldn’t----”

“Yes, you could,” he contradicted grimly. “You brought me out. You can
take them in.”

“It would be different.”

“It would be. Thank God.”

“No.” She laid her cheek against his sleeve. “No, I couldn’t do that.”

“Hold on a minute.” This was awful. This wasn’t like her. She would be
sorry later if he let her have her way now. If only he could make it
easier for her, somehow. If only she had had time to get used to it. He
should have told her weeks ago. He himself had known, weeks ago. But he
had gone on foolishly hoping for a miracle.... Miracles didn’t happen.
Not after soft-nosed bullets. Poor Sandy. She was taking it much too
hard, though. How little she looked, there on the floor. If only
one could pick her up.... She wasn’t--_crying_? “Pull yourself
together, Sandy,” he said, looking down at her helplessly. “You’re not
a sentimentalist. There’s work to be done--such as it is. _Our_
work--such as it is. Come, now--how about it?”

She got to her feet slowly, pushing back her hair with the old gesture.
No, she wasn’t crying.

“I’ve got to think,” she said. “I can’t--think.”

They watched her pityingly, while she paced the room’s length and back,
and drifted out through the open windows into the garden above the sea.
Then their eyes met and Bob shook his head once, like a man who has
overshot.

There was silence in the room. Bob stooped above a candle to light
another cigarette. The sound of the sea came up, a murmur only, for the
night was calm. Jenny was singing very softly, very sweetly, in the
kitchen. No one would have heard, if it hadn’t been so still.

“Oh, damn the robe!” said Dorin suddenly.

“Agreed.”

“Bobby--I mustn’t try to hold her. That wouldn’t do. She must think
I want her to go. But it’s not safe, you know.” He was only thinking
aloud, as they could, with each other. “Lewis is a reckless fool. He
thinks it’s like Egypt. Tombs. It’s not Egypt. She oughtn’t to go.”

“Compared to the little party _you_ took her on, the Lewis
expedition is safe as houses,” Bob reminded him mercilessly.

“I know that.” He sighed. “_Not safe!_ Well, I’ve lived to say it!
Things look different from this end, somehow. Oh, very different--at
the end, Bobby! Remember that. Not that it matters. Serves me right,
doesn’t it, any way you look at it. Jolly good for me. Good for the
spirit of a mortal who was proud. I thought I knew it all. And then--we
shaved so close--she was so splendid--it was so ghastly a gamble, with
her life as the stake! Oh, she loved it! Gloried in it! And she must
go on, I suppose, taking chances in the good old way till she comes a
cropper as we all do, sooner or later. And I won’t be there!” His head
went down into his hands. “She was born to it. Mustn’t try to hold her.
Mustn’t be an old woman, Bobby. Must--let her have her head.”

“You don’t think--” began Bob, and stopped.

“No,” said Dorin, from between his hands.

“Might be better----”

“No. _You’d_ hate it.”

“But after all--she is a woman.”

“If you’d seen her in the temple you might not be so sure.”

“I’ve seen her since then.” Bob rose and walked round his chair,
aimlessly. “You see--the point is--she loves you.”

“So do you. But you’ve loafed about England long enough, for all that.”

“You know what I mean.”

“Yes. But she loves the life I lead--led. And so she loves me. We
belonged together--out there. But if it comes to me without the fun or
the fun without me, there’s not much choice, is there! Put yourself in
her place.”

“You could keep her here, if you tried.”

“Perhaps. But could I keep her happy, there’s the rub.”

“She loves you,” repeated Bob stubbornly.

“Don’t harp on it, there’s a good chap.”

“Sorry. But--I’m not sure you’re right to let her go.”

“If I were whole, I’d have some right to try to steer her in a
moderately safe course from now on. If I had two good legs again
I’d feel more like--putting my foot down.” He grinned one-sidedly,
hopefully, but Bob didn’t seem to see the joke. “But as it is--I can’t
presume. Why, it would be worse than the unlamented Clem! Sandy married
to me now would be like the blind man’s dog! I----”

“Dodo, you do exaggerate. Damnable habit.”

“Oh, good Lord, Bobby, do you suppose I haven’t been over this a
million times and seen her farther beyond my reach each time I looked?”

“But, old man, you could travel! You might not be able to climb things
and ride things and chase things--but you’re a long way from bedridden,
you know!”

“She’s got to be free, and not be thinking about me all the time.”

“Freedom,” said Bob, kicking at the carpet, “is a state of mind.”

“But don’t you see,” Dorin went on heedlessly, “if I should go mad and
beg her not to risk her precious neck a second time for that infernal
yellow rag with bits of glass stuck on to it--if she should marry me
now out of loyalty or pity--!” He hunched his shoulders in a sort of
shudder. “No,” he said. “Oh, no. It isn’t good enough.”

“All the same----”

“No,” repeated Dorin dully. “I can’t see it at all.”

“Look here. Give her a chance, won’t you?”

“A chance to what?”

“Go out there and talk to her, that’s all I ask.”

“Talk?” said Dorin, horrified and helpless. It was the last thing he
saw himself doing.

“Right. Talk.”

“But--there’s nothing to say. That is----”

“_Nothing to say!_ Oh, my God! What have you _been_ saying! To me,
just now! To her, all these weeks! To anybody that would listen, there
at the Fort while you were out of your head! _Nothing to say!_”

Dorin was looking interested.

“In the Fort? Did I talk about Sandy in the----”

“Did you--! Nothing else _but_! I blushed for you! Upon my word, I
blushed for you! Didn’t think you had it in you!”

Dorin was still looking interested. Perhaps what the situation really
required was more of the same.

“What did I say?” he inquired respectfully of the oracle.

Bob stood still and looked at him with something like disgust.

“I didn’t take it down,” he said. “You’ll have to make up some more as
you go. It came easy enough to you then.”

“But I’m not delirious anymore,” Dorin reminded him gently. Again his
tentative grin drew a blank.

“When you come at last to the pearly gates where St. Peter keeps the
keys,” said Bob severely, “may I be there to see if you can talk sense
just once. _I_ can’t do anything with you!”

“Well, but what was I talking at the Fort?” insisted Dorin, but more
feebly.

“Something about violets, dammit. And something about tigers.”

Violets. That settled Dorin. He leaned his head against the back of the
chair and closed his eyes. That went home.

“What do you suppose I brought you down here for?” demanded Bob
aggrievedly. “To lend a hand. To let her know she’s wanted here.”

“She knows.”

“They like to be told.”

“If I whine now she’ll stick at any price. I can’t have that.”

“So you’ll sit here and let her think you don’t care one whoop in hell
whether she goes or stays!”

“She’ll know better than to think that.”

“Oh, you consummate ass! Can’t you see----”

“I can see that I _must_ keep out of this. A word from me now
might make her do something she would regret all her life.”

“Three sensible words from you now would put the whole thing right! ‘I
want you.’ Down your stubborn pride and say ’em quick, for God’s sake!”

_I want you._ Was that all one had to say? It sounded easy enough.
Could one possibly set this thing right with three words? And would it
be right when one had done so? What _was_ right? What in heaven’s
name was one to do? To people who had been in love all their lives,
or to people who were not and never had been in love, it might appear
simple. But he was so new to it. He loved Sandy so much. Having her was
not the thing. She must be happy. And how could she be happy with a
man who couldn’t ride things, and climb things, and chase things? And
yet--she did love him, in her way. They belonged together. They had
been so long finding one another. It was terrible not to know what to
do. He wasn’t used to it.

“It’s not pride,” he began. “It’s----”

“_Oh, don’t argue!_”

Bob threw up frenzied arms to heaven. In the very act, he caught sight
of Dorin’s face and went to him, and gathered him up in a bear-like
embrace and held him, muttering penitent things.

Once more, Bob was very near to hating her. That she could hesitate
at all! That she could weigh Dodo for one instant against the whole
continent of Asia! Couldn’t she see that Dodo always had had, always
must have what he wanted? He was of a mind to go out there and talk to
her himself!




                               CHAPTER V


MEANWHILE, Alexandra sat on a low rock-bench in the garden above the
restless, murmurous blackness that was the sea. A feeble crescent moon
was smothered in drifting cloud. Except where the candlelight made
a dim square on the ground outside the windows it was quite dark in
the little, rocky garden, and except for Jenny singing softly in the
kitchen it was quite still. But Alexandra, trying so hard to think, sat
with her elbows on her knees and her hands over her ears and her eyes
shut tight.

It was the queerest thing the way her mind wouldn’t work. She couldn’t
go back to Dodo till she had decided, and all she wanted was to go
back. He wouldn’t know what to make of her like this. He liked the way
she always knew at once exactly what she wanted to undertake. And now
she couldn’t think. It was partly because of Dodo’s eyes. She kept
seeing them, even with her own eyes screwed tight shut. And Dodo’s
voice. She heard it, even with her hands pressed over her ears. She
wanted to go back to him. There seemed to be nothing else in the world
but going back to Dodo. Love. This must be it. Whatever did one do with
it? One couldn’t think.

_I want you to go without me._ She must carry on, then. It was
their work--such as it was. There was only one of them now. And Dodo
would fret about the robe’s being left there, so long as there was a
chance of having it. She must go back and fetch it, then, so that it
wouldn’t be always on his mind, a sort of derisive monument to his last
job. His last job. Oh, that was horrible. Dodo--never to sit a horse
again! But she mustn’t stop for that now. She must think.

_You brought me out. You could take them in._ Yes, perhaps she
could. Her sense of direction, her eye for landmarks, had never failed.
She had had that from her grandfathers. It had only wanted a chance.
But to go without Dodo. To see again the place where their last fire
had been built and where they had talked together in the dawn.... But
she must pull herself together. She must not be a sentimentalist.
How simple things had looked that morning in the Hills! It was life
that was difficult, not death. They had never dreamed of--this--that
morning. Then, if they got through alive they were going on together.
And if they died-- They had never dreamed, that morning, of not being
together, somehow. She had sworn never to leave him, and now he was
sending her, as he had tried to send her then. That time she had
mutinied. But this was different, wasn’t it? He was safe now, and
she had to go on alone, whether she liked it or not. She couldn’t
have Dodo disappointed in her. She couldn’t very well go to Dodo and
bury her face against his coat and say, “That’s all over. I’d rather
just be with you now, if you don’t mind.” That wouldn’t be playing
the game--their game. Just this one more job, then, since he wished
it. And then she would come back and be near him. She must be very
careful--must be very sure to get back this time, with Dodo waiting
helplessly instead of sharing the fun. It was no way to go, though,
with your mind always on getting back safely. She didn’t like it at
all. It was going to be so different, trying to get back to Dodo.

_I’d give my blundering soul to marry you_. He did want her, then.
It wasn’t that he didn’t want her. But if he wanted her like that and
she wanted only to be with him--why couldn’t the robe just go to the
devil?

She sat up at that, staring widely out to sea. Well, why not, she
argued, breathlessly. After all, what did the robe matter? They had
books to write and books to read, and there was always so much to talk
about, with Dodo. What did anything matter, really, unless they were
doing it together? Couldn’t he see that? Dodo always saw things. Her
breath came more quickly between her parted lips. They could live here,
with the sea at the bottom of the garden.... She would marry Dodo and
they would settle down.... It was a tremendous idea. A great adventure.
Adventure was Dodo. Dodo was adventure. Hang the robe!

“Dodo!” she called, jumping up and running toward the windows. “Oh,
Dodo, I--” She paused on the threshold and hung there a moment,
radiant, a little uncertain, and then came on to where they sat
waiting, Bob on the arm of the chair. “Dodo,” she began again, above
the foolish thumping of her heart, “_would_ you mind--that is--I’d
_so_ much rather marry you and stay here!” They were blinking
at her stupidly. She knelt beside the chair, and slid her hand into
Dorin’s. “_Please_ don’t send me back there,” she insisted softly.
“Just for that bit of junk!”

Then Bob began to laugh. It was just too much for him. He laughed all
up and down the room, he couldn’t help it, waving his arms and holding
his head in a kind of sublimated hysteria, moaning something about the
blind man’s dog. Alexandra, comfortably close in the sudden circle
of Dorin’s arms, watched him in astonishment over her shoulder. But
Dorin’s face was pressed against her hair and this time he failed to
see the joke.


                                THE END

THE SINGLE TRACK




THE SINGLE TRACK




CHAPTER I

YEARS OF DISCRETION


Janetta crossed her pretty feet and then considering that posture
undignified for an attorney’s office, uncrossed them again and jingled
her platinum mesh bag in impatience much as a child would twiddle its
pencil in the last trying hour of school.

“I came because you said I must, Uncle Andy, but it’s perfectly silly
to talk to me, for I don’t understand a thing about mines and stocks
and dividends!” She glanced with a little pout at the lawyer’s dour
face. “Besides it’s my birthday, and I think it is mean----”

“It is precisely because it is your birthday, my dear Janetta, your
twenty-first birthday, that it is necessary for you to take your mind
from frocks and frills and flummery long enough to try to understand
your financial situation,” Andrew Geddes interrupted sternly. “You are
no longer a child in the eyes of the law and the time has come for you
to take an active and intelligent interest in your own affairs.”

Janetta glanced at the jeweled watch on her slender wrist and sighed.
She would certainly be late for that luncheon! Then hopefully she
favored Mr. Geddes with a swift, engaging smile.

“But Uncle Andy, I prefer to leave everything in your hands and
Ollie’s; I do, really! You’ve always managed so splendidly since
grandfather died that I would much rather just trust you.”

“You’d trust anybody, if it saved you from bother and responsibility!”
the lawyer snapped, but there came a little tender twinkle into his
shrewd eyes. “It won’t do you a bit of good to smile at me like that,
Janetta Gildersleeve! You got my watch away from me that way and
smashed it when you were a matter of three years old, but you can’t
wheedle me now. Of course, you’d rather leave everything in my hands
and go on leading your butterfly existence; but you may find that it
will last just about as long as the existence of a butterfly does! What
then?”

A certain grimness had crept into his tone, the twinkle disappeared,
and Janetta looked again at him in bland bewilderment.

“What do you mean, Uncle Andy?” she asked wonderingly. “A butterfly
lives about six weeks, doesn’t it? What has that got to do with
dividends and things?”

“I mean, Janetta, that sometimes property depreciates, and dividends
