The other made a face and nodded. “Hard luck,” he commented. Then: “I
say, though! Maybe he’s a friend of yours?”

“No, he isn’t.” Richard’s tone was extremely dry, and the other boy’s
mouth curved in another grin.

“He’s a poor fish,” was the pronouncement. “What’s your name, by the
way? Mine’s Ravenel.”

“Dodd,” said Richard.

“Short and sweet! You’re in the third, aren’t you? I think I saw you in
Latin 5 yesterday. You must be blooming smart.”

“Smart?” echoed Richard.

“Yes, to be in third class. Why, I’m sixteen.”

“How old do you think I am?”

“Fourteen; nearly fifteen maybe.”

“I’m nearly sixteen.”

Ravenel whistled. “You don’t look it.”

“It’s because I’m so small,” said Richard sadly.

Ravenel viewed him judicially. “Yes, you are small,” he said, “but you
look pretty well-built and awfully fit.” He had been gently propelling
the canoe toward midstream and now he shipped his paddle and relaxed,
gathering his knees between slim brown arms. “I’m no giant myself,”
he went on, smiling. “Glad of it, too. It lets me out of all kinds
of trouble. When they come scouting around for football or crew or
baseball material they just look at me and go on. It’s not so bad,
being a pigmy.”

“I wouldn’t call you that,” laughed Richard. “You’re a lot bigger than
I am. But――but don’t you like to play football? Or row?”

“No, I don’t. I’m too busy, for one thing.”

“Oh!” Richard wondered what the occupation might be that precluded his
new acquaintance from those sports, but he didn’t quite like to ask.
Perhaps Ravenel guessed the other’s curiosity, for he went on gravely.

“You see, Dodd, I’m here at North Bank for two things principally.
One is to study very, very hard and the other is to enjoy myself.” He
paused as though expecting comment, and so Richard said:

“I see.” He didn’t though; not exactly. The statement sounded queer.
Ravenel went on, hugging his white-flanneled knees tightly and
regarding his _vis-à-vis_ with really sobering gravity.

“Of course study takes up a lot of my time, Dodd. If a fellow is really
conscientious about it he’s bound to spoil a couple of hours a day
studying.”

“A couple!” exclaimed Richard in amazement. “Why I’ve been putting in
three and four!”

“Really?” Ravenel frowned. “Well, some fellows are like that, I
suppose. I learn very quickly. Anyway, two hours out of what you have
left from recitations and meals doesn’t leave much time for enjoyment.
You see that, eh? Now suppose I go in for baseball or football――Well,
not football, for I’m too light, but some other sport: lacrosse, say,
or basket ball; why, I wouldn’t have any time left!”

“No, I guess you wouldn’t,” acknowledged Richard, “but――but what do you
want the time for? I mean――”

“For enjoyment, of course.”

“Yes, but what sort of enjoyment?”

“Why, this, for instance. All sorts of jolly things. Sometimes I go
down to the bridge and fish. Sometimes I take some lunch and go up
the river and have a picnic. There are so many things to do, you see;
really important things. I like to swim, too. I like to photograph. I
like to――to――oh, just mess around in the woods. Those things are fun.
Getting all heated up and covered with dirt playing baseball, or having
my head slammed at lacrosse――well, I can’t just see that, Dodd!”

“Of course, what it amounts to,” said Richard after a moment’s
consideration, “is that you don’t like sports.”

“I don’t like some kinds of sport,” corrected Ravenel gently. “Canoeing
is sport, swimming is sport, walking is sport.”

“I ought to have said competitive sports,” amended Richard.

“Maybe, but when it comes to that I’m ready to take on any one at the
things I like. I’ve got nothing against competition. I won the mile and
two-mile races on the ice last winter and I’m no slouch at swimming if
the distance isn’t too far.”

“But don’t you think it’s a fellow’s duty to――to do anything he can? I
mean, for instance, if he can play baseball oughtn’t he to do it? Or
football? Or――or anything else?”

“Duty to whom?” asked Ravenel.

“Why, to the School!”

“Oh, that! Old stuff, Dodd, old stuff!”

Richard looked plainly puzzled, even a little shocked. “But you
_have_ a duty, Ravenel,” he insisted. “In a way a fellow’s school is
like――like his country.” Richard flushed a trifle. “I mean, you know,
he believes in it and wants it to be the best and does all he can to
help it be the best. At least, that’s the way I feel about it,” he
ended a trifle embarrassedly.

“Your sentiments do you credit, Dodd,” said Ravenel gravely. “It’s
certainly a fine thing to hear the youth of the country talk like that.
I can remember when I used to say just that sort of thing. Patriotism!
School Spirit! Gee, I was chock-full of them! But they’ve gone out of
style now. It’s every fellow for himself these days.”

Richard peered closely at his companion’s countenance before replying.
Was there, perhaps, a hint of raillery behind the soberness of his
eyes? Richard couldn’t be sure. “I don’t believe that,” he answered
firmly. “I guess you don’t, either. I guess there are lots and lots of
fellows here who think just as I do. I don’t believe that things like
patriotism ever go out of style, Ravenel.”

“_Omnia bona bonis_,” murmured Ravenel. “Retain your innocence, sweet
child. I would do naught to disillusion you.”

Richard hesitated, doubtful. Then he smiled. “I guess that means that
you know I’m right, doesn’t it?” he asked.

The other shook his head, but he smiled gayly. “It means, Dodd, that
your faith is too beautiful to destroy. By the way, what particular
line of patriotic endeavor do you go in for?”

“How do you mean?” asked Richard.

“What sport. Football, baseball, tennis, soccer――”

“Oh! Not any, I’m afraid. You see, I’m too small. At high school they
wouldn’t let me on any of the teams, not even basket ball. They say I’m
not strong enough.”

“You? Fiddlesticks! I’ll bet you have more strength than I have. Still,
you should worry. You’ll escape a lot of bother.”

Richard smiled ruefully. “The trouble is,” he said, “I’d like awfully
well to play things. Of course, I couldn’t play football, I suppose,
not even on a scrub team, but it seems to me I might try for baseball
next spring. I’ll be sixteen then, and maybe I’ll grow some, too. I eat
everything I can that makes a fellow grow.”

“Oh, you’ll grow all right,” comforted the other, “but I guess you’ll
never be very large. Are your parents small?”

“My mother’s quite tall, but father’s smallish. He doesn’t _look_
small, but he is. I guess I’m like him.”

“Well, for my part, I don’t see why you want to make teams, but every
fellow to his taste. You go and talk with Mr. Tanner. He’s physical
instructor, you know. Seen him yet? Well, you’ll have to in a day or
two. He will go all over you with a stethoscope and dig you in the ribs
and make you take long breaths and say ‘A-a-ah’ and lift yourself on
your toes twenty times――or maybe it’s twelve――and feel very silly. You
see him some time when he isn’t busy and tell him what you want to do.
He’s a good old goat. I dare say he will pass you for something, if
it’s only lacrosse.”

Richard’s face brightened. “Gee, I’d like lacrosse!” he exclaimed. “Do
you think he would?”

Ravenel smiled pityingly. “Search me, Dodd,” he said. “He will let you
do something, though, something to help the dear old school! By the
way, do you swim?”

“Yes, pretty well. I like swimming, but folks say I oughtn’t to do much
of it. It’s too taxing on the heart or something.”

“Folks talk a heap of nonsense,” grunted Ravenel. “Ever go in with your
clothes on?”

“Why, no! What for?”

“It’s good practice,” replied Ravenel inscrutably. “You never can tell
when you may have to, you know. No fellow really knows how to swim
until he can do a half mile or so with everything on.”

“I should think it would be pretty hard,” said Richard.

“Not very. Of course, you can always kick off your shoes, if you don’t
mind losing them. It’s hard to carry them along. You ought to try it
some time.”

“I wouldn’t mind,” was the answer. There wasn’t much enthusiasm in the
tone, however.

“Of course,” pursued Ravenel, who seemed quite in love with the
subject, “when a fellow has a pretty good watch he rather hates to get
it wet. Most watches leak after three or four minutes.”

“I guess water wouldn’t hurt mine much,” laughed Richard. “It only cost
three dollars, and it’s always twenty minutes slow every night!”

“Oh, well, in that case――”

The canoe had floated to the south shore of the river where a rounded
promontory thrust its well-wooded slope outward, creating a back-water
in which reeds and rushes found a shallow much to their liking and
where dragon flies hung lazily about in the sunlight. Suddenly――so
suddenly that Richard could only stare amazedly through one fleeting
instant――Ravenel threw his body sidewise. Over went the blue canoe!
Over went both occupants! Richard, falling into depths of greenish
water, choking and thrashing, still grappled with his sense of utter
amazement.




                               CHAPTER IV

                                 JIMSY


“Fetch the paddle, will you?”

Richard, coughing and sputtering, his head at length above water,
looked about him. A few yards away floated the upturned canoe. Nearer,
Ravenel was treading water, the canoe seat under one armpit and the
cushion in one hand. Dazedly, Richard searched for the paddle and found
it bobbing gently behind him. With a final sputter and choke he seized
it and struggled toward the canoe. Swimming with rubber-soled shoes
on his feet, with his arms fettered by the clinging sleeves of his
coat, was no easy task. But a half dozen desperate strokes gave him a
hold on the canoe, and from there he faced the calm, smiling Ravenel
indignantly.

“You did that on purpose!” he gasped. “I saw you!”

“Of course I did,” was the untroubled reply. “Stick your paddle on the
bottom and we’ll push her in.” He laid his own burdens on the hull and
began to propel the unwieldy craft toward the rushes. “You said you
wouldn’t mind it, you know,” he went on, “and there’s no time like the
present. We’ll dry out in the sun in a little while. Put your feet
down. You can walk in now.”

Richard obeyed and between them the canoe was pushed into shallow
water. There, removing the seat, paddle and cushion to the stones,
Ravenel directed and Richard helped and the canoe was lifted, drained
and set down again right side up. When that was done Richard looked
up to find his companion smiling quizzically at him. After a moment
Richard grinned. Then Ravenel laughed. Then Richard laughed, although
less mirthfully, and after that the _entente cordiale_ was quite
restored and they took off their outer clothing and laid the garments
in the sun and stretched themselves on the little beach of small,
waterworn stones.

“I don’t just see why you did it, though,” said Richard presently.
Ravenel stopped flicking pebbles into the water and looked around.

“I did it for fun,” he answered tranquilly. “It was fun, wasn’t it now?”

Richard observed him doubtfully. “For you, maybe.”

“Rot! For both of us. Look here, Dodd, you’d never been dumped out of
a canoe before, had you? No! Well, then, it was an experience, wasn’t
it? Sure! And experiences are what every fellow’s after. Of course you
were surprised, and maybe you were scared just for a second, but that
didn’t last. After that you liked it. You liked getting your head out
and thrashing around and spitting out the water and finding you were
better than the river! You were proud of being able to keep afloat even
if you did have your clothes on! And now it’s all over, and you’ve
done something new, and you can remember it, and talk about it, too, if
you like. And you’re feeling great, just as I am, and you’re glad I did
it. Am I right?”

“Well,” began Richard hesitantly.

“’Fess up! Tell the truth, Doddie!”

Richard grinned and then laughed. “I guess so,” he answered. And then:
“Say it _is_ hard to swim that way, isn’t it?” he went on. “It seems
like your clothes weigh about a million pounds!”

Ravenel chuckled. “You bet! If you’ve got a long swim ahead the best
thing to do is get everything off that you can――shoes, coat, trousers.
It isn’t hard if you keep your head.”

“Yes,” agreed Richard, “I suppose it wouldn’t do to take your head off,
too!”

Ravenel chuckled, “Why, the kid has a sense of humor!” he exclaimed
delightedly. “Dodd, I’m glad I found you. By the way, you have another
name, haven’t you?”

“Richard,” acknowledged that youth.

“Fellows call you ‘Dick’? I suppose.”

“Yes, sometimes.” Richard hesitated, and then went on with candor.
“Generally they call me ‘Dicky,’ though,” he said.

“They would, of course.” Ravenel grinned. “I shall call you ‘Dick,’
though, according you proper respect.”

Richard nodded. “What’s your name?” he asked.

“James Hamilton Ravenel,” replied the other with great dignity.

“Oh!” Richard deliberated. “Well, James is a――a nice name.”

“It’s rotten,” returned James emphatically.

“I suppose they call you ‘Jim’?”

Ravenel shook his head.

“Ham, then?” laughed Richard.

Ravenel shook his head again. Richard looked puzzled. Ravenel sighed.
“I guess I might as well tell you,” he grumbled. “You’d find out soon
enough. They call me Jimsy.”

Richard laughed enjoyably, more, though, at Ravenel’s tone of disgust
than at the oddity of the nickname. “Why, that’s jolly,” he declared.
“Jimsy! Mind if I――” Richard stopped embarrassedly.

“No,” answered Ravenel. “Go ahead. I’m used to it. Even my folks call
me ‘Jimsy.’ They ought to know better, too.” He appeared to become
immersed in tragic reflection. Richard respected his silence and fell
to tossing pebbles at the canoe paddle. Suddenly Ravenel spoke again,
this time with no hint of tragedy. “Got over your homesickness?” he
asked slyly.

Richard flushed slightly. “I wasn’t exactly homesick,” he denied.

“Weren’t you? Well, you looked mighty down-in-the-mouth,” responded the
other dryly. “That’s why I asked you along. I’ve been homesick often
enough, and it’s a punk feeling.”

“Maybe I was homesick,” acknowledged Richard. “I was wishing I was
back home, anyway. You see, I don’t know any one here, except like I
told you, and――and everything’s quite different from what I expected.”

“Everything always is, if you ask me,” said Ravenel pessimistically.
“Still, that’s half the fun, I guess. It would be rather tiresome if
things always happened the way you expected them to. What is it that’s
wrong here, Dick?”

“Oh, I don’t know,” replied Richard vaguely. “I suppose I had funny,
high-faluting notions about preparatory schools.”

“I know.” Ravenel chuckled. “You’d been reading books. Especially those
English books. I did, too. I thought life was going to be one jolly
round of――of heroic adventures. I was all set to rescue my deadly
enemy from drowning and die in the infirmary with the principal and
the faculty weeping by my bedside and planning a bronze tablet in my
memory. But it hasn’t worked out that way at all. I can’t even scare
up an enemy, dog-gone it! I haven’t even fought the school bully
yet. There isn’t any! Think of a school without a bully, Dick! Gee,
the fellows who write the school stories wouldn’t believe it! It’s
positively fierce!”

Richard laughed, and then, becoming quickly serious, asked: “Do
they――are you allowed to scrap here, Rav――Jimsy?”

“Scrap? Hm, well, if they don’t actually catch you doing it; _flagrante
bello_, so to speak; if you can get away with it. What’s doing?”
Ravenel looked extremely interested.

“Nothing. I just wondered.” Richard’s gaze wandered to the river. After
a moment he added: “It’s that fellow Lodge, the fellow I’m rooming
with. He’s bigger than I am, and older and all that, but by gum, Jimsy,
if he doesn’t quit nagging me I’m going to go for him some day!”

“That’s the spirit! Dick, I knew I was going to love you the first
moment I saw you! But, say, hold on! Bert’s inches taller than you, and
heavier, and you won’t have a chance. Take my advice and get him some
other way. It won’t be any real satisfaction to have him beat you up,
Dick!”

“I don’t know any other way.”

“Well, we’ll think of one. Bert’s a pig, and anything short of poison
will answer. We’ll cook up some scheme, all right. By Jove, life is
brighter already, Dick! Something tells me that you and I are going to
have some whaling good times around here!” Ravenel kicked his shoeless
feet in the air and whooped with glee. After that he said “_Ouch!_”
with great expression and rubbed a shoulder blade where a stone had
bored into it.

The clothing took longer to dry than they had counted on, and in
the end they had to get back into very damp garments. But before
that came about they had discussed many subjects; swimming, “snap”
courses, photography, camping out, Doctor Heidler, the principal, and,
according to Ravenel, “a beany old scout”, the faculty in general,
fishing, third class English, the comparative merits of five prominent
universities, scouting, literature, postage stamps and pearls. The
last subject was brought up by Richard, who had picked up a broken
shell, and enlarged on by Ravenel, who knew a place up the river where
there were millions of pearl mussels. He had never, he acknowledged,
discovered a pearl in one of them yet, but they were the right sort and
he was certain that if they undertook a systematic search they would
find plenty. It was unanimously voted to go pearl fishing on Saturday
afternoon.

Just before supper time they lifted the blue canoe back on its rack
and climbed the hill on their way to Baldwin House, for――which was
something of a coincidence in the estimation of each――they both resided
in the “Apple Box,” Richard on the second floor and Ravenel on the
third. It might be explained in passing that each of the four dormitory
buildings had a nickname. McCrea, occupied solely by the seniors, was
known as “Mickey,” Follen, which housed the fourth class, was called
“The Nursery,” and Ellicot was “The Cot.” Richard eagerly accepted his
new friend’s invitation to visit Number 33 that evening, and, much
happier than he had been since he had arrived at school, went on to
Number 12 and the unwelcome society of Bert Lodge.

He found Bert bathing his nose with almost passionate solicitude and
muttering, “O-oh! Ugh!” whenever his wash-cloth came in contact with
that abbreviated feature. Some one, it developed in the course of
a subsequent conversation that was rather more of a monologue, had
rudely planted the sole of a shoe against Bert’s face with unpleasantly
painful results. Richard, viewing the injury, reproved himself for the
pleasure he felt, and offered some witch hazel. Bert refused the offer,
scoffed at the remedy and went on bathing and groaning. A few minutes
before supper time Richard left him to his agony, being by that time
weary of Bert’s lamentations. From remarks that followed him into the
corridor it was evident to Richard that his roommate considered him
unfeeling, uncharitable and otherwise lacking in Christian attributes.
Which fact didn’t prevent Richard from making a very excellent meal.

He discovered that Alan Linscott sat at a table at the far end of the
big hall, one of twelve first class youths of unmistakably athletic
build. Probably, thought Richard, they were all crew fellows. He was
wrong there, however, for, since the football table was not to start
until the next Monday, a good half of the dozen were gridiron toilers.
Richard was, though, far less interested in Alan Linscott this evening
than he had been previously, and his attention soon wandered away from
the crew captain. The feeling of loneliness and friendlessness was
gone and he was looking forward almost excitedly to the coming visit
to Jimsy Ravenel and his roommate, one George Ferry, who, Jimsy had
assured him, was a “top-holer.” Richard wasn’t quite certain what a
“top-holer” was, but it sounded reassuring. He ate a good deal of
everything that was placed before him or that he could get his hands
on, caring less than before that his table companions were too busy
with each other to address him save to request the milk or the bread or
some other viand that was momentarily out of their reach. Jimsy himself
sat two tables distant, his back to Richard, but he had spied the
latter on entering and had waved a greeting. There was a great deal of
merriment at Jimsy’s table, for much of which Jimsy himself appeared to
be accountable. Richard more than half wished that he sat there, too.




                               CHAPTER V

                         IN NUMBER THIRTY-THREE


George Ferry proved to be rather different from Richard’s preconceived
idea of him. It had seemed that the roommate of a fellow of Jimsy’s
characteristics must be sprightly, fun-loving, debonair. George wasn’t
anything of the sort. He was a rather tall, lanky boy of seventeen
with good features and coppery-brown hair. He said very little on
the occasion of that first visit of Richard’s, sitting propped up by
cushions on the window seat, regarding the others gravely when he was
not dipping into the book held open against his long legs. Richard
didn’t feel quite comfortable, for he had the sensation of being
examined minutely and, he thought, disapprovingly. Yet George Ferry
could smile, and did it two or three times during the evening, and he
had a manner of expressing himself that made Richard feel that his own
remarks were horribly entangled. Richard gathered before his visit was
ended that George was a good deal of a student――or, in school parlance,
a “hound”――and that his only passion aside from books was lacrosse. He
and Jimsy Ravenel came from neighboring towns in Delaware, which fact
doubtless had first brought them together. After that it may have been
a total dissimilarity that had fostered friendship. George was in the
second class and already nibbling at extra work which would, two years
hence, make his entrance examinations for college easier. Jimsy poked a
good deal of fun at him, which George received with a tolerant twitch
of his lips which, usually, did for a smile. Richard departed uncertain
whether he liked or disliked the fellow, and even more uncertain
whether George Ferry liked or disliked him!

His surprise was all the greater, therefore, when Jimsy, hailing him
from the steps of Hall the next forenoon, incidentally let fall in the
course of conversation that George had congratulated him on his new
acquaintance. “Said he was glad to see me pick up with a fellow of
intelligence,” chuckled Jimsy. “I told him prolonged association with
him had driven me to it! Old George seems to approve of you mightily.
Got quite chatty after you went last night. Said you had ideas and
ambition. Hinted that I hadn’t. Silly old idiot! Say, don’t forget
Saturday.”

“Saturday? Oh, the pearls, you mean.”

“Yes. We’d better go in the morning. There’s a game in the afternoon.”

“I thought you didn’t care for football.”

“Me? Oh, I like to see them play it. I only meant that I didn’t care
for it for little Jimsy. We’ll go right after chemistry; that’ll give
us nearly three hours before the game begins.”

“What about dinner?” objected Richard.

“Take some lunch with us. It’s lots more fun. You leave that to me.
I’ve got a drag at the kitchen. They’ll give me a hand-out. I’ll see
you before that, though. What you doing this afternoon?”

“I ought to study a bit,” said Richard.

“Good idea! So ought I. We’ll take our books and go up on the hill. I
know a corking place. I’ll stop in at your room at three-thirty.”

The place was “corking” without any doubt. From it they could look for
miles up and down the river valley and across to Annapolis and, beyond,
far down the bay. But there was very little studying done. Jimsy used
the two books he had brought along to pillow his head on, and whenever
Richard started to read his companion’s voice broke in on him. Before
long he gave up all attempt. After an hour or so Jimsy got restless and
so they deposited their books in the cleft of a tree and explored the
hill that ascended behind them. They made no momentous discoveries, but
they had a good deal of fun, and afterwards they spent a good twenty
minutes locating the books, finding them at last a long way from where
they had thought them, and swung down the hill, across an old tobacco
field, in the yellow glare of a setting sun and so reached the red clay
road a quarter of a mile from school.

That was the beginning of a companionship from which Richard derived a
great deal of happiness. He was making other friends but slowly, and
without Jimsy he would have been very lonely at North Bank during that
first fortnight. At first he thought that Jimsy had been like himself,
at a loss for companionship, arguing very modestly that otherwise
Jimsy would not have struck up the friendship. But he soon discovered
that this was far from the fact. The whole school knew Jimsy Ravenel
and liked him. And Jimsy knew the whole school and liked them. But
Jimsy had few close friends, preferring his own society to that of most
of his acquaintances. As he explained to Richard one day, he could have
a heap more fun by himself than he could with other fellows who didn’t
like the things he liked. Just because he didn’t seek the society of
others, most fellows, even some of those much older, felt flattered
when Jimsy bothered himself with them. That Jimsy was so astoundingly
friendly with Richard soon had the effect of placing the latter in a
position of some importance, and toward the middle of his second week
at school he found that he was accumulating quite a list of speaking
acquaintances. Some of these would have become closer friends had
Richard encouraged it. That he didn’t was because, after those first
days of solitude, it didn’t occur to him that any one really wanted to
know him, and because, too, his friendship with Jimsy supplied all his
needs.

Knowing Jimsy was not, he soon discovered, conducive to overwork as
regarded studies. Jimsy, in spite of his fine phrase about studying
very, very hard, shirked lamentably. Quick wits and an excellent
memory, however, stood him in good stead and he was seldom in trouble.
But Richard hadn’t yet learned the gentle art of faking his way through
a recitation. In fact he never did learn it, which was just as well.
Consequently a certain amount of attention to his books was compulsory,
and to give that attention when Jimsy was forever dragging him away on
some exploit was most difficult. Not that Richard’s six courses were
proving hard, for there were times when he suspected that by tutoring
the least bit during the summer just past he might have entered the
second class instead of the third. With the exception of mathematics,
which had always been a bugaboo to him, and English, which was far more
advanced than he had expected, none of his studies troubled him. He
liked his instructors and so far had maintained friendly relations with
them all; and he very much wanted those relations to continue. That
they would continue he very much doubted, however, unless he gave less
time to the pursuit of pleasure with Jimsy!

The search for pearls was fruitless, but not for lack of effort. They
accumulated nearly a half bushel of the bivalves and opened them
without discovering treasure. Jimsy called the things mussels, but
to Richard they looked more like clams. Whichever they were, they
certainly failed of thrills, although just at first both boys were
hopefully excited. After they had finished they sought a secluded spot
and went in bathing. This was a necessary as well as a pleasurable act.
Even after they were out again and had dried themselves and donned
their clothes Jimsy declared that he still smelled “mussely.” However,
that didn’t take the edge off his appetite, and they dined enjoyably,
albeit scantily, on the fare he had brought along.

“Grandfather used to say,” remarked Jimsy reminiscently and a trifle
sadly as he picked a crumb from his knee and consigned it carefully
to his mouth, “that you ought always to get up from the table still
feeling hungry. I reckon grandfather would be mightily pleased if he
were here now!”

Richard pointed out that, as they had nearly three miles to walk before
they were back at school, the fact that they had not over-eaten had its
advantage. Jimsy agreed rather dubiously and replied that he always
walked better on a full stomach. They found some late raspberries
presently and ate a few, but they didn’t help much. After that, with
one accord they set their faces homeward. Jimsy regretting that they
had not traveled by canoe since, with the tide in their favor, they
could have reached home speedily and at the cost of no exertion. On the
way back Jimsy covered half again as much ground as his companion did,
for he continually made side excursions to get the view from a hill, to
examine a strangely twisted tree trunk, to pick curiously at a ledge
with the point of his knife, to pick up an oddly shaped stone or, as on
one occasion, to disappear for quite ten minutes in the forest while
Richard swung his legs from the top rail of a fence and awaited his
return. On that occasion he explained a bit breathlessly that he had
pursued a woodchuck which, contrary to his hope and expectation, had
not revealed his burrow but had headed straight for the next county.
When Richard asked what he would have done with the burrow had he
found it, Jimsy didn’t know. He had, however, brought back an oak gall
of surprising size, and that appeared to comfort him. Jimsy always got
back to school after his wanderings with his pockets filled with a
variety of such trophies, but Richard couldn’t discover that he ever
kept any of them.

They eked out their meager lunch with biscuits in Jimsy’s room after
their return and then hied them to the football field, arriving there
just in time to see Norwell, the North Bank left guard, kick off to Mt.
Saint Anne’s. It was the second game of the schedule, for the Light
Blue had triumphed over Bayside the week before to the one-sided score
of 19 to 0. To-day, however, Mt. Saint Anne’s was a different sort
of opponent and the two boys saw and enjoyed a close and thrilling
contest that was only won in the last quarter――and close to the end of
that――when the North Bank left half, Benson, got away at the enemy’s
forty-three yards and tore through a broken field for a touchdown.
Captain Trumbull missed the goal and the final score was 6 to 0.
Richard, his patriotism rampant, cheered and shouted all through the
contest, to the amusement of Jimsy who only contributed to the acclaim
when the cheer leaders insisted that “every fellow get into this!” Of
course Jimsy did get to his feet and yell a little when Jerry Benson
tore off that sprint for the winning touchdown, but he seemed rather
ashamed of it afterwards and even had difficulty in recalling it when
Richard laughingly reminded him of it. Richard was beginning to
suspect that Jimsy’s attitudes on some subjects were only poses!

In fact, George Ferry as much as said so one evening some few days
later. The talk in Number 33 Baldwin had worked around to the
characteristics of different schools, a subject that Richard knew
little about, and which Jimsy discussed quite knowingly. Richard asked
what North Bank’s chief characteristic was and Jimsy promptly replied:
“Seriousness.” George smiled.

“As exemplified by one Jimsy Ravenel,” he murmured.

“Me?” exclaimed Jimsy. “I’m pretty nearly the only chap here who
doesn’t look and act like he had the world on his shoulders! Honest,
George, I sometimes wonder what the place is coming to! Why, I get up
in the morning feeling fairly chipper. The old world looks right good
to me. Then I go to prayers and the change begins. After breakfast I’m
thinking about my great-great-uncle who was hung for sheep stealing in
Ireland. By noon I’m wondering whether to jump into the river or stick
it out another day. By night I’m so filled with gloom that even suicide
looks too cheerful for me!”

The idea of Jimsy being filled with gloom seemed to amuse his
roommate, for he positively chuckled. Richard laughed aloud. Jimsy
viewed them both disapprovingly. “Why,” he continued, “just as a
sample, you fellows. Yesterday I had to go to the library to look up
something――I’ve forgotten what it was――I didn’t find it, anyway, so
it doesn’t matter. Well, there was a kid, a freshie he was, sitting
over by a window with a big book spread on his knees. He looked almost
cheerful and so I wondered what the book was. I sneaked up behind him
and looked over his shoulder, and what do you reckon? Why, he was
looking at the pictures in Dante’s _Inferno_! You know, those awful
things by Doré! Can you beat that? He was having an awfully good time
and I went out on tiptoe so as not to disturb him.”

“In my opinion,” said George after a proper appreciation of his
friend’s tale, “North Bank’s too small to have any character or
atmosphere. We’ve only got about two hundred fellows here. It takes
more than that to create a distinct quality, to give a school what
you might call individuality. Of course Jimsy’s merely fooling when
he says we’re serious, but I do think that we’re earnest. I think we
take our duties earnestly, realize that we’re here, first of all, to
learn. Some of the schools we’ve spoken of are not much more than――than
playgrounds. Fellows go to them with the idea of having a good time for
four years. Study is just incidental. Sports are fostered, even nursed,
and as long as the school turns out a winning football team or baseball
team or track team each year nothing else much matters. You know of
schools like that, Jimsy.”

“I’ve heard of them,” sighed Jimsy, “but they sound too good to be
true! We’re not like that here, are we, Georgie?”

“No,” agreed George, smiling, “we aren’t. Although, goodness knows,
we go in pretty heavily for sports considering the size of the place.
Football, baseball, rowing, lacrosse, soccer, basket ball, tennis――even
track games of a sort! Doesn’t sound as if we were so very serious,
Jimsy!”

“Oh, doesn’t it? Mean to tell me that the fellows get any _fun_ out
of those things? Not a bit of it! It’s decided that we ought to have
a football team to beat Cumbridge, so they round up a lot of fellows
who look like they could stand the wear and go to it. They feed them
raw meat and drill them two hours a day. Do you think they enjoy
it? Why, say, if some one should laugh at training table he’d be
drawn-and-quartered!”

“Oh, piffle, Jimsy! Don’t you think I have a good time playing
lacrosse?”

“You? Oh, you’d make believe you liked it if you were playing cricket.
You’re a stoic! No, you’re an Indian fakir, like one of those guys who
put their feet in their laps and sit and grin for thirty years just to
prove they’re happy!”

“I don’t believe,” ventured Richard, “that many fellows play football
who don’t want to.”

“Nor I,” said George. “Fact is, only about a third who want to play get
a chance. Same way with other sports; baseball, rowing, lacrosse.”

Jimsy sniffed disdainfully and Richard looked thoughtful. “You don’t
think then, Ferry, that patriotism is out of fashion here?” asked the
latter.

“Patriotism? Oh, you mean school patriotism! Of course it isn’t! That’s
some more of Jimsy’s guff, I suppose. You mustn’t take our young friend
too seriously, Dodd. He doesn’t always mean what he says nor jump the
way he looks. Jimsy likes to talk right well.”

“There’s not a nickel’s worth of patriotism in North Bank,” declared
Jimsy stoutly. “It’s the most indifferent school I ever heard of.
All any one here ever thinks of is getting his bean full of useless
Latin and algebra and such rot. We have a lot of poor chaps who
are――are――what’s the silly word?――intimidated into playing football
and rowing in the boat and all that, but if they weren’t scared to
death they’d be back in their rooms cramming their heads full of this
stuff they call knowledge and not giving a hang whether the dear old
school was licked at soccer or baseball or anything else. Patriotism!
Patrio-piffle!”

George laughed softly. “You talk a lot of foolishness, Jimsy, don’t
you?” he asked kindly. “Do you know, if you’d take half the trouble
studying your lessons that you take evolving these crazy theories of
yours, and arguing them, you’d be an Honor Man?” George turned to
Richard. “I’m not at all sure,” he went on, “that our little Jimsy
is good company for you, Dodd. He won’t be if you listen to all his
nonsense. He says his great-uncle, or some one, was hung in Ireland and
I believe it. That is, I believe he’s got a lot of Irish in him, for
he’s always ‘agin the government.’”

“Not me,” denied Jimsy, grinning. “I’m agin the governed. Anyway, I
hope I have got some Irish in me, for the Irish are the only folks
who’d rather have a good laugh than a cry. What this school wants to
do is get more Irish here. It wants to wake up, be-dad! And the Irish
are the folks to do it. The Irish,” ended Jimsy, laughing, “can wake
anything up.”

“Your idea then,” said George, “is that the school is dead and needs an
Irish wake. Jimsy, I’d miss you horribly if the faculty should decide
to get along without you. For my sake, do a little Latin to-night.”




                               CHAPTER VI

                           CRIMINALS CONVERSE


On an afternoon of a lazy, languorous day about a week after the last
recorded events Dick and Jimsy reclined on the bank above the river
near the western confines of the school. (No one called the former
boy Richard, and I don’t see why we should. Jimsy called him Dick,
George Ferry and a number of random acquaintances called him Dodd and
Bertram Lodge called him whatever came into his mind.) It was about
four o’clock and very warm in the sun. The Severn was calm and dazzling
to the eyes if one gazed too long on its burnished surface. Behind the
two, casting shadows athwart their faces, the trees edging the grove
stood, sun-flecked and hushed, peering down the steep descent as if
longing to lave their thirsty roots in the cool water. Late October
may be very warm in Maryland, and nearly a month without rain had
parched the sod and caused the leaves to hang limp and listless. Some
of that same listlessness had, it seemed, pervaded the bodies of the
two boys. Jimsy, who held a number of long black horsehairs, collected
painstakingly from the stable premises, had long since ceased tying and
looping them and, with his hat brim pulled over his eyes, was staring
silently at a bank of fleecy white clouds in the south. Dick, supported
on one elbow, gazed down toward the boathouse, some two hundred yards
distant. A mocking bird was practicing a few notes in the grove behind
them and a troop of sparrows were bustling about the grassy slope
below, noisy and busy in the pursuit of grasshoppers. Suddenly Dick
propped himself higher on one hand and gazed more intently.

Down there on the float the long slim nose of the second crew shell
came into sight through the boathouse door. Dick called Jimsy’s
attention and the latter turned slightly and watched, too. Eight
stalwart, white-clad forms moved under it, slowly, carefully, and
from the distance the thing took on the appearance of some strange
insect. In the stillness the coxswain’s voice came to them clearly.
“Hold her! Easy, now! In she goes!” The hearers paused at the edge of
the float, the long shell turned over and came slowly down to rest on
the still water. The crew returned indoors for the sweeps. The cox,
slim, quick-moving, fitted the rudder into place and looped the lines
carefully across the seat. Then, strapping the small blue megaphone
against his mouth, he took his place. One by one the oarsmen followed,
bending to lace their feet in the shoes on the stretchers. A short,
wide-shouldered little man in a faded green sweater appeared, followed
by four substitutes bearing a scull. The larger boat moved away from
the float and waited, its sharp nose turned upstream, a blue-tipped oar
dipping occasionally, now to port, now to starboard, to hold her there.
The green-sweatered man seated himself in his single scull and paddled
away, too. Then appeared the other shell, the first crew bearing it
down the incline. They, too, were boated and moved into the stream.
In the scull, Coach Carmichael――“Mike” behind his back and out of
hearing――fastened a small megaphone across his mouth and called through
it.

“All right, First! Take her up! Keep that stroke long!”

The first crew coxswain barked orders. “Touch her, Seven! Steady! Ready
all! Forward! Row!――Row!――Row!――Row!――” His voice dwindled. First was
moving easily, rhythmically upstream, past where the two boys sat.
Dick, looking down, could see Alan Linscott at Number Two. The second
crew followed, half a dozen short lengths behind, with the coach
hanging on their port, his bare, muscular arms making no work of their
task. North Bank owned no launch for coaching purposes, although in
spring one was hired over in Annapolis. During fall practice the coach
followed in a scull. The second, a little more ragged than the first,
passed upstream, Mr. Carmichael’s voice occasionally floating up to the
watchers.

“Get together, Second! Finish out, finish out!”

After the crews had disappeared around the first bend Dick’s thoughts
still remained on Alan Linscott. Alan had taken no notice of his
overture. He had neither called on Dick nor answered his note. Dick
didn’t mind so much now, but it did seem strange that Alan should
be so discourteous. Jimsy declared that the crew captain was a fine
fellow; none better, said Jimsy. Jimsy, of course, had not been told
of the unanswered note. Dick was too proud to tell him about that. Dick
wondered whether that note had failed to reach Alan. It didn’t seem,
though, that it could have. That fellow he had left it with, Whittier,
wouldn’t have failed to deliver it. Whittier had remembered Dick and
always spoke to him when they met, and Dick held a high opinion of him.
No, the more plausible explanation was that Alan, being a pretty busy
fellow, had just forgotten all about it. Dick preferred that theory to
one less flattering either to himself or Alan. Alan had been a hero to
Dick for several years past, and one dislikes to discover faults in
one’s heroes. Occasionally he entertained the idea of calling again
at Number 6 McCrea, but he knew very well that he couldn’t do it. His
mother had asked him long since in one of her letters if Alan was
looking after him, and Dick had so far avoided an answer. His mother
had counted so much on Alan’s friendship and protection for Dick that
he hated to tell her the truth.

Well, he could do without Alan well enough, he reflected. There was
Jimsy, a most satisfying chum, and there might be others if he cared to
cultivate them. He had plenty of interests now, had jostled down into
his place in the school and was having a good time. Perhaps he wasn’t
getting along in classes quite as well as he should, but he meant to
do more studying from now on. He had, he reflected, made that promise
to himself several times already, and so far he had failed to keep it.
Well, the weather was so hot just now that a fellow didn’t have much
ambition. Just as soon as it got a bit cooler――

“Let’s get on with these,” said Jimsy, sitting up with sudden and
unexpected animation. “Hold this, Dick, while I get a loop on here.”

They were entering a career of crime, having decided to become poachers
and snare rabbits. The fact that the land thereabouts was not posted
and that no one cared a bit whether rabbits were snared on it might
have detracted somewhat from their pleasure had they considered it.
But they didn’t. They simply disregarded it by mutual understanding.
They were poachers, and every one knew that poaching was beautifully
illegal and punishable by long terms of imprisonment. They had embarked
on their criminal career, you see, with eyes wide open to its risks
and possible penalties, and they were desperately determined to pursue
lawlessness to its triumphant or bitter end, or, as Jimsy simply
phrased it: “We’ll get a rabbit or something, I’ll bet――if it’s only a
skunk!”

Jimsy, searching the library shelves for information regarding a
person named Gladstone, who, it appeared, had been of some prominence
in British politics at one time, had come across a volume entitled
_Every Boy’s Handbook of Outdoor Sports_. With regret I am obliged to
state that Jimsy forgot Mr. Gladstone immediately and took refuge in
a corner with the Handbook on his knees. It really wasn’t altogether
his fault, for _Outdoor Sports_ had no business in the section of the
library marked “Biography: A――J.” Jimsy read interestedly of fishing,
of falconry, of coursing, of otter hunting, of ferreting, of snaring
and trapping and of many other things. But when it came to putting this
newly acquired knowledge to practical use he was at once faced with
difficulties. Falconry required the services of a hawk, and he doubted
his ability to capture one, to say nothing of training it afterwards.
Of course, he could fish, but not for the strange fishes referred to
in the book――excepting trout, and Jimsy had his own ideas on trout
fishing. Coursing necessitated dogs, and so did otter hunting――to say
nothing of otters. In the end rabbit snaring promised the only field
for his skill, and he set about a thorough and exhaustive study of the
poacher’s art. Several materials were well spoken of for use in making
nooses, but horsehair seemed to Jimsy the more sporting, and so he had
laboriously collected a large number of long black strands that had at
some recent date adorned the tails of the two horses which conveyed the
carriage between school and station. Collecting had been done under
difficulties, for Cicero, the black coachman and general factotum,
viewed with suspicion all trespassers on his domain. But Jimsy had
succeeded, as Jimsy had a way of doing, and now it only remained to
tie clever knots and running nooses, and subsequently, with amazing
cunning, to arrange these athwart the rabbit “runs.”

In a measure Dick had been pessimistic. He had, first of all, expressed
doubt as to the presence in the vicinity of rabbits. He had then
questioned Jimsy’s ability to recognize a “run” if he found it,
and had flatly declared that, while English rabbits might confine
themselves to certain paths, American rabbits, in his belief, were far
too independent to do anything of the sort. But Jimsy was not the sort
to be easily discouraged. When Jimsy once believed in anything, that
thing simply was until――well, until Jimsy chose to abandon it. Just
now he believed implicitly in rabbits, rabbit “runs,” horsehair snares
and poaching. Just as he had a fortnight ago believed in pearl-bearing
mussels, and, more recently, in his ability to manufacture writing ink
from green walnuts.

“Hold tighter,” directed Jimsy. “Pull it toward you. That’s better.”
He frowned in concentration as his fingers busied themselves with
intricate knottings.

“What I don’t see,” said Dick, “is how we’re to hang these loops at
just the right height. What’s to keep Mr. Rabbit from walking under
them or putting his foot in them instead of his head?”

“The book tells you,” responded Jimsy. “That part’s all right. What’s
bothering me is how we’ll get the rabbits cooked after we’ve caught
them. We can’t take them to the kitchen because some one would ask
questions. I suppose we could cook them in the woods――”

“Do we have to eat them?” asked Dick alarmedly.

“Sure! Why not?”

“I don’t think I like rabbit. At least, I’ve never eaten any.”

“Time you did then,” said Jimsy firmly. “They’re bully. Just like
chicken. And, say, we can sell the skins. I’ve got a paper in my room
that has dozens of advertisements from folks who buy all sorts of furs.”

“Are rabbit skins fur?” asked Dick ignorantly.

“Of course! Why, they make all sorts of things out of rabbit skins:
felt hats, coats――er――muffs, all sorts of things. I guess they fetch
good prices, too.”

“Well, if we can get money for the skins maybe we don’t have to
eat them,” said Dick hopefully. “I mean eat the rabbits,” he added
explanatorily.

Jimsy shook his head. “No use wasting them,” he replied reprovingly.
“We’ll get a skillet and――and some things and have some bully feeds,
Dick. We’ll have to cure the skins, though――pelts, I mean. You use salt
and pepper, don’t you? Or is it alum? I’ll send off and get a book that
tells about it. There, that’s the last. Put your hand in that and pull
it toward you. Not too hard! How’s that? Guess if you were a rabbit
you’d be in a fix, eh? Say, I want you to know those things are strong.
Look here. Well, that was a weak one.” Jimsy viewed the broken noose
philosophically. “Besides, I pulled a heap stronger than any rabbit
could. Shall we set these now?”

Dick shook his head. “It’s too hot, Jimsy. Let’s wait until to-morrow.”

“It’s getting cooler, though,” responded the other. But he didn’t
insist on immediate action, and Dick was relieved. It was getting
cooler, but the thought of the breathless heat of the woods held no
appeal for him. He preferred to lie there and watch the river. Several
canoes had followed the shells into the water and four crew candidates
for whom there was no room in the boats were pulling lustily upstream
in pair-oars.

“I wish,” murmured Dick, “that I had a canoe.”

Jimsy nodded, bundling his snares up and slipping them into a pocket.
“So do I. Too hot to-day, though, for the river. Look at those fellows
over there. Just dawdling. There’s a lot more air up here.”

Dick’s thoughts traveled up the river in the wake of the crews. “Jimsy,
do you have to be pretty big and strong to row?” he asked.

“Row? No, not if you have a light boat. I’d rather paddle a canoe any
day, though. You get somewhere in a canoe.”

“I meant row on the crew,” said Dick.

“Oh! Why, yes, of course. They used to have a junior crew here, I’ve
heard. Four-oared, you know. But it died out. Only the big chaps like
your friend Linscott can make the eights. You might get a job as
ballast, though,” Jimsy chuckled.

After a long silence Dick spoke again, a bit wistfully. “I wish I could
do something,” he said.

Jimsy emerged from a deep reverie. “Eh?” he asked. “Let’s set the
snares, then.”

“I meant something like row or play football or baseball,” said Dick.
“I’d like to make a team, Jimsy. Of course, I never could, I’m so
small, but I’d like to awfully.”

“Well,” responded Jimsy reflectively. “There’s tennis. And second team
basket ball. And you might try lacrosse. Can you run?”

“Pretty well. But I guess I wouldn’t stand much show. I guess most of
the fellows are pretty big, aren’t they?”

“I don’t know. Old George isn’t a mammoth. Still, he’s one of the
smaller ones. Ever play basket ball?”

Dick shook his head. “Not really. I’ve fooled around a little in the
school gym at home, but they wouldn’t let me try for a team; not even
the Midgets. I don’t think I’d care so much for basket ball, though.
I’d rather do something out of doors. Maybe I’ll grow some this winter
and have a chance at baseball.”

Jimsy shook his head wonderingly. “You’re a funny little tike, Dick,”
he said. “I don’t see why you want to _look_ for trouble. It comes easy
enough. You get on one of the teams and you’ll wish you hadn’t, son.
They work you to death, and you have no time for anything; not even for
studying. That,” added Jimsy, plainly as an afterthought, “is why I
don’t go in for anything.”

Dick smiled. “Well, maybe next year I can do something. I wonder why I
was made such a little runt, Jimsy.”

“Oh, you’re all right,” Jimsy consoled. “I’d rather be small and have
right good sense, like you, than be a big bull of a fellow like Joe
Whittier and no use except to pull an oar.”

“I like Whittier,” replied Dick. “And I don’t think he’s so very big,
Jimsy.”

“Oh, yes, he’s all right. I like him, too. Every one does. But he’s
just a mass of muscle. Good-hearted, but――but no refinement, Dick.”

Dick sighed. “I wish I were like that, Jimsy.”




                              CHAPTER VII

                            BENSON GOES OVER


October became November. Rains came copiously and east winds blew
low-lying clouds across the bay and brought autumn at last. The woods
were thinning fast. Maples were flaming and walnuts were dropping their
fruit. In warm corners the roses still bloomed sparsely, however, and
along the curving path that fronted the dormitories white and orange
and pale purple chrysanthemums nodded bravely. Fall baseball came to
an end, the crews boated in sweaters and only the football players and
a few lacrosse enthusiasts scorned the chill. Ten days of unvaried
cloudiness hinted strongly of winter. Yet when the Saturday of the
St. John’s game arrived the sun arrived, too, and summer seemed for
the while to be back once more. The game was played in Annapolis and
all North Bank attended, floating down the river in boat or canoe,
journeying by railway or, in fewer cases, putting the distance behind
on foot.

North Bank had had varied fortunes so far. A good start had been
followed by an early slump during which she had been defeated by West
Shore and tied by Fernwood. A week ago she had recovered sufficiently
to win a ragged game from Severn, 10 to 10. To-day she hoped for
victory but expected defeat, for St. John’s College had been playing
excellent football all season and was heavier both in the line and
behind it than the Light Blue. Of course Dick and Jimsy went, and
George Ferry went with them, marching along the rutted clay road to
the little box of a station in the company of nearly a hundred others
and subsequently hanging to as much brass railing as they could get
their hands on and dangling precariously all the way across the river
and into Annapolis. It was a noisy ride, for North Bank always became
intensely vocal when it went forth to do battle, and from the station
to the field the marching horde of invaders, blue banners aloft,
informed the residents of College Avenue that they would

    ... Cherish the Light Blue, the bright blue, the right blue,
    Unfold it, uphold it, and fight for it, too!

Because the Navy team was playing away from home that afternoon,
Annapolis turned out in numbers for the North Bank game and the
gridiron was surrounded five and six deep. St. John’s doesn’t supply
seats, save for the contestants and a few honored guests, and Dick soon
realized that his chance of seeing much of the game was very slim. But
Jimsy had reached a similar conclusion. “It’s all right for a tall gawk
like you, George,” said Jimsy as they strove to see between the heads
and shoulders of the earlier arrivals, “but Dick and I aren’t giraffes.
We’re going to try for front row position. Want to come?” George was
satisfied to remain where he was. “All right,” said Jimsy. “Wait for
us up by that goal, afterwards, will you? And, say, got an old letter
in your pocket? Or an envelope? I’ll give it back to you.” George
found the desired article and Jimsy beckoned to Dick. “Come on,” he
whispered. “We can do better than this.”

Jimsy led the way back toward the corner of the field where the throng
was less dense, Dick following him doubtfully. There Jimsy held his
letter in plain sight and began to press authoritatively forward
“Beg pardon,” he said, “but I’ve got to get through.” The spectators
shuffled and made way and Jimsy and Dick squirmed toward the front. A
group of midshipmen aided good-naturedly. “Gangway!” they bawled. “A
reprieve! Stop the execution! Gangway there!” Jimsy emerged inside the
enclosure, and Dick, clinging like a limpet, emerged likewise. Still
brandishing the letter, Jimsy turned and made for the North Bank bench.
Once out of sight of those who had let him through, however, he thrust
the letter into a pocket. Dick felt very uncomfortable as he followed
along the edge of the throng. Some North Bank boy saw Jimsy and set up
a gleeful howl of “Jimsy! Come out of there! Oh, you faker!” The howl
became general, for hereabouts North Bank held the field solidly. Jimsy
thrust up an imperious hand and looked stern and haughty, but that only
had the effect of calling forth more laughter and cheers. “Hep! Hep!
Hep!” chanted the audience in time to Jimsy’s dignified pace. Dick felt
his face getting red and wished he hadn’t come. Then, however, they
had reached the bench. The first and second squads were on the field,
at practice, and only a few substitutes, the managers, the trainer
and Coach Thorne were there. Jimsy seated himself beside Johnny Pell,
the team manager, and fell into whispered converse. Dick, not knowing
what else to do, edged behind the bench and hoped that his ears weren’t
as red as they felt. Then, after a moment of evidently important
conference, Jimsy nodded to Dick and winked. Dick approached along the
back of the bench to meet the grinning countenance of Pell.

“Sit down on the ground at the end of the bench,” said the manager,
_sotto voce_, “and keep out of sight. You, too, Jimsy. You’ve got more
cheek than a cage of monkeys. If Thorne sees you, though, he will
probably throw you out.”

But the coach was intent on the players and Jimsy and Dick settled
themselves on the worn grass, occupying as little space as possible
and trying to make themselves invisible, while from behind them came
good-naturedly sarcastic comments from the less fortunate spectators.
“Slick work, Jimsy! I’ll say so!” “Oh, you fakers!” “Get up out of
there, Jimsy! You’ll catch cold!” “Got room for me, Johnny? Be a good
fellow, will you?” “Say, Jimsy! Let me sit in your lap?”

But Jimsy was deaf to all this. “Awfully low, common lot,” he confided
to Dick. “Bourgeoisie, you know, very.”

“How did you do it?” whispered Dick.

Jimsy flecked an imaginary speck from his sleeve and smiled in a
careless and very superior manner. “Influence,” he replied, “merely
influence.”

Then the players trooped back, blankets were donned and Captain
Trumbull followed the referee out to the middle of the field and shook
hands with the rival leader. A coin spun in the air, Trumbull walked
back, Coach Thorne said: “All right, fellows. Play hard. Let’s go!” and
blankets were off again. Then, presently, a whistle piped and the game
was on.

North Bank found hard sledding from the first. St. John’s took the
ball on the kick-off and ran it back almost to the center of the
field. Plunges at the center of the Light Blue line produced amazing
gains, and, almost before the contest was well under way, North Bank’s
supporters were desperately chanting: “Hold ’em! Hold ’em! Hold ’em!”
The Light Blue did hold them that time and St. John’s was forced to
try a field goal. North Bank strove desperately to block the kick, but
the strong enemy line held like a wall. Fortune, though, had not yet
utterly deserted the visitors, and the ball missed the goal, albeit by
inches only.

North Bank tried to rush from her twenty yards, but, after two failures
to advance, punted well into her opponent’s territory. St. John’s
again began her journey, and, although she moved more slowly now, she
moved no less certainly, and just before the first quarter was up she
piled her back field through the right side of the light blue line
for the first score. A goal followed. The second twelve-minute period
was a repetition of the first inasmuch as St. John’s again started
from the kick-off and took the ball to within striking distance of the
opponent’s goal, was again halted, lost possession on a forward pass,
and, later, pulling down Trumbull’s long punt, marched up the field to
a second touchdown.

North Bank was no match for the enemy in any department of the game
save, possibly, kicking. Trumbull and Gray both punted farther and with
more science than did St. John’s experts, and could the North Bank ends
have seconded their efforts there might have been a slightly different
tale to tell. But neither Dimond nor Clary nor the substitutes who
succeeded them late in the contest――Bert Lodge was one of these――were
fast and clever enough to get the catcher, and the long punts were
almost invariably run back for good distances. The first half ended
with the score 14 to 0, and Dick, among many others, was disappointed
and sad. Dick was an ardent football “fan,” had sat through every
game of the schedule, rain or fair, secretly considered every member
of the team a hero and would have given almost anything he possessed
or hoped to possess to have had a speaking acquaintance with Captain
Trumbull or Jerry Benson or Gurney James. Even sitting so close to them
had thrilled him wonderfully after the first moments of frightened
embarrassment, and he wondered if it would be near enough to the
truth to write home that he had sat on the bench with the players! To
have his heroes meet with adversity always filled Dick with dismay
and sorrow, and to-day his heart was leaden when the blue-stockinged
warriors came, panting, dirty, streaked with perspiration, in many
cases even disfigured, back to the bench for their blankets ere they
walked over to the gymnasium. Rather to his surprise, no countenance
showed any such grief as he was experiencing. Some faces were still
lighted with the ecstasy of battle, some were smiling, a few were tense
and grave; but there was neither discouragement nor downheartedness
visible. Dick took hope. There was another twenty-four minutes, he
whispered to himself, and although what had gone seemed to promise
little encouragement it might be that Coach Thorne had something up
his sleeve, that the team hadn’t found itself yet, that――that――well,
sometimes things happened in football that were scarcely short of
miracles. Dick hoped hard for a miracle.

Behind him the ranks of North Bank supporters were singing lustily. He
turned and studied the neighboring faces. They didn’t look much as if
they were saddened by impending defeat. Smiles, laughter, pranks were
mingled with the singing. Two fellows he knew, seated cross-legged in
the front line, were playing stick-knife, just as if, thought Dick a
bit resentfully, defeat for North Bank was a thing of no account. He
turned to Jimsy, not for sympathy, for Jimsy was not one to be downcast
by athletic misfortunes, but in hope of a diversion from his gloomy
contemplations. Jimsy was smiling and untroubled. “There’s going to be
fun in the next half,” he confided.

“You mean you think we’ll do better?” asked Dick eagerly.

“We? Oh, the team! No, I guess we’ll do a lot worse. We aren’t in the
same class with these fellows this year. They play football. No, what I
meant was the dust. See how those bare spots out there are drying out
in the sun? Well, you wait until the players begin kicking that dirt up
again. Dust! Oh, boy! I’ve seen it before. Watch the girls over on the
other side scatter when that nice red dust begins to blow their way.”
Jimsy laughed joyously. “Lucky we’re on this side, eh?”

Dick said it was, but he secretly thought that Jimsy’s mind occupied
itself with extremely trivial affairs. Cheering broke forth all about
the field and the two teams jogged in simultaneously. Once more Dick
thrilled as he realized his proximity to those twenty-odd heroes in
blue. He stared at Trumbull and Benson and James and wondered what they
were thinking behind their cheerfully inscrutable faces. Wondered,
too, if Jerry Benson knew that the deep gash along one cheek was
bleeding from under the plaster. To Dick it seemed a wonderful and
much-to-be-desired thing, that gash. He guessed that Benson, in spite
of his nonchalance and sober smile, was secretly pretty proud of it.
Dick knew that he would have been. The players who were to start the
third quarter bent above the bench for Coach Thorne’s last reminder and
then, Trumbull leading, spread over the end of the field. The cheering,
which had momentarily lapsed into individual efforts, began again, the
leaders casting aside their big megaphones and gesturing impellently.
“Ray, ray, ray! Ray, ray, ray!” thundered the chorus. “North Bank!
North Bank! Ray, hooray! Ho-o-o-_rah_! Ho-o-o-_rah_! North Bank! North
Bank! North Ba-a-ank!”

Dick gripped his hands tightly between his knees and watched. His
throat felt a little choky, just as it always did when that long cheer
crashed out, and his heart was pounding and, as it felt, missing an
occasional beat. Somewhere at the back of his mind he was saying an
unconscious prayer for victory. Jimsy was watching the bare expanses of
red loam that showed here and there over the trampled field, watching
expectantly, gloatingly. Perhaps Jimsy, too, was praying. If he was, it
was a prayer that the breeze might increase.

North Bank took the kick-off, and Nagle, the quarter back, evaded the
enemy ends and reeled off nearly twenty yards before he was downed.
North Bank shouted joyously. Then followed three tries at the St.
John’s tackles and ends that netted but six yards, and Trumbull
punted. For once the kick was short and carried only to the enemy’s
thirty-eight yards, where it bounded out. St. John’s pierced the light
blue line twice for good gains and made her distance outside Hickson.
A plunge at center lost her a foot or more, and then she heaved a long
forward pass that was gathered in by a waiting end far down the field.
But an off-side penalty brought the ball back and a second heave
grounded. A punt to North Bank’s fifteen yards was caught by Benson and
that sturdy runner raced back to the twenty-three before he was laid
low. Then began North Bank’s one glorious effort, and Dick, a small,
strained-faced, wide-eyed youth, felt his heart sing and for many
breathless minutes believed that the longed-for miracle had come to
pass.

It was a fake kick on third down that started the Light Blue’s journey.
Trumbull ran wide around his right wing, eluded a tackle behind the
line and, guided by Fortune, raced for thirty-two yards before he
was thrown out of bounds. Behind Dick pandemonium reigned. Concerted
cheering failed to express the joy of the North Bank contingent and
every lusty young throat yelled as the spirit urged. The result was
deafening and wonderfully satisfying, and it only ended when Benson
was stopped short and thrown for a loss on the next play. But Benson
was seldom stopped twice in succession, and when Nagle tossed him the
ball again he ploughed past the St. John’s left tackle and reconquered
the lost ground and added two yards to it for good measure. The ball
was on the home team’s thirty-nine now, on third down. Trumbull walked
back to kicking position, caught the pass from center and, as the enemy
poured through, passed across the line to Clary. The latter was downed
where he stood, but again the Light Blue had made her distance and
the pigskin was close to the thirty-yard line; and again North Bank
supporters shouted themselves breathless.

There is always a weakest spot in every line if the opponent can find
it, and it seemed now that North Bank had found that spot. Using Benson
again and again, Nagle pointed the attack this way and that way yet
continually hammered the St. John’s right tackle. Twice Benson got
through for five yards; once for four. Gray gained two at the same
place. St. John’s backs were plugging the hole desperately now, and
the gains were less certain. From the enemy’s seventeen, Nagle risked
a forward pass over the line on third down. It grounded between a
knot of struggling players. There was three and a half yards to go on
fourth down. North Bank yelled for a touchdown, but the crossbar loomed
close and inviting, promising a certain if lesser triumph. Trumbull
stepped back and the St. John’s cohorts began their chant of “Block
that kick! Block that kick! Block that kick!” Dick’s heart seemed to
be trying to turn completely over at one moment and at the next to
be crawling inconveniently into his throat. Hearts do strange things
at such crises. He heard Trumbull call hoarsely: “Hold that line,
fellows!” He heard Nagle shrilly give his signal. He watched Trumbull’s
outstretched hands, waited interminable minutes for the ball to reach
them, felt his heart sinking sickeningly. Then he saw that the lines
had broken, were confusedly mingled, that the backs were speeding
toward the farther side of the gridiron. And still the ball was not in
sight to him. And then he did see it. Benson had it, and Benson had
already made the distance and was still ploughing forward, halted but
not yet stopped, tearing himself loose from clutching hands, pivoting,
side-stepping, staggering, but always going forward. Then the enemy
fairly bore him down by numbers and the whistle piped, and all along
one side of the field lunatic youths were hurling megaphones and caps
in air and shrieking mere sounds that, while wordless, were certainly
not meaningless.

The ball lay three scant yards from the goal line when the dust of
battle subsided and it was North Bank’s first down. None doubted that
the Light Blue would score, probably not even the enemy. Yet before
the next play the ball must be taken to the far end of the field, for
the third quarter was up, and in that minute’s pause the St. John’s
coach hustled in two fresh linemen. But even new blood couldn’t avail.
Nagle thrust Trumbull straight at center for something less than a
yard, sent Benson slanting off tackle for a second short gain and
then, while Dick added his pæans to the unceasing shouts of friend and
foe, and while Jimsy so far forgot his indifference as to pummel his
companion enthusiastically on his back, shot the left half again at the
desperate, defiant wall and saw him go through and down and over.

While North Bank still celebrated, Captain Trumbull cocked the ball to
his liking and sent it, slowly revolving, well above and safely between
the bars. And the score changed from 14 to 0 to 14 to 7; which anybody
with North Bank sympathies can see is a far more attractive array of
digits.

I wish that I might leave the game as it stood then, while North Bank
was still puffed with success and glowing with delight, but there
still remained some ten minutes of contest, and in those ten minutes
St. John’s set herself grimly to the task of wreaking vengeance. What
she sought she found. Before the last whistle sounded she had scored
a third touchdown, from which no goal followed, and had kicked a
field-goal from the thirty-two yards. So the final figures were 23 to
7, and North Bank trailed back across the river conclusively defeated.
Yet, somehow, that desperate and successful rally by the Light Blue in
the third period seemed to atone for a great deal, and I think most of
the school felt about as Dick did. How Dick felt may be judged from
a remark he made to Jimsy and George as they went back along College
Avenue to the station.

“Of course,” said Dick thoughtfully, “we got beaten, but I guess
getting beaten isn’t so bad if――if you fight――” he paused, seeking a
word, and then ended half defiantly, half apologetically――“nobly.”




                              CHAPTER VIII

                         TRIBULATIONS OF A POET


    See our banners bravely flying
    ’Gainst the golden sunset, dying,
    Hear the cheers....

Dick sucked the end of his pen and gazed abstractedly at the window.
“Hear the cheers,” he murmured. “Hear the cheers――crying, lying,
trying, shying, buying, fry――oh, gosh!” He sighed, pushed his hands
into his pockets, tilted back in his chair and eyed the paper
discouragedly. It was Sunday, the day following the St. John’s game,
and just such a day as yesterday had been. The time was a half hour
before dinner and Dick had Number 12 to himself. He didn’t especially
want to sit up there in the room and compose poetry, for the sunlight
was warm, the river was blue and dazzling and out-of-doors called
loudly. But for more than a week Dick in his spare moments――of which
there weren’t very many――had been trying to write a football song.
To-day was the last day, for the efforts must be turned in to-morrow
morning before nine. The call for new songs had been made a fortnight
ago. Kirkham, of the second, had written the tune, which was not more
than ordinarily reminiscent and which really had a fine martial swing
and which had seemed to Dick most inspiring. He had come away from
the cheer meeting quite certain that he could write words for the
tune which would satisfy the committee, and even on his way to the
room he had composed several lines. Unfortunately, the lines were not
consecutive, however, and the next day, when he had tried to fill in
between them he had had no luck. Occasionally, sometimes in class, he
had tried again, but he couldn’t seem to find the right rhymes. He
had given up the idea of entering the competition, and, with it, all
hope of hearing a song of his sung at the Cumbridge game, until last
evening. Then the enthusiasm generated by that hard fought battle with
St. John’s had supplied him with the first two lines of a stanza and
with a perfectly corking chorus, and this morning before church, and
after, he had been struggling heroically. He had abandoned the first
start and tried numerous others, and now, in despair, he was back at
the first. If there was only a word, a right word, to rhyme with――

Eureka! He had it!

Defying!

“Hear the cheers tum-tum defying!”

That was it! Only, he had to have another word in there. Confident?
Hopeful? No, those wouldn’t do. “Hear the cheers――hear the cheers――” He
looked startledly at the little clock. It was three minutes to one. He
hid the scribbled sheets in a drawer and dashed for the lavatory. But
all during dinner his mind kept busy. Taking a mean advantage of his
absorption, young Endicott, his right-hand neighbor, stole his butter.
Dick never discovered it. With the frozen pudding came victory! As soon
as might be, disregarding the frantic signals of Jimsy, he hurried out
and back to the room.

    Hear the cheers that, hoarse, defying,
      Thunder o’er the field!

Written down, it was a bit disappointing, but it would do for the
present. He went on to struggle with the next line. He was still
struggling when Bert Lodge came in. Dick resisted the inclination to
slip the papers into the drawer. Instead, he shuffled them together
in the hope that Bert would think he was writing his Sunday letter,
which was just what Bert would have thought had it not been for the
strange, rapt, almost ecstatic look on Dick’s flushed face. Bert stared
curiously.

“What are you up to, Midget?” he asked. Midget was one of the least
disagreeable nicknames he had invented.

“Just writing,” answered Dick, lowering his head and forming meaningless
words on the uppermost sheet of paper. Bert laughed incredulously, but
seemed to accept the explanation. He busied himself at his chiffonier
and then walked back to the table, yawning loudly. The next instant he
had reached across and swept the sheets from under Dick’s hand. Dick
snatched after them but missed and jumped to his feet.

“Bert! You give those back!” he cried. “You’ve no business――”

But Bert was already reading, his face one broad grin of malicious
amusement. “‘Oh, North Bank, to you our allegiance we pledge,’” read
Bert grandiloquently. “‘’Neath your banner of Heaven’s cerulean
hue――――’”

Dick tried to reach the papers, but Bert held him off, laughing. “Keep
off, kid,” he warned. “You’ll get hurt! Say, you’re some poet, aren’t
you? Where’s the rest of it?” He tried another sheet. “‘See our banners
bravely flying.’ Bully, kid! Hot stuff!”

Short of actual combat, there was nothing for Dick to do but accept the
situation with what dignity he might. He seated himself on the window
seat and sullenly waited for Bert to finish his banter.

“Ah, here we have it!” Bert had come to the last sheet.

    Hear the cheers that, hoarse, defying,
      Thunder o’er the field!

“Wow! What do you know about the Midget being a real, gosh-dinged poet?
Some genius, I’ll tell the world. What comes next, kid?”

“That’s all I’ve written,” muttered Dick defiantly.

“What’s it for? Don’t tell me you’re trying to write one of those
football songs. By jiminy, that’s it, isn’t it? Well, let me tell you,
young Dodd, that this is the mushiest stuff I ever read. Can it, kid,
can it! You make me sick, rotting in here on a corking day like this.
Grab your cap and beat it.” Bert tore the sheets into bits and tossed
them in the general direction of the wastebasket.

Dick bit his lips and then shrugged. “You’re a rotten bully, Bert,” he
said almost dispassionately. “I wish I was a bit bigger.”

“You do, eh?” Bert laughed contemptuously. “What would you do if you
were, youngster?”

“I’d lick you good and hard,” replied Dick evenly.

“Would you now? Takes more than size to do that, you little runt!” Bert
stepped across and made a grab for Dick’s nose, but Dick struck the
hand aside and jumped to his feet.

“You touch me, Bert,” he said in a low voice, “and you’ll be mighty
sorry.”

Bert laughed again, hesitated and turned on his heel. “I’d take you
over my knee,” he growled, “if I wasn’t afraid of breaking you. You and
your silly rhymes. ‘See the banners bravely flying.’ Better get out and
get some air in your lungs, you dear little girl. Why don’t you get
some sewing? Ever try tatting?”

“If I did I’d do it better than you play football,” answered Dick hotly.

He was sorry the instant he had said it, for the expression on Bert’s
face said plainly that the shot had told and hurt. Bert had made rather
a mess of his playing yesterday, and he knew it, and the subject was a
very sore one. After all, Dick didn’t like to hurt others’ feelings,
even if they had hurt his.

“Sorry, Bert,” he said contritely. “Forget that.”

The apology, however, seemed to Bert as great an insult as the original
cause for it, implying as it did that Dick had touched on an open wound.
Bert’s face flushed darkly and he glared across the room as though
minded to take the table at a flying leap and wreak vengeance. He was
not, though, destined to get his revenge just then, for there was a
knock on the door behind him and, after a last malevolent look, he
turned and opened it, revealing the smiling Jimsy.

“Hello,” growled Bert. Then, as Jimsy, with a curious glance at him,
entered, he slipped past him and was gone along the corridor. Jimsy
looked after him amusedly, closed the door slowly and softly and then
leaned against it, regarding Dick with upraised eyebrows.

“I seem to have interrupted something,” he said.

Dick smiled ruefully. “Glad you did. Bert and I were having some words.”

“Words? Gee, I thought it looked more like actions. What was the row?”

He seated himself in Bert’s chair by the table and listened to Dick’s
recital. When it was ended he chuckled. “You certainly handed him a
stiff one, Dick,” he said. “From what I’ve heard, he and two or three
others got raked over the coals in great shape yesterday. They say
Thorne was pretty sore.”

“I didn’t mean to be nasty,” said Dick regretfully, “but he got me
pretty sore.”

Jimsy shrugged. “He’s a pill. I wouldn’t worry. But, say, what’s this
about the song? You didn’t tell me you were trying it. Where is it?”

“He tore it up,” answered Dick evasively.

“Well, you remember what you wrote, don’t you? How does it go?”

“Oh, I didn’t have much luck with it. I guess I’ll forget it.”

“Piffle! Look here, Dick, I’ll tell you what we’ll do. Get some paper
and we’ll go and find a quiet, peaceful spot and finish it. I’ll help.
I’m a regular Henry Wadsworth Tennyson when it comes to poetry.”

But Dick shook his head. “There isn’t time. It’s got to be in the first
thing in the morning.”

“What of that?” Jimsy laughed derisively. “Why, we’ve got all the
afternoon and evening.”

“You may have,” replied Dick virtuously. “I’ve got to study.”

“Well, sakes alive and everything!” Jimsy spoke exasperatedly. “You
don’t have to study all the rest of the day, do you? Come on. Besides,
there’s nothing else to do.”

“We might snare rabbits,” said Dick slyly.
