Jimsy grinned. “Shut up,” he said pleasantly. “You’re not teasing me
any, son. I’d have had those rabbits if there’d been any. You can’t
snare rabbits where they ain’t. Besides, we had lots of fun, didn’t we?”

Dick acknowledged that they had. Jimsy helped himself to the major
portion of one of Bert’s scratch pads and thrust the paper into a
pocket. “Come on,” he insisted. “You can’t stay in here a day like
this, anyway. If you don’t want to write poetry we’ll just take a
walk. For my part, though, I feel just like composing sonnets and
things. I feel the divine whatyoucallit working inside me.”

“You probably ate too much pudding,” said Dick. But he got his cap and
followed.

In a sunny place overlooking the river they sat themselves down and
Dick at length consented to put on paper as much of the football song
as he had arrived at and submit it to Jimsy. Jimsy was loud in praise
of it. “Why, that’s fine!” he declared. “How does the tune go?” Dick
hummed it and Jimsy sang the words as far as they went, ending with a
series of tumty-ti-tums and then breaking forth majestically on the
chorus:

    Wave the flag of Heaven’s hue!
    Hail the heroes tried and true!
    Cheer to victory the blue
      Of Old North Bank!

“Say, that’s corking! You’re a genius, Dick! You mustn’t quit now.
Finish it up. You only need three or four more lines, don’t you? How
many verses do they want?”

“One, with a chorus, will do, they said. But it’s the other four lines
that I can’t get.”

“Why not? Let’s see.” Jimsy studied the verse a long moment, handed it
back, seized some paper, unlimbered his fountain pen and frowned down
at the sun-shot river. Several times he wrote and as many times his
frown deepened and he erased. Finally, tired of waiting for results,
Dick set about the matter again himself. Many minutes passed. From the
river below came voices and laughter as canoes and boats drifted past.
The shrill whistle of an electric train sounded from the cut that led
to the bridge, and Dick, his mind busy with the verse, watched the
cars crawl into sight, slow at the draw and then go speeding on again
toward the farther shore. He shot a glance at his companion. Jimsy had
relinquished paper and pen and was frankly idle, a grass stem between
his teeth and his gaze fixed on the river. Dick smiled to himself.
The divine afflatus of which Jimsy had spoken had not lasted long, he
thought! But there he did his chum an injustice, for a moment later the
latter came out of his daydream, picked up paper and pen and began to
scribble rapidly. This fact, though, Dick missed, for he was bending
intently over his own task and had forgotten, for the time, Jimsy and
all else.

Twenty minutes later Dick stopped writing, read the completed verse
through and turned in smiling triumph. “Got it,” he announced. “At
least, it doesn’t sound so bad.”

Jimsy waved his pen, but made no answer. Plainly he, too, was in the
throes of poetic composition. The sheet of paper on his knee was
covered with writing. Dick tried to read it, but couldn’t. Jimsy added
a last word and waved the sheet proudly. “Listen to this, Dick,” he
cried. “Talk about your football songs! Wait till you get this one,
son! All ready?” Jimsy cleared his throat impressively and began to
read.

    Down the field our team is rushing!
    Back the enemy we’re pushing,
    Cumbridge hopes beneath us crushing
      Deep into the mud!

    There goes Trumbull through the center!
    Gray and Benson, too, will rent her,
    Every rush will badly dent her,
      Like a raging flood!

    Smear ’em, smash ’em, bust ’em, too!
    Kick their slats as we go through!
    Paste their eyes and paint ’em blue
      For Old North Bank!

“How’s that for pep?” demanded Jimsy triumphantly. “And feeling?
And――and poetry, what? Might as well tear yours up, Dick. You can’t
compete with Byron W. Keats! Gosh, that’s a rhyme, too! It’s getting to
be a habit! Like cabbage with a rabbit! Stop me, some one!”

“What I like best,” laughed Dick, “is that line about the raging flood.
‘Dent them like a raging flood,’ isn’t it?”

“‘Every rush will badly dent her, like a raging flood,’” quoted Jimsy
complacently. “Of course, floods don’t usually dent things, but I had
to have a rhyme for ‘mud.’ Pretty slick, isn’t it?”

“It’s wonderful,” chuckled Dick. “The――the sentiment is so sweet!”

“Sweet? You don’t want sweet sentiment in a football song, you idiot!
You want pep and punch. I call that song inspiring. Get the fellows to
singing that and the team will do murder! Trouble with most football
songs is that they’re too tame, Dick. I claim that I’ve managed to get
away from the old style. I――I’ve sounded a new note, as you might say.
If,” he concluded modestly, “I hadn’t written that myself I’d say it
was mighty good!”

“It isn’t like you to let that interfere,” responded Dick blandly.

“Envy,” retorted Jimsy. “That’s your trouble. Now read your song. Of
course it isn’t up to mine, but read it just the same. Might as well,
now you’ve gone to so much trouble with it.”




                               CHAPTER IX

                    “SEE THE BANNERS BRAVELY FLYING”


“The committee,” announced Benson, senior class president, from
the edge of the platform, “was disappointed at the number of songs
submitted in response to its request. It has received only twenty-two,
and as there are over two hundred fellows here this year, that’s not
doing well. I reckon a whole lot of you didn’t take the trouble to try.”

“How about you, Jerry?” demanded a voice in the audience. A laugh
greeted this, and Jerry Benson joined it.

“Members of the committee weren’t allowed to compete,” he replied.
“Well, the result is that we’ve chosen two songs from those submitted,
and we’re going to ask you all to try them over and see which you like
best. We think they’re both pretty good, but we don’t want more than
one, I reckon. The first is by――” Benson referred to a piece of paper
he held――“by Thomas Hale Nichols, second class, and the other by R. S.
Dodd, third class. You’ll find the words of both on the sheets that
have been distributed. In case you’ve gone and forgotten the tune,
the――the orchestra will play it through first.”

Benson retired amidst applause and laughter, the latter occasioned
by his reference to Cas Kirkham, who presided at the piano, as the
orchestra. The occasion was the regular Wednesday night football mass
meeting, and the hall was pretty well crowded. Dick, seated between
Jimsy and a second class fellow known as “Ducker” Coy――why Dick never
learned――was warm with embarrassment, and, as the piano began the
martial strains of Kirkham’s music, he took up the little sheet of
paper he held and gazed again at the two sets of verses and refrains.
Nichols had written lines rather less heroic than his, and Dick thought
them better. Or perhaps it would be more exact to say that he thought
the other fellows would think them better! Still, it was something to
have emerged even second best out of a competition of twenty-two!

The piano stopped and Warden raised his baton. “All ready, fellows!” he
called. “We’ll take the first one. Get into it!”

They got into it and the hall rang with boyish voices. Dick sang
loudly, resolved to do his duty by the rival anthem. Jimsy sang, too,
but he sang his own words, or as many as he could remember, and his
rendition of the chorus, with the bloodthirsty “Smear ’em, smash ’em,
bust ’em, too!” occasioned much surprised interest in the immediate
neighborhood. The song ended in a long-sustained note and was followed
by enthusiastic applause; clapping, stamping, cries of “A-a-ay!” Dick
clapped louder than any, while Jimsy cried “Rotten! Rotten!” and
hissed, again becoming the center of local interest.

“Cut it out,” begged Dick. “Fellows will think it’s me!”

“What’s the difference? Every fellow has the right to express his
convictions. It’s a punk song. Wish I’d sent mine in! Say, Ducker, I
wrote some words that were corking, but I didn’t want to squeeze Dick
out of it. I’ll sing ’em to you after the show.”

Ducker, who was a big, loose-jointed chap, crewman and left fielder on
the nine, grinned and chuckled. Ducker did one or the other, or both,
in lieu of speaking whenever possible.

“Now we’ll try the next one,” announced Warden. “Same tune, you know.
We’ll take the chorus a bit slower, Kirkham, and see how it goes. All
right!”

Dick knew these words without reading from the slip of paper, but for
some reason his voice was scarcely audible. Probably it was because
he wanted to hear how his song sounded when sung by others. Once more
nearly two hundred hearty voices joined and once more the piano crashed
out the accompaniment.

    See the banners bravely flying
    ’Gainst the golden sunlight, dying,
    Hear the cheers that, hoarse, defying,
      Thunder o’er the field!

    See the vaunted foe retreating,
    All his onslaughts we’re defeating,
    While our battle-cry repeating:
      “North Bank does not yield!”

    Wave the flag of Heaven’s hue!
    Hail the heroes tried and true!
    Cheer to victory the Blue
      Of Old North Bank!

To Dick it seemed that the applause that followed was louder than
before, more spontaneous. Certainly there was less polite handclapping
and more vociferous shouting and thumping of feet. Perhaps, though,
Jimsy was making such a racket that Dick couldn’t estimate the rest of
the applause very nicely. Jimsy was clapping, stamping and shouting at
one and the same time. Ducker, who probably had no choice between the
two compositions, was shouting “A-a-a-ay!” very loudly and out of sheer
friendliness. When quiet was restored Jerry Benson joined Tom Warden at
the front of the platform.

“I reckon we’ll have to take a vote,” he announced. “Those who like the
first song best will please stand up.”

Many stood, but many more remained seated and loudly called on the
standers to “Sit down, you chumps!” and earnestly begged to know how
they got that way! Pandemonium threatened while Benson and Warden
craned their necks to estimate the vote. Kirkham seemed uninterested in
the matter, and picked out soft notes on the piano with one finger.

“All right,” said Benson finally. “Sit down, you all! Now those in
favor of the last song will please stand.”

To Dick it looked as if the entire audience was on its feet, including
even those who had voted before! Jimsy tried to drag him upright, too,
but Dick resisted. He had remained seated before and had no notion of
getting up now. From behind the backs of those in front of him he
heard Benson speaking again.

“I reckon there’s no doubt about it,” said Benson laughingly. “We’ll
adopt the second version, written by Todd. Eh? Oh! Not Todd, Dodd! All
down, fellows!” The speaker’s face again came into Dick’s vision. He
was still talking. “Now I think we’ve got a rousing good song there
and we ought to learn it thoroughly, and so we’ll sing it again. But
before we do that I want to thank all those fellows who sent in verses.
I’m thanking them in behalf of the committee.” Applause greeted this.
“And I want more especially to thank the two fellows whose songs were
selected for trial to-night, Messers――er――Nichols and Todd――I should
say Dodd.” Laughter here. “If Nichols is here I’d like to have him
stand up, please.”

After some hesitation Nichols did so. He was a round-faced, good-natured
looking boy, and he smiled sheepishly at the cheers that met his
appearance.

“Thank you,” said Benson. “And now, Dodd――or――no, that’s right! Dodd.
Will Dodd please stand also?”

Seemingly Dodd wouldn’t, for after a moment, during which there was an
unseemly disturbance from the left of the hall, near the rear, Benson
resumed. “Apparently he isn’t with us this evening, so――”

“He’s here, all right,” announced the voice of Jimsy Ravenel, “but I
can’t get the silly beggar up!”

After that there was but one thing to do, and Dick did it. He stood
up, a small, slight, greatly embarrassed youngster, while laughter and
good-natured joshing greeted his appearance and Jimsy intoned “Dodd!
Dodd! Dick S. Dodd! Dodd! Dodd! Dick S. Dodd!” over and over. Very red
of face, Dick endured the publicity for one wretched moment and then
sank hurriedly from sight.

“Thank you,” said Benson, above the dying tumult. “And now, fellows,
let’s have it again. There’ll be another cheer meeting Friday night,
and I want every one of you to know the words by heart. All right, Tom.
Make them sing it!”

After they had gone through it again they went back to the older
favorites; to _We’ll cheer for Old North Bank_ and _Rush them, crush
them_ and, finally to the School Song, _By the Side of the Severn_.
Last of all they cheered mightily, for the Team, for the players
separately, for the coach, for North Bank, and so went their ways,
rather hoarse, somewhat exalted of spirit.

Perhaps Dick was the happiest of all those who poured out of the hall.
Even when he was in bed, with the light out and Bert’s unmusical
respirations alone breaking the silence, the happiness remained. He had
heard his song sung by the whole school, had thrilled to the wonder of
it, and the thrill still lingered. On the morrow he found that he had
become a person of prominence in a small way. Fellows congratulated
him, sometimes laughingly, but always sincerely, and the third class
members drew public attention to the fact that Dodd was one of them. Of
course it was only for a day or so, but it was pleasant while it lasted.

Dick might have been very fully satisfied with life those days had it
not been for one thing. The one thing was Bert Lodge, or, more exactly,
Bert’s behavior. He had neither forgiven nor forgotten that episode of
the Sunday afternoon, and he made the fact evident on all occasions.
Dick’s aspersion on his football playing had struck in a vulnerable
spot, for Bert was failing to please the coach and was seeing his
chance of getting into the big game grow dimmer and dimmer each day. In
some vague way he blamed Dick not only for the criticism but the truth
beneath it. Perhaps, since he couldn’t vent his wrath on Mr. Thorne,
Dick was the natural recipient of it. At all events, life in Number 12
was anything but smooth and sunny those days between the St. John’s
game and the Cumbridge contest, and Dick grew to dread the hours he
was forced to spend in Bert’s society. The latter never let pass an
opportunity to sneer or nag, and he perfected a system of insults that
cunningly stopped just short of an excuse for physical retaliation.
Dick often wished very heartily that Bert would provide that excuse,
even though, as he was certain, he would be badly worsted in a fight.

In a measure he sympathized with Bert’s frame of mind, for he knew
how hard the latter had set his heart on making the first team that
fall, or had hoped, failing that, at least to win the position of
second-string end. Perhaps few of his team-mates had expected him to
succeed in either endeavor, but Bert had entertained early in the
season no doubt in the matter. He held a very excellent opinion of
Bert Lodge and of that young gentleman’s abilities, and his failure to
make good surprised him almost as much as it pained him. He explained
the matter to those who would listen long enough by dark hints of
personal animosity toward him on the part of the coach. This may have
salved his sensibilities, but it didn’t fool the hearers. Even Dick,
who knew little of inside football affairs, couldn’t credit the theory.
Dick believed that Coach Thorne ranked in greatness just under the
President of the United States and was above all criticism. Of late,
of course, Bert had ceased confiding in Dick, but the latter never
missed a practice, unless the session was a secret one, and it wasn’t
difficult to see how things were going. Barring a marvelous reversal
of form, Bert would do no better than third or even fourth choice the
day of the Cumbridge game, and his chance of getting his letters was
extremely slim.

Taking all this into consideration, Dick found it in his heart to be
rather sorry for his roommate on occasions, although the occasions were
becoming few and of short duration. Jimsy, who held Bert in deep and
abiding contempt, and never troubled to disguise the fact from him, was
all for reprisals. He advanced many plans having as their object the
disciplining of Bert. Mostly they were more spectacular than practical.
Of course, he pointed out, Dick couldn’t fight the obnoxious one and
derive any satisfaction thereby. Dick wasn’t so sure about that, but
didn’t argue it. Therefore, Jimsy expounded, it was necessary to adopt
strategic measures. For instance, they might decoy Bert to the river
and push him in. Or they might tie him to the bed some night and paint
him over with gear grease. Or they might smear his nose-guard with
capsicum vaseline. Jimsy had heard of a case where that treatment had
been most successful. He evolved a new scheme almost daily, but somehow
none seemed quite appropriate, and Bert pursued his way if not serenely
at least unchallenged.

Two mornings after the memorable evening when he had heard his football
song sung for the first time, Dick met Jerry Benson face to face in
front of Founders’ Hall. Dick didn’t doubt that Benson would remember
him, and his heart took several violent somersaults as they drew
closer. Dick wondered whether the football hero would speak to him or
just nod. The football hero did neither. Perhaps he wondered a bit why
the small youngster gazed at him with such wistful appeal, but there
was no recognition. Dick was terribly disappointed, but he didn’t blame
Benson. A fellow like Benson had so much on his mind!




                               CHAPTER X

                            FOOTBALL MADNESS


Dick heard his song――well, of course it wasn’t all his, for Cas Kirkham
had contributed the music; though, as any one knows, it’s easier to
write the music of a song than the words; all you have to do is take
some one else’s tune and change it a bit! Well, anyway, he heard _the_
song sung out of doors on Saturday, and wished that he was on the other
side of the field so that he might get the full effect of it. Sitting
right in the middle of it, so to speak, he only heard the voices
close by him. But he thought it sounded mighty well, even under such
circumstances, and wondered if Cumbridge would bring a song with her
next Saturday that would be as good.

The North Bank students spent the entire fifteen minutes between
the halves in practicing songs for the big game, and the hundred or
so Brackett’s School representatives who had followed their team to
North Bank were appreciative and generous with applause. Perhaps the
fact that the songs were aimed at Cumbridge, a team which had, two
weeks ago, beaten Brackett’s, 19 to 3, had something to do with their
appreciation.

When half time came North Bank was well in the lead, having scored
two touchdowns to Brackett’s one field goal, and there was no reason
to doubt that she would do equally well in the next half unless Coach
Thorne used his third-string men in the final period, which was
predicted. Brackett’s, in spite of having been heralded as a strong
team with a mighty offense, had proved rather easy. Indeed, North Bank
might have had a third touchdown save for an unfortunate fumble by
Nagle on Brackett’s twelve yards that had been recovered by the enemy.
North Bank’s back field had been irresistible. Trumbull and Benson
had done almost as they pleased with the opposing line, and Gray,
whose forte was speedy running of the ends rather than line plunging,
had managed several good dashes. At the ends, though, Brackett’s was
stronger than from tackle to tackle, and all during the first two
quarters North Bank had used old style football, the back starting from
close up and concealing the ball as long as possible. She had worn out
the Brackett’s left guard by the end of the first period and had then
transferred her favor to the left tackle, with the result that that
player had also shown every indication of fatigue when the whistle had
blown.

North Bank started the third period with three substitutes in her
line-up; new ends and a new right tackle; Clary, however, was out
because of a weak knee and not for faulty work. Thorne needed Jim next
Saturday and was taking no chances with him to-day. It was the Light
Blue’s kick-off, and Brackett’s pulled the ball down on her eight yards
and hustled it back to her fifteen. Two tries netted four yards off the
new tackle and then she punted well and far. For several minutes the
ball exchanged hands frequently, and then a stumble by Benson, catching
a punt on his thirty-two, resulted in his being downed in his tracks.
Brackett’s crowd applauded that break in the luck loudly. They hadn’t
had much to applaud so far and they made the most of this.

The Light Blue sent Trumbull back to kicking position and Nagle hurled,
on first down, to Temple, left end, and Temple caught the ball for
eight yards’ gain. Benson made more than the distance at right guard.
Then, although Benson again gained, some one was off-side and a penalty
resulted. Gray tried a run around left but was thrown for a two-yard
loss, and Trumbull punted.

The kick was low and outdistanced the Light Blue’s ends, and the
Brackett’s quarter came back nearly twenty yards before he was stopped
on his thirty-two. Then began Brackett’s one supreme effort of the day.
She concentrated on the middle of the North Bank line and made her
distance by inches, and reached the forty-two yards. Another plunge
straight at Norris gained two, a second went for three. The North
Bank backs stopped the third attack at the same place, and Brackett’s
deployed for a kick. But the small, chunky right half, who, in spite
of his build, had lots of speed, tore straight through the North Bank
center and reeled off seven yards, placing the ball well over the
fifty-yard line. Brackett’s became quite delirious with joy. As Norris
was showing the pace, Canton was sent in to replace him. Brackett’s
tried an off tackle play to her left and made it go for three. A second
attempt, inside the tackle, was stopped. Then, faking a line-plunge,
she threw down and across the field and caught the opposing right end
napping. The runner was on North Bank’s thirty-seven yards when he was
hurled out by Benson.

Brackett’s failed at a crisscross that shot the runner against Hickson,
and then netted three on a quarter-back run around left. Coach Thorne
sent Bert Lodge in at right end and substituted Jansen for Gray. On
third down Brackett’s again attempted a forward pass, but Jansen
spilled the play. The pigskin was on the thirty-four yards when it was
brought back, and the distance to the North Bank goal doubtless looked
discouragingly great to the Brackett’s left half when he retreated to
kicking position. From across the field came imploring cries from the
visiting audience.

“_Kick that goal!_” chanted the enemy. “_Kick that goal!_”

North Bank believed the attempt a hopeless one, and the answering
slogan of “_Block that kick!_” was but half hearted. Then comparative
silence fell and the ball shot back, the teams plunged into action
and, back at the forty-two yards, a tall, brown-stockinged youth swung
a long leg in the direction of the distant crossbar. The ball started
true, but it was low, and Gurney James, leaping high toward its path,
struck it down with one big hand. Perhaps it would have been better if
he hadn’t, for the pigskin had been aimed too low to top the crossbar.
The ball shot sidewise, disappeared into a confusion of striving,
jostling bodies, trickled out into sight, bobbed along for several
yards and was then scooped up by the Brackett’s quarter.

At the moment there was none between him and the goal line, some
thirty-five yards away, and he had a good start before North Bank saw
the danger. He shot away like a sprinter from a mark, straight and
swift, and the Brackett’s supporters raised a wild pæan of passionate
delight. But he was not to reach the goal line, for Hickson saved the
moment for the Light Blue. His tackle, made in an instant of frenzied
alarm, was poor, but it served to throw the runner out of his stride
and in the next moment Benson had dragged him down on the eight yards.

From the eight to the goal in four downs was very far from impossible,
and the visiting cohorts shrieked and howled, crowding along the side
line about the corner of the field. Time was called for North Bank,
though it appeared that Hickson’s injury was slight, and Coach Thorne
took advantage of the interruption to send in two substitute forwards,
Norwell and Lansing retiring. North Bank supporters grumbled at that,
for to them the moment seemed inauspicious for the introduction of
second and third-string players.

One plunge at the left of center netted less than a yard to the
attackers and before the next play could start the whistle ended the
quarter and Brackett’s supporters had to pace the length of the field
to reach their vantage point again. Changes were made in the brown
eleven, a new end and a new right half back entering the arena. Then
the last period started with a mass attack on North Bank’s center that
bore it back to the five-yard line. But that play settled the matter,
and North Bank cheered approvingly. No team of Brackett’s strength
could conquer five yards in two rushes, and, barring a successful
forward pass, the enemy could do no more than add a second field goal
to her score.

But Brackett’s had the courage of her convictions and scorned to accept
a paltry three points when six beckoned. She shot her interference to
the left and sent the quarter to the right in search of a hole. He
found it, but it let him through for only a scant yard. Near at hand
the visiting contingent, wracked by suspense, shouted and howled and
swayed about the corner of the gridiron. The Brackett’s captain held a
conference with his quarter, and North Bank accepted the incident as a
confession of weakness and jeered a bit. Then the attack poised itself
once more, hoarse voices entreated or warned, the ball went back and
the two lines surged together. Followed a long moment of doubt, for
the ball was gone from sight and half the players on the field seemed
inextricably piled on the ground, like a bunch of human jackstraws.

Then the referee, a slight man in an immaculate white sweater, plunged
into the confusion, pawing, digging, like a small terrier after a
buried bone, and one by one the writhing players were scattered
aside until, on his knees, one arm buried from sight, the referee
looked toward the sideline and waved his free arm back up the field.
Brackett’s had failed! No touchdown! North Bank’s cheer leaders sprang
to duty and a long cheer vented vast relief. When the ground was
cleared of bodies the ball lay less than a yard from the last white
line. Brackett’s had, after all, nearly done the impossible!

So far as excitement went, that finished the game, for what followed
was tame and lacking in thrills. As the period drew on Coach Thorne
threw substitutes in bewilderingly until, at the last, only Nagle
remained of those who had started the contest. Not to be outdone,
or, more probably to seek revenge by the use of fresh material, the
Brackett’s coach used his substitutes generously, and, as a result, the
fourth period was as halting as it was devoid of interest. The teams
remained of about the same relative strength and toward the last of the
period North Bank added a third touchdown when, unable to get closer
to the enemy’s goal than her twenty-yard line, she threw a successful
forward pass that was easily converted into a score. No goal resulted,
however, and the final score was 19 to 3, which was, oddly enough, the
identical score by which Cumbridge had triumphed over the Brown! Those
who had hoped to judge of the comparative merits of the Light Blue and
the Dark by to-day’s game were disappointed.

There was an impromptu celebration that evening, and perhaps because it
was impromptu it was a great success from the standpoint of noise and
enthusiasm. Dick and Jimsy joined the cheering procession and paraded
around the grounds, arm in arm, and did their utmost to make the fact
of their presence known. Dick was thrilled and ecstatic, but Jimsy, it
appeared, would as lief have cheered for Free Trade or the State of
Maryland as the football team. The important thing to Jimsy was the
noise he could make and the fun he could have making it. Prolonged
demonstrations in front of the houses elicited brief remarks from
various of the faculty, from Coach Thorne, from Captain Trumbull and,
eventually, from Doctor Heidler. The principal said the usual things
in much the same way he had been saying them on similar occasions for
years past, ended with a mild joke and retired indoors as a final cheer
was called for. The celebration terminated in front of Founders’ Hall
with the singing of the School Song.

In those days, though, it wasn’t the School Song that one heard about
the campus, in the corridors and from behind the curtains of the
showers. It was that more recent ditty known now as “Banners Flying,”
for want of a more official title. Dick heard it whistled or sung or
hummed on all sides, and felt rather proud. He wished that he had
written the music, too, and wondered how one wrote music, and, seeking
to solve that problem, spent a half-hour in the parlor in Baldwin one
afternoon when the house was fairly empty strumming tentatively on the
piano with unsatisfactory results.

Dick passed through the week following the Brackett’s game in a
condition bordering on nervous collapse. Jimsy called his trouble
_dementia footballitis_, and made fun of him. Jimsy certainly wanted
North Bank to win next Saturday’s game, but Jimsy wasn’t losing
any sleep over the matter. He didn’t wear out the daily papers
following the fortunes of the rival teams as narrated by the school
correspondents, nor did he haunt the field whenever a pair of soiled
khaki breeches appeared on it. Dick, however, did those things and
more. Dick lived and even dreamed football, and no anxious trainer
ever watched his charges more carefully than Dick watched the members
of the team. If he passed Hickson on the way to morning prayers and
detected a frown on that youth’s countenance, Dick became the prey to
deep forebodings. If Benson’s tanned, good-humored face seemed to the
younger boy to be a shade paler than usual the latter told himself that
the left half back was worrying about Saturday’s game, and was less
happy than before. Dick was football mad, in all truth, and Jimsy’s
diagnosis was not a mistaken one. Dick couldn’t bear to consider a
defeat for his school, and when some pessimistic acquaintance predicted
a Cumbridge victory he had to bite his lips to hold back the flood of
indignation that surged within him. Mass meetings were held almost
nightly, and Dick never missed one. He sang loudly and cheered with a
passionate enthusiasm that usually left him hoarse for the rest of the
night.

The final practice was held on Thursday, and the whole school marched
across to the field with banners snapping in a chill east wind and
stood around while the substitutes and the scrubs played a short
game and the first-string men walked through a few plays and kicked
or passed the ball about. Cheers and songs floated away on the wind,
the khaki-clad heroes trotted back to the gymnasium and the gathering
broke up. Dick, much moved by his emotions, walked silently back beside
Jimsy and scarcely heard the flippant chatter of his chum. There were
times, such times as this, when Jimsy seemed to Dick to be lamentably
light-minded and his conversation of no moment.

Dick was not the only occupant of Number 12 whose nerves were aflutter
in those poignant days. Bert Lodge suffered as much as did Dick from
suspense, although perhaps he was a trifle less concerned with the
outcome of the game than with his participation in it. Bert was still
hanging on and still hoping. The fact that he had survived every cut in
the squad gave him reason to hope. If Thorne didn’t mean to use him, he
argued, he would have been dropped long since. On the other hand, there
were three fellows ahead of him, aside from the two regulars who played
the end positions, and it was only in moments of extreme optimism that
he could picture himself getting into the big game. He had another
year ahead of him yet, and if he failed this fall he still might
succeed next, but Bert wanted those letters on his sweater, wanted the
privilege of going home in the spring wearing the light-blue and white
ribbon of the football man on his straw hat, wanted the distinction
that privilege would lend him.

He was a very trying companion to one who was himself keyed to a high
nervous tension, and Dick fairly ached at times to throw a book at
his head, or, hurling himself across the barrier of the study table,
to bear Bert backwards and hammer his fists in the sneering, snarling
face. One of Bert’s pet amusements just then was to sing “Banners
Flying” while Dick was trying to study――and in those days trying
was usually as far as he got――supplying silly, idiotic words to the
tune. If Dick protested Bert apologized with mock regret and began
again a minute later. Still, save that the endless repetition of
sound was difficult to stand, the singing was of little consequence.
Dick couldn’t get his mind on his lessons and it really made little
difference whether he was disturbed or wasn’t. Most every one else was
having the same difficulty, however, and the faculty, while sorely
tried, made generous allowance.

Friday night’s mass meeting was something to remember long afterwards.
There was the usual singing, the usual cheering to start the affair,
and then the speeches began. Trumbull spoke, and so did Coach Thorne,
and Jerry Benson, in his position of first class president, and Alan
Linscott, crew captain, and Tom Warden and Jimmy, the trainer, and two
or three more, and each was cheered when he arose and cheered when he
sat down. And between whiles the Glee Club and the Musical Clubs added
their bits.

Coach Thorne was earnest and brief, and it wasn’t until the meeting
was over and Dick was lying, very much awake, in his bed that he
realized that not once had the coach predicted victory for his charges.
Dick consoled himself with the explanation that the coach was one of
the careful and conservative kind and remembered that almost all the
other speakers had spoken of victory on the morrow as though it was an
accomplished fact. His head still rang with the wild, exultant cheers,
and, staring upwards into the darkness, he could still see the sober
yet confident face of Captain Trumbull as he had ended his remarks
with: “We’ll do our part, fellows. You do yours. Stand behind us every
instant and let us know that you’re there!” Yet Dick’s last waking
thought was: “I wish he’d _said_ we were going to win, though!”




                               CHAPTER XI

                           THE CUMBRIDGE GAME


Saturday dawned lowering and chill. A cold wind blew up the river from
the Bay. It was ideal football weather, doubtless, but Dick would have
appreciated sunlight. There was something depressing for him in the
low-hanging clouds and leaden appearance of the river. Victory for
the Light Blue seemed less assured than it had yesterday. He ate very
little breakfast, thereby following the fashion of the day, since only
the phlegmatic few were capable of finding savor in the morning meal.
Excitement and suspense were in the air. All recitations were canceled
for that day, leaving six long hours to be lived through before the
game without the diversion of lesson periods. A scrub game between
McCrea and Ellicot to decide the house championship was played at ten
o’clock, and Dick watched it, cheering for Ellicot’s team because
Ducker Coy, who was a resident of “The Cot,” played left tackle on
it. Jimsy cheered on all occasions and showed no preference. The game
served to help pass the better part of two hours, what with delays and
arguments over decisions, and in some way it was dinner time before
either Dick’s mind or his stomach proclaimed it. He managed to do
rather better at the noon repast, which was held half an hour earlier
than usual, and then joined the crowd on the steps to cheer the team
when it came out. Most of the players were smiling when they appeared;
only a few of the substitutes, fellows who had yet to face Cumbridge
for the first time, looked a bit nervous or pale. Dick felt heartened
by that view of the team. You couldn’t beat those fellows! No, sir, you
just couldn’t do it!

He and Jimsy sought seats early. George Ferry sat beside Dick. George
wouldn’t subscribe to Dick’s statement that North Bank was bound to
win. “We’ve got a good team, Dick,” said George, “but so has Cumbridge.
I’ll give you an opinion after the first quarter’s done. I wouldn’t
expect too much, though. Then you won’t feel disappointed if things
don’t go just right.”

Dick set George down as a pessimist. Jimsy confided that old George was
always like that. Wouldn’t say a team was going to win until the game
was over; and didn’t like to even then!

Long before two o’clock the stands were full and the late comers were
taking possession of the side lines. Cumbridge had brought a band with
her, not a very large band nor a very excellent one, but it made a good
deal of noise and added to the general excitement and confusion. The
rival school boasted of a much larger student body than did North Bank,
and it seemed that every Cumbridge fellow must have accompanied the
team. Across the gridiron the visitors’ stand was a solid mass of dark
blue.

Cumbridge’s warriors came on first, cheered by friend and foe, and
began warming up. Then North Bank appeared and Dick fairly strained
his throat when the cheer leaders tossed their big megaphones aside
and waved their arms. That was a wonderful cheer! Sitting down, he
intercepted an exchange of amused glances between Jimsy and George, but
he didn’t mind. They were probably quite as excited as he, only they
pretended not to be. The next moment he was singing, again on his feet,
his gaze fixed unswervingly on Tom Warden’s swaying hand.

    We’ll cheer for Old North Bank!
      She’s got the right team,
    She’s got the right spirit,
      She’s got the right steam!
    She’s got the right coach and
      She’s got the right men!
    She’s got to make good for
      Old North Bank again!

    So it’s rip up the Cumbridge team,
    Tear up the Cumbridge team,
    Smash up the Cumbridge team!
      Fight, fellows, fight!

Then came a long cheer that seemed to shake the stand, and the teams
were trotting out, spreading about the faded green of the field, the
dark blue players to the west and the light blue in front of the east
goal. Some one pulled Dick back into his seat just as the whistle blew,
and a voice called “Down in front, Freshie!” an insult that Dick might
have resented at any other moment! But he scarcely heard it then, so
intent was he on watching the flight of the ball. Nagle caught it
straight in front of the goal, hesitated the barest fraction of a
second and was off, slanting to the left, then to the right and then,
eluding a Cumbridge end neatly, straight ahead, the quickly formed
interference about him now. Ten yards, fifteen! Then he was tackled,
was down, was crawling ahead, was stopped. The ball was just short of
the thirty-yard line and North Bank was cheering madly.

Three minutes later, though, Trumbull had punted and the play was
at the other end of the field. Cumbridge lost no time in trying out
the adversary’s line. Her backs dived in, there was an instant of
confusion and then North Bank lined up again four yards nearer her
goal. Cumbridge cheered as wildly as North Bank had a few minutes
earlier. The Dark Blue shifted and a single figure ran back, caught
the quick pass and was off to the right. A sudden stop to let an enemy
end spill himself on the turf and then a long overhand heave that sent
the pigskin far up the field and to the left, well over the heads of
the struggling lines. There was just one player awaiting that ball,
and that player had dark blue arms to pull it down with and dark blue
legs to bear it speedily over the intervening lines toward the North
Bank goal. He was never seriously challenged, although Clary ran him a
wonderful race and reached the goal line but a fraction of an instant
behind him. Cumbridge scored her first touchdown in just five minutes
and twenty seconds after the kick-off, and two minutes later she had
kicked the goal!

Somehow that incident failed to disturb North Bank’s equanimity very
greatly. The thing had seemed so much of a fluke that it was not taken
too seriously. Of course, it gave Cumbridge seven points, but, well,
just wait until North Bank got going! So Dick and all the others
cheered defiantly, encouragingly and the Light Blue kicked off to the
enemy and the game went on again. Once more Cumbridge came back, but by
smaller gains, and only to lose the ball finally on downs just short
of North Bank’s forty. Nagle brought the home team supporters to their
feet with a startling run of twelve yards around the Cumbridge left,
but succeeding efforts were vain and Trumbull booted to Cumbridge’s
five yards. The quarter ended after another brief march by the Dark
Blue and another exchange of punts.

So far, excepting for that forward pass that had caught the home
team napping, the rivals had shown football of much the same style
and caliber. Each team seemed afraid to let herself go lest some
miscalculation should be seized on by her opponent. Attacks between
tackles diversified by an occasional end run and followed by a kick was
the order of the day. Neither team had gained consistently through the
opposing line and neither had shown superiority in punting. When it
came to the ends, however, Cumbridge had decidedly the best of it, and
there were those who watched who wondered that the visitor did not more
frequently send her plays outside tackles. But that, as it was proved,
was to come later.

Meanwhile, during the second quarter Cumbridge still smashed at the
North Bank line and North Bank still hurled Benson and Trumbull and
Gray against the almost impregnable front of the enemy. There were
gains, on both sides, but only once did the Dark Blue make her distance
in the second period by line bucking, while North Bank failed of even
that. The Light Blue twice made a good advance by dividing her attack
and sending Nagle, with the ball, inside of tackle, quite alone. But
that play was good only so long as its novelty lasted, and after
that, since the Light Blue was not using the forward pass, there was
little to do save punt. Although there were few stirring incidents
in the second fifteen minutes, excitement continued at its highest.
Over-eagerness twice set the visitor back, once for holding and once
for being off side, and thrice North Bank suffered from penalties.
When the half ended the ball was in North Bank’s possession on her own
forty-one yards.

When the teams had trailed their blankets out of sight Dick settled
back with a sigh that spoke eloquently of the nervous tension under
which he had been. About him discussion was rife and argument was
heated. Fellows who had never played the game in their lives were
eloquent with criticism. A discussion behind him, in which Jerry Benson
was blamed and defended for not playing the game he was capable of,
irritated Dick until to drown the sound of it in his ears he turned to
George Ferry and asked: “Do you think we can score, George?”

George nodded. “Bound to, I think, Dick.”

“So do I,” agreed Dick stoutly. “That touchdown of theirs was just a
piece of luck, wasn’t it?”

“Luck coupled with mighty fine playing,” agreed George. “Also with some
punk work by our end. Butterfield lost his man completely. Too bad.”

“He’s done pretty well since then, though,” said Dick generously,
and George nodded. The cheer leaders called for noise then, and
conversation was ended for the time. Songs followed, and again Dick
listened pleasurably to “Banners Flying.” North Bank went through her
repertory and Cumbridge sent back a tuneful defiance. Occasionally,
through the voices, could be heard the strains from the Cumbridge band!
Surprisingly soon, a mad cheer arose from the North Bank stand, and
fellows jumped to their feet. The team was coming back! Cheer leaders
ran to their places. “Long cheer, fellows! Long cheer! Make it good!
_Come on!_” It was good, although the final “North Bank!” was drowned
by the crashing welcome that Cumbridge hurled forth as the Dark Blue
warriors trotted into sight.

Jimsy voiced prophecy as the teams took the field and the cheers died
away. “We’ll score once and they’ll score again,” said Jimsy with the
impersonality of a Fate. “No matter how you figure it, fellows, we’re a
gone coon!”

“You shut up,” begged Dick. “You don’t know anything about it, anyway.
We’re going to win this, aren’t we, George?”

“Let’s wait and see,” was the unencouraging answer. “You never can tell
till it’s over, Dick.”

Dick had to be satisfied with that as he squirmed forward to the edge
of his seat and thrust his tightly clenched hands into the pockets of
his trousers. It was cold enough for heavy overcoats to-day, but North
Bank eschewed such garments. It was a sort of a principle there that a
sweater was enough for any occasion, and there were many on the stand
who were suffering for the principle!

North Bank ran foul of ill luck soon after the second half began. All
season long the team had escaped serious injury to any of her members,
and now, when such injury could be least endured, it happened, and not
once but twice in a brief five minutes! First it was Norris, the big
center, who was led limping away with something wrong with a shoulder
or an arm, and then, after a pile-up, Jim Clary remained on the ground
and when time was up was helped off between two substitutes. It was
then, I think, that North Bank first saw the shadow of defeat hovering
over her. With Clary out of the line, the Light Blue was a poorer team
by far. She could have better lost any man in the rush line than Jim.
Some predicted comfortingly that he would be back when the last quarter
started, but the prediction proved false and Sinclair played the game
out at right tackle, and played well but not as Jim would have played.
Canton went in for Norris and gained fame that day.




                              CHAPTER XII

                            BRIEF AND TRAGIC


North Bank was less steady in the line after the retirement of Jim and
Cumbridge began to make gains where, before, she had met repulses.
She took the ball down to North Bank’s twenty-four yards, running the
ends for variety, and then was stopped. A forward pass on third down
grounded and she tried a placement kick that, fortunately for the Light
Blue, failed widely. North Bank opened up with a few tricks late in the
quarter and Gray twice got away inside tackle for good gains, while
Benson brought every North Bank fellow to his feet with a wide end run,
with good interference, that placed the pigskin on Cumbridge’s nineteen
yards. That was the Light Blue’s opportunity to even the score, and the
cheerers did their part loyally, but something went wrong. Afterwards,
some said that Trumbull got his signals crossed and some said that the
fault was Nagle’s. The facts never appeared, which was just as well,
for even a football hero is human and fallible and accidents will
happen, and so why attach the penalty of blame?

An accident happened in this case, for after Benson had made two yards
through the Cumbridge center and Gray had failed to find a hole at the
right, Trumbull went back to kicking position, the ball was passed
to Nagle and there was none to take it! Cumbridge piled through,
and Nagle, running back and seeking a chance to toss forward, was
downed eight yards behind the line! It was fourth down then, on the
twenty-seven, and North Bank played it safe and wisely, and Trumbull
sent the ball over the bar for three points.

Three points was so much better than none that the Light Blue cheered
exultantly and prolongedly, and accepted the incident as an augury of
further success. The quarter, however, ended without further scoring
by either side and the teams changed goals. Coach Thorne sent Temple
in for Butterfield, but that was the only change he made then. Dick
remembered Bert Lodge and tried to pick him out on the bench below, but
he couldn’t identify him. Dick just then felt a bit sorry for Bert, for
Mr. Thorne had used but three ends so far and Bert’s chance was still
distant. But Dick had bigger things to worry about than his roommate
and his thoughts speedily went back to them. First, there was the fact
that even if Cumbridge failed to add to her present score North Bank
would have to do better than secure another field goal, for she would
in such case still be a point behind. A touchdown was imperative and
some one had to make it inside the next fifteen minutes, and Dick
prayed hard that some one would!

Cumbridge pushed her way across the center of the field and then placed
the ball on the forty-two yards by means of a short forward pass. A
minute later, however, a fumble brought the advance to an end and the
ball went to the Light Blue. Benson made four on a split-attack play
and Gray got two right through center. Trumbull faked a kick and ran to
the left, but was downed for no gain and Nagle punted to the opponent’s
seven yards. Again the North Bank ends were slow and the pigskin was
brought back to the twenty-one. Cumbridge tried two rushes and kicked.
Nagle caught near his thirty-five and made two strides before he was
tackled. Again North Bank tried Benson and then Trumbull and then
Benson again and made seven yards. Trumbull prepared to kick, but Nagle
changed signals and the backs returned to three-abreast formation. But
Cumbridge refused to believe her and when Dimond, skirting the line
behind, took the ball from Nagle and went on to the right he found a
comfortable hole and dashed through for six yards. A bedlam of cheering
rewarded that gain. But a few moments later Trumbull was forced to
punt and the ball rolled over the goal line and the teams lined up
on Cumbridge’s twenty. North Bank chanted “Touchdown! Touchdown!
Touchdown!” But the Dark Blue, with a comfortable lead in the scoring,
was taking no chances, and on second down she punted out of bounds at
North Bank’s forty.

Time was slipping away fast. The twilight of a cloudy day was making
the figures at the farther end of the field hazy and uncertain from
where Dick sat. Coach Thorne threw in two substitutes, relieving Gray
and Hickson. The big left tackle had played a fine game and was about
ready to fall. Nevertheless, he fought stubbornly against retirement,
so stubbornly that it required the efforts of Trumbull and the umpire
to get him off the field.

Some one announced that but six minutes remained, and Dick’s heart
sank sickeningly. A moment later it was bobbing about in his mouth,
for Nagle had shot a superb forward pass to Benson, and Benson was
speeding like a shot along the further side line. With luck, he might
have gone half way to the goal, but luck wasn’t smiling on the home
team much this afternoon. At Cumbridge’s forty-two yards he was tackled
and thrown, and a groan of sorrow went up from the Light Blue stand.
Again Nagle threw forward, but this time it was a Dark Blue player who
pulled the pigskin out of the air and shot away with it. Dick watched
that fleet-footed quarter back despairingly. Time and again he was
almost stopped, time and again he stumbled, time and again he was
forced toward the side line, yet on he went for what to one watcher at
least seemed interminable aeons. In the end he was brought to earth,
though. Dick could almost hear his inert body thump against the sod and
he was not surprised when, after Benson had unwrapped his arms from the
foe, the latter lay where he had fallen. But that quarter back wasn’t
made of glass, not he! After a minute he was up again, shaking his
head impatiently, thrusting aside the trainer. He had taken the ball
thirty-three yards straight through the whole North Bank team, and he
wasn’t to be discommoded by a little thing like a hard tackle!

Cumbridge was howling wildly, triumphantly. It was the Dark Blue’s ball
on the enemy’s twenty-five and she could see no reason why another
touchdown shouldn’t eventuate. But North Bank did see. Cumbridge ripped
off five yards on the first try, getting past Dimond. Two rushes
took the ball the rest of the distance and made it first down on the
fourteen. But there the Light Blue stood fast. Two smashes at the
center netted but three yards. A fake forward pass, left half aiming at
tackle, added another. Cumbridge set herself for a try-at-goal, or, it
might well be, a forward pass. The North Bank stand was silent. Every
fellow stood, straining his eyes through the gray murk of evening. Back
shot the ball. The player in kicking position held it aloft on one
palm and stepped back and to the left. Confused cries filled the air.
Bodies shot hither and thither. Then the ball launched forward. Back of
the goal a mass of straining arms showed momentarily. A horn squawked
ominously. An excitable youth behind Dick shouted: “Game’s over! Game’s
over!”

But it wasn’t. Instead a Cumbridge player was nestled to earth back of
the North Bank goal with half the opposing team about him. Cumbridge
cheered doubtfully. The horn squawked again. The referee had the ball,
was stepping back from the ten-yard line. At the fifteen he placed
it down. “Cumbridge off-side!” The joyous cry turned into a cheer
of relief and the Cumbridge stand became silent. Dick had stopped
thinking of victory now. But three minutes remained, maybe less for
aught he knew. North Bank couldn’t win. He realized that at last.
But, oh, if she could only save herself from the added humiliation of
another score! He prayed for that and that only, clasping his hands so
tight that his finger nails bit into his palms, stretching himself on
toes that trembled.

Two more substitutes were sent into the North Bank line. Then the
whistle piped once more and Cumbridge’s signals floated down the field.
Back went the kicker again. This time, it seemed, there could be no
doubt about it; it was to be a try-at-goal. And it was. But it was only
a try, for North Bank, defeated but never so desperate, broke through
the enemy line as if it had been of paper and the ball went bounding
off up the field!

A dozen players trailed it, reached it, missed it, stumbled, fell, in
a veritable comedy of errors. Then one, at last, captured it, strove
to run and was pulled down. Cumbridge cheered and North Bank cheered,
for at that distance dark blue and light blue were much the same.
But it was North Bank’s ball and the teams lined up once more on the
thirty-two. Coach Thorne was emptying the bench now. Dick saw Bert
Lodge go sprinting on, one hand frantically seeking attention. One by
one the veterans came trudging slowly off, limping sometimes, their
heads turned to watch the game they were leaving.

“One minute,” some one announced, and: “That’s enough,” declared
another. “Just let Benson get away once! We aren’t beaten yet!”

Hope dies hard, and Dick for a moment felt an almost agonized thrill of
confidence. Then the lines were swaying together again and some one had
shot through for several yards. There was a wait. Some one was down.
Then he was up again and again the lines faced each other.

The timekeeper, watch in hand, hovered ominously between side line
and players. Something went shooting through the air toward the
further side of the gridiron. Forms followed it. A single player ran
back and back, followed desperately by a second. The ball came down,
was clutched by the first. The two forms went down together close to
Cumbridge’s forty-yard line and the field streamed up. The North Bank
cheers burst forth imperiously. Another gain like that and victory
might yet come to the Light Blue!

Hurriedly North Bank lined up. The timekeeper walked a few steps
nearer, his gaze alternating between watch dial and players. Trumbull
was going back. Surely not to punt! No, it was another forward! And
there went Dimond almost alone! He had it! He had it! He was running
now, but two of the foe were close on his heels. If he could make it――A
great groan went up from the North Bank stand. He was down! But he had
almost reached the twenty, and if there was time――

A horn blatted. The teams drew away from each other. Around Dick
fellows were moving and stretching. Across the field the stand was
emptying. Dick watched dazedly. Surely it wasn’t over? It couldn’t be.
Why, just when another minute would have meant victory? The Cumbridge
band was playing loudly and the visitors were forming behind it to
march about the trodden field and under the goals. Jimsy’s voice
reached Dick as from a long distance.

“Dog-gone the rotten luck!” said Jimsy feelingly.

Beaten! Dick wanted to cry, wanted very badly to cry. But no one else
seemed to. Fellows all about him were talking and even laughing, though
not very joyously. He wondered how they could. He looked up to find
George observing him half smilingly but very understandingly. George
put an arm over his shoulders.

“Got to take the bad with the good, youngster,” he said softly. “Our
fellows played well and there’s another year coming.”

Dick looked up, swallowed, smiled soberly and nodded. Below them
they had started the School Song. Dick joined in, rather tremulously
at first and then more strongly. Singing those words seemed to give
him courage to stand the disappointment. Jimsy was singing, too; and
George. It was something to stand like that, shoulder to shoulder with
your comrades, and meet adversity with a brave countenance. Dick’s
voice gathered volume and his heart swelled until it hurt him, but the
pain was very pleasant.

    Old North Bank, to you our allegiance we pledge,
      To you we will ever be true.
    Though far we may wander our heart still will be
      Back here ’neath your banner of Blue!
    We’ll cherish the Light Blue, the bright blue, the right blue,
      Unfold it, uphold it and fight for it, too!




                              CHAPTER XIII

                          THE GREAT CONSPIRACY


A week of cold weather followed, and Maryland’s winter, seldom severe
when judged by Northern standards, seemed to have begun nearly a month
too early. The crews came off the river and the shells were stowed
back in winter quarters. The football gridiron was deserted save for
an occasional group of very small youths who disported themselves
joyously and noisily with a battered old ball. The tackling dummy was
gone from the “gallows” in the corner of the field and would be seen no
more until spring. The disreputable old fellow, headless and footless,
with a dark blue C painted on the front of his stuffed canvas body, had
retired to private life for the while. And so, too, had many of those
who had so rudely assaulted him a fortnight back: Trumbull and Benson,
Nagle and Norris, and various other erstwhile heroes. Already their
fame was waning. Every dog has his day, and the gridiron bulldog must
now give place to the lither terrier of the basket-ball floor.

Dick for awhile was one of those terriers.

He had followed Jimsy’s advice and had a heart-to-heart talk with Mr.
Tanner, the physical director. Mr. Tanner was a small, broad man with a
countenance almost entirely enshrouded in whiskers. He looked rather
like a benign old English sheep dog, Dick thought. Dick wanted to know
if he might go in for basket ball, and Mr. Tanner asked him why not.
Dick soon discovered that the physical director was much fonder of
asking questions than answering them. Dick explained that at home he
had been told to abstain from all athletic activities calculated to tax
his heart unduly. Mr. Tanner said: “Humph! Ever noticed anything wrong
with your heart?”

“N――no,” answered Dick. “Only sometimes it――it sort of jumps.”

“Jumps? When?”

“Well, when I get excited, I guess.”

“So does mine. Strip down to your waist.”

Five minutes later Mr. Tanner stopped tapping him and pressing a
whiskered cheek ticklingly against his chest and laid aside the funny
instrument with two tubes. “All right,” he said, and Dick got his
clothes on again. “What sort of things do you want to do?” asked Mr.
Tanner.

“I’d like to play basket ball and baseball, sir. And, maybe, next year
I’d like to try for football.”

“Never mind next year yet. Basket ball? All right, but don’t overdo
it.――Baseball? Certainly.――No reason why you shouldn’t. There’s nothing
the matter with your heart, my boy. It’s as good a heart as they make.
Lungs are sound, too, but you’ve never given them a chance to develop.
You ought to be two inches bigger around the chest. Muscles aren’t
bad, either, considering. You’re small, but you’re quite normal. Well
built, I’d say. Good bone structure, straight spine. How are your feet?
Better take the left shoe off. All right. Put it on again. General
health good? Ever have fever? Scarlet fever? Measles? Measles, eh? Much
trouble? Good. Well, you’re all right.” Mr. Tanner delivered a hearty
blow on Dick’s back that almost upset him. “What you should do is join
one of the gymnasium classes. Let’s see.” He drew a book from a corner
of his desk and leisurely turned a few pages. “I’ll put you down for F
Class. Four-thirty every afternoon but Saturday――and Sunday, of course.
We’ll get you breathing right in a month, and put two or three inches
on you. Wouldn’t be surprised if we helped you grow a bit, too. Stretch
your spine a little. All right. Good morning.”

“Then――then you don’t think,” began Dick.

“Not a bit of it! Pooh, pooh! Some one’s been trying to scare you.
Nothing to it, Dodd. Better if you’d done what other fellows do. That’s
your main trouble. Haven’t had enough play. A good year behind in
development. But we’ll fix that. Easy. Good morning.”

When some one has said good morning to you twice it is time to go. So
Dick went, although he had thought of several other questions to ask.
On the whole, though, he was quite satisfied. He didn’t know what his
folks would say when they learned that he was playing basket ball, but
then, maybe he wouldn’t play it. There was nothing certain about it
yet. And if he did play, why, perhaps his folks had best not hear of
it until he got home at Christmas time. Then he could break the news to
them gently.

As it turned out, he didn’t play basket ball. That is not much. He
reported with some forty-five other candidates and practiced nearly a
week, but he was included in the first cut of the squad. After that
he tried to make the junior team, composed of third and fourth class
students, and lasted another week. It wasn’t that he didn’t show
ability or speed, but he was too small to last long against the other
players. Most of them, even those of the junior team, topped him by
head and shoulders, and they had a most mortifying way of tossing him
about, if he happened to impede their progress over the floor, much
as if he had been something that had dropped down from the balcony
and didn’t belong there! That was very discouraging, and when he was
informed that his connection with the third squad of the junior team
was at an end he took it philosophically and retired to splash more
witch-hazel on his various bruises.

Jimsy was condoling and sympathetic, but seemed to imply that any one
silly enough to try such things deserved disappointment. Dick went
regularly to the gymnasium at four-thirty and, in company with some
fifteen or sixteen others, performed rather monotonous feats with chest
weights, dumb-bells and clubs and contorted his body into strange
shapes. After a fortnight, though, the program became more diversified
and included interesting stunts with bars and rings, and he spent less
time lying on a mattress and waving his legs in the air. Before he went
home a few days before Christmas he had, in fact, increased his chest
measurement by one and a half inches and could breathe in a manner
never before conceived of!

But there were other things beside physical development to engage his
thoughts. There were, for instance, studies. Following the end of the
football season, Dick had discovered that all was not well with the
relationship existing between him and certain of his instructors. The
fact was forcibly impressed upon him when he was invited to visit the
office of the principal and there discuss the subject of preparation.
It seemed that mathematics and English were not, according to the
reports received, getting as much attention from Dick as, in the
opinion of Doctor Heidler, they deserved. The discussion was quite
amicable. The Doctor was reasonable. He acknowledged to Dick that
there was a temptation on first entering school to lose sight of the
more important business and to become too greatly concerned with
such fascinating things as football and similar interests. He added,
however, that they looked for a change about this time; indeed, rather
insisted on it! Dick couldn’t think of any good reason why they
shouldn’t, and so there was no argument. He went away a bit chastened
and resolved to improve, and since improvement depended principally
on devoting more time to study he succeeded. Jimsy, who had also been
riding for a fall, followed his example, although he didn’t, as he
frankly explained, believe in taking the bread out of his preceptors’
mouths.

“If a fellow learns everything before he goes into class,” said Jimsy,
“what good’s the instructor? First thing he knows he won’t have any
job. Best way’s to divide the work, Dick. You learn part of the stuff
and the instructor teaches you the rest. Live and let live, that’s my
motto.”

Fortunately, aside from a fortnight of basket-ball endeavor, there
wasn’t much to prevent a decent application to studies, and Dick was
soon back on terms of mutual respect with the faculty. The month that
intervened between the Cumbridge game and the holidays was devoid of
great events, even of excitement, although there was one interesting
incident to break the not unpleasant monotony. That concerned Bert
Lodge.

Bert had won his football letters, but the fact had not seemed to
improve his disposition. Bert’s outlook on life remained as pessimistic
as ever and his regard for Dick was no warmer. It must be acknowledged,
though, that Bert was a trifle less obnoxious after the football season
was over. Either that or Dick had become callous. Bert had struck up
a sort of friendship with a senior named Walker. Walker had been a
substitute guard and, like Bert, had won his letters by two minutes of
play in the last period of the Cumbridge game, a fact which perhaps
brought them together. Walker was also a crew candidate, and Bert
informed Jimsy one evening, in a burst of unprecedented confidence,
that he guessed _he_ would go in for rowing after the holidays. The
emphasis is Bert’s. Jimsy looked extraordinarily grave and replied,
“That’ll be fine, Lodge,” adding hopefully in the next breath, “You
can’t swim, can you?” Bert seemed slightly puzzled, but said that he
could, and the glad light in Jimsy’s face faded.

Of course Bert knew of Dick’s basket ball ambitions, and, although he
seldom if ever looked in on practice, he possessed an uncanny knowledge
of his roommate’s progress――or, rather, lack of progress. Consequently,
Dick had to stand a good deal of malicious joking on the subject;
although perhaps joking is too charitable a word to use. When Dick
retired from basket ball activities Bert spent a full quarter of an
hour condoling with him, and Dick wanted very much to hurl a dictionary
at him.

Then, one night, Bert happened to catch Dick in the act of inflating
his lungs and observing the result, with considerable satisfaction,
in the glass. That gave the older boy a new idea, and after that Dick
was continually twitted about his physical development. Bert pretended
to detect a striking likeness between Dick and a certain gentleman
whose portraits adorned the advertising pages of the magazines, a
gentleman with a chest like a pouter pigeon’s and muscles that would
have shamed Samson himself. Bert declared that Dick might have sat for
that picture, it was so like him! He envied despairingly what he called
Dick’s manly strength and hoped that some day he, too, would be big
and powerful and able to break matches between his fingers! Dick never
dared so much as glance at his reflection in the mirror after that, for
fear that Bert would see him and start nagging. One evening some ten
days before the end of the term Dick went up to Jimsy’s room about nine
o’clock looking so close to tears that Jimsy noticed and questioned.
George was not there and Dick found relief in pouring out the tale of
his woes. He had had to study pretty hard that evening, and Bert had
been at him more than half the time, and he hadn’t learned a thing for
to-morrow, and Mr. Logan would jump on him, and――and he was just tired
of the whole thing! What between some difficult problems in algebra and
Bert’s attentions he was quite pathetically unnerved.

Jimsy was silent awhile. Then he said decisively, “Dick, we’ve got to
stop that fellow’s nonsense. The time’s come!”

“How are we going to do it?” asked Dick dolefully.

“Don’t know yet. We’ll have to think of a way. We’ve got to get
something on him so that when he starts to rag you you’ll have a
comeback. Shut up and let me think. What’s the guy’s big weakness,
Dick?”

“You told me to shut up,” answered Dick, smiling wanly.

“I want you to, son. I’m just thinking aloud. Let’s see now. Conceit?
Surest thing you know! That’s the lay! Wait a minute!”

Dick had to wait more minutes than one before Jimsy, with an
exclamation of glad triumph, seized a block of paper and began to
write. Dick refrained from intruding on his frenzy, and at last Jimsy,
smiling modestly, handed the result across. Dick read the effusion,
doubtfully at first, and then with a chuckle of appreciation. We
won’t concern ourselves with what he read, for it was but the first
rough draft of the finished article. Drawing a chair beside Jimsy’s,
Dick lent his enthusiastic aid and counsel, and word by word, line by
line, the composition was amended until at last the two leaned back in
triumph. Then Jimsy read it aloud. It bore an address in New York City,
was dated two days later and ran as follows:

    BERTRAM LODGE, ESQ.,
        _North Bank School,
            North Bank, Md._

    DEAR SIR:

    It is the intention of the publishers of _Who’s Who on the
    Gridiron_ to make the coming volume more comprehensive than
    ever, and to this end it will be extended to include those
    players of the more important preparatory institutions who have
    made their marks during the past season. Every effort will be
    made to keep the volume at the same standard of excellence,
    however, and to maintain its value as an authoritative
    reference. Your name has been suggested to us as one deserving
    inclusion in the forthcoming edition, and, should the plan meet
    your approval, we would be grateful if you would favor us with
    a brief sketch of your career, more especially that portion
    concerning your school life and athletic success. Such sketch
    should not exceed two hundred words and should include place
    and date of birth, height, weight, and all particulars of your
    football activities. If possible this information should be
    accompanied by a photograph of yourself, preferably in football
    costume, suitable for reproduction.

    As this invitation is of necessity extended to but a very
    limited number of representative football notables, you are
    asked to treat it as confidential, whether you decide to accept
    it or not. The acceptance places you under no obligation. You
    will, of course, want a copy of _Who’s Who on the Gridiron_
    when ready. The price to contributors is $1.50, and that amount
    may be sent with your sketch and, we hope, photograph. The
    book will be forwarded to you by post as soon as published.
    If, however, you do not find it convenient to make payment in
    advance, a written acceptance of this offer will suffice, and
    you will be notified when your copy is ready for delivery to
    you.

    Trusting that we shall be favored with an early and favorable
    reply, we beg to remain,

                                                THE EDITORS,
                                      _Who’s Who on the Gridiron_.

    Kindly address your letter and all later communications to
    Gerald P. Thompson, Chief-of-Staff.

“It’s simply corking!” gurgled Dick. “But do you think he will fall for
it?”

“Like a ton of bricks,” answered Jimsy confidently. “And I’ll bet he
will send half a dozen photographs, too!”

“I don’t believe he has any,” said Dick doubtfully.

“Then he’ll have some taken,” chuckled Jimsy. “Why, say, that letter
would fool any one! I’ll copy it off to-morrow morning on Ducker’s
typewriter. I wish, though, we had a sheet of paper with printing on
it. You know, ‘Editorial Offices of _Who’s Who on the Gridiron_,’ or
something like that. But we’ll have to make the best of it. He won’t
think about that, probably. I’ll write a note to Thompson to go with
this and tell him to be on the watch for a letter, and send it to me
as soon as it comes. Oh my, oh my, what a rag! If only it goes right,
Dick, that chump downstairs won’t dare to open his mouth again while
he’s in school!”




                              CHAPTER XIV

                              BERT OBLIGES


Three days passed during which the conspirators watched and waited.
The letter to Bert Lodge from _Who’s Who on the Gridiron_ should have
reached him by that time, unless, as Jimsy owned was not impossible,
Gerald Thompson was away from home. Nothing occurred to indicate that
the letter had come. It was easy enough for Bert to receive it without
Dick’s knowledge, but Dick was pretty certain that he hadn’t. Then, on
the fourth day, their anxiety was set at rest. Returning to Number 12
about half past two, Dick saw the letter on the table, spread out at
Bert’s elbow. Bert was writing a reply. There could be no doubt as to
that, for every few moments the scribe re-read portions of the letter,
always laying it aside again with every indication of satisfaction. In
fact, it seemed to Dick that Bert would have been highly elated had
his roommate referred to the letter and so given him an excuse for
exhibiting it. He moved it about the table as though seeking to draw
Dick’s attention to it while the latter was busy at the other side
with his books, and Dick, inwardly convulsed with mirth, had hard work
keeping his face straight. He hurried off to find Jimsy and impart the
glad tidings, leaving Bert still struggling importantly with his answer.

The next afternoon Bert was seen making his way to the railway
station with a large bundle under one arm. That the bundle contained
his football togs and that he was on his way to Annapolis and a
photographer was quite beyond question, and Jimsy and Dick fairly
hugged each other. That evening Bert moved about in a mood of
exaltation and pride, a strangely benign mood that knew naught of
nagging. He hummed happily and, instead of studying, sat for long
minutes staring into space, his saturnine visage fairly transformed by
the radiant pictures his mind was conjuring up.

The following day Gerald Thompson was heard from. Gerald, an erstwhile
crony of Jimsy’s, was most complacent. He said he hoped the joke
was a good one and that Jimsy must tell him about it when they met.
Meanwhile here was the letter, and Jimsy would kindly note that he had
to pay postage like any one else and so settle up like a gentleman
when the business was concluded. Eagerly Jimsy slit an end of the
enclosed envelope. The missive that he drew forth was, at first glance,
disappointingly brief, but a perusal of it brought only satisfaction.
Here, shorn of salutation, is what Bert had written:

    I’ll be pleased to be represented in your publication, as per
    yours of Dec. 15. I am preparing the sketch and will forward
    it within a day or two. Also photographs. There will be two
    of these. Please select the one you consider the best for
    publication and return the other to me soon. Put me down for a
    copy of the book and let me know when it is ready and I will
    send the money. Trusting this will be satisfactory,

                             Respectfully,

                                                 BERTRAM C. LODGE.

    P. S. The sketch and photos will surely reach you within four
    days, so don’t forget me. B. C. L.

“Isn’t it a scream?” demanded Jimsy joyously. “Did he fall for it? Oh,
no, he didn’t fall! He――he just collapsed! Oh, boy, when we get those
photos!”

“What’ll we do with them?” asked Dick, grinning with anticipation.

“Do with them? Why――” Jimsy stopped and his smile languished. “Gee, I
don’t know, Dick. We might put them on the notice board in Hall, eh?
No, I guess that would be too raw. Well, I don’t know as we can do much
with the photos. It’s the letter we want, the sketch of his football
activities. Wonder if he’ll own up to playing only a minute and a half
in the Cumbridge game. Bet you he’ll get around that somehow, Dick! Has
he got the photos yet?”

“I don’t believe so. It takes about a week, generally, doesn’t it?”

“Maybe, but friend Lodge isn’t going to let it take any week this time.
He’s scared blue the _Who’s Who_ folks won’t wait for him. Did you get
that pathetic postscript? ‘Don’t forget me!’ Oh, we won’t, Bertram, we
won’t!”

The photographs must have arrived when Dick wasn’t about. Or perhaps,
unnoticed, Bert made a second trip to Annapolis and got them from the
photographer. Jimsy favored the latter theory, adding that Bert had
doubtless taken the sketch with him to town and mailed it with the
photographs there. As for the sketch, Dick had watched its composition
fascinatedly during two evenings, what time he should have been
studying. Bert had labored hard with it, had written and erased, had
corrected, amended, deleted, extended, copied and recopied. He had
gazed unseeingly at the wall, had writhed and groaned and sighed, had
written feverishly, had written falteringly, had, on one occasion,
caused Dick’s heart to sink by savagely tearing up the entire result
of an hour’s labor. Dick had not been present at the triumph of
completion, but that that stage had been reached was beyond doubt, just
as it was beyond doubt that the photographs had been received, for on
the Monday preceding the Wednesday of exodus came a second consignment
from Gerald Thompson. Gerald drew attention to the obvious fact that he
had had to put four two-cent stamps on the package and hoped to hear
from Jimsy soon.

In the seclusion of Jimsy’s room the package was opened amidst a
breathless silence and the contents revealed. The conspiracy had
succeeded beyond their wildest expectations. There were two panel
photographs of Bert in football attire. In one he was standing, his
feet slightly apart, his hands on his hips, against a vista of meadow
and forest that recalled the backgrounds of Sir Joshua Reynolds’
masterpieces. Bert wore a stern, heroic expression, and the beholder
felt at once that here was one of those brilliant, hard playing, hard
fighting youths whom the writers of football fiction took for their
heroes. Even Jimsy was momentarily impressed and said “Gee!” half under
his breath in unwilling admiration. The second portrait showed Bert in
a more careless, genial moment. He was seated, staring smilingly at the
