beholder, a football clasped carelessly to his stomach and one hand
resting negligently on a khaki-clad knee. Before him lay head guard and
nose guard, as though, having led his companions to victory a moment
before, he had thrown them aside for an instant’s relaxation. This
latter photograph was less impressive, although, as Dick pointed out,
it was even more remarkable than the other, inasmuch as it portrayed
the hero good-natured and smiling. Jimsy said they were both “corkers”
and that he wouldn’t take a hundred dollars for them!

But the masterpiece, when all was said and done, was the “brief sketch
of your career.” Jimsy read it aloud unctuously.

                         BERTRAM CHARLES LODGE

                  _North Bank School, North Bank, Md._

    Born Ellsworth, Pa., June 9, 1904. Attended school in Ellsworth
    and became prominent in athletic circles. Founded the Keystone
    Junior Athletic Club, 1917. Captain Ellsworth Grammar School
    Baseball Team, 1918. Played on Ellsworth Grammar School
    Football team two years, during which period Ellsworth defeated
    all teams of its weight. Entered North Bank School, 1919.
    Played with freshman team and made the School Second the next
    year. Joined the School Team last autumn, playing end. Missed
    taking part in early season games because of illness. Played
    left end against Cumbridge School. Height, 5 ft. 8 in. Weight,
    136 lbs.

    Lodge is an unusually brilliant player for his years, his style
    reminding the spectator strongly of the renowned Pierson of
    undying fame. Although light, he is particularly strong on
    offense, and his speed is phenomenal. He is a heady player,
    always diagnosing the enemy’s intentions with certainty.
    His ability as an end was finely exemplified in the North
    Bank-Cumbridge game when he was never once stopped when
    carrying the ball and never missed a tackle. He also displayed
    an all-round brilliancy worthy of a more experienced player.
    This promising player will undoubtedly make even more of a name
    for himself next year.

“Gee!” breathed Dick. “He’s pretty good, after all, isn’t he?”

“He is the way he tells it,” answered Jimsy, grinning. “Wait a sec.
Let’s count the words.” After a moment he added: “Just two hundred and
one! Say, it’s like him to try and sneak over an extra word on us!”

“Well, maybe he didn’t count right,” said Dick charitably. “Or maybe
you didn’t. He――he writes pretty well, doesn’t he?”

“Great! I’ll bet he sweated blood over this! That about reminding the
spectator of the renowned Pierson is a little bit of all right. Say,
who the dickens is Pierson? Ever hear of him?”

Dick shook his head. “Some one before our time, I suppose.”

“Must be. Well, we’ve certainly got the goods on Brother Bert! Now the
question is what’s to be done with these photos.”

“I think we ought to send them back,” said Dick.

Jimsy considered long, holding them before him and gazing admiringly
upon them. “Well, I don’t know but that you’re right, Dick. We sort
of got them by false pretenses. How would it do to write and tell him
that they’re both so good we couldn’t choose between them, and so we’re
sending them both back?”

“It doesn’t sound just right, somehow.”

“What do we care how it sounds now? We should worry! That’s what we’ll
do. Now let’s read this sketch once more. Say, Lodge would make a fine
press agent, wouldn’t he? Do you know, Dick, I believe he could be
almost as great a publicity man as he is a football player?”

Now that the deed was done, Dick had misgivings. After all, it didn’t
seem quite fair. Even if Bert was a pest, and worse than a pest, the
trick they had played on him looked, now that it was accomplished,
rather mean and small. That thought did not, however, seem to occur to
Jimsy. Jimsy re-read the sketch and commented and chuckled, and in the
end it was pinned to Bert’s letter and laid safely away in a drawer.

“I don’t believe,” said Jimsy contentedly, “that we’ll ever have to
show those to any one. Fact is, I’d rather hate to, Dick. I’d do it,
though, if I had to, all right. But I fancy Brother Bert will take the
hint and be good!”

Strangely, though, Brother Bert was good without any hints. Perhaps
elation over inclusion in the forthcoming volume of _Who’s Who on the
Gridiron_ sweetened his disposition, or perhaps he was too concerned
with the approaching recess to bother with Dick. At all events the few
remaining days passed without further nagging, and Dick had no excuse
to make capital of the secret documents. This rather disappointed
Jimsy, but up to the very moment of leaving for home he remained
hopeful. “You wait till he gets those photos back again,” advised
Jimsy. “Then he won’t be so sweet tempered.” But the photographs didn’t
return. Perhaps Gerald Thompson was away from home, or perhaps he had
decided to render no further service until he had been reimbursed for
postage. Be that as it may, the end of the term arrived and North
Bank was practically depopulated one forenoon, and Bert went off to
Ellsworth, Pennsylvania, still convinced of his fame.

Dick and Jimsy parted in Baltimore, each regretful. Still, as Jimsy
said, vacation lasted only eleven days and they’d soon be together
again! Jimsy sent Dick a silver pencil at Christmas――silver pencils
were much in vogue that winter――and Dick sent Jimsy a silver pencil,
too. As each wanted one, each was pleased. Dick saw Alan Linscott
just once during recess, which was later explained by the fact that
Alan had spent but three days with his folks, going to Joe Whittier’s
for the rest of the time. The one sight of Alan was brief, occurring
on Main street the afternoon before Christmas Day. Whether Alan saw
him, Dick didn’t know. If he did there was certainly no recognition
forthcoming. Fortunately, Dick’s father and mother took it for granted
that he and Alan were friendly at North Bank, and so Dick was spared
embarrassing explanations that, he feared, would have aroused Mr.
Linscott’s ire and might have made unpleasantness for Alan. And even if
it seemed to him that Alan hadn’t been altogether courteous, he didn’t
want to be the cause of any trouble for him. Dick was faithful in his
allegiance still.

Dick had a very pleasant visit at home, renewed old acquaintanceships,
attended several parties, posed a bit quite unconsciously and finally,
one cloudy, wintry morning, set off again for school. Although at
school he had often and often wished himself at home, now, having been
home ten days, he was impatient to be back at school. The fact came to
his notice, but he didn’t trouble himself to explain it.




                               CHAPTER XV

                         “THE RENOWNED PIERSON”


He got back to Number 12 Baldwin House to find that Bert Lodge had not
yet arrived, a fact that caused him no regrets. Even if Bert never
arrived he would, he told himself, manage to survive and even derive
some pleasure from life! Having set his bag down, he contemplated
running upstairs to see if Jimsy had come, for their carefully
arranged plan to meet in Baltimore had miscarried. Then he decided
to get unpacked and settled down before Bert’s arrival complicated
the process, and a minute later, placing some books on the table, his
glance roved to Bert’s side of it and fell on a largish brown-paper
packet. He didn’t need to look at the address to know what the packet
contained, but he did. Bert’s photographs, rejected by _Who’s Who on
the Gridiron_, had arrived by mail during his absence and been placed
on the table. Dick resolved to be absent from the room when Bert found
them!

Ten minutes later he climbed the stairs to Number 33 and discovered
George Ferry admiring a new lacrosse stick that had come to him at
Christmas. George hailed Dick with evident pleasure, shook his hand
warmly and dragged him down to the window seat beside him, inviting
his admiration of the crosse. Jimsy, it appeared, had not yet put in
his appearance. But he arrived not many minutes later to drop a big
kit-bag, alarmingly new and hugely monogramed, inside the door and
strike an attitude depicting some strong emotion, possibly joy. When
quiet had again fallen――comparative quiet, that is――Jimsy told a moving
tale of missed connections and a long and fruitless search for Dick
in the Baltimore station, while George, having produced a hard rubber
ball, was running it tentatively up and down the new stick, registering
supreme satisfaction in his sober way. Later, Dick told Jimsy about the
photographs, adding: “You’ve got to go down with me when I go back,
Jimsy. I’m scared to go in there alone. He will be wild, I guess!”

But he wasn’t. They found him sullen, sarcastic and generally
unpleasant, but no furniture was broken and he didn’t attempt to bite
any one. The packet was gone from the table. Jimsy stayed long enough
to assure himself that no bodily danger threatened Dick, and then
returned upstairs to unpack. It was an unpleasant feeling of guilt that
prompted Dick, when Jimsy had departed, to ask in a friendly tone:
“Have a good time, Bert?”

“No, I cried all the time I was gone,” replied the other with snarling
sarcasm. “Why wouldn’t I have a good time, you silly little fool? Say,
you been mussing around my side of the table? I left a tin box here
when I went away with――”

“It’s on your dresser,” said Dick calmly.

“Oh! Well, I didn’t leave it there. You quit moving my things about,
kid, or I’ll rumple that nice slick hair of yours. Was mama glad to see
her little darling?”

“I didn’t touch your box,” said Dick warmly. “And never mind my mother,
Bert.”

“Gosh, we’re touchy, aren’t we? They must have fed you raw meat, kid.
You’ll be stronger than ever, eh? How are the little muscles coming
on? Take a long breath for papa and let him see little Sweetie’s chest
expand!”

“Cut that out, won’t you?” asked Dick patiently. “Let’s start the term
fresh, Bert, and see if we can’t get on without――without that sort of
thing.”

Bert stared in surprise. “You’re starting it fresh, all right,” he
ejaculated. “Listen to me, young whippersnapper, if you don’t like
what I say, why, you can”――Bert had to think a moment――“you can lump
it! Talk’s free here and I say what I please.” Bert grinned. Then he
scowled disgustedly. “Gosh, it’s tough enough, anyway, being stuck
with a little two-for-a-nickel runt like you always under my nose! Why
didn’t they keep you at home where you belong when they had you there?”

Dick was silent a moment. Then he said pleasantly: “I’ll tell you,
Bert, why they didn’t. I wanted to stay, but my father wouldn’t let
me. He said if I was ever to be like Pierson I’d have to go back and
finish.”

“Pierson?” said Bert. “Who’s Pierson?”

“Why, the renowned Pierson,” answered Dick innocently.

Bert stared hard, puzzled.

“Of undying fame,” added Dick casually.

Bert shot a glance toward the table and then returned an uncertainly
suspicious glare on Dick. Two small red disks showed over his cheek
bones. He opened his mouth to speak, thought better of it and closed
it. Dick viewed him calmly. Finally, “Say, you’re crazy, I guess,”
muttered Bert. He dropped his gaze and turned silently to his dresser
and began a rather feverish rearrangement of the contents of the top
drawer. Dick, inwardly smiling, outwardly grave, picked up a magazine
with which he had passed the time on the train and pretended to read.
But he only pretended, and Bert’s frequent puzzled glances over his
shoulder were not lost on him. After many minutes Bert spoke again.

“Where’d you get this stuff about Pierson?” he growled.

“Eh?” Dick looked up a bit vacantly. “Pierson? Oh, every one knows
Pierson. The renowned Pierson, you know.” He dropped his gaze to the
magazine once more. He heard Bert gulp. Then the drawer was shut very
softly, in defiance of Bert’s usual manner of closing a drawer, and
again there was silence. Dick peeked over the top of a page. Bert
was standing motionless by the dresser, his gaze fixed thoughtfully,
frowningly on the wall. After awhile he moved suddenly toward the
table, drew out the drawer there and, out of sight of his companion,
slipped something from the drawer to his coat pocket. He seemed to
feel more comfortable then, for he cleared his throat loudly, kicked
a chair out of the way and left the room, pulling his cap down with a
gorgeous assumption of ease.

Left alone, Dick winked gravely at the closed door. Then he tossed the
magazine aside, laughed, stretched and jumped to his feet.

“Got to tell Jimsy,” he chuckled.

Jimsy dropped in at Number 12 that evening after supper. He wasn’t in
the habit of doing that, for he didn’t take much pleasure from Bert
Lodge’s society and Bert never failed to indicate his distaste for
Jimsy’s. To-night, though, Jimsy made the visit gladly, in spite of
the fact that he knew Bert would be in. The latter’s greeting was as
ungracious as usual.

“Hello, Ravenous,” he said with his unpleasant smile. “You back, too?”

“Back again, Logical!”

“Don’t get fresh,” warned Bert. “Fellows who get fresh get put out.”

“Not me,” answered Jimsy cheerfully. “It takes a lot to put me out, I’m
that good-natured.” Jimsy sank into a chair and smiled blandly about
him. “Have a good time, Lodge?”

“I sure did! A whale of a time! Spent Christmas in the city.”

“What city’s that?”

“Philadelphia.”

“Oh, well, I like a quiet time, too.”

“Is that so?” snarled Bert. “I suppose you had a wild time in the
country where you were!”

“No, things were quiet there, but I wasn’t home long. Just over
Christmas. Spent the rest of the time with Pierson.”

Bert jerked his head up and shot a startled look at Jimsy.

“Who――what――who’s he?” he asked anxiously.

“Pierson? Never heard of him? Why, the fellow’s famous, renowned. One
of the greatest football players of the century, Lodge. Guess you’ve
got a rotten memory!”

Bert glared for an instant. Then he swallowed hard and looked away.
Jimsy continued chattily. “Nice fellow, Pierson,” he confided to Dick.
“Unaffected, too. Modest, you know. You’d never think he was any one at
all to listen to him.”

“Really?” asked Dick. “You’d rather expect a fellow like Pierson to be
stuck-up, wouldn’t you?” From the corner of his eye he could see Bert
watching them, his lowering, disquieted gaze moving from Jimsy to him
and back to Jimsy.

“Rather!” agreed Jimsy. “That’s what I liked about him, though,
his――his naturalness. No airs at all, Dick. Just like you or me or
Lodge, say. Do you know, Lodge, you――” Jimsy half closed his eyes and
cocked his head on one side――“you sort of remind me of him?”

“Never you mind about that!” snarled Bert. “You fellows think you’re
pretty smart, don’t you? Reading other folks’ letters! You’re――you’re a
couple of little sneaks!”

“Them’s hard words!” exclaimed Jimsy with great surprise. “Whatever do
you mean?”

“You know what I mean!” Bert’s angry gaze sped to Dick. “You little
bounder, you got into my desk! Yes, you did! I never left that letter
around!”

“Letter!” echoed Dick. “Why, Bert, I never went near your desk! What
letter do you mean?”

“You’re lying! If I――――”

“My, my!” interrupted Jimsy reprovingly. “You oughtn’t to say such
things, Lodge. Pierson would never talk like that!”

Bert choked, his sallow face red with anger. He started to speak but
stopped, his mouth open, as a crafty expression crept into his eyes.
His mouth closed into a sardonic grin and he laughed. “You fellows
think you’ve got something on me, don’t you?” he asked jeeringly.

“The whole episode,” murmured Jimsy, looking questioningly at Dick,
“leaves me at a loss. I merely mentioned Pierson, a fellow of undying
fame, and Lodge flies quite off the handle!”

Bert flinched, but laughed again contemptuously. “Go on, you smart
Alick! I don’t mind. What you saw was just something I was writing for
a joke, a――a――”

“A sort of brief sketch of your career?” asked Jimsy helpfully.

“Go to thunder!” snapped Bert. “You fellows think you’re mighty clever,
but you’ve got nothing on me, nothing at all!”

“But we never said we had!” expostulated Jimsy.

“Anyway, no one would believe you,” added Bert triumphantly.

“We wouldn’t expect anyone to,” said Jimsy calmly. “That is, not
without documentary evidence.”

“Sure,” agreed Bert. “And a copy wouldn’t be evidence!”

“No, that’s so. One would need the originals.”

Jimsy’s gaze and Bert’s held for a long, silent moment. Then Bert’s
eyes fell. He laughed a bit discordantly and shrugged his shoulders.
“Oh, you make me sick, Ravenel,” he growled. “You don’t know anything
about it. Go on and spring your joke. No one will believe you.”

“I do wish I knew what you were talking about,” said Jimsy plaintively.
“I come in to have a chat with Dick and you get all excited and queer.
What was it we were talking about, Dick? Oh, I know, Pierson! I was
telling Dick about the renowned Pierson when you――”

“Oh, shut up!” bellowed the harassed victim. He jumped up and seized
his cap. “Go on and jabber, you――you little fools!” He strode to the
door and jerked it open. “I don’t have to listen to you!” The door
closed with a crash.

“First,” murmured Jimsy, “he tells us to shut up and then he tells us
to go on! Most bewildering!”

Dick laughed, and then sobered. “Do you think he knows that we have
the――the sketch, Jimsy?” he asked.

Jimsy nodded. “I think he do, Dick, I think he do. And what’s
bothering him more than anything else right now is curiosity, consuming
curiosity! He’s trying mighty hard to dope out how we can have the
stuff he mailed to New York, and he will hatch more――more theories than
enough before he’s through. But――” Jimsy arose, stretched luxuriously
and smiled contentedly――“but I think, Dick, that we’ve cut his spurs.
Unless I’m much mistaken Brother Bert is going to sing small for a long
while!”

That, in fact, is just what Bert did do. For days afterward it was
apparent to Dick that his roommate was still seeking an explanation.
Glancing up while at study, Dick frequently encountered Bert’s gaze
fixed questioningly on him, and there were times when it seemed that
Bert was going to yield to curiosity and ask outright what he was dying
to know. But Bert never did. Only twice after that evening of Jimsy’s
visit did Dick have to introduce the word “Pierson” into his discourse.
Bert accepted the bargain. He gathered that so long as he was careful
not to displease Dick the brief sketch would remain unseen of the
public and the name of the renowned “Pierson, of undying fame” would
remain taboo. It wasn’t easy for Bert to live up to his part of the
implied agreement, for the incident had not increased his affection for
Dick, and the habit of being disagreeable died hard, but he did succeed
fairly well. Life in Number 12 did not become exactly joyous for Dick,
but, at least, he was spared the constant heckling that had made it a
misery.

Whether Bert guessed that the affair of _Who’s Who on the Gridiron_
had been a hoax or whether he expected the volume ultimately to
appear neither Dick nor Jimsy ever knew. Nor did they much care. The
deception, of which each was, I think, a little bit ashamed, had
accomplished its purpose and, in so far as his relations with Dick
were concerned――yes, and with Jimsy, too――Bert Lodge was a chastened
youth. Perhaps in the course of time Bert would have outlived his fear
of ridicule and returned to his old form as a pest. That will never be
known, for in February occurred an incident that changed the course of
Dick’s affairs amazingly.




                              CHAPTER XVI

                                CAPSIZED


A letter from home summoned Jimsy away from North Bank the last week
in January. His father was dangerously ill with influenza and it was
thought best that Jimsy should be at home. There was a good deal of
influenza that winter, although no case of it had developed at school.
Dick’s mother had had a slight attack, and each letter from her
recorded the severe illness, once the death, of a near neighbor. Jimsy
went off very hurriedly one Friday forenoon looking grave and anxious.
Dick and George went to the station with him and waved him good-by as
the electric train went on toward Baltimore. Jimsy had promised to
write as soon as he got home, and, of course, he would be back again
before long. But Dick was rather down in the mouth as he and George
walked back to school over the hard and rutted road. The weather had
been severely cold for more than a fortnight, and to-day a blustering
wind buffeted them rudely and forced Dick to put his bare hands in
his pockets for warmth and to step out briskly at George’s side. The
prospect of shelter and a good dinner raised his drooping spirits
toward the last of the journey, and after dinner he managed to forget
Jimsy’s absence for a while. But life threatened to be pretty dull,
and was.

There was no word from Jimsy until Tuesday. Then he wrote cheerfully
that his father was out of danger, although “the old boy” was still
pretty sick, and that he wasn’t returning until Sunday. The letter was
addressed to George, but there were many messages to Dick, and so,
after all, it was quite like getting a letter himself. He remained in
Number 33 quite a while after the letter was read, and he and George
talked about the absent one and about lots of things while the shadows
deepened over the room and the lights appeared one by one in Ellicot.
When Dick finally left, apologizing for staying so long, George was
very nice.

“Long?” he repeated. “Nonsense! Glad to have had you, Dick. Come any
time and stay as long as you like. Jimsy says you and Lodge don’t
get along very well, so don’t think you have to stay down there just
because Jimsy’s not here. If I’m busy you won’t mind if I don’t talk.
Just make yourself at home. I sort of miss Jimsy, and it’ll be nice to
have someone around.”

Dick made the most of the invitation during the rest of the week. He
got in the habit of taking his books up to Number 33 and studying,
stretched out on the window seat, while George occupied his place at
the table and bent over his own books. Such visits always ended in a
lazy, leisurely talk that Dick thoroughly enjoyed. George’s topics
of conversation were different from Jimsy’s; usually more serious;
usually more interesting. It was quite remarkable what weighty matters
they discussed at such times, and Dick always departed feeling not
a little proud that George, who was two years older and far more
experienced, should enjoy discussing them with him.

One evening Dick confided his secret sorrow, which was his inability to
“do something.” “Mr. Tanner said I might play basket ball and baseball,
but I tried basket ball and didn’t have any sort of a chance, and I
guess it will be just the same in the spring. I’m too small. I might
get on a scrub team, I suppose. Maybe I can make the Baldwin team, but
I doubt it. Jimsy says the fellows on the house nines last year were
all pretty old and big. There doesn’t seem to be anything I _can_ do!”

“You’ve got two years after this,” responded George consolingly. “Most
fellows don’t get into anything until their third year. You’ll probably
be considerably larger next fall. You keep up the gymnasium work, Dick,
it’s fine stuff for you. You might try lacrosse in the autumn. Size
isn’t a very great factor there. If you have lots of speed and can keep
going, all you’ll need to do is learn stick work and a few things.
Lacrosse is the best game there is, Dick, and I think you’d like it.
You could have a try this spring, for that matter, but I wouldn’t
advise it. In the first place, you need training; and then, in the
spring a new candidate hasn’t the chance that he has in the fall. There
isn’t the time then to try out new men. If you think seriously of it,
I’d advise you to join the track workers in March and develop your
speed and your wind. You’ll need good lungs for lacrosse. And then keep
up the training during the summer. Do a few sprints every week and jog
a mile, maybe, every two or three days. Of course, I’ll help you any
way I can, especially in the fall.”

“I’d like it a lot,” replied Dick warmly. “If I did that I wouldn’t try
for baseball at all, George. I’d just put in all my time at running.”

“Well, don’t overdo it. You’re quite a youngster yet. Take it easy,
that’s the wisest way. Tell the track trainer what you want to do and
he will work out a schedule for you.”

Dick was quite cheered up by the possibility of lacrosse and went back
to gymnasium work the next day with increased interest. Now that the
drudgery might lead to something it seemed far more worth while. On
Saturday, though, there was no gymnasium class, and when dinner was
over he found himself at a loose end. Outdoors the sun was shining
brightly enough, but there was a regular gale blowing out of the west
and the thermometer showed the mercury hovering around thirty. It was
no day for a walk, Dick decided, for he detested being blown about. A
little after two he went up to Number 33 and ran into George at the
door.

“Hullo,” said the latter, who was capped and sweatered. “Sorry, Dick,
but I’m just going out. I promised to paddle Browning over to Ferndale.
He’s going over to spend the evening with some friends and I told him
I’d save him the trip by rail. Want to come along?”

Dick hesitated. He had seen the river from his window not ten minutes
before, and the idea of being tossed about by whitecapped waves and
assailed by the cold wind wasn’t appealing. Nevertheless, he would have
accepted if George hadn’t rescinded the invitation the next instant.

“Guess you’d better not, though,” said George. “It’s fairly rough and
it’ll be hard going. Three might be one too many, Dick. I’ll be back in
an hour or so. Drop around, won’t you?”

Dick agreed and parted from George on the floor below, returning
disconsolately to Number 12. Now that he couldn’t go, it seemed to him
that he had wanted to badly. He picked up a book and tried to read, but
couldn’t. Presently he was on his feet again, wandering about the room.
He felt blue and lonely, so lonely that he almost wished that Bert
would come in! From the window he looked past the Hall to the sunlit
Severn. From shore to shore and for as far as he could see downstream,
the surface of the river, very blue to-day under the wind-swept sky,
was dancing with whitecaps. It looked decidedly rough, Dick thought,
although he had frequently seen the waves much bigger. He tried to
discern Bert’s canoe――or, rather, Browning’s――but it was not in sight.
Probably the Hall hid it from his view, since Ferndale, which wasn’t a
town but only a community of a dozen scattered residences, lay across
the river in that direction. They would probably paddle straight toward
the stone landing over there, keeping the sea on the stern quarter.
Dick didn’t know a great deal about canoes and canoeing――only what
little he had learned on such occasions as he and Jimsy had been able
to borrow a craft for some excursion――but it seemed to him that when
it came to getting back alone George would have his hands full. Dick
got a bit uneasy, watching the antics of wind and current, and recalled
dimly a remark that Jimsy had once made when they had been discussing
swimming. Dick wasn’t certain whether Jimsy had said that his roommate
didn’t swim at all or that he didn’t swim well. No one who didn’t swim
strongly, Dick thought sternly, had any business in a canoe on a day
like this. George had been crazy to try such a stunt, even for Rod
Browning. Browning was a corking fellow, the sort that made you eager
to do things for him, but he oughtn’t to let George make that return
trip alone. If Jimsy was here he would have stopped him. Dick wished
Jimsy _was_ here!

Half an hour later, after another determined but unsuccessful attempt
to find interest in the book, Dick put on his coat-sweater under his
jacket, pulled his cap down tightly and left the room. He just couldn’t
stay indoors any longer. There were very few fellows in sight. Voices,
borne on the gale, came to him around the corner from the volley-ball
court as he left the house and took the curving path past McCrea. A
fellow curled up amidst cushions in one of the first floor windows
tapped on the pane and waved to him. Dick waved and went on to the end
of the gravel and then toward the grove of trees by the river bank.
The wind wasn’t so bad here, for the plantation held many evergreens
and they provided some shelter. He passed through the fringe of the
grove and found the spot where Jimsy and he had loafed one afternoon in
the fall. He remembered watching the crews come out and go gliding up
the river, remembered that Jimsy had been fashioning rabbit snares of
long black horsehair, snares that had caught no rabbits but that had
provided a deal of fun. He sat down on the slope of the bank. He knew
he couldn’t stay there long, for, although the worst of the wind swept
over his head, it was much too cold for comfort. Being outdoors wasn’t
any better than being in, he reflected morosely. If you had the blues
you might as well have them where it was warm!

His wandering gaze caught sight of a two-car train moving slowly along
the distant bridge. It looked very small, and there was no sound from
it, for the wind took care of that. Perhaps Jimsy had come on that
train! But that was only a make-believe thought, for Jimsy wasn’t
coming until to-morrow. He remembered George then, and bent his gaze
toward the landing under the red clay bluff at Ferndale. It was time
he was coming back, but he saw nothing of him; nothing until, his gaze
returning across the dazzling expanse of sun-flecked, wind-tossed
river, it encountered something darker than the blue and white of
water and the yellow gold of sparkling sunlight, something that he
lost again instantly and had to search for ere it again took shape.
Then he saw that it was a canoe holding a single figure, a figure that
knelt too far aft, to Dick’s thinking. The bow of the craft was out of
the water and catching the wind badly. Dick stood up and went slowly
along the path, peering intently, a little anxiously, at the voyager.
That George was having a hard time of it was obvious enough. He had,
probably, tried to paddle directly across for the boathouse float and,
finding it impossible to keep that course with the wind blowing the
bow downstream, had pointed the craft upriver, almost into the gale,
doubtless meaning to reach a point well above his goal and then cut
across and down. But paddling against wind and tide was no mean task,
and Dick could see that George was making very little progress. Now
and then a stronger gust would sweep the bow around and George would
have to paddle desperately to regain his course. Dick waved once,
meaning to convey encouragement, but George probably didn’t see him.
Even if he had he couldn’t have ceased his labor long enough to answer.
Dick, braced against the gale, forgot to be cold and kept his eyes set
anxiously on the distant canoe. He wished he had gone along. He wasn’t
a very capable paddler, but he could have helped. If no more he would
have kept that bow down in the water. It was strange that George didn’t
realize that he should be further toward the bow. Afterwards Dick
learned that George had realized it, but not until he was well away
from shore. Then, since a thwart had barred his way, he had not dared
try to change.

Ten minutes had passed from the moment Dick had first sighted the
craft――possibly more. George had reached a point nearly opposite the
Hall now, and Dick expected each instant to see him turn the nose of
the canoe toward the landing. Gazing so intently that the dazzle hurt
his eyes, Dick had to close them occasionally for a moment. He did so
now, and, opening them again after a brief respite, he stared at first
in puzzlement and then in alarm. The one object had become two! There
was the canoe, bottom up, a dark maroon line on the water, and there,
well upstream, was a dark speck that came and went as the whitecapped
waves intervened!

For an instant, an instant that seemed interminable in retrospect
but that in reality endured no longer than it took his heart to beat
chokingly a half-dozen times, Dick stood rooted to the spot. Then he
was off, running toward the boathouse steps at first, then plunging,
sliding down the bank beside them, the center of an avalanche of earth
and gravel and broken tree roots.




                              CHAPTER XVII

                        RESULTS OF BEING A HERO


Afterwards he could recall little of what happened until, coatless and
bareheaded, he was plunging his oars into the broken water, heading
the little skiff straight out into the current. Vaguely he remembered
struggling with the heavy boat, heavy enough to call ordinarily for the
strength of two, and of looking despairingly for oars where only canoe
paddles rewarded his search. Yet he must have found oars eventually,
just as eventually he had worked the skiff down the run and across the
float to the water. Now, buffeted by the gale, dragged seaward by the
tide, he was rowing with all his strength toward midstream. To reach
that was his first thought.

The capsized canoe must soon be opposite the landing. Indeed, it might
be there even now, and the thought put new power into Dick’s already
aching arms. He wanted to look, but dared not yet risk the loss of a
single stroke. Time enough for that when the boathouse lay further
astern. It receded very slowly, and, in spite of his efforts, it was
already upstream a bit. That, though, was not important. It might
prove fortunate in the end. Speed was the main thing, for the current
was running strong and the wind was aiding, and he must be where he
could act swiftly and certainly when the canoe came abreast. He was
taking it for granted that George had reached the canoe, although the
alternative lurked in the back of his mind. If he had not reached
it――but Dick wouldn’t think of that!

Presently he dared pause for an instant at his work, turn his head and
look about him. Then he was bending frantically at his oars once more,
turning the skiff’s nose further downstream, for not a dozen yards away
was the overturned canoe, almost opposite him, floating sluggishly.
There had been no time to see whether George was clinging to it, and
not until he had spent himself in another dozen strokes did he look
again. Then his heart sank leadenly. The canoe was beside him――he could
have touched it with an oar――but no hand clutched it!

Despairingly his gaze flew upstream, toward the further shore,
downstream. The canoe was beyond reach now, for Dick’s oars still dug
the water, although he no longer had any conscious plan. His eyes met
only glinting, whitecapped river. And then, faintly distinct above the
splash of the waves and the rushing sound of the wind, came a cry!

“_Here! Dick!_”

Dick saw then. Between him and the North Bank shore something dark
bobbed above the surface. He swung the boat desperately and bent at the
oars. Every stroke carried with it now a sob of exhaustion, but that
horrible moment of despair had passed and hope and joy lent him a new
courage and a final remnant of strength. Twenty hard strokes, and he
looked over his shoulder. Ten more would do it!

He tugged again. Those last strokes taxed his endurance to the breaking
point, but he made them. Then he looked. George’s face, set and white,
stared entreatingly at him but an oar’s length away. He was almost
past exertion, ready, it seemed, to give up. Somehow he kept himself
afloat, striking out weakly with numbed limbs, but he made no progress
toward the boat. Even in the moment that Dick looked, he moved past the
boat’s bow, borne on the current. Dick dug one oar, shipped both and
leaned over the side. George was beyond aiding in his own rescue, for
it was only by almost overbalancing that Dick’s hand was able to reach
the other’s wrist. As it did so George ceased even the slight struggle
he had been making, and his weight fell on Dick’s arm, and his body
settled into the water.

“George!” panted Dick. “You’ve got to help! I can’t get you in here
alone! Take hold of the gunwale!”

George thrashed weakly with his legs and managed to clasp one hand
on the edge of the skiff. Dick guided his other hand to the edge and
changed his own grasp to George’s armpit. Then for an instant he
rested, fighting hard for breath, longing for strength to complete the
task. “I’m going to try and pull you in, George,” he said finally.
“You’ve got to help, though. Can you?”

There was no answer, but the lolling head straightened for an instant.
Then: “Now!” said Dick. He tugged. The gunwale dipped toward the
surface. George thrashed and his fingers strained weakly at the edge.
Then one arm was over the side, and a shoulder, and Dick quickly
changed his hold and was straining at a handful of cloth that went
slipping from his fingers. But in the next moment he had seized one
of George’s legs and, with a final heave, had conquered. The water
poured over the gunwale, but George was in the boat, limp, exhausted, a
huddled, sodden form between the seats.

Dick tried to prop his shoulders up, but George shook his head slowly.
His lips moved, but Dick caught no sound. His eyes were tightly closed
and great, long breaths tore at his lungs. Dick sank to the seat,
nerveless, even a little sick, and the boat floated on down the stream,
pitching crazily, the water it had shipped swashing from side to side.
After a long minute Dick roused himself and reached wearily for the
oars. Then his eyes sought the shore. They had drifted far below the
school already and the railway bridge, although still far distant, was
moving toward them. He must work out of the current and make the shore
as best as he could. The thought of working the oars again filled him
with despair, for it seemed to him that he could not lift them, much
less use them, and the nausea that had seized him still lingered. But
he did manage presently to get the oars back into the rowlocks and even
to head the skiff about with a few weak strokes. It was then that he
heard a hail and, looking over his shoulder, saw two boats pulling
down on him from the direction of school. After that he attempted only
to keep the skiff headed into the seas. Overwhelming relief gave him
the strength to do so much, but further effort was beyond him. At his
feet, George stirred and opened his eyes. His gaze encountered Dick’s.
His lips moved as his eyes closed again.

“Thanks,” whispered George.

At the boathouse landing it was a question with the rescuing party
whether George or Dick needed attention most, and they solved the
problem by carrying them both, Dick expostulating faintly, George not
at all, up the hill and to their rooms. Dick was aware of passing many
staring faces but was too done up to recognize any. In fact, he had no
curiosity in the matter. He longed for warmth and rest, and oh, he did
want to be left alone! When, however, they had his clothes off and he
was tucked in bed and had swallowed a whole tumblerful of something
very hot, rest didn’t seem so essential. Of course, he was tired, but
he could see no reason for spending the rest of the day in bed, as he
was instructed to. He asked after George, but no one seemed to know
much about him. Joe Whittier, however, promised to find out about
George and let him know shortly. What Joe Whittier was doing there Dick
couldn’t make out, not knowing that Joe had been one of the first to
witness the accident and had, with two others, formed the first rescue
party.

Presently Joe and several other fellows had gone and Dick was left to
himself. He felt deliciously warm and, save when he moved, thoroughly
at peace with the world. He started to go over, rather hazily, the
recent astounding events, but fell asleep almost at once. Later he
awoke to find that Bert was sitting at the table and observing him in
an oddly respectful, even awed manner. But Bert wasn’t interesting just
then, and Dick went off to sleep again.

When he awoke once more the room was dark and he was alone. His muscles
ached frightfully when he moved, and he abandoned his impulse to get up
and turn the light on. After all, it didn’t matter much what the time
was. He did hope, though, that some one would see that he had supper!
Even when you are aching in every inch of your body you still need food!

He wasn’t forgotten, however, although it seemed to him that supper was
rather skimpy. Afterwards Bert returned and asked gruffly, yet with an
apparent desire to be cordial, how he felt. And Dick told him that he
felt fine thanks, and would he please stick that tray out in the hall.
Bert wanted to hear just what had happened, but Dick was so sketchy
that he got disgusted and went out to seek information elsewhere.
Dick got up and made his way in a rather wobbly fashion to the table.
A fellow had to study, he supposed, whether he had been put to bed
or hadn’t! Back in bed once more, with his books beside him, he felt
interestedly of his arm muscles. Gee, but they were sore! Pinching
them until they responded painfully was quite a fascinating occupation,
but it palled after awhile. He guessed George’s muscles were worse than
his were, and he wondered how old George was.

Just then, as if in answer to his thought, there was a loud knock at
the door and Joe Whittier entered, and with him, a most amazing fact,
came Alan Linscott! Dick, hugging his knees, stared incredulously. But
it really was Alan, and Dick found himself getting red of face and
embarrassed, although it wasn’t at all clear to him why he should. The
visitors came over to the bed and Joe asked cheerfully: “Well, how
are you feeling now, Dodd?” And then, without waiting for answer, he
continued: “By the way, you know Linscott, don’t you? He tells me you
used to be friends once.”

Dick nodded and then found himself shaking hands with Alan.

“I thought you’d forgotten me, Dick,” said Alan smilingly. “I tried to
find you in the fall, when you first came, but you were out. Why didn’t
you come and see me? Sort of haughty, weren’t you?”

“Had a right to be,” grunted Joe. “Told you you ought to look him up
again.”

“I――I didn’t know,” stammered Dick.

“Didn’t know I’d called here? That’s funny. I told your roommate to
tell you. Left word with him that you were to come to see me. Perhaps
he forgot.”

“He must have,” agreed Dick thoughtfully.

“Looks as if he could forget pretty easy,” commented Joe.

“Dick, I’m sorry,” exclaimed Alan contritely. “I got your note, you
know, and came over here, the next day, I think it was, and you weren’t
in. So I told that idiot to tell you I’d called and that you were to
come over right away. When you didn’t come I thought you didn’t care
to. I looked around for you several times, but you’ve changed a lot
since I saw you last, and I never recognized you. You’ve sort of filled
out, haven’t you? I guess it’s two years since we met, eh? You must be
sixteen now, I suppose.”

Dick shook his head. “Fifteen, Alan. I’ll be sixteen――”

“Some stunt for a fellow your age, Dodd,” broke in Joe Whittier warmly.
“And you aren’t so blamed big, either, even for fifteen, if you don’t
mind my saying so! The fellows are still talking about it. School’s
proud of you, youngster.”

“You certainly showed pluck, Dick,” said Alan. “How did it happen,
anyway? No one seems to know exactly. Mind if I sit here?”

The idea of his objecting to having a hero like Alan sit on the side of
his bed seemed so incredible to Dick that he forgot to answer. So Alan
sat down where he could lean his broad shoulder against the footrail,
and Joe pulled a chair up with: “Yes, let’s have the real dope, Dodd.”

So Dick told what had happened, too much impressed, though, with the
wonderful fact of Alan’s presence to give a very succinct account, and
it was only by subsequent questioning that the audience got the events
straight in their minds.

“Mean to tell us,” said Joe, “that you snaked that skiff out of the
boathouse all alone?”

“I think so. I mean, I must have. You see, I don’t remember much about
that part of it. I do remember, though, that it was awfully hard to get
started. Probably that was because the boat was sort of heavy.”

“Heavy!” ejaculated Joe. “I’ll say it’s heavy! It’s the heaviest old
tub in the lot, Alan. Wasn’t it hard rowing out there?”

Dick nodded emphatically. “Yes, it was, because the wind and tide were
together. That boat――” he paused reflectively――“that boat seemed to
pull sort of hard, anyway.”

“It certainly does,” corroborated Joe. “I’ve pulled it! Well, I say you
did a man-sized job in a mighty nifty manner, Dodd. You put some inches
and beef on you, youngster, and we’ll have you pulling stroke in the
boat some day!”

Dick smiled to signify that he realized that Joe was just fooling, and
then asked: “Have you heard how George is?”

“Yes, he’s doing all right,” answered Joe. “Silly ass to try a stunt
like that, anyway. Deserves to feel rotten, I say. Fellows who can’t
swim ought to keep out of boats. Especially canoes.”

“Looks to me,” said Alan, “as if Ferry managed to do quite a bit of
swimming.”

Joe shrugged. “Paddled around. Kept his head out. A decent swimmer
would have either got back to the canoe or struck out for shore. Ferry
would have drowned if Dodd hadn’t got him when he did. Says himself
he’s a rotten swimmer. Blamed idiot, I say.”

Alan spoke about home and asked after Dick’s folks, and then, rising to
go, added: “Guess you’ll be feeling top-hole in the morning, Dick; hope
so, anyway. Now don’t feel sore about what happened. I mean because
we missed each other. You know where I am. Come and see me, Dick, and
we’ll get acquainted again. If you don’t like me you’re bound to like
Joe here. Every one does!”

“I like him already,” said Dick impulsively. He wished, the next
instant, that he hadn’t, but Joe laughed and clapped him on a
particularly sore part of his arm.

“Glad to hear it, youngster!” he said. “That’s a sure-enough compliment.
School hero says he likes me, Alan. Get that? Must be some good in me,
eh? Come on before he changes his mind!”

They went out merrily, calling good night to him from the doorway, and
Dick sank back on his pillows with a sigh of content. Alan hadn’t gone
back on him after all! His hero was still without reproach! He was so
glad of that that when, a few minutes later, Bert Lodge came back, he
didn’t bother to tax him with that lapse of memory. Of course Bert
hadn’t really forgotten. He had purposely withheld Alan’s message. But
now that Dick had found Alan again it didn’t seem to matter.




                             CHAPTER XVIII

                      JIMSY COMES BACK ON THE JOB


George Ferry seemed to be quite himself again by the time that Jimsy
returned, although he did not accompany Dick to the station. The two
had spent much of the morning going over yesterday’s events. George
remembered far more clearly than Dick did. “I was just about giving
up when I saw the boat,” said George, “I couldn’t swim well enough to
reach the canoe, so I tried to make for the shore. All I could do was
keep afloat. I never was anything of a swimmer, perhaps because I was
born on the coast and have lived there all my life! It’s the fellows
who come from away inland who know how to swim! I was――well, pretty
scared. That is, I was quite certain that I could keep going only a
short time and that after that I’d drown. Perhaps scared isn’t the
exact word. I was awfully panicky for a minute after I was turned out,
but afterwards I wasn’t so much frightened as――well, sort of amazed,
incredulous and sorry for myself. I didn’t want to die a bit. It didn’t
seem fair, somehow. Toward the last, after I’d swallowed a good deal
of water and was plumb tired, I didn’t care so much. In fact, I got to
wishing for the time to come when I couldn’t struggle any longer. Just
as long as I could struggle, though, I knew that I had to, no matter
how much it hurt. And it did hurt, Dick. Then, all of a sudden, I saw
your boat. I didn’t know at first who was in it, and it looked as if
you weren’t looking for me. I tried two or three times to shout, and
couldn’t make a sound. Then, finally, I did, but it didn’t seem to me
that I’d called loud enough for you to hear me. I tried to get toward
where you were, but it wasn’t any use. Then I saw you turn the boat
around and start my way, and the relief was so great that I mighty near
quit trying any longer. I guess I just shut my eyes and sank, for I
swallowed a lot of water and had to thrash to get into the air again.”
Then he ended gravely, even a little solemnly: “You saved my life,
Dick. If it hadn’t been for you I wouldn’t be here now. That’s――that’s
a queer thought, isn’t it?”

Dick squirmed and nodded.

“I’d know how to thank a fellow for――well, for most things, Dick, but
I don’t know how you do it, what you say, when some one has saved your
life.” George looked across in puzzlement. Dick squirmed some more.
Then, after a moment of silence, he said:

“I don’t see why you need to thank any one for pulling you out of the
water. Gee, it’s a perfectly natural thing to do, isn’t it? What else
could――could a fellow do? He couldn’t just look on, could he?”

“No, but he might not risk his own life, Dick.”

“I didn’t risk anything,” declared Dick impatiently. “If I’d overturned
I’d have hung to the boat and kicked ashore somehow. I’m as glad as
anything I got there in time, George, but there’s no sense in fellows
making a scene like they did this morning. It was sickening! And then
Doctor Heidler, last night, and――” his voice died into morose silence.

George smiled faintly. “At breakfast?” he asked.

Dick nodded gloomily and reddened. “I didn’t suppose they were going to
act like a lot of――of silly girls, or I wouldn’t have gone in there!”

“I heard something about it,” answered George sympathetically, although
he seemed secretly amused by Dick’s indignation. “They got up and
clapped, didn’t they?”

“They――they cheered!” exploded Dick resentfully. “Stood up and howled!
Made me feel like――like a lead nickel! Gee!”

George laughed frankly now. “Don’t be an ass, Dick,” he said soothingly.
“You did something mighty fine, and every decent fellow likes things
that are fine. You’d have cheered just as hard as they did if some one
else had been the hero.”

“Wouldn’t,” grunted Dick. “I’d have had some――some regard for the poor
chap’s feelings!”

“Dick you’re a joy!” laughed George. Then: “If you’re going to get to
the station before that train gets in you’ll have to move, won’t you?”

Dick cast an alarmed look at his watch and sprang up. “I’ll have to run
half the way, I guess,” he exclaimed. “See you later!” At the door he
stopped to ask: “Quite sure you’re all right?”

“Sure,” assented George. “Beat it!”

Dick beat it and reached the little box that did duty as a station just
as the electric train clattered into sight around the turn beyond.
Dick’s fear that Jimsy might not come after all was quickly dispelled,
for Jimsy leaped from a car before it had stopped rolling and the next
instant they were squabbling good-naturedly as to who should carry
the bag. Once on the road, Dick unfolded his news. It wasn’t very
sensational news, as he told it, but Jimsy was properly thrilled and
flatteringly exclamatory.

“Gosh! It was lucky you were around!” said Jimsy. “He’s a perfectly
punk swimmer and I’ll bet he’d have gone and drowned himself if you
hadn’t picked him up. He hadn’t any business going out in a canoe on
rough water, anyway. I’ll bet he wouldn’t have done it if I’d been
there, the silly old goose!”

To all this Dick agreed and, after Jimsy had asked more questions
and had received answers which, he dimly felt, were not altogether
satisfactory, the talk turned to other things, and it wasn’t until he
and George had been left together by a reluctant Dick that he got a
full and true story of the accident. Ten minutes later he was banging
at Dick’s door downstairs, and, not waiting for an invitation, was
inside. Dick gazed at him with mingled apology and defiance.

“You’d better look like that,” exclaimed Jimsy, shaking a finger at him
threateningly. “You’d better look ashamed of yourself! I’ve heard what
you did yesterday, you deceitful little cuss! A nice stall you gave
me! You were in a boat and picked him up! What did you tell me all
those lies for?”

“I didn’t lie,” muttered Dick.

“Might as well have then, you――you bloomin’ hero!”

“I’m not!”

“You are!” Jimsy strode forward and ruffled Dick’s hair ungently.

“Jimsy, I’m not!” Dick cried indignantly. “Don’t you act the silly fool
like――like all the rest of them!”

“I will, too!” Jimsy tweaked Dick’s tie up under one ear and punched
him affectionately in the ribs. “Bloomin’ hero, that’s you!”

Dick pulled his tie back into place and stared morosely at the blotter.
“I thought,” he muttered finally, “you’d have more sense. I wish you
would, Jimsy! I――I’ve had to put up with a lot since it happened.” He
looked up to find Jimsy grinning broadly. “Gee,” he almost wailed,
“it’s enough to make a fellow wish he hadn’t done it!”

“Oh, well!” Jimsy sobered. “It won’t last long, Dick. Fellows’ll let
up on you in a day or two. I won’t say anything more about it if you’d
rather I wouldn’t. Only――only, honest, Dick, I’m mighty proud of you!”

“You needn’t be,” muttered Dick. “I――I wish you’d shut up!”

“All right. What are you doing this afternoon? Aren’t going to study,
are you?” Jimsy glanced disapprovingly at the open book. “Come on out.
It’s a gorgeous day.”

Dick shook his head. “I’ve got some Latin to do. You stay here.”

“And watch you work? What’s the fun? Bring your book along and we’ll
find a nice sunny place.”

Dick shook his head again. “I’d rather――I can’t, Jimsy.”

A light dawned on the visitor and he whistled softly. Then he grinned
and walked to the window and peered stealthily out. “Honest, Dick,
there isn’t a soul in sight,” he said.

Dick flushed. “There would be if I got out there,” he sighed.

“Well, you know you’ve got to face them some time!”

“Maybe they’ll forget it by to-morrow,” said the other hopefully.
“It――it’s fierce, Jimsy!” Then, in a sudden burst of confession: “I
didn’t have any dinner!”

“_What!_” Jimsy stopped grinning. “You blamed little idiot! Honest,
Dick, you ought to be spanked! Where’s your spunk? Gosh, think of a
fellow doing what you did yesterday――Oh, shut up! I’m not talking about
it!――doing what you did and then being afraid to face a few fellows!
You make me tired! Aren’t you hungry?”

“Not so very,” answered Dick wistfully.

“You are, too! You’re starved! Come on out of here!”

Jimsy seized him by an arm and pulled. Dick resisted. “Where to?” he
asked suspiciously.

“Upstairs. I’ve got some eats in my bag. Figs and dates with nuts stuck
in ’em. And old George has some crackers, I think. Come on before I
beat you up!”

So Dick went. Only, at the foot of the stairs he clutched the speeding
Jimsy and detained him. “Don’t tell George I didn’t――didn’t――”

“I won’t,” agreed Jimsy. “You’re an awful fizzle for a hero, Dick!”

“You cut that out!” wailed Dick.

Jimsy’s prophesy came true. The school did forget in a day or two.
Or, more truthfully, the school acted as if it had forgotten, which,
from Dick’s point of view, was quite as satisfactory. That Sunday
night Jimsy had finally persuaded him to go to supper and Dick, not
very happy, had walked half the length of the dining hall to his
seat without awakening a demonstration. Fellows had stared, and some
had called to him as he passed, and at his own table his arrival had
been greeted with jesting remarks and inquiries as to his whereabouts
at dinner time, and he wasn’t allowed to forget that he was still a
celebrity. But it hadn’t been nearly so bad as he had feared, and
he had been extremely hungry and had managed to forget everything
save satisfying his appetite until, looking up unguardedly, he had
encountered Jimsy’s mocking grin. But on Monday he breathed easier.
Fourth class youngsters still embarrassed him by watching his passing
with round eyes and audible whispers, and older fellows observed him
with respectful curiosity, but by keeping his own eyes averted Dick
was able to weather these things. Then, on Tuesday, something happened
that made him forget self-consciousness. Jimsy came into Number 12
while Dick and Bert were still dressing with the news that George was
awfully sick and the doctor had been sent for.

“He woke me up about four o’clock,” narrated Jimsy. “He had a lot of
pain, he said, and he was as hot as anything. I didn’t know what to
do for him, but I got him some water and put a wet towel on his head
and sat around awhile, and pretty soon he went to sleep. But he had me
up again about five and I hustled on my clothes and got Mr. Hiltower
up there, and Hiltower said he had pleurisy and telephoned over to
Annapolis for the doc. He hasn’t come yet. The matron gave him some
stuff, though――I mean George――and he’s asleep, sort of. I don’t like
the way he looks, though, fellows. Gosh, he’s all sort of funny!”

“Pleurisy’s awfully tough,” said Bert. “My sister had it once and
nearly died.”

“Gosh, you’re comforting!” said Jimsy disgustedly. “Well, I’m going to
get some breakfast. I’ve been up since five. I’ll let you know what the
doctor says, Dick.”

An hour later George was moved to the little infirmary in Ellicot
and it was known that not pleurisy but pneumonia had seized him.
George’s mother arrived that evening, rather tall, very calm and very
capable-looking; as Jimsy said, a whole lot like George.




                              CHAPTER XIX

                         DICK STUDIES AQUATICS


Anxious days followed. Jimsy fairly haunted Ellicot to learn of
George’s condition and Dick dogged Jimsy’s footsteps to get the news
from him. The news wasn’t reassuring. George was very ill indeed,
and the nurses who took turns at his bedside seldom gave encouraging
reports. The night nurse was Jimsy’s special abhorrence. He invariably
awaited her as she went off duty and, as Jimsy put it, she “always
looked as if old George had just passed away!” Another anxious youth
was Browning, for whose sake George had made that hazardous trip across
to Ferndale. Browning blamed himself bitterly and became something of
a nuisance to Jimsy. Jimsy declared that things were bad enough anyway
without having Browning almost weeping on his shoulder every day! Jimsy
found relief at that period in an irascibility usually quite foreign to
him.

Dick, deprived of Jimsy’s society more than usual, went over to McCrea
on Friday afternoon and knocked at the door of Number 6. There was
no answer, however, and he departed not ill satisfied. He had kept
his promise to call on Alan and had been saved the exertion of making
conversation and listening to it when he didn’t feel a bit like it. He
would try again some evening, he told himself. He would be more likely
to find Alan in after supper.

Then came the day when the crisis of George’s illness was due to occur,
and Jimsy lugged Dick off for a walk, a long, mad walk that took
them all over the surrounding country, it seemed, and was made more
than half the time in silence. They got back just before supper time
and went right to Ellicot. Dick remained downstairs while Jimsy went
anxiously up to the infirmary. Jimsy soon returned. They didn’t expect
the crisis until that night, he told Dick. Doctor Morton had just gone,
but was coming back later. Dick didn’t find much appetite for supper,
in spite of all the exercise he had had, and afterwards he and Jimsy
sat in Number 33, pretending to study, until nearly ten. Then Jimsy
made another trip to Ellicot and returned with no news.

“Guess we won’t know until morning,” he said dully. They were standing
in the entrance of Baldwin, where Dick had awaited his return. The sky
was bright with millions of twinkling stars and the night was frostily
cold. Jimsy sighed. “Poor old George!” he whispered.

“Somehow,” said Dick, “I think he’s going to get well, Jimsy. You know
the doctor said he was so healthy that he had every chance.”

Jimsy nodded. After a minute he said, half defiantly: “I’ve been
praying for him every night, Dick.”

“So have I,” answered Dick simply.

“Seems to me that ought to――ought to help,” murmured Jimsy.

“I think so, too.”

They parted rather silently at the head of the first flight.

In the morning Dick got the good news before he was well out of bed.
Jimsy burst in, all excitement and joy. George had passed the crisis
and was going to get well! Jimsy overturned Dick on the bed and
pummelled him breathless, and Dick, too happy to defend himself, took
the punishment. Even Bert looked less sour, although he coupled his
expression of pleasure with the hope that Ferry would have more sense
after this!

That evening Dick said: “You know Alan Linscott, don’t you, Jimsy?”

“Yes, pretty well. I guess I know him better than he knows me, though.”

“Let’s go over and see him. Will you? I ought to, you know.”

Jimsy looked dubious. “I don’t believe I know him well enough for that,
Dick. You know how it is. Those first class fellows have kind of short
memories sometimes.”

“Oh, well, I know him,” answered Dick, “and I’ll introduce you. You
know Joe Whittier, anyway.”

“Yes, but, I guess you’d better go by yourself.”

“Shan’t! You’ve got to come along.”

So Jimsy surreptitiously felt of his tie and smoothed his hair down
and went. He didn’t really want to, but the good news of the morning
had made him very happy, and, being happy, he was willing to oblige.
The incident was robbed of any embarrassment for Jimsy owing to the
fact that when they reached Number 6 McCrea only Joe Whittier was in.
Joe said that Alan would be back in a few minutes. No one ever felt
embarrassed with Joe, and by the time Alan did come the visitors were
quite at their ease.

Alan greeted Dick warmly and Jimsy with flattering cordiality. It was
evident that for one brief instant he didn’t remember Jimsy’s name,
but he recalled it almost at once. Dick was proud of Alan, proud that
he was his friend, for the crew captain was so very good-looking, with
the sort of good looks that boys admire, so big and kind of splendid!
He glanced at Jimsy to see if the latter was properly impressed and
gathered from Jimsy’s attitude and tone of voice that he was. There
were inquiries about George Ferry first, and then the conversation
wandered from one subject to another in an easy, comfortable fashion,
and the visitors found themselves feeling surprisingly at home in the
attractively furnished room.

The evening was half gone and Dick was about to drag himself out of the
comfortable chair in which he sat when Joe, harking back to Dick’s
rescue of George, again expressed his wonder. “What gets me,” he said,
“is a fellow no bigger than a piece――I mean no bigger than Dodd is――”

Jimsy’s chuckle interrupted him and Joe turned an apologetic look on
Dick.

“No offense, Dodd,” he said. “You aren’t very big, you know, but I’ll
say you’re all there!”

“Dick isn’t touchy about his size,” Jimsy reassured him, “although he
does trouble about it a good deal. You see, Linscott, Dick wants to do
big things: captain the football team or pitch for the nine or――”

“Shut up,” said Dick earnestly.

“Wouldn’t wonder if he’d take Whittier’s job, at a pinch!” continued
Jimsy. “Dick has a six-foot ambition, believe me!”

Alan laughed. “Dick will grow, I guess, eh, Dick?”

“He doesn’t need to,” said Joe. “He’s got everything any of the big
ones have, and then some! Can’t see that he needed any more inches the
other day when he pulled Ferry out of the water!”

“He’s got plenty of pluck,” agreed Alan heartily, and Dick hoped that
he wasn’t blushing. “Tell you what he would make, Joe. He’d make a
corking cox!”

“Wouldn’t he, though? By Jove! Say, that’s an idea! Would he have any
show, Alan?”

Alan shook his head. “Not this year, of course, but I wouldn’t wonder
if he’d cop it hands down next fall. Gage will be gone and there’s only
that little simpleton of a Warren left. Ever think of coxing a crew,
Dick?”

Dick shook his head, blankly. “Could I?” he asked.

“I’ll bet you could!” interposed Joe with enthusiasm. “You’ve got the
size and the grit, youngster, and if you knew rowing――”

“Nonsense!” Alan cut in laughing. “No cox we ever had knew anything
about rowing, Joe! Don’t ask too much.”

“There’s something in that,” Joe agreed, with a grin. “Still, it
wouldn’t hurt if Dodd did learn port from starboard! Say, what harm
would there be in his coming out this spring? Mike wouldn’t mind his
getting some training, especially as Tommy Gage will steer his last
boat in June. Ever do any rowing yourself, Dodd?”

“Not that sort,” said Dick. “Do you really think Mr. Carmichael would
let me try, Alan? Is it hard? A coxswain doesn’t do any rowing, does
he?”

“Now you’ve started something,” sighed Jimsy, viewing Alan
reproachfully. “Who’s going to play center on the football team next
fall if Dick becomes a coxswain?”

Dick only frowned on the levity. He was too excited to join in the
chuckles that followed the sally. He listened to Joe’s explanations
of a coxswain’s duties with all ears, deaf to Jimsy’s flippant
interpolations.

“Tell you what,” said Joe finally. “If you really want to try it, Dodd,
I’ll speak to Mike about you when he gets back. I think he will be
mighty glad to start you in training against next fall, for he’s got
to have a cox for the second, anyway, then. If you make good, and I’ll
bet a hat you will, you’ll be coxing the first boat a year from this
spring. You’ll be a member of the crew, youngster, and wear the crossed
sweeps on your shirt and the blue-white-and-blue on your hat. What do
you say? Want to try it?”

“Y-yes!” blurted Dick.

He walked back to Baldwin with Jimsy a few minutes later treading
on air. He asked so many questions that Jimsy threw up his hands in
despair and declared that he was neither a Courtney nor a Rice. “You
beat it over to the library to-morrow, Dick,” he advised. “There are
heaps of books on rowing there, I guess. Anyway, plenty of ’em have
been written. Maybe you’ll find one that’ll answer about half of your
questions. Sorry I can’t, but I never coxed an eight in my life.”

“Well, but, Jimsy, do you think I could do it?” asked Dick intensely.
Jimsy shrugged.

“Why not?” he responded. “I’ve seen many a fellow sitting in the stern
of a shell who didn’t look to have any more sense than you!”

On the morrow Dick, still chock-full of enthusiasm, sought the
library. Jimsy’s assertion that he would find heaps of books on
rowing was proved erroneous, but he did find four. Three of them
were by English authorities, two of whom had coached American crews
with but scant success. But Dick didn’t know that and so read the
works with veneration and respect. For the next month he divided his
leisure about equally between the school curriculum and the science
of rowing, and Jimsy, after finding that levity was not favorably
received, sympathetically aided and abetted by placing before Dick any
and all matter pertaining to the subject. This matter ranged from
clippings from the newspapers and magazines through a really helpful
book borrowed from a friend back home to a dissertation on the Roman
war galleys discovered in an ancient tome in the school library. Much
of what Dick read was hard to understand, since he had never swung a
sweep, but in a fashion he assimilated it all. He got Joe Whittier to
go down to the Hall basement with him one day and show him the two
shells which were stored there and explain the matter of rigging and
much more. Dick looked almost with awe at the tiny seat in the stern,
and handled the rudder with its two white lines, laid carefully on the
floor, with deep reverence. Joe was always willing to talk rowing,
always willing to answer questions, and from him Dick heard many epics
of the river that added new fuel to his enthusiasm. And so February
passed and March came, and with March the opening of the spring rowing
season. But before that, other events occurred deserving of record.

George’s recovery was slow, but there finally came a day when he
left his bed and sat in a chair by an open window in the sunlight. By
backing tightly against the wall of Follen and getting on your toes you
could just see George’s thin face peering out of a nest of blankets. If
you said “_Hi, Ferry!_” you got a smile and a wave of a hand. Then one
day still later Jimsy was allowed to call, and then the next day Jimsy
and Dick both called, and after that they regularly spent an hour or
so up there. Browning got his spirits back and no longer buttonholed
Jimsy on campus or stairway. But when a fortnight had passed it became
evident to the doctor that George had reached his limit of recovery. He
stood still, and didn’t want food and didn’t seem to care whether he
went back to Number 33 or spent the rest of the year in the infirmary!
So, in the end, it was decided that George was to go home and not
return to North Bank until the fall, and that he was to spend the
summer somewhere in the mountains and not do anything but breathe pure
air into his lungs and put good food into his stomach.

George accepted the verdict placidly. His only regret was for missing
spring lacrosse, although, as Jimsy pointed out to him, he would have
been just about as much use to the team as a rubber dumpling in a stew!
George replied that he guessed the rubber dumpling would have him beat,
for he wouldn’t even _look_ like a player! “You and Dick had better
hitch up after I go,” said George the next day. “Dick doesn’t like the
fellow he’s in with, and I guess the faculty will let him change.”

Dick demurred on the score that George might decide to come back later
in the spring, but George assured him that he wouldn’t, so when one day
George went off in an automobile with his father beside him, and Dick
and Jimsy had waved a last good-by, they went together to the office
and saw Mr. Ledyard and obtained permission. The next morning Dick
transferred his possessions up to Number 33, leaving behind him a very
surprised and disgruntled Bert. Bert declared a great number of times
that the arrangement suited him all right, but it was plain to be seen
that the prospect of being alone didn’t really please him a bit.

Two days after George’s departure Dick and Jimsy hung over the edge of
the balcony in the gymnasium and saw North Bank defeat Cumbridge in
the second basket ball game of the series. Cumbridge had won the first
contest on her own floor by a score of 28 to 22, and as the rivals
played only two games the championship was decided by the final total
of points. Therefore it was necessary for North Bank to accumulate
at least seven points more than Cumbridge on this occasion. And she
did it quite handily, just doubling the Dark Blue’s score. Dick got
frightfully excited toward the end of the first half and would possibly
have fallen over the railing if Jimsy hadn’t kept tight hold of him.

Tom Warden, captain and center of the North Bank five, gathered scoring
honors by tossing five goals from the floor, two of which were long,
diagonal shots. Cumbridge shifted her line-up continually, using in
all more than two full teams, while North Bank stuck to her original
make-up until just before the contest ended, when several substitutes
were sent in that they might get their letters. Cumbridge’s defensive
play was much better than her offensive, and in the first half she
stood an intensive bombardment stubbornly. She clung closely to North
Bank and reached the intermission on the short end of a 12 to 8 score.
North Bank scored first with a long shot from near the center of the
floor by Debrion, left forward. Cumbridge tied the game at 3-all and
again, later, at 5-all, but after that the Light Blue forged ahead.
Debrion’s ability to throw goals from fouls counted considerably in
both halves. Cumbridge, on the other hand, was woefully weak in that
department, and although three of her players tried free throws during
the forty minutes of playing time, she accumulated but four goals from
sixteen attempts.

During the second half Cumbridge scored but two field goals. She clung
throughout to the short, diagonal passing game and, although she was
frequently able to work the ball under North Bank’s basket she didn’t
seem able to lift it in. North Bank varied her attack, in the first
half relying on a quick toss over the heads of the players and in the
second half alternating with a long, high toss to a player under the
basket that usually took Cumbridge by surprise. That second half was
monotonously North Bank’s, though the audience seemed to approve of
the monotony. When the last whistle sounded the Light Blue was 26 and
the Dark Blue 13, and the former had won the series by the safe margin
of 19 points. As that was the first victory over Cumbridge that year
it was vastly appreciated. If it didn’t take all the sting from the
football defeat it was at least soothing!

The Prize Debate came off toward the last of February, too, and if
Dick didn’t get quite as excited over that as he had over the basket
ball game he at least enjoyed it. As a matter of fact, there was a
surprising amount of suspense and interest in the affair, and a good
deal of cheering when the prize was awarded to Cas Kirkham. Dick
tentatively added debating to the select list of worthwhile things
deserving his attention next year. Just now his mind was too occupied
with aquatics to have room for much else.

Jimsy had pointed out Tom Gage to him one day on the campus and Dick
had been extremely surprised. Gage wasn’t at all Dick’s idea of the
flashing-eyed, stern-browed, shrill-voiced occupant of the coxswain’s
seat. Tom Gage was eighteen, fairly tall and about as thick through
as a broomstick. So far as absence of weight went, well and good,
but there wasn’t any flash to Gage’s near sighted brown eyes and if
he could ever look stern his present expression belied him. Gage, in
short, looked like a very quiet, mild-mannered youth who would much
prefer a book to rudder-lines. Jimsy, though, said he guessed Tom was
a pretty good cox; that, anyway, he had been coxing quite awhile and
still held his job! Dick wondered if his notion, gathered from rowing
stories, of what a coxswain should be was all wrong. Certainly, the
thin, lanky fellow carrying a load of books from the library didn’t
tally with either text or pictures!

Then March came in and Coach Carmichael appeared one day on the campus
in a suit of loud-checked tweed, and Dick’s heart leaped.




                               CHAPTER XX

                         IN THE COACH’S LAUNCH


March Seventh!

Ever memorable day!

On the boathouse float was activity, confusion and color. The two
slender cedar shells had been carefully carried down from the Hall
and now lay on their trestles side by side while Coach Carmichael and
several of the crew members were going over them carefully. About them,
frequently getting in their way, were a dozen or more muscular-looking
youths in “shorts” and sweaters and woolen stockings, while about the
doorway lounged a sprinkling of on-lookers attracted by the crews’
first appearance. Amongst the onlookers was Richard Dodd. Dick hoped
to be more than an observer presently, but as yet he was only one of
the chorus, in a manner of speaking. He watched the coach fascinatedly,
for that short, wide-shouldered, thick-chested person in an old green
sweater and very dirty gray flannel trousers and a funny little round
cloth hat held Dick’s destiny in the capable-looking brown hands that
were busy about the first crew shell.

Coach Carmichael was forty-two years old. He had a roundish, deeply
seamed face from which a pair of sharp gray eyes looked. Under a
beaklike nose a rather long mustache, once red-brown but now grizzled
to an indeterminate shade, hid most of a generous-sized mouth. The
fellows said that that mustache was “Mike’s” one vanity. In any case
it is true that he carried a small mustache comb in his pocket and in
moments of leisure abstractedly brought it forth and ran it through
that adornment. Mike was no longer first of all a rowing coach. That
day had passed. He had been a good one once, it was said; for that
matter he was a good one still, but now coaching was only a sideline
and his real business was the conduct of a shoe store in Baltimore.
He had coached North Bank six years, had, indeed, taken hold there
when the first Light Blue crew had dipped oars in the Severn. No one
outside the faculty knew what salary Mike drew for his services, but it
was generally believed that it was less that salary than the love of
boating that attracted him.

Dick was on the float by direction of Joe Whittier. Joe had spoken to
the coach about Dick, and, while Mike had made no promise, it had been
agreed that the new candidate for a coxswain’s seat was to report for
what Joe called “the swift glance.” Now Dick was waiting for the coach
to finish with the shells and for Joe to come and get him. Joe was
doing something with a screw driver near by and grunting hard. At the
side of the float the little rented launch, the “Sprite,” was lying
ready, Bromley, of the first class, in overalls and jumper already well
grease-smeared, in charge. The afternoon was bright but far from warm,
and Dick appreciated the shelter provided by the boathouse wall against
whose sun-warmed surface he was leaning. A southeasterly breeze was
ruffling the blue surface of the river and bringing a fascinating odor
of gasoline and hot metal from the launch to his nostrils. Far down the
river the tall chimneys and golden dome and gleaming walls of the Naval
Academy stood sharply against the blue sky.

Beside Dick, Grantley, a large, heavy, second-class fellow was nibbling
peanuts and trying to hold converse. Grantley was always nibbling
something, a large freckled hand making periodical excursions from
pocket to mouth. Dick had nothing against him, but he was too intent on
the coach to do much talking. Several late comers clattered down the
steps and joined the fringe of the little crowd. Tom Gage, his thin
legs covered with green golf stockings and a knit cap on his head, a
blue sweater enfolding him loosely, came out of the boathouse with the
rudder under an arm. Gage looked a little more alert to-day. The second
shell cox, Warren, was on hand, too. Warren was small and weasel-faced,
with a pair of gimlet eyes and a high-pitched voice. The first crew’s
boat was ready for the water now, and it was lifted from the supports,
turned bottom up, borne to the edge of the float, righted and lowered
into the dancing water. Gage fitted his rudder and took his place in
the stern. Sweeps were fetched and laid on the float.

“Four!” called the cox, and Tom Warden stepped into the shell. The
others followed by numbers. The coach examined stretchers and slides.
Then: “Take ’em away, Tommy, and paddle around. Some of the stretchers
may want changing. Keep your sweaters on, fellows.”

“Ready,” called Gage. “Forward!” The eight oarsmen moved up with their
slides. “Paddle!” The oars dipped and the slender shell moved from the
float.

“All right with this one,” said the coach, and the second crew boat
went over. The oarsmen laid their sweeps down and awaited the word.
Warren was strapping the tiny blue megaphone to his mouth. The coach
watched impatiently. “What’s the matter, Kid? Has your head grown since
fall? Don’t keep your men waiting!”

“Places!” piped Warren. “Four!”

The second shell slid away, too, and the “Sprite” began to chug
impatiently. Dick’s heart was in his boots, for Joe had gone off in
the first shell and doubtless Coach Carmichael had forgotten all
about the coxswain candidate. The coach was addressing a handful of
substitutes left on the float. “You fellows get the pair-oars out and
do some paddling. Don’t try racing strokes to-day. It’s cold and your
