muscles are stiff. Go down to the red bank and back, and take it easy.”
Then, turning to the little throng of onlookers: “Dodd here?” he asked
crisply.

Dick’s heart jumped as he stepped forward. The coach looked at him
sharply, critically, as he crossed the landing. Then he put a broad
hand out and Dick’s was swallowed up in it. “Glad to meet you, son,”
said the coach. “Come along.” He jumped down to the float and climbed
into the launch. After an instant of doubt, Dick followed. He wasn’t
certain that he had heard correctly, but evidently he had, for the
coach motioned to one of the uncushioned seats that ran lengthwise of
the launch and said: “Make yourself comfortable. Let her go, Ben!”

The “Sprite” chugged more loudly, choked, chugged faster and swung
into the stream. Coach Carmichael stood at the bow, one hand on the
wheel. The “Sprite” was only sixteen feet long, an open launch with
neither glass nor spray-shield. Further aft, Ben Bromley presided over
the small four-cylinder engine. Bromley cared little about rowing, but
he cared a lot for launches and gas engines, and now he was in his
element. The “Sprite” had speed, if few refinements, and almost as soon
as they had started Mike was holding up his hand and the launch was
slowing down. A little distant lay the second crew, sweatered, capped,
their faces turned toward the launch. The “Sprite” floated closer.

“All right, Second,” called the coach. “I want you to go easy to-day.
Remember that this is your first work-out and don’t put much into it.
Take ’em up to the second bend, Kid, and go slow. Coming back you’d
better keep over near the other shore. Keep your strokes long and slow,
fellows. Give ’em about a couple dozen hard ones coming back, Kid, and
see that they finish out. That was one big trouble with most of you
last fall. You didn’t finish your strokes out. Number 4, look after
your hands and remember what I told you. Let her go!”

The second slipped easily upstream through the choppy water and the
coach turned his attention to the First which was coming slowly up.
“That’s rotten, Number 3!” he called. “You’re not catching. Put some
water on that blade. All right, way enough!” And when the shell was
floating placidly near by: “All I want to-day is some paddling, you
fellows. It’s a good time to study your stroke and see what’s wrong
with it. You’ve got a lot of work ahead of you before your first race,
and the sooner you make up your minds to get down to business the
better. Last fall you were rowing every man for himself. See if you
can’t get together. Tommy, watch Three and Five. They were clipping
badly just now. Slow and long, fellows, and finish out. Take ’em up to
the second bend, Tommy. All right.”

“Touch her, Seven! Steady! Ready all! Forward! Row!”

The shell went off with slow strokes of the long, blue-tipped sweeps
and the “Sprite,” her engine throttled down, followed. The coach turned
to Dick, “Come up here, son,” he said, and Dick slid along the seat
to the narrow bow. “Joe Whittier tells me you want to be a cox,” Mike
continued. “Well, that suits me all right. Glad to have you try it.
Know anything about rowing?”

“I’ve been reading a good deal about it,” answered Dick. “And Joe has
been telling me things.”

“Reading, eh?” mused the coach dubiously. “Well, I don’t know. Better
than nothing, I dare say. Guess you’ll learn more out here, though, in
one afternoon. Ever row any yourself?”

“Only in a skiff or a dory, sir.”

“Well, that’s something. You know why a boat moves forward when you put
the blade of an oar in the water and pull the haft toward you. More
than some fellows ever do know. Have a look at that boat ahead there.
Seeing anything wrong with it?”

Dick looked at the slowly moving shell that, from the launch, had
the appearance of a big bug walking up the river. After a moment he
answered doubtfully: “She’s sort of uneven, isn’t she? I mean she rolls
a good deal.”

“Sure does! So you could see that, eh? Know why she’s rolling?”

“No, sir, I don’t.”

“Watch the starboard oars then. See the second and third ones? They’re
doing it. Rowing light again.” He picked up the long blue megaphone
from beside him and roared through it. “Three! Five! Help the boat
along! You’re catching badly and you aren’t finishing. Get a hold
and pull through! Lengthen that stroke, Joe! Don’t hurry it! I said
lengthen it! That’s better. Eyes in the boat, Five! Tommy, keep ’em
steady! Watch ’em!”

Mike set the megaphone down again and leaned against the coaming, his
face toward Dick but his gaze fixed for the most of the time on the
shell ahead. “We’ll need a new cox next fall,” he went on. “Gage leaves
and Warren will have to take the first, I guess. That leaves a place
for you, son, if you can get the hang of it. Trouble is, though, that
coxing a crew is something that you can’t learn by reading. Something I
can’t tell you, either; not much, anyway. You’re a nice size and a nice
build for a cox, though, and I guess you’ve got gumption. Know what
gumption is?”

Dick smiled. “Horse sense,” he hazarded.

Mike grunted. “Sort of. Gumption’s what tells you where the current’s
fastest and what to do when your crew lays down on you in the last
quarter and how water looks when the eel-grass is reaching for you
and how to steer when a launch drags her anchor and comes down on you
to port and an empty barrel lies ahead and a course buoy is close
astarboard. That’s gumption. Think you’ve got it?”

“I don’t know,” said Dick, doubtfully.

“Well, I think you have!” The coach smiled down at him. “Didn’t you
pull a fellow out of the river here awhile back? Sure! That took
gumption, I guess. I wouldn’t wonder――” He broke off to seize the
megaphone again. “In the boat! You’re all rowing too short again!
Lengthen out, lengthen out! Bow side, keep your hands up! Number Seven,
you’re bending your arms too soon! Steady down now! Let me see you do
twenty clean strokes. Come on! One!――Two!――Three!――”

Presently he was addressing the boy beside him once more. “I wouldn’t
be surprised, Dodd, if we made a cox out of you by the fall. You stick
around and keep your eyes open, son. See if you can tell when a crew’s
rowing right, and why. Find out where the mistakes are. Some day I’ll
let you go out in the four and hold the lines. Meanwhile you show up
afternoons and help me coach. Lots to see if you keep your eyes peeled.
Little things that may help some day. Coxing isn’t an easy job; good
coxing, I mean. Any one can steer a shell after a fashion, but it takes
brains to bring a racing crew over the mile-and-seven-eighths ahead
of the other boat. I’ll say it does! You’ve got to learn your men and
know ’em as well as you know yourself; got to know what you can get
out of ’em and how to get it out. You’ll find eight different sorts of
fellows in a ’varsity shell; no two alike, all different. One will be
high-keyed and another low, one will loaf if you’ll let him and the
next’ll row his heart out. That’s the way it goes from bow to stroke.
Got to know ’em, got to watch ’em, got to handle ’em. Some coxswains
think the boat’s all they need to have on their minds, but they find
out different. There’s――For Pete’s sake!”

Mike grabbed the megaphone again.




                              CHAPTER XXI

                         DICK LEARNS THE RIVER


Almost every day thereafter for many weeks Dick “helped coach.” Mike
jokingly referred to him as “my advisory.” Between the two quite a warm
friendship sprang up. Dick enjoyed every instant of those afternoons on
the “Sprite” and Coach Carmichael seemed to enjoy having Dick beside
him in the bow. He talked to the boy quite as though the latter was,
indeed, a skilled and experienced oarsman, and spoke of things still
beyond Dick’s comprehension. Mike seemed to find relief in speaking his
thoughts aloud, and if, returning to the float, Dick had repeated only
a few of the things he had heard, many a self-satisfied member of the
first or second crew would have been surprised and dismayed. For Mike
didn’t believe in scolding unnecessarily, nor in risking discouragement
by too captious criticism.

But there was time for instruction, too, and interspersed with
comments, often caustic, were many hints that the boy stored away
against future needs. Before March was over he had learned a whole lot
about the tides and currents in the river thereabouts, where the slack
water lay and where the fast, and how far out at Fletcher’s Bend the
weeds and shoals extended, and how, negotiating the bridge at the draw,
you had to bear hard aport until you picked up the wireless tower far
down the river. He learned, too, what to do when you were holding the
lines and a “false current” swung your bow, and how, by changing your
course two boat-lengths upstream of the mile marker, you could shave
the buoy and gain half a length. And he learned many things that were
not told him, just by keeping his eyes and ears open and putting two
and two together in the long-established fashion. He discovered for
himself, as an instance, that when a shell rode badly you looked first
to the stroke-oar for the cause, and that when an accident happened
there was just one thing you shouldn’t do, and that was lose a stroke.
A broken oarlock or outrigger meant one man lost to the crew, but
it mustn’t slow the boat. You just went right on, rowing seven men,
and won if you could. And the idle man didn’t jump into the river in
the old spectacular fashion, for that rocked the shell and lost you
distance. Instead, he repaired the damage if such a feat was possible,
or, failing that, he just made himself small and prayed hard!

There was many a day on the river in March when Dick had to huddle
himself up and keep his hands in his pockets for warmth, days when the
wind blew cold and the river showed whitecaps, even in the sheltered
stretches, and the shells went out with the canvas spray strips
stretched along the sides. But there were other days, especially
as April drew near, when the Severn was a smooth, blue, laughing
reflection of the cloudless sky, when the sun shone warmly and the
little “Sprite” fairly danced up and down the course. Such days grew
more frequent as time went on and Dick acquired a perceptible coat
of tan on face and hands. He made friends with Bromley, listening to
wise words anent the peculiarities of gas engines and the freakishness
of ignition, and hearkening with no sign of boredom to the technical
explanation of the engine _he_ was going to build some day. Dick could
almost have qualified as assistant engineer along in April!

He saw much less of Jimsy afternoons, but since they were together most
of the rest of the time that didn’t matter greatly. Life in Number 33
Baldwin was splendid. Jimsy was an ideal roommate, and now that Dick
had reached a point beyond saving, in his strange ambition to “do
something,” Jimsy no longer made fun of him. Instead, Jimsy displayed
a real interest in rowing affairs and in Dick’s slow progress toward
the goal of his desire, which goal was now some few square inches of
polished seat in the stern of the second boat. Together they spent many
evenings in Number 6 McCrea when study was over. Dick had not lost his
secret worship of Alan, but he had added Joe Whittier to his company
of heroes. Joe was such a “corker” that you couldn’t help sort of
loving him. Alan was perhaps grander to Dick, more exalted, but he was
also, and for that reason, less approachable. Alan tried to be nice,
and was nice, but he hadn’t Joe’s comradely ways. Alan always found
it difficult to step down off his pedestal, even for a minute. Oddly
enough――or perhaps not oddly at all!――Jimsy got on better with the
crew captain than Dick did. Alan took to Jimsy right off, found him
amusing and enjoyed talking to him. That generally left Joe and Dick to
make their own converse, and, needless to say, it was usually on rowing
matters. Frequently there would be others there when Dick and Jimsy
arrived: Tom Warden and Ducker Coy, Hickson and Lee, sometimes Tommy
Gage, of the crew; Caspar Trumbull or Jerry Benson of the football
crowd. Always there was plenty of talk and entertainment, and, although
Dick and Jimsy were out-aged, the youngsters never felt awkward in the
company. Perhaps Jimsy wouldn’t have under any circumstances!

The evening they found Gage there proved more than usually interesting
to Dick, for the first crew coxswain attached himself to the neophyte
and talked to him as though to a brother cox. Dick suspected that Gage
would have appreciated a few confidences, such, for instance, as what
Mike’s opinion of Tommy Gage’s recent work was, but Dick made believe
he didn’t suspect and Gage accepted failure gracefully. He said one
thing that made Dick a little happier.

“If you can please Mike,” said Tommy, “you’ll pop into the first boat
next fall, Dodd. This is between us, you understand, and no offense to
Purley Warren. Warren isn’t a cox and never will be, and Mike knows
it. If you had ever steered a crew he’d have you in the second boat
right now, I’ll bet a doughnut! So just you say nothing and saw wood,
boy. Mike’s taken a shine to you, all right, and he’ll put you through
hard and fast. Glad of it, too, for you look like a peppy guy to me,
and you ought to make a rattling good chap for next year’s boat. I’ll
put you wise to one thing, though. Don’t ever try to argue anything
with Mike. He’s a good old scout, but if he tells you you’re wrong,
why, you be wrong! Don’t make any cracks, Dodd. Just sit still and take
it.” Gage stared reflectively at the toes of his rusty shoes a moment.
“Generally,” he added then, “you will be!”

Dick was glad that Gage had added that, for he secretly believed that
Coach Carmichael was infallible, or, at least, as infallible as one can
be in this fallible world. Gage raised himself in Dick’s estimation
by that bit of candor. When, presently, Gage’s attention was summoned
elsewhere Dick had decided that he liked the first crew cox immensely.

There had been several letters from George Ferry since his departure
in each of which he had reported cheerfully that he was feeling a lot
better. He was at Atlantic City in March and sent Dick a postcard
photograph of himself and his mother in a wheel chair. Jimsy, studying
it, remarked that George might be better but was a long way from being
best! One letter contained this: “You and Dick had some patter about
‘the renowned Pierson of undying fame’ just before I left. It was some
crazy secret you had, I suppose, but I understood that Pierson was a
football player. I came across this the other day in a newspaper and
wondered if this was your man. If so, you had the name wrong, you
funny kids!”

“This” was a few lines cut from the columns of a daily paper and pinned
to the top of the sheet of hotel writing paper “‘Scrapper’ Presson, the
former All-America football end of 1907 and 1908, was a guest of Mr.
and Mrs. Frederick Eddy at the Wavefront on Tuesday. Those who recall
Mr. Presson’s wonderful playing in the Princeton-Yale game in ’08 would
scarcely have recognized him on the board walk. He has put on weight
since those good old days and would look more at home in the center of
the line than at the end.”

“Gee,” laughed Jimsy, “that’s a good one! Brother Bert didn’t even get
the fellow’s name right!”

“It would be rather fun,” mused Dick, “to send him that. Only, we
wouldn’t be around when he read it.”

Perhaps that was the reason Bert didn’t see the clipping, but more
likely it was because he had ceased to be of interest to the occupants
of Number 33. Or maybe because Dick’s thoughts were centered on more
serious things in those days; such, for example, as the first boat race
of the season to be rowed on Saturday between the North Bank first crew
and the Navy plebes.

As a contest, that race wasn’t much, for the Navy youngsters took the
lead at the first quarter-mile flag and increased it all the way, until
at the finish of the mile course they were seven lengths ahead. Some
said nine lengths, but it is well to be conservative, and a length
more or less doesn’t matter in such a case! Dick and Jimsy watched
the contest from the shore, close to the finish, not because they
preferred to view matters from so long a range but because they could
neither borrow a canoe nor beg accommodations. North Bank didn’t do
so badly, when all was said, for the Navy’s first year crew was an
exceptionally good one, as later events proved. But there were two
changes in the Light Blue boat on Monday, nevertheless, for there is
nothing like a real race to show up the weak places. Tom Warden, rowing
at Six, changed places with Ducker Coy, at Three, and Chase yielded his
place at Five to McKim, of the second. Dick couldn’t say that the new
arrangement improved matters, but Mike seemed better satisfied, and so
the “advisory” concluded that the change was for the best.

It was two days after that race that the coach made good his early
promise and gave Dick his first test with the rudder-lines. A four-oar
was manned with Chase and three other substitutes and Dick was placed
in the stern. Mike counseled the new coxswain with grave countenance.
“Don’t bring ’em in, Dick,” he ordered, “until they can do thirty
strokes that you’re satisfied with. See that they finish out every
time. Chase, use your legs and don’t finish sitting up. That goes for
you, too, Debrion. Walker, look after your body and don’t swing out
of the boat. Lobell, watch your catch. All right, Dick. Better go
upstream, I guess.” He waved a hand and Dick swallowed and called:
“Ready all!” He had no megaphone, nor needed one, but he wished that
he did have one since it would have hid much of his face and helped
conceal the fact that he was far from at ease. Walker, rowing Stroke,
grinned at him sardonically and, in spite of the command, turned his
head long enough to say something to Chase over his shoulder. Dick was
glad that the crews had gone off and that there were few loiterers
about the landing, but he was horribly embarrassed as he issued the
next order and tried not very successfully to make his voice sound deep
and authoritative.

“Touch her, Three! Steady! Forward! Paddle!”

The four oars dug into the smooth water and the little shell slid out
into the river. Dick pulled anxiously at one rudder line and the slim
bow crept to starboard. He pulled the other, surprised that the result
had been so instant, and the boat straightened. Walker was setting
a slow stroke and rowing well, Dick thought. Beyond him, Chase was
following satisfactorily, but, in the bow, Lobell was late. “Bow,
you’re late,” warned Dick. Then: “Pick it up, Stroke, now.”

Walker shot a quizzical glance at the coxswain and added a couple
more strokes to the minute. Dick counted ten and then eased himself
in his little seat and looked about. Quite a ways up the river was
the first, swinging along with Joe setting what Dick judged to be
about thirty-four. It passed from sight about the first headland as he
watched. The launch, with the coach erect in the bow, came charging
along from the landing, its little engine pulsing loud and fast.
Mike raised his megaphone and his voice came startlingly across the
intervening water.

“Lengthen out, lengthen out!” he called. “Keep in the boat, Walker!”




                              CHAPTER XXII

                         MUTINY IN THE FOUR-OAR


The “Sprite” went past, Ben Bromley winking gravely at Dick, leaving
a parted wake behind her. Dick watched Walker closely for a moment,
but the big chap seemed to be doing his honest best, catching sharply,
pulling strongly well through, recovering cleanly and moving back
easily on his slide to the accompaniment of a well-feathered oar. Chase
was getting more length into his efforts, too, and it was not until
Dick studied the bow oar that he found cause for criticism. Lobell was
again catching late and the boat was rolling a bit as a result.

“You’re late, Bow!” called Dick sternly. “Watch your stroke! That’s
better!”

The four-oar crept up to the first bend and Dick swung obliquely across
toward the further side. The First would be coming down presently on
a time trial and it wouldn’t like broken water. Well out of the north
course, Dick turned the bow upstream and said: “All right, fellows. Let
her run.” The rowers ceased and the long sweeps hung dripping above the
still water. “Better rest a minute,” said Dick. He looked upstream for
the First and saw it coming fast, the launch boiling along behind. The
others turned in their seats and looked, too.

“Mike’s sweating them, all right,” commented Walker. “Doing
thirty-eight, or I’m a Dutchman!”

“Some one’s splashing a bit, too,” said Chase. “Warden, isn’t it?”

“Yes, he can’t hit it up without splashing,” answered Walker. “I may be
rotten, but I’ll bet I could pull Warden in a circle!”

“You might mention it to Mike,” suggested Debrion dryly, and Dick
smiled faintly. Unfortunately, Walker saw it and frowned.

“I might mention a lot of things to him,” he growled, “but I don’t want
my head bitten off.” Then, to Dick: “What are we waiting here for, kid?
Think we can do better with stiff muscles?”

“Just letting the First come down,” replied Dick. “You won’t get stiff
a day like this.” The First swept past them across the stream. Warden
still splashed now and then, but on the whole the boat was moving
nicely. Tommy Gage, swinging back and forth in the stern, looked very
thin and very small as, clutching the lines beside him, the little
blue megaphone hiding half his countenance, he leaned tensely forward.
Voices floated across, Tommy’s first, then Mike’s. Then the sound
of the “Sprite’s” exhaust drowned the voices and the rattle of the
oarlocks and the shell became foreshortened and the afternoon sunlight
gleamed crisply on the blue tips of the eight blades as, leaving the
water in unison, they swept forward again over the oily swirls and
were again buried from view. It was a fine sight, thought Dick, and he
experienced a thrill at the recollection of Gage’s prediction. Next
year he might be in the picture himself! He came back to the present
to find Walker’s gaze set sarcastically on him. He flushed a bit, for
it seemed to him that the Stroke had guessed his thoughts, and to cover
his discomfort he drew the lines taut again and called: “Ready all!”

The oarsmen wrapped their hands about the oars, slid forward at the
next word and then dug the blades into the water again. After a
moment Dick pulled gently at the line in his right hand and the shell
turned into midstream. Then, with the stroke side oars paddling,
the nose was turned down the river again. “Touch her, Bow! Steady!
Let’s try those thirty strokes now, fellows. See if you can do them
perfectly. Remember, use your legs, Two. Make them long and finish
clean, fellows. Touch her, Two. Steady! Ready all. Forward! Row!
One!――Two!――Three!――Four!――Lengthen out, Stroke! Five!――Steady;
all! Six!――Seven!――Eight!――Nine! That’s the ticket! Ten!――Two,
you’re not in time! Eleven!――Twelve! Finish out, Three! You’re
clipping! Thirteen!――Fourteen! Pull through, Three! Finish your
stroke! In the boat, Stroke! Fifteen! Half way, fellows! Keep it up!
Sixteen!――Seventeen!――Eighteen! Stroke, don’t rush your slide! Steady!
Nineteen!――Twenty! Lengthen that stroke! You’re all clipping! Lengthen
out! Lengthen out, Stroke! Get the time, Two! Twenty-two――_Let her
run!_”

“What’s that for?” panted Walker indignantly. “What’s wrong with us?”

“Lots,” replied Dick crisply. “You weren’t pulling through, any of
you. You did about twenty and then went to pieces. Bow, you were
taking about a two-thirds stroke. You’ve got to catch harder and carry
through. You’re much too short in the water. Two, you weren’t in time.
You ought to watch the man in front of you and follow him. And you
weren’t getting your legs into the pull. Three, you were all right
until you tried to do it all with your body. You’ve got legs, too.
Stroke――”

“Yeah? What about me?” asked Walker belligerently.

“I guess I don’t have to tell you,” answered Dick, returning his
incensed gaze squarely. “You lean outboard when you get to the end of
the stroke, and that throws the boat over and spoils your recovery,
besides. You rowed a pretty stroke halfway through and then began to
weaken on your finish and rush your slide. The boat wasn’t traveling
for beans at the last. We’ll float awhile and then try it again.”

“Say, how long have you been coxing, anyway?” demanded Walker.

“About forty minutes, maybe; perhaps less.” Dick glanced imperturbably
at his watch. “To be exact, thirty-two.”

“Yes, well, you want to get down to earth, kid. We’ve been rowing for
two years and I guess we know a blamed sight more about it than you do,
and――”

“I’m sure you do,” interrupted Dick calmly, although he wasn’t feeling
calm. “That’s why I expect something better from you.”

“Oh, chase your blind aunt,” advised Walker peevishly. “We were pulling
a good enough stroke for anybody that knows anything. You make me
tired, Dodd. You’ve got a swelled bean, kid; that’s your trouble.
You’ve been picking up a lot of lingo, talking to Mike, and you don’t
know what it means!”

“Oh, shut up, Frank,” said Debrion. “Dodd’s all right. I know when I’m
jazzing my stroke. We did go to pieces, and you know it, old son. Let’s
have it again, Cox.”

“That’s all right,” answered Walker, “but this smart Alick will have us
rowing all over the river! He doesn’t know anything but a lot of words
he’s picked up!”

“Touch her, Two,” said Dick. “Steady! All right, we’ll have another
try, fellows. Just keep your minds on the job this time and see if you
can’t do better. Ready all. Forward. Row!”

Down the river they went again, the current helping greatly now.
Dick found that he no longer had any conscious thoughts of steering.
That matter looked after itself, it seemed. One just steered without
knowing he was steering. Ten strokes brought the shell almost
abreast of the boathouse. All four oars were in time and all four
backs were bending and straightening in unison. Twenty strokes
brought them past the bathhouses, and now again Walker was throwing
his body to the right as his hands came up and, in the bow, Lobell
was catching late and skimping his stroke all through. Dick warned
them and caught up the count again: “Twenty-three――Twenty-four!
Keep it up! Not bad!――Twenty-five! Five more now! Steady,
all!――Twenty-six! You’re short, Stroke! Pull it through! Watch the
stroke, Three――Twenty-seven! Catch hard, Bow! Come through with it!
Steady!――Twenty-eight!――Twenty-nine! Keep it long, fellows!――Thirty!
Let her run!”

Four panting youths lay on their oars and bent inquiring looks on the
small coxswain. Walker’s, though, was more than inquiring; it was
challenging.

“Well, how were we?” he asked.

“Better,” said Dick. “You almost did it.”

“Almost! Where do you get that ‘almost’ stuff?” Walker exploded.
“That’s as good as you’re likely to get, kid, and you might as well be
satisfied with it. Let’s try a couple of starts, fellows, and call it a
day.”

“I guess we’ve had about enough,” agreed Chase. “Want to try us on a
start or two, Dodd?”

“Not yet, I think.” Dick shook his head resolutely. He was smiling, but
his mouth was rather set. “We’ve got to do a smooth thirty before we go
in, fellows. You heard what the coach said. Touch her, Bow!――Steady!
Might as well make up our minds to it, I guess. We’ll have another try
presently. There’s the Second coming up. The First, too.”

Walker turned to look, but his face was gloomy. “All right, I’ll go you
once more, kid, but that’s the limit. I don’t intend to stay out here
all night. Got to get my breath first, though.”

“Oh, your breath’s all right, Frank,” said Lobell from the bow. “Let’s
get it over with. Let’s have it, Cox. Say, wasn’t I better that time?”

“Yes, you rowed pretty well until about the twenty-fifth stroke,”
replied Dick encouragingly. “See if you can’t keep it up for thirty
this time, Bow. Same with the rest of you. It’s got to be thirty good
ones, fellows, so let’s have them!”

Coach Carmichael waited at the landing. The first and second boats
were housed, the sweeps were in the rack and the oarsmen had climbed
the hill to the gymnasium and grateful showers. Scripps, the manager,
kept Mike company; and a few fellows, lately out of canoes, lingered to
find out what was up. Mike looked again at his watch and then searched
the river. The hour was getting late. The shadows of evening fell far
across the darkening surface of the water and supper time was drawing
near.

“You say they went downstream?” he asked Scripps. “How long ago was
that?”

“About three-quarters of an hour, I think. It was about ten minutes
before the Second came in.”

“Something must have happened,” muttered the coach. “Don’t see what
could, though, in water like this. Unless young Dodd steered ’em into
the bank. The boy hasn’t had any experience with the lines, and I guess
I was a fool to send him out. Still, Chase and Debrion are old hands;
Walker, too. I suppose you can’t run that launch, Johnny?”

The manager glanced at the “Sprite,” lying silent at the shore end
of the landing, and shook his head. “Don’t know anything about the
things,” he answered.

Mike turned to the half-dozen loiterers. “Any of you fellows know how
to run a launch?” he asked crisply. One, an angular youth in a faded
baseball shirt and a pair of soiled flannel trousers stepped forward.

“I guess I can,” he said. “I’ve run one a goodish bit. Anyway, I’ll
take a chance, Coach.”

“Then I guess I’ll have to,” said Mike grimly. “See if you can get her
started, will you?”

“Wait a minute!” exclaimed Scripps. “There’s something in sight; just
under the bluff, there. Can you see it, sir? It’s in the shadow now,
but――”

“I get it,” answered the coach. “Guess that’s the boat. Never mind
about the launch.”

In a minute or two the small object struck a patch of lighter water
and became recognizable as the missing four-oar. It came on slowly,
very much as if the four oarsmen were tired, and many minutes elapsed
before, at last, it reached hailing distance. Then: “In the boat!”
bawled the coach. “Anything wrong?”

“No, sir!” That was Dick’s voice. “Coming in, sir.”

“‘Coming in;’” echoed Mike to Scripps. “Well, I’d hope so!”

“Way all!” came from Dick. The little shell floated closer. “Back
water!――Steady all!” Scripps seized the nose of the boat and led it
along the float while oars were unlocked and, at last, five youths,
four very tired and one very stiff, stepped ashore.

“Where the Sam Hill have you been?” asked Mike, addressing Dick
curiously.

“Pick her up,” directed Dick. “Steady, Three! All right! Take her in!”
Then, replying to the question: “We’ve been down around the bridge for
the last hour or so, sir,” said Dick. “There seemed to be less current
there. You see――”

Walker came out of the boathouse and strode up to the coach.

“Coach, this kid’s kept us out there two hours! Wouldn’t bring us in,
sir, and made us do about a million strokes. Kept us rowing long after
we were played out. Said those were your orders. I’d like to know if he
had authority to make goats of us!”

Mike heard the speaker patiently. Then he faced Dick again. “What was
the trouble, Dick?” he asked.

“Why, you said I wasn’t to bring them in until they’d done thirty
strokes and done them right.”

“And they didn’t? Just a minute, Walker, please!”

“No, sir, they didn’t, not quite right. The last try wasn’t so bad,
though, and it was getting late, and I thought I’d better bring them
back.”

“Forget it, Dodd!” said Walker. “We rowed the thirty all right, two or
three times! You just got stubborn, that’s all! Why――”

“If you rowed thirty strokes the way they should have been rowed,”
interrupted the coach firmly, “you did more than I thought you could
do, Walker. You never did it for me, boy! Now lay off Dodd. He had his
orders, and he obeyed ’em. He had a right to keep you out until black
dark. Seems to me you were lucky to get in so early. To-morrow you’ll
have a chance to show me what you learned!”

Walker scowled, started to speak again, thought the better of it and
turned away to the steps. Scripps was locking the door beyond which lay
the shells. The others were already ascending the bank. Mike put an arm
over Dick’s shoulders. “You beat it up there and get under a shower,”
he said kindly. “Don’t wait for me. Can’t have you catching cold,
Dick, for you’re about the only man in the bunch who knows how to obey
orders!”




                             CHAPTER XXIII

                              “READY ALL!”


Dick threshed it out with Jimsy that night very earnestly.

“You see,” he explained, “I couldn’t do anything else, Jimsy. Mike said
keep them out until they’d done it right, and they simply wouldn’t do
it right. So I just had to, didn’t I?”

“Abso-lutely!” agreed Jimsy, grinning. “Oh, but I wish I could have
been there, Dick! It must have been rich!”

Dick shook his head soberly. “It wasn’t,” he answered. “It was beastly.
Walker got madder and madder and wouldn’t half row. And Chase got
grumpy, too, although he was pretty decent, I suppose. They _were_
tired, you see! If it hadn’t been for Debrion and Lobell standing by me
they’d have come in half an hour before we did. Once Walker threatened
to chuck me overboard.”

“He must have been waxy!” said Jimsy. “What happened?”

“Nothing. Chase told him to shut up and not spill the boat. Of course,
if he had tried to put me over the shell would have turned turtle. So I
wasn’t afraid of that. After awhile they saw that I meant what I said,
and they really tried. Even Walker. He _can_ row if he will, Jimsy.
They didn’t do a perfect thirty, of course. I had to shut my eyes
toward the last, but they did a lot better than at first. It was more
Walker’s fault than any one’s, for if the stroke doesn’t put his heart
into it the others can’t do their best. He thought when we started out,
that we were just going to have a nice easy paddle, that I didn’t know
a decent stroke when I saw it and that all he had to do was go through
the motions. I don’t see how he expects to make the boat if he goes at
it that way.”

“Walker? He hasn’t any more chance of making the First than I have,”
said Jimsy. “He will have to fight good and hard to even get into the
second boat. He always was a bluffer. Glad you wore him out, Dick. If
I’d thought you were still on the river I’d have been down there when
you got back. But I supposed you were in long ago. It was white of Mike
to back you up.”

“Why, he couldn’t do anything else, could he?” asked Dick. “I was only
following instructions!”

The fate of the four substitutes was soon known throughout the school,
and the school laughed consumedly. None laughed more heartily than
Joe Whittier. Joe laughed until the tears fairly streamed down his
weather-tanned cheeks. “Think of those four big hulks out there being
bossed by that little tike, Alan!” he gasped. “Can’t you see it? Frank
Walker, the big goof, getting madder and madder, and trying to mutiny?
And the others not daring to! And the youngster, about as big as a
good-sized bite, sitting there and telling them they’re rotten and
that they can’t quit until they’ve delivered the goods! My sainted
aunt, it’s grand!”

Alan agreed that it was grand, and after a moment he added, while Joe
wiped his eyes: “Looks to me as if young Dick was a born cox, Joe.
Funny if he made the boat next fall!”

“Funny!” said Joe indignantly. “How do you get that way? It would be a
blamed sight funnier if he didn’t!”

Dick didn’t go out in the four-oar again. For that matter, the four-oar
didn’t go out itself. Chase and Debrion displaced Crane and Nelson in
the second boat, and Walker and Lobell paddled about in a pair-oar
or substituted on occasions. The coach’s big job now was to get the
first crew in shape for the three-cornered race with West Shore and
Brackett’s, and all his energies were being bent to that end. May came
in very warm and stayed so, and the river was like a mill pond most of
the time. Standing on the bluff any week-day afternoon one could, in
the course of an hour, sight at least a half-dozen crews at work, for
the Navy was out with her Varsity and her second Varsity and her third
Varsity and her plebes, and there were the light-blue-tipped blades
of the North Bank first and second. Launches sped after the toiling
eights, canoes bobbed lazily about, sail boats got in the way, rowboats
plied from shore to shore and the old Severn became busy and colorful.

Ashore, baseball and lacrosse squads were hard at work. Indeed, both
teams had already played several games. The tennis courts were filled
at all hours and one might have wondered how the two hundred and odd
young gentlemen ever found time for study; whether, for that matter,
studies were still pursued at North Bank. But they were. Dick knew it
well, and so did others. Still more, briefly losing sight of the fact
in the press of outdoor engagements, were due to become thoroughly,
even rudely, cognizant later. Dick had survived midwinter examinations
without great difficulty; had even attained some slight credit; but now
that rowing affairs had become so important it wasn’t to be denied that
lessons seriously interfered with his career! Still, he didn’t make the
mistake that some made. He tried honestly to do what was required of
him, even if by so doing he lost precious hours that might have been
more pleasantly spent. As a result, he was keeping his end up when May
came and could take thought of the onrushing finals without having his
heart sink into his shoes. Jimsy, too, was playing it safe, although
his idea of safety was not Dick’s. To Dick it seemed that his chum was
always treading precariously on the very edge of misfortune!

Frank Walker had never forgiven Dick for that incident on the river.
He might have forgiven the thing itself in the course of time, but the
joking and “ragging” he had received as a result of it was too much for
him to overlook. He invariably met Dick with a ferocious scowl that
was intended to convey contempt and hatred and that succeeded fairly
well. As they met frequently, at the boathouse if nowhere else, Dick
would have led a miserable life had he allowed Walker’s manifestations
to trouble him. But he didn’t. To more than make up for Walker there
were plenty of other crew men who liked Dick and let him know it.
Unofficially at least he was a member of the rowing squad, for although
he didn’t sit at training table he was always on hand at rowing time,
helping at this task or that, smiling, quiet and ready. Almost always
he took his place beside Coach Carmichael in the launch when the crews
were boated and went off up or down the river, as the case might be,
“helping coach.” And so affairs went until the Tuesday preceding the
race with West Shore and Brackett’s. That afternoon, when the first was
out of the way, the coach sprung a surprise.

“Get a move on, Second,” said the coach, turning from watching the
first get away. “Anstruth, how’s the shoulder? All right? Good boy!
Hold on, Paine. You needn’t row to-day. Nelson, you go in at Two.
That’s right, I guess. And Dodd――Where’s Dick Dodd? Oh, there you are!
You take the lines to-day, Dick. Kid, you come along with me in the
launch.”

Warren yielded his megaphone to Dick with patent surprise, but without,
so far as the younger boy could see, any resentment. Warren, however,
was not one-half so surprised as Dick was. Dick accepted the megaphone
rather dazedly and turned a blank look on the coach. But the latter
was talking to Paine, and Dick’s glance, going past him, encountered
Walker’s sneering scowl. That steadied him and he went inside,
squeezing past the crew who were bringing out the shell. In the dimness
of the shed, odoriferous of paint and varnish and cedar scrapings, he
took a long breath. Then he followed out with the rudder. The shell
was righted, lowered, and the men tramped up the slope again for the
sweeps. Dick fitted the rudder and cautiously seated himself, bringing
the lines past him and crossing the ends on his lap. Then he fitted his
feet into place. The sweeps were on the float and the men ready.

“All right,” he called.
“Four!――Five!――Three!――Six!――Two!――Seven!――Bow!――Stroke!”

Oars were locked and sweaters peeled. Dick looked along the boat.
Anstruth, facing him, smiled back. Further forward, Debrion grinned and
gave his head a sidewise shake as if saying, “We’re getting on, Dodd!”
Dick smiled back. They were a fine, eager-looking lot, he thought,
and he sincerely hoped he wouldn’t make a mess of his part of the
proceedings. Coach Carmichael was speaking to him now.

“Better let Stroke work the boat to-day, Dick,” he said. “He knows the
programme. Watch ’em sharp, though, and see if you can help smooth
the stroke out. They’re still rowing ragged. I’ll pick you up later
at the head of the course. All right, Second. Remember you’ve got a
race to-morrow over the full course, and for Pete’s sake get together
to-day. Take ’em out, Cox.”

“Up or down?” asked Dick of Anstruth.

“Up, Cox. We’ll take it slow for awhile and then try a good breeze from
about the first point. Keep her inshore going up, for the current’s
setting out pretty strong. And, say, watch for a roll, will you? One of
our troubles of late has been to keep an even keel. All right, if you
say so.”

“Ready all! Forward! Paddle――Way all! Five and Seven, back water!
Stroke and Six, paddle!――Steady all!――Touch her, Stroke! Steady! Ready
all! Forward! Row!”

The eight blades caught together, the slides traveled forward, the
shell slipped ahead, the oarlocks rattled musically, the wet blades
emerged from the swirling ripples, paused in air and again disappeared.
But now bow side was a little late and Dick began to time them:
“Row!――Row!――Row!――”

The locks clicked in unison again and the slight rock of the shell was
gone. It was traveling evenly once more. Anstruth smiled at the Cox.
“That’s Norwell,” he said softly. “Number Five. Watch his catch, Dodd.”

Dick watched, and then: “Five, you’re catching late!” he called
sharply. “Watch Seven! Get your time from him! That’s better!”

Anstruth quickened his stroke a little and the shell began to travel at
a good speed. It was exhilarating to feel the air in his face and to
watch the eight rowers moving forward and back, the muscles of their
brown arms swelling into cords as the oars caught at the blue water.
This, thought Dick happily, was different from steering the four;
different in more ways than one. Here were fellows not only willing to
work and do their very utmost but eager, even anxious. The very feel of
the lines was different, for the long shell was like a horse with the
bit in his teeth. It paid but slight heed to the gentle tugs that would
have veered the four-oar widely from her course, and when, at the first
point, Dick sought to steer to starboard he was forced to a second
attempt and so lost water that in a race would have been invaluable.
Anstruth saw and smiled again.

“Got to pull her,” he grunted. “Give ’em ‘Way all,’ Dodd.”

They rested on their oars a minute under the shadow of the bluff and
watched a Navy crew go rattling past, her Cox hoarsely exhorting them
to “Get her up! Get her up! Get her up!” Anstruth shook his head.
“That’s rowing, fellows,” he said. “I’ll say that’s rowing!”

“That was their second, wasn’t it?” asked Dick.

The Stroke nodded. “Yes, and it’s just as good as their first, if you
ask me! Gosh, those guys can certainly handle a sweep! Well, let’s go,
Cox. Better try a racing start, I guess.”

Dick nodded. “Racing start, fellows!” he called. “Ten strokes and then
lengthen out. Get deep and don’t splash any more than you have to.”
Dick was repeating stuff he had heard a score of times. “Touch her,
Seven! Steady! Are you all ready? Forward!――Row!――Two! Three! Row! Row!
Five! Six! Seven! Eight! Nine! Steady down! Lengthen out! That’s it!
You’ve got ’em! Row! Row! Row!”

Anstruth gradually let down the stroke and they went on at a thirty-two
clip, rowing very well for aught Dick could see. “Good start,” he
megaphoned. “Nice work, Second!”

Short of the second turn they ceased rowing once more. Anstruth looked
approvingly at the new cox. “Dodd, I wish you were going to be here
to-morrow. You’ve got real pep, boy.”

“He’s a _cox_,” said Number Seven, with warm approval. “Let’s get Mike
to let us have him. What’s the chance, Dodd?”

Dick shook his head, trying not to look too pleased. “Guess I’m not up
to a race yet,” he answered. “I’ve only been out once before; in the
four-oar.”

“Seems to me I’ve heard something about that,” laughed Norwell. “How
about it, Deb?”

Debrion grinned. “Dodd’s the heartless tyrant, all right,” he replied.
“Any fellow got a bottle of pop handy?”

“Shut up!” growled Bow. “I’m as thirsty as a sponge!”

“Well, wet your wrists,” said Anstruth. “Let’s try another start, Cox.
We can do better than the last one.”

Twenty minutes later the first crew came up with the launch hard on
its heels and Mike’s voice bellowing through the big horn. Then the
“Sprite” swung about and came sidling down on the second.

“Tried your starts, Captain?” asked the coach.

“Two, sir.”

“How’d they go?”

“Pretty good, I think.”

“What do you say, Cox?”

“Good, sir.”

“All right. I’ll take you down a ways and then you can go in. Hit up
a thirty-two to the big maple and then run it up to thirty-eight and
let’s see if you can keep together. All right!”

Behind the shell came the launch, the water curling away from her sharp
nose, the big blue megaphone and the coach looming in the bow. These
things Anstruth could see, but not Dick. Dick only got the occasional
booming of Mike’s voice as the shell went rushing through the water.
Stroke’s muscles swelled and his breath came hard and fast. Thirty-six
to the minute now. “Slower back, Five!” warned Dick. “Watch your man in
front!” Thirty-eight, Dick guessed. The shell was certainly traveling!
The nearer shore slipped past rapidly. The first point was coming up to
port. “Watch your catch, Two!” shouted Dick. “You’re late!”

“Get together!” roared the voice through the megaphone in the launch.
“Bow side, you’re ragged!”

Dick tightened his grasp on the left line, ready for the turn, but
before he needed to pull Mike’s voice came again. “That will do,
Second!” called the coach.

“Way all!” said Dick.

The launch came nosing into sight beside him. The crew were leaning
heavily on their oars and breathing hard, their eyes, however, seeking
the coach’s face.

“Not so very bad,” said Mike. “You aren’t together half the time, of
course, and you won’t be until you learn to use your ears as well as
your arms and legs. If you’ll listen for the rattle of the locks you’ll
get the time. There ought to be just one sound instead of two or three
or half a dozen! Five, you start your slide too soon. Get your weight
onto your stroke before you drive your slide. Two, you don’t get your
blade out clean. Drop your hands more. Bow, you were a lot better
to-day. You’re getting more out of your legs. You, too, Stroke. You’re
improving right along. All right. Take ’em in, Cox. Better paddle back.
You’ll have a real job on your hands to-morrow!”

Back at the boathouse, the shell housed, Dick waited to see the First
come in. Scripps and Anstruth leaned beside him in the shadow, for the
sun, although well down, still shot its hot rays athwart the landing.
“I wish,” said the second crew captain presently as he watched the Navy
plebes go swinging downstream, “that Mike would let us have Dodd here
for keeps. I like Kid Warren all right, but Dodd’s got him beat to a
froth as a cox. Think he would, Johnny?”

The manager looked a bit surprised. “Gee, I don’t know. Maybe.” He
looked past Anstruth at Dick. “You’ve been out only twice, haven’t
you, Dodd?” Dick nodded. “Well, I don’t know,” repeated Scripps
thoughtfully. “If you like, I’ll throw out the hint, but you know how
Mike is. He has everything doped out a month ahead.”

Anstruth nodded, and Dick said relievedly, “There they come!” and
walked toward the float. The First was coming down fast, Joe Whittier
setting a thirty-eight stroke. Some one on the bow side, probably
Warden, was splashing, although not badly. Anstruth, joining Dick,
looked and commented.

“They’ll beat us by about ten lengths to-morrow,” he said sadly.

The “Sprite” circled outward and came up to the landing from downstream
as the shell glided up to the float. Dick caught an oar-blade and led
it along the edge. The crew lay tiredly on their sweeps, their eyes
fixed on Mike, standing in the bow of the launch as it puffed slowly
up. There was silence when Bromley shut the motor off, silence save for
the lapping of the water against the float. Mike shook his head slowly
as he leaned on the big blue megaphone and looked across at them.

“Not so good, to-day,” he said regretfully. “You’re still not together,
and you’ve _got_ to get together before you can hope to win a race.
I wish you could carry one day’s form over to the next day, but it
seems that you can’t. You were better yesterday, individually and
collectively, than you were to-day. Stroke, you weren’t bad, but you’re
still trying to feather under water. Try to correct that. Number Seven,
what’s the matter? You crumple right up at the finish. Pull it through,
pull it through! Number Six, you’re still slow at the catch. I’m tired
of telling you about that. Number Five, you did better about splashing.
You’re not pulling clear through yet, though. Number Four, watch the
angle of your blade in the water. Number Two, not bad for you to-day.
You’re improving. Bow, you’re finishing in the air. Keep your hands
out of your lap, for Pete’s sake! Cox, your steering might have been a
sight better. Some day you’ll run the nose into the bank! All right.
That’ll do.”

“Well, I don’t know,” confided Anstruth as he and Dick climbed the
steps together. “Maybe they aren’t such great shucks after all, Dodd.
Maybe we’ve got a chance with ’em, eh? What do _you_ think?”




                              CHAPTER XXIV

                               “FORWARD!”


The Second did have a chance to win the race on Wednesday, but lost
it when, near the three-quarters, Purley Warren steered the shell
too close to the shore and lost the aid of a good, strong current.
Perhaps, as Warren claimed afterwards, the first actually did crowd him
there――there were no course markers――but, as Coach Carmichael dryly
reminded him, since he was in his own water he was not required to
give way to the first. Possibly the second would have been beaten even
if that incident hadn’t occurred, for the bow-side oars were rowing
pretty raggedly at the finish, Norwell, at Five, messing his stroke
badly. It was, however, a pretty race, and the first crew had to extend
themselves to get the length and three-quarters lead that was theirs at
the finish line.

Dick saw the contest from the launch, in company with Johnny Scripps
and ex-Captain Trumbull; and, of course, Coach Carmichael and Bromley.
It is doubtful, though, if Bromley looked more than twice at the
shells. The “Sprite’s” engine was acting hysterically that afternoon,
and Bromley spent his moments watching it sternly. If Dick entertained
a hope that he might pilot the Second down the river that afternoon,
he was disappointed, but I don’t think he did. If Scripps ever
followed his own suggestion and hinted to the coach regarding Dick and
the coxswain’s seat, Dick never knew it. When the race was over and
Dick was helping on the float Captain Anstruth let fall a remark that,
while it buttered no parsnips, pleased Dick. “We could race ’em again
now,” said Anstruth, a trifle bitterly, “and beat ’em. We’d have beaten
’em then if we’d had you in the cox’s seat instead of that fried egg
over there!”

However, the “fried egg” continued to steer the second. There was no
more racing, but on Thursday the first went over the full course in 11
minutes and forty-one seconds, a performance that brought no joy to
any one. Conditions were not ideal that afternoon, though, for there
was only a sluggish current and a brisk wind quartered the course. The
crew rowed fairly smoothly for the first mile and a half, but after
that it was every man for himself, to use Mike’s dejected words. Still,
they finished strong, and that was promising. Friday saw a few short
stretches rowed while Mike tried to smooth out individual rough places.
Then, on Saturday, West Shore, who had come down the bay in a big
launch, her shell in tow, appeared off the boathouse in the forenoon,
and Brackett’s School arrived about twelve. After that events came
fast. The race was started upstream at five o’clock. Dick had half
expected that Coach Carmichael would invite him to see the contest from
the “Sprite,” but he didn’t. Instead, the “Sprite” held three members
of the second, Anstruth one of them, Manager Scripps and the coach.
Probably Bromley was there, too, but if he was he was so hunched over
his beloved engine that Dick didn’t see him when the launch came;
dancing past the spot where Dick and Jimsy were watching.

The race went to West Shore by a length and a half, with North Bank
second and Brackett’s trailing six lengths behind the Light Blue.
North Bank cut twenty seconds off her trial time, but that wasn’t good
enough to nose out West Shore, who finished sitting up and who, it was
generally conceded, might have added another length had she cared to.

There were, however, encouraging features for North Bank. Her crew,
four pounds lighter than the winners, had rowed steadily, had, between
the mile and the mile and a half marks, picked up two lengths on the
leaders, and had finished the race, if not untuckered, at least in
extremely good condition. As Scripps said later to Dick, if the course
had been two miles instead of a mile and seven-eighths North Bank would
have evened matters up with West Shore. Her attempt to spurt at the
end had not been successful, but she was, declared Scripps, getting
more out of her stroke before that than West Shore. Moreover, added the
manager, there remained three weeks before the Cumbridge race, and he’d
trust Mike to do a whole lot in three weeks!

Mike did do a lot in those three weeks, and several unforseen
things happened during them. On Thursday of the week following the
three-cornered event Dick became permanent coxswain of the second boat.
No one seemed much surprised save Dick. Even Warren appeared to have
been anticipating it and, on the whole, took it very well. Debrion
did quote him as having remarked that “there was no use putting up a
fight against a fellow who lived in Mike’s pocket!” But Warren may be
excused some slight expression of chagrin. Dick went to the second crew
training table and sat between Anstruth and Nelson, where, fortunately,
he was on the same side as Walker and so did not have to see that
gentleman’s disapproving looks. Anstruth called him “D. D.” and teased
him because he ate so little, and liked him immensely. For that matter,
so did the others, with the exception of the unrelenting Walker, and
boasted in the hearing of first-crew fellows that they had the best cox
on the river. In something like three days Dick became “Dicky.” For
several years he had dreaded that appellation, had on occasions fought
glorious battles to protect his name from the diminutive termination,
and now it had come and he didn’t mind it a bit! He liked being “Dicky”
because there was no loss of dignity entailed. The second crew adopted
him enthusiastically, renamed him to please themselves and were proud
of him. He was, they declared, the smallest cox on record and the
pluckiest and the cleverest. Debrion would catch him up and sit him on
a broad shoulder and parade the length of the float. Lobell, from the
bow of the boat, would beg him to take his megaphone off a minute so
he could see him. They all made affectionate fun of him and babied him
until he felt almost ashamed. When, however, he tried to assert his
dignity they laughed harder and “roughed” him gently and quite spoiled
his effect.

At North Bank, as at every place where feet lace into stretchers, there
was one inviolable rule regarding new coxswains, and Dick fell foul
of it two days after his promotion. It was Saturday afternoon. The
First had boated and was lying off the landing. The “Sprite” awaited
the coach’s pleasure. The second crew fellows and a small gathering
of onlookers were standing about while Mike and Scripps discussed
something earnestly at the doorway. Dick, megaphone in one hand and
polished rudder in the other, was talking to Ben Bromley when Debrion
and Chase joined him.

“Let’s see that rudder,” said Debrion. Dick yielded it. At the same
moment Chase tugged at the megaphone. Dick yielded that, too, glancing
up wonderingly from his conversation. Something in Chase’s grin warned
him, and he stepped back. He had no suspicion of what was coming, but
Chase’s expression certainly hinted at mischief. He reached forth for
the megaphone, but Chase only laughed and set it down on the edge of
the landing beside the rudder. Dick stepped forward to rescue both
articles, keeping, however, a wary eye on Chase.

“What’s the idea?” he asked.

They were all about him then, quite suddenly, a group of big,
bare-legged, bare-armed, laughing captors. “New cox! New cox!” they
shouted gleefully. “Bathe the baby!” Dick knew then what was coming and
submitted gracefully enough, although he did kick and squirm some as
he was lifted and passed from one pair to the next down the runway and
across the float to where, finally, Anstruth and Crane swung him twice
backward and forward and then sent him, turning and twisting, far over
the water!

Dick was aware of a mighty splash, realized that, in a manner of
speaking, the splash was he, and then struck upward from the green
depths. When he had shaken the water from his eyes he saw them
there all lined up, laughing, and ready to help him out. “You big
dumb-bells,” he sputtered. “You wait till I get you out!” He wasn’t
in the least angry, but he knew that they would expect some show of
dignity, would be disappointed if he took it too calmly. His threat
redoubled their laughter, while Dick struck out for the float and was
hauled out in a trice by many hands. Coach Carmichael, grinning until
his bristly mustache pointed acutely upward, called: “Better get into
some dry things, Dick. Some of the crowd can fix you up.”

Dick, shaking himself, was taken into the boathouse by Debrion and was
soon in possession of a pair of shorts and a rowing shirt some six
sizes too large for him. His reappearance caused renewed merriment, and
Chase, gathering a handful of Dick’s upper garments, shook it, crying
anxiously: “Shirt! Shirt, where’s Dicky?” Dick squirmed away, gathered
up his rudder and megaphone and sternly ordered the shell out; and
then became aware that the first crew, still lying off the landing, had
joyously witnessed the incident.

During his first week with the Second Dick learned the ropes fast.
He got to know the river, from the sand spit to the railway bridge,
extremely well. Along the three miles there were certain landmarks
of recognized importance, each of which the crewman’s vocabulary had
provided with a name. These Dick learned from Anstruth, who was an old
timer on the river: Blue Ledge, Fletcher’s Bend, The Walnut, Second
Point, Red Bank, First Point, The Beach, High Rock, the Boathouse,
Laurence’s, Ferndale, Three Trees, Big Hole. “Hit it up, Stroke!” Dick
would bark. “Swing her down to High Rock at thirty-four! Let’s see you
push some water!” Or: “Keep it up, Second! There’s Laurence’s! Ten
more strokes! Don’t let down! Eyes in the boat, Three! That’s fine!
Come on, now! Right on down to Ferndale! Get the time, Six! You’re
slow! That’s fine! Ten more now! Row! Row! Five more! Come on, Stroke!
Three!――Four!――_Five! Let her run!_”

It might be stretching it a bit to say that the second crew was a
better crew after Dick’s arrival in the cox’s seat, but certain it
is that it showed more snap and did things in a swaggering, cocky
fashion that would have pleased a veteran oarsman. When the Second
brought the shell out, put her over and took their places, or, having
returned from work, reversed the process, it was worth seeing. Dick,
megaphone against one small hip, very straight and slim and stern,
said “Hep!” and they “hepped” as one man. They might grin as Dick
barked his orders, catching the size of him from the corners of their
eyes, but they obeyed like soldiers at drill and loved doing it. Coach
Carmichael, watching, would smile, too, but it was an approving smile.

Thrice a week now there was a brush between the two crews, and some
ten days after Dick’s initiation the Second won by a full boat-length
in a mile race and got words of commendation from the coach, bellowed
through the big blue horn as the launch swept by. That victory cost
them dear in wind and muscle, but it was worth it, and they were a very
cocky lot for two days, or until the First came back at them and rowed
away from them at the finish. Once a week, usually Saturday, the two
shells sped over the full course in competition, and always on those
occasions it was Dick’s lot to watch the long, bent back of Tommy Gage
as the line was neared, for the Second never won over the full course.

There were three such races during the interim preceding the final
contest of the year. In one of them the First took the lead at the
start and was never headed. In another the Second held her shell in
the fore all the way to Ferndale, only to be beaten by more than a
length at the line. The third――that was on the Wednesday preceding
the Cumbridge race――was a heart-breaking affair from start to finish.
Theoretically, the first crew should have won handily, for here it was
but three days from the Big Day and “Mike’s Pets” were supposed to
have attained the height of their form. But Second grabbed the lead in
the first six or eight frenzied strokes and kept it to Second Point.
There Dick saw the rival shell edge up on the stroke side and from
there to the half distance the First lapped and hung. Off the boathouse
Dick called for a spurt and got it, Anstruth hitting up the stroke
without losing drive, and the First shell’s nose receded from his
sight. But Anstruth couldn’t stroke a mile-and-seven-eighths at full
speed, and for the last half-mile the two boats see-sawed until, at the
very last instant, the First shot ahead and won by less than a length.

That race didn’t bring the victors many compliments. The coach
said harsh things at the landing and the school began to wonder
whether Saturday’s race was to be the walk-over that of late it had
anticipated. The time had been slow, everything considered, and there
had been a good deal of splashing in the middle of the shell toward
the end. On the whole, North Bank’s chances to win from Cumbridge were
considered far less bright that Wednesday evening than before the race,
and Coach Carmichael plainly showed that he was disappointed.

Anstruth bitterly reviled himself after the race and wouldn’t be
comforted by his mates. If he could only have come across with a last
spurt, he declared, they’d have won or tied. Every fellow had rowed
a corking race but he, and he had failed them! Debrion told him to
forget it. “Why, you slab-sided, double-jointed Piute,” said Debrion
scornfully, “we couldn’t have answered you if you’d gone a single
stroke higher in that last hundred yards! We were all in and pulling
with our nerves. Ask any of ’em, you lobster. Ask Dicky. Dicky knows we
were rowed out, every mother’s son of us!”

And Dicky, who didn’t know anything of the sort, but who was too fond
of Anstruth to withhold consolation, nodded vehemently. “It wasn’t your
fault, Cap,” he said, “any more than it was theirs――or mine! You rowed
a corking race. Why, gee, if you’d done any better you wouldn’t have
been there! They’d have you in the other boat!”

“Yeah,” answered Anstruth dolefully, “that’s right! If I was any good
I’d have been there long ago!”

“Oh, well, forget it,” counseled Debrion. “We made ’em mighty near kill
themselves. Half the lot were draped on their oars when they finished.
We did all right, every one of us. So did Dicky. Dicky steered like an
old-timer all the way. Never lost an inch of water and took us past the
second turn so close you couldn’t have dropped a match between my blade
and the marker!”

“Dicky’s a little wonder,” said Anstruth. “He knows the rowing game
already better than a lot of us. Dicky did his part, and if I could
have come across the last time he asked for it――” The Second crew
captain shook his head sorrowfully and turned away.

It was on the Monday before that the letter from George came. George
wrote Jimsy that he was feeling fine once more, was back at home and
had been tutoring for more than a month. He was coming back next fall
to try for the first class and expected to make it. He wanted Jimsy
to visit him in August, he wrote: Dick, too, if Dick could manage it.
But he would talk about that when he saw them, for he was running down
to North Bank the following Saturday to see the baseball game and the
boat-race; and so that would be about all for the present.

“That’ll be corking!” exclaimed Jimsy. “We’ll see what we can of the
ball game and then get over in time for the race. Gosh, it’ll be like
old times, won’t it? The three of us together again, I mean!”

But Jimsy was planning without the sanction of the future. When
Saturday arrived, although George arrived with it, looking a very
different George from when last seen there, and although Jimsy was
still enjoying the possession of his bodily and mental faculties, there
was no Dick to make the third at the reunion. Dick had a more important
rôle to play that day than that of mere observer, for on Thursday the
strong hand of the faculty reached forth and lifted two members of the
first crew from the boat, with no thought, as it seemed, for what their
absence might mean two days later. The faculty only knew that repeated
warnings had failed to keep the two in good class standing, and now,
like an impersonal and inscrutable Fate, the faculty acted, and Coy, at
Number Six, and Gage, at Cox were eliminated from rowing affairs for
the rest of the season.

The school, revolted by the tragedy, endured an agonized period of
speechlessness, and then made itself heard in no uncertain voice. The
faculty was a lot of dunder-heads, the faculty was this, the faculty
was that. Principally, the faculty was a Traitor! But, although the
storm waxed mightily, the faculty, like a bleak and solid headland,
neither shook nor wavered. Appeals to Doctor Heidler were vain. A
petition circulated all Friday morning and signed by more than half the
students was politely tabled. The storm rumbled away, leaving a gloomy
and sullen world behind.

Alan Linscott became almost lyric in his fervid denunciations and
tragic expressions of grief that Thursday evening, and Dick and Jimsy,
who had unwisely intruded, wished themselves back in Baldwin. Joe
Whittier, gloomy enough though he was, accepted the matter with fair
philosophy. Joe pointed out that Coy wasn’t the whole crew, and――

“It isn’t that,” declared Alan passionately. “We can replace Coy.
There’s Anstruth, Debrion. But you can’t shake a crew up like this
almost the day before the race without playing hob with it! You smash
the whole works, I tell you! We had a slim chance of winning yesterday.
To-day we haven’t. That’s all. We’re beaten before we start, Joe. Oh,
it’s all right for you to sit there and shrug your fat shoulders!
You’re not captain. I am. There’s the difference. What about Tommy?
Think you can fill his place easy? Tommy’s worked with us two years and
knows the river, and knows you and me and how to handle us. Oh, well,
we’ll get licked, but it won’t be our fault! Licked by the faculty!
That’s us! Licked by a foozling old bunch of grannies! That’s fine,
isn’t it? Laugh now!”

But Joe didn’t laugh, and after awhile the temperature lowered and they
talked things over more calmly if no more hopefully.

“Who rowed six in your boat, Dick?” Joe asked.

“Never mind,” said Alan irritably. “I want Debrion. He’s the fellow
for us. We’ll get him shaken in somehow to-morrow. You’ll have to cox
us, Dick, I suppose.” Alan’s tone didn’t hold any flattering note of
pleasure. “Warren’s no earthly use. Do you know the course?”

“Don’t be an ass,” said Joe pleasantly. “Dick knows the course well
enough to steer us over it. He hasn’t had any trouble getting the
Second down on our necks two, three times!”

“I know,” agreed Alan, more amiably. “Well――Say, I’ve got to see Mike!
And Scripps! What’s the time? Geewhillikins! I’m off!”

Joe watched his departure sympathetically. “Hard lines on old Alan,” he
said softly. “Rotten hard!”

The next day Debrion was snatched from the débris of the discarded
Second and fitted his feet into the lacings of Number Six stretcher,
and Dick, not a little tremulous and doubtful, was thrust into the
stern, and the First went out on the river to learn a new cohesion
and, if possible, by so doing, wrest to-morrow’s supremacy from the
husky dark-blue crew that followed it up the stream, a half mile back,
like a gloating Nemesis!




                              CHAPTER XXV

                                “_ROW!_”


Saturday dawned warm, still, lifeless. Not rowing weather, unless by
chance the breeze came up later and cleared the haze away. The race was
set for three-forty-five, which meant, in the light of experience, four
or four-fifteen. There was a ball game with Cumbridge at two, the first
game of the series, and optimistic fellows believed that they would be
able to see the last man put out before it was time to seek a vantage
point along the river.

George arrived quite early, so early that Jimsy, who had expected
to meet him at the station, was taken by surprise, for the visitor
walked in on him while he was still searching for a blue-and-white tie
appropriate to the day. George was quite himself again. Indeed, he
looked far better than Jimsy remembered ever having seen him. Presently
they set forth on a search for Dick, but failed to find him. Dick was
out with the crew, for, contrary to custom, Coach Carmichael had sent
his charges up the river for a quiet paddle along the still reaches.
It was a long wait for four o’clock to come and some of the fellows
were restless and nervous. Mike could have wished for less enervating
weather to-day. Dick returned to Number 33 about half-past ten, warm
and inclined to be silent. But the meeting with George acted as a
tonic and the three of them sat as close to the open window as they
could get and talked hard.

“I see,” said George, “that we’ve lost you for lacrosse, Dick, but I’m
mighty glad you’ve found this other job. Like it, don’t you?”

Dick nodded earnestly. “I love it, George.”

“Going to win this afternoon?”

Dick’s face sobered and he hesitated perceptibly before answering. “I
hope so,” he said finally. “Some of the fellows seem fairly confident,
and Mike says we’ve got a good chance, but――I don’t know. There seems
to be a sort of――sort of downheartedness in the air.”

“That’s just this beastly sultry weather,” said Jimsy. “It would take
the starch out of a potato. Thank Heaven I don’t have to row in a boat
race or play baseball to-day!”

George was observing Dick thoughtfully. “Don’t let it get on your
nerves,” he advised. “Those fellows are going to take their cue from
you, Dick, and if you look worried they’re going to feel so. Keep the
upper lip stiff, boy, and even if you think you’re in for a licking,
don’t let them know it.”

“But I don’t,” said Dick quickly. “That’s just it. I think we can win
if we really do our best, but――but the others don’t! That is, a good
many of them. Alan smiles and talks cheerful, but he overdoes it and
the others don’t believe him. Joe Whittier is the only one of them who
really expects to win, I guess. If they’d only make up their minds to
it, they’d do it, George. I’m sure they would!”

“What’s wrong with the boat? You know I haven’t heard much of the news
since I left.”

“Well, of course losing Coy sort of upset things; Coy and Gage, too. We
did pretty well yesterday in practice, though. Then Cumbridge has done
the distance in nearly twenty seconds under our best time, and she was
out yesterday afternoon where the fellows could see her and there’s
no denying that she rows more evenly than we do. She has a shorter
stroke, with a quick drive, that gets her along awfully smoothly. She
looks hard to beat, and that’s a fact. Oh, I guess it’s just one thing
and another――nothing special――we’re in a sort of funk, maybe. Two or
three of the fellows are a bit on edge. Alan’s one of them. I’m scared
about him. If any one breaks before the race is over it will be Alan, I
guess. He’s all nerves and make-believe.”

“I know the symptoms,” answered George. “He will probably get over it
after things start. It’s the suspense that’s wearing him out. Who’s got
the weight, we or Cumbridge?”

“There’s not much difference according to the figures. They have a
pound or two on us. I heard Mike say that they weren’t boated any too
well, though; that they’ve got too much beef in the bow. Nice-looking
crew, those Cumbridge fellows. I sort of wish I hadn’t seen them row
yesterday. They came down the river after us, when we were coming back,
doing thirty-eight to the minute and not tossing a drop of water. It
was mighty pretty, but it sort of got me scared.”

“That was showing off,” said George. “They wanted to scare you, Dick.
Thirty-eight doesn’t mean so much when the stroke’s a short one, too.
Don’t worry about them. Forget them entirely. Just get your boat down
the river as fast as you can. That’s your job.”

“I know.” Dick nodded thoughtfully. “I wish it was over, though!”

About two o’clock the air freshened somewhat, but the heat was still
severe and over on the baseball diamond the male portion of the
audience folded their coats across their knees and pulled their hats
down over their eyes. Jimsy and George, roasting side by side, hoped
to witness a North Bank victory before they left to see the race, but
the game dragged, for neither pitcher was effective and hits and runs
were plentiful――and errors, too――and at three-thirty, the score being
then 12 to 10 in Cumbridge’s favor, North Bank was just starting her
half of the sixth inning. It was largely the lure of the comparative
coolness of tree shade on the river bank that took them away then,
for since boat races never did start on time they might safely have
watched another inning though. But they unwedged themselves from their
perspiring neighbors and made for the river, and were glad that they
had done so for here there was a breeze which, though hardly more than
a zephyr, dispelled the worst of the heat. They chose a point about
an eighth of a mile from the finish, joining a sprinkling of onlookers
who had already gathered. From there the starting point was out of
sight, but they would have the boats in view from the half distance to
the end. Cumbridge had already gone up, they learned, the crew aboard
the launch and the shell in tow. The judge’s boat was anchored at the
finish line and all seemed ready. The time was twelve minutes to four.

A mile and three-quarters upstream the two crews were listening to the
referee’s final instructions at that moment. He was speaking to them
through a small megaphone from the bow of an immaculate white launch.
To the left the black launch flying the dark-blue of Cumbridge floated
down with the current and churned back to position again. To the right
the little “Sprite” lay throbbing softly at a distance. Between the two
shells, their sterns even, lay some forty feet of gently flowing water.
The rowers, hatted, their white shirts plastered to their bodies,
waited. No eye roved toward the starter. Every face was set toward the
stern. Save for the lapping of the water, the chugging of the launches
and the crisp voice of the referee everything was very silent. Once
Dick glanced across the intervening space at the rival coxswain. He
seemed, thought Dick, no older than himself, a slight, earnest-faced
youth, his dark-blue megaphone pointing downstream in a queerly
determined manner. Dick wondered if his own face looked, under its tan,
as pale as the other boy’s did. The speaker’s voice stopped and Dick
jerked back to attention.

“Touch her easy, Two! Steady!”

“Are you ready?” asked the referee.

“Forward!”

The slides answered. Dick’s heart beat convulsively as he waited. The
time seemed eternal. Then a pistol shot rang out.

“_Row!_”

Oars caught, bodies lurched in frenzied haste, locks rattled,
blue-tipped oars swept forward and back, water churned. Ten seconds of
wild confusion in which the shouts of the coxswains, the encouraging
cheers from the launches, the beat of oars, the splash of water made
bedlam.

“_Row!――Row!――Row!――Row!――_” bellowed Dick, his pulses leaping. Then:
“_Steady down! Steady down!_” he shouted. From the corner of his eye he
saw the Cumbridge shell sweeping along beside them, but they had caught
the jump in those frenzied strokes and the bow of the Cumbridge boat no
longer ranged even. “Lengthen out, Joe!” said Dick. “We’re ahead!”

Joe Whittier grinned as he answered. Down the length of the shell the
rowers followed the slower, longer stroke. Behind, although Dick could
not see, came the launches, gliding easily over the smooth water.
Ahead, over the shoulders of the crew as they finished their strokes,
Dick could see the wide blue river, almost unruffled, the course
markers growing smaller and smaller in the distance, here and there a
canoe, or a sailboat with listless sail, some spots of white and faint
colors along the bank where groups of spectators congregated. His small
brown hands clutched the rudder-lines convulsively and his heart raced
and stopped agonizingly. Beside them hung the boat with the dark-tipped
oars, neither gaining nor losing.

Dick had been told that somewhere between the start and the first turn
of the course Cumbridge would go into the lead. That, Mike had said,
was certain. Cumbridge was rowing a shorter and faster stroke and was
due to lead at the half distance if not before. North Bank’s business
was to keep her stroke long, finish hard and wear the enemy down.
“When she gets a length ahead, hang onto her rudder,” directed Mike.
“Don’t get worried, fellows. Just keep your stroke long and bide your
time. You’ll get her later. She can’t keep up that high stroke for the
distance, and once she lowers it you’ll have her. The race will come in
the last half-mile. Be ready for it.”

To Dick it seemed that Joe was pulling a lower stroke than the
instructions called for, but Cumbridge was not drawing away and so that
must be all right. They were down to the quarter-mile now, all in an
instant as it seemed to him. Somewhere a launch whistle was shrilling
wildly. Then the Cumbridge shell began to move up and up. Dick looked
at Joe and knew that Joe saw. But Joe’s expression was as untroubled
as ever. Beside him, across the little space of water, the Cumbridge
coxswain moved into Dick’s range of vision. Cumbridge was leading
now by a third of a length, perhaps more. The quarter-mile flag was
astern, the half mile was coming toward them. In the other boat the cox
was doubled over, shouting stridently. Dick couldn’t hear the words.
The boat crept past until its rudder was even with Alan. For twenty
strokes it hung there, and then again it moved forward. Dick watched it
anxiously. Then:

“They’ve got a length, Joe,” he said.

Joe nodded as he swept his slide forward. His stroke quickened a
little. Hickson, at Four, was clipping, and Dick shouted warningly. Joe
looked interrogation and Dick answered with: “We’re holding them!”
