Cumbridge kept that lead to the half-mile flag and then on to the next.
The work was beginning to tell now. Dick could see the tenser set of
the jaws as the eight heads came forward for the catch. He shouted
encouragement through his megaphone at intervals, “We’ve got hold of
their rudder! They can’t do another foot! Keep it up, North Bank!
Number Five, you’re slow! Four, you’re clipping again! Keep it long and
slide it out! Come on! Come on! We’ve got them! They’re showing the
grind! Row, North Bank! Row!”

Down to First Point the two shells swept, Cumbridge just showing open
water between her stern and the North Bank bow. Then came the turn
and Dick watched for the distance, swung slowly, steadily, saw the
mile flag go past, almost grazing the sweeps, straightened out again.
Cumbridge had lost water there, had steered poorly, and now the North
Bank shell just lapped the other.

“We’re on them!” cried Dick. “On them by six feet!”

But his triumph was short-lived. The Cumbridge boat suddenly regained
her lead and lengthened it. She was a length and a quarter to the good
now and still drawing away. “Hit it up, Joe!” cried Dick. “They’ve got
more than her length and we’re past the half!”

And Joe hit it up, to thirty-six, to thirty-eight, and the open
water lessened from yards to feet and disappeared. North Bank was
lapping! But thirty-eight was no stroke to maintain at that distance
from the finish and gradually Joe came back to thirty-four and then
to thirty-two. Cumbridge moved away again slowly. How those fellows
could keep up that fast stroke and still put the power into it that
they did Dick couldn’t understand. The next flag came bobbing toward
him and passed. Why, they were nearing the finish now! And Cumbridge
was still leading! He sought for signs of weakening in the rival but
could see none. Rhythmically, desperately the eight sweeps pushed the
river behind them. The dark-blue oars had again opened water between
them and the light-blue. Dick felt suddenly horribly sick. They were
being beaten! Cumbridge was rowing away from them! He raised his voice
huskily.

“Don’t lose them, fellows!” he begged. “We’ve got them if you’ll stick
it out! Don’t weaken now! Only a half mile more, fellows! Two! Two,
eyes in the boat and pull it through! Hit it up, Stroke! Thirty hard
ones now! Let’s go!”

“Not yet!” gasped Joe. “Wait!”

Dick got command of himself again. The boats about the finish line were
plainly in sight now. Cumbridge was a good length and a half ahead.
Dick watched the intervening water during a dozen strokes. It hadn’t
broadened! They were holding Cumbridge now! If only, when the final
test came――

“_Two! Alan! Don’t do that!_” Alan’s head was hanging at the finish and
he was “riding his oar.” “Row, man! We’ve got them now! They’re coming
back to us! We’ve got them, I tell you! Buck up, Two!”

Alan pulled himself together and bent harder at his oar. He was ghastly
pale under the brown sunburn, and his mouth was drawn wide open. He
would never last the race out, thought Dick hopelessly. Others, too,
were weakening; Hickson and McKim weren’t half rowing. Debrion was
splashing badly. He scolded and entreated. Another marker went past.
“Half a mile to the line, Joe,” he called entreatingly. “We can do
it! Come on now! Make them hard! Get together and row them down! Row
them down! Come on, North Bank! We’re beating Cumbridge! Get that?
_Cumbridge!_ Don’t weaken now! It’s almost over! Less than half a mile,
fellows! Come on for North Bank!”

Up went the stroke and the others pulled to it. At last Cumbridge was
tiring, tiring fast. Three and five were splashing badly. The two
shells drew together slowly. The last marker went past. There was only
a quarter of a mile left to cover. North Bank’s bow lapped the stern of
the other boat. Dick shouted the tidings and urged them on. “We’ve got
them! Keep it up! Only a little longer, fellows! Two, don’t quit now!
Five, pull it through! You’re losing the race for us! Buck up, man,
buck up!”

And then it seemed that they never would do it, after all. Cumbridge
had come back until her cox was almost opposite the middle of the North
Bank shell, but there she remained. Joe, the perspiration running down
his face and neck, still held on valiantly, and valiantly the others
strove to do their parts. But the stroke was a killing one. Bow was out
of time, the shell was rolling, Alan was hardly more than a passenger.
Yet Cumbridge, too, was breaking under the strain, and if only there
had been another eighth of a mile, another hundred yards, even――

Then Dick shouted frantically, a new note in his voice. “We’ve won!” he
shrilled. “They’re coming back fast! Almost even now! There’s the line
just ahead! Ten strokes, fellows, only ten! Oh, you yellow dogs, don’t
give up! Two! Four! Five! You quitters! You beastly quitters!” Dick was
almost sobbing. “_Can’t_ you even try? Only ten strokes, ten hard ones!
Oh, you――you――”

The Cumbridge shell was almost even and the line was under them! Dick
lifted his voice in one last and frantic appeal: “_Lift her! Lift her
over! Row! Row! Row――_”

There was the dull report of a pistol, many sounds, cheers, the
shrieking of whistles.

“Let her run!” called Dick.

There was silence in the shell as it went on out of the lane, the
silence of exhaustion. Presently Joe lifted a drawn face.

“Did we――” He didn’t try to finish. Dick looked back toward the judge’s
boat.

“I’m afraid not, Joe,” he said sorrowfully. “But it――it was a good
race. You fellows worked like――like――” Dick broke down then and cried
frankly.

“Never mind, youngster,” said Joe. “You did your part.”

“I――I called you quitters,” sobbed Dick. “I didn’t mean it! I was――”

“We’d have been beaten worse if you hadn’t,” growled Debrion.

“Look!” Lee was pointing weakly upstream. “The flag! We _did_ win!”

Dick turned again. On the stern of the judge’s boat a big light-blue
flag was fluttering lazily. There was a hail from close by, and Coach
Carmichael, his face wreathed in smiles, waved from the bow of the
“Sprite.”

“Good work, North Bank! Rowed, you fellows rowed! Well steered, Cox! A
close race, but you won it, by gravy! Won it by a quarter of a length!”

                   *       *       *       *       *

They paddled back, scorning the proffered hospitality of the referee’s
launch, paddled back proudly, untiredly, passing the clustered boats
at the finish with the superb indifference of conquerors, smiling
tolerantly at the cheers that greeted them. Dick, in a happy haze of
unreality, clung to the rudder-lines and beamed at an excellent world.
They had won. North Bank had won; his school! A voice disturbed his
rhapsody. It was Joe speaking.

“Happy, Dicky?”

Dick nodded and grinned a bit sheepishly. He hadn’t forgotten that
he had wept weakly back there, like a mere kid! Joe nodded, too,
understandingly.

“Nice race,” he said simply.

They were approaching the boathouse now. On the landing and float and
along the rising bank above waited the school. Dick thought he could
see Jimsy and George at the right, close by the steps. They’d be
awfully happy, too, just as he was. Not quite so happy, of course, for,
as he realized now, his happiness came less from the victory, than from
the knowledge that he had “done something,” something for the School!


                                THE END
